supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Let the laboratory region and its chart be those of [[def-em-lab-geometry]], with
the units of [[def-em-si-conventions]].

(a) [Charge parameter] The framework takes a real **charge parameter**
$q\in\mathbb R$, measured in coulombs, attached to a source; its sign is the
sign of the source and it is a parameter of the model. Charge quantisation is
not asserted.

(b) [Smooth source fields] A **smooth (volume) source field** on
$\Omega\times I$ is a pair $(\rho,J)$ of maps $\rho:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R$,
$J:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ that is continuous on $\Omega\times I$ and of
class $C^1$ wherever a displayed equation differentiates it; $\rho$ is the
**frame charge density** (C m$^{-3}$) and $J$ the **frame current density**
(A m$^{-2}$). For each fixed $t\in I$ retain the compact Jordan branch: if
$V\subseteq\Omega$ is compact and Jordan measurable, define

$$Q_R(V,t):=\int_V\rho(y,t)dy$$

by [[def-riemann-integral-over-a-jordan-set]], with integrability supplied by
[[thm-continuous-functions-on-compact-jordan-sets-are-integrable]]. For the
full measurable-volume branch assume Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]),
as required by the published Lebesgue-measure interface. If $V$ is any bounded
Lebesgue-measurable subset with compact closure $\overline V\subseteq\Omega$,
define

$$Q(V,t):=\int_V\rho(y,t)d\lambda_3(y)=\int_{\mathbb R^3}F_t(y)\mathbf{1}_V(y)d\lambda_3(y),$$

where $F_t=\rho(\cdot,t)$ on $\Omega$ and $0$ elsewhere; the signed integral is
defined through its positive and negative parts
([[def-integral-over-a-measurable-set]],
[[def-integrable-real-and-complex-functions-and-their-integrals]]). The
function $F_t$ is Borel, and hence Lebesgue measurable: for every open
$O\subseteq\mathbb R$ its preimage inside the open set $\Omega$ is relatively
open in $\Omega$, hence open in $\mathbb R^3$, and the closed complement of
$\Omega$ is added precisely when $0\in O$
([[thm-continuous-preimages-of-borel-sets-are-borel]],
[[thm-borel-sets-are-lebesgue-measurable]]). This integral is absolutely
finite: $\rho(\cdot,t)$ is bounded on the compact $\overline V$ by
[[thm-extreme-value-metric]], $V$ has finite Lebesgue measure by
[[prop-lebesgue-measure-is-sigma-finite-and-finite-on-bounded-sets]], and the
monotonicity and homogeneity of the nonnegative integral
([[prop-order-and-scalar-rules-for-the-nonnegative-integral]]) bound
$\int|F_t|\mathbf{1}_Vd\lambda_3\le M_t\lambda_3(V)<\infty$, the indicator
integral being its simple-function value
([[prop-the-nonnegative-integral-agrees-with-the-simple-integral]]); the
positive and negative parts are measurable by
[[prop-closure-properties-of-measurable-functions-used-by-the-integral]]. On
the compact Jordan branch, under the same Countable Choice assumption,
$Q=Q_R$ by [[lem-riemann-lebesgue-comparison-for-distribution-test-integrands]].
The
empty region has charge zero in both branches. The current flux remains
defined independently: for each oriented surface patch in $\Omega$ the current
flux at time $t$ is the surface integral of $J(\cdot,t)$ in the induced
orientation, as defined in [[def-oriented-unit-normal-and-flux-of-a-surface-patch]].
Point sources and sheet sources are not source fields in this sense; they are
different objects, defined by their own pairings when the framework uses them.

(c) [Covariant identification] Write $j:=(c\rho,J)$, so $j^0=c\rho$ and
$j^i=J^i$. The framework adopts as a model premise the identification of the
charge-current of a source with a vector field of the affine Minkowski model,
and hence the component transformation law of
[[thm-sr-tensor-and-current-transformation]] for $j$ between inertial charts.
This is a model premise, not a theorem about physical currents.

(d) [Frame density, scalar multiplier and the normalized material branch]
Suppose additionally that the identified $j$ is $C^1$ and $j=\rho_0U$, with a
$C^1$ future timelike vector field $U$ and a $C^1$ real scalar multiplier
$\rho_0$. Since $U^0>0$, define the normalized chart direction $u:=U/U^0$, so
$u^0=1$, $u^i=U^i/U^0$. Then $j=(\rho_0U^0)u$ and, because the electromagnetic
convention is $j^0=c\rho$,

$$\rho=\rho_0U^0/c,\qquad J^i=\rho_0U^i=c\rho\,u^i.$$

Pointwise equality $\rho=\rho_0$ holds if and only if $\rho_0(U^0-c)=0$,
including the zero-multiplier case. Where $\rho_0\ne0$, equality is equivalent
to $U^0=c$, which does not alone imply $U^i=0$ for an arbitrary future timelike
$U$. Thus a scalar multiplier is not automatically a Lorentz rest charge
density. The direction $u$ is chart normalized, with no unit or
proper-four-velocity normalization imposed in this general branch; if its
coordinate velocity interpretation is adopted, the spatial velocity is
$v^i:=cu^i$.

For the separate convective source model, explicitly assume that $U$ is the
material proper-time four-velocity, normalized by $\eta(U,U)=-c^2$ as in
[[thm-sr-proper-time-and-observer-decomposition]]. This is an additional model
condition, not a consequence of the factorization $j=\rho_0U$. In that branch,
$U=\gamma(c,v)$, $|v|<c$, $\gamma=(1-|v|^2/c^2)^{-1/2}$, and

$$\rho=\gamma\rho_0,\qquad J=\rho v.$$

Here $\rho_0$ is the rest charge density of this stipulated convective model:
in a comoving inertial frame $U=(c,0,0,0)$ and $j=(c\rho_0,0,0,0)$. The
equality $\rho=\rho_0$ then holds exactly where $\rho_0=0$ or $v=0$
(equivalently $\gamma=1$). Both signs of charge and the zero-density case are
retained.

(e) [Scope] This definition fixes the source objects of the smooth branch and
their transformation interface. It asserts no conservation law (that is proved
for stated source classes) and no regularity of singular sources.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$), used through the sphere and polar integrations below ([[def-countable-choice]], [[def-polar-surface-measure-on-the-unit-sphere]], [[thm-polar-coordinates-formula-for-lebesgue-measure]]). Let $c>0$, write $Q:=\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$, $\mathcal D:=\mathcal D(Q)$ for the test-function space of [[def-test-function-space-d-of-an-open-set]], and $C:=\{(y,t)\in Q:t=|y|/c\}$ for the retarded cone. Define the functional $K$ on test functions by

$$\langle K,\psi\rangle:=\frac{1}{4\pi}\int_{\mathbb R^3}\frac{\psi(y,|y|/c)}{|y|}\,dy\qquad(\psi\in\mathcal D).$$

Then: (a) the integral converges absolutely for every $\psi\in\mathcal D$, the functional $K$ is a distribution on $Q$ ([[def-distribution]]), $(K,\psi)=0$ for every $\psi$ with $\operatorname{supp}\psi\cap C=\varnothing$, and for every $(y_0,t_0)\in C$ and every neighbourhood $U$ of $(y_0,t_0)$ there is $\psi\in\mathcal D$ with $\operatorname{supp}\psi\subseteq U$ and $\langle K,\psi\rangle\ne0$; consequently $\operatorname{supp}K=C$. (b) For every $h\in C_c^\infty(Q)$ the function

$$(K*h)(x,t):=\int_{\mathbb R^3}\frac{h(y,\,t-|x-y|/c)}{4\pi\,|x-y|}\,dy$$

is well defined (the integral converges absolutely), of class $C^\infty$ on $Q$, and for every $\psi\in\mathcal D$

$$\langle K*h,\psi\rangle=\langle h,\,K\circledast\psi\rangle,\qquad (K\circledast\psi)(y,s):=\langle K,\psi(y+\cdot,s+\cdot)\rangle=\frac{1}{4\pi}\int\frac{\psi(y+z,s+|z|/c)}{|z|}\,dz;$$

moreover $W(K*h)=h$ on $Q$ in the classical pointwise sense, where $W=c^{-2}\partial_t^2-\Delta$ is the wave expression of [[def-wave-equation-cauchy-data-and-wave-speed]] and [[def-laplacian-of-a-c2-function]]. (c) Read $W=c^{-2}\partial_t^2-\Delta$ as the distributional operator built from [[def-distributional-derivative]]; then $WK=\delta_{(0,0)}$ in the sense of [[def-dirac-delta-and-its-derivatives]], that is, $(WK)(\psi)=\psi(0,0)$ for every $\psi\in\mathcal D$. This identifies $K$ as the retarded fundamental solution of $W$; no smoothness of $K$ itself on the cone is asserted, and the advanced fundamental solution is not treated.
supplier_excerpts.relevant_hypotheses_and_conventions: For every $h\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R)$, $K*h(x,t):=\int h(y,t-|x-y|/c)/(4\pi|x-y|)\,dy$ is absolutely convergent, is jointly $C^\infty$, and satisfies $W(K*h)=h$ pointwise, with $W=c^{-2}\partial_t^2-\Delta$. Adopt as a physical assumption of this framework the following solution-selection rule for the classical vacuum model on the laboratory region $U\cong I\times\Omega$ of [[def-em-lab-geometry]], with the constants and SI units of [[def-em-si-conventions]] (so $c>0$, $\mu_0>0$, $\varepsilon_0=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$).

(a) [Formulation] In the potential formulation of [[pthm-em-lorenz-gauge-wave-form]] with the conventions of [[def-em-potential-gauge-and-field-conventions]], for a $C^2$ potential pair in Lorenz gauge the sourced Maxwell system of [[post-em-vacuum-maxwell]] is equivalent to the decoupled sourced wave equations $W\varphi=\rho/\varepsilon_0$, $WA=\mu_0J$, where $W=c^{-2}\partial_t^2-\Delta$. The wave expression $W$ is invariant under $t\mapsto-t$; where explicit retarded or advanced constructions for a prescribed history exist, they give distinguished particular solutions built from the corresponding forward or backward fundamental kernels. Every other solution differs from a chosen particular solution by a source-free addition; retarded and advanced particular solutions also differ by such an addition. This describes the affine free-solution freedom, not a claim that arbitrary histories have exactly two solutions or that either construction always exists.

(b) [Adopted rule] The framework adopts the retarded branch with no free field added: the physical potential pair of the model is the retarded one, that is, the one whose support and propagation lie in the forward light cones of the source and which carries no field arriving from the past independently of the source. For the zero-incoming model the selected sourced solution has no independently prescribed homogeneous addition. If nonzero Cauchy data are instead prescribed, their compatible homogeneous addition is a separate initial-data model; it is not equivalent to setting every free addition to zero. The advanced construction and independent incoming free fields are excluded by the present retarded selection.

(c) [Status and scope] This is an adopted extra temporal condition carrying the model's arrow-of-time content. It is not a theorem, not a consequence of the time-symmetric wave or Maxwell equations (which admit advanced and free solutions as mathematical objects), and not a deduction from experiment; it asserts no existence, uniqueness, regularity, support or decay for any source class, all of which must be supplied separately by theorems of this page. It selects a solution only of the models to which it is applied; it introduces no product of distributions, no source model, no self-force, no radiation reaction, no measured signal and no statistical claim. The retarded compact-source branch to which this selection applies is developed on this page as a conditional theorem, and the point-source branch is developed later on this page; neither existence statement is part of this postulate. For the separately declared point-source branch assume Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]), as in its exact source/field interfaces, and adopt the same no-free-addition retarded selection in the weak equations of [[post-em-distributional-vacuum-maxwell]], for the locally integrable field and proper point-current types of [[def-em-weak-sources]]. This extends the selection's model scope explicitly; neither existence nor an arbitrary convolution of noncompact distributions is postulated.

Adopt as a physical postulate of this framework the following four equations for
the fields of [[def-em-fields]] and the sources of [[def-em-sources]] on the
laboratory region $U\cong I\times\Omega$ of [[def-em-lab-geometry]], with
$\mu_0>0$, $c>0$, $\varepsilon_0=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$ and the SI units of
[[def-em-si-conventions]].

(a) [Smooth branch] Let $E,B$ be jointly $C^1$ fields with the additional
derivatives required by each equation existing and continuous, and let
$\rho,J$ be continuous. Then, with the divergence and curl of
[[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]] and the partial derivative
$\partial_t$ at fixed position of
[[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]],

$$\operatorname{div}E=\rho/\varepsilon_0,\qquad \operatorname{div}B=0,\qquad \operatorname{curl}E=-\partial_tB,\qquad \operatorname{curl}B=\mu_0J+c^{-2}\partial_tE.$$

(b) [Weak branch] Let instead $E,B$ be locally integrable $\mathbb R^3$-valued
fields and $\rho,J$ locally integrable scalar and vector fields on
$I\times\Omega$, identified with their regular distributions
([[def-regular-distribution-from-a-locally-integrable-function]],
[[thm-locally-integrable-functions-embed-in-distributions]]). Let
$\operatorname{div}$, $\operatorname{curl}$ and $\partial_t$ act as
distributional derivatives, componentwise, and let $\psi$ range over
$C_c^\infty(I\times\Omega)$ ([[def-test-function-space-d-of-an-open-set]]).
Then the same four identities hold in the sense of [[def-distribution]]: the
pairings

$$\langle\operatorname{div}E-\rho/\varepsilon_0,\psi\rangle,\qquad \langle\operatorname{div}B,\psi\rangle,\qquad \langle\operatorname{curl}E+\partial_tB,\psi\rangle,\qquad \langle\operatorname{curl}B-\mu_0J-c^{-2}\partial_tE,\psi\rangle$$

all vanish for every such $\psi$, all derivatives being distributional
derivatives ([[def-distributional-derivative]]).

(c) [Scope] The postulate contains no magnetic charge: $\operatorname{div}B=0$
and no magnetic-source term appears in $\operatorname{curl}E$. Sources that
are not locally integrable functions (point or sheet sources) are covered by
neither branch and require their own definition. The equations are adopted
classical vacuum physics in the named inertial chart; they are not deduced from
charge conservation, from empirical agreement or from the special-relativity
postulates, and this item by itself asserts no covariance under changes of
inertial frame.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Let $c>0$, let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be open, let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an interval with at least two elements ([[def-interval]]), and let $(\varphi,A)$ be a potential pair of class $C^2$ jointly on $\Omega\times I$ in the restriction convention of [[lem-em-joint-smooth-potentials]] ([[def-em-potential-gauge-and-field-conventions]]): for open $I$ this is the ordinary open-domain class of [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]], and for non-open $I$ the pair is the restriction of a $C^2$ pair on an open neighbourhood of $\Omega\times I$, with relative derivatives at included endpoints and no time jet beyond the restricted values. Write $(E,B)$ for the field pair of $(\varphi,A)$ ([[def-em-fields]]) and

$$G:=\operatorname{div}A+c^{-2}\partial_t\varphi,\qquad W:=c^{-2}\partial_t^2-\Delta$$

for the Lorenz divergence and the wave expression of [[def-em-potential-gauge-and-field-conventions]], with $\Delta$ the Laplacian of [[def-laplacian-of-a-c2-function]]. Let $\rho:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R$ and $J:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ be continuous source fields of the framework ([[def-em-sources]]).

(a) [Exact identities] Independently of any field equation,

$$\operatorname{div}E=W\varphi-\partial_tG,\qquad \operatorname{curl}B-c^{-2}\partial_tE=WA+\nabla G\qquad\text{on }\Omega\times I.$$

Consequently the sourced Maxwell equations of [[post-em-vacuum-maxwell]] hold for $(E,B,\rho,J)$ if and only if

$$W\varphi-\partial_tG=\frac{\rho}{\varepsilon_0},\qquad WA+\nabla G=\mu_0J\qquad\text{on }\Omega\times I,$$

with $\varepsilon_0=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$ the constant of that postulate.

(b) [Gauge shift] If $\chi:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R$ is a gauge function of class $C^2$ jointly on $\Omega\times I$ ([[def-em-gauge-transformation]]), then $G(T_\chi(\varphi,A))=G-W\chi$ on $\Omega\times I$ and the transformed pair has the same field pair $(E,B)$ ([[pthm-em-gauge-invariance]]); hence $T_\chi(\varphi,A)$ is in Lorenz gauge if and only if $W\chi=G$ on $\Omega\times I$.

(c) [Decoupling in Lorenz gauge] Suppose in addition that the given pair is in Lorenz gauge, $G=0$ on $\Omega\times I$. Then its field pair solves the sourced Maxwell system of [[post-em-vacuum-maxwell]] if and only if the pair satisfies the decoupled sourced wave equations

$$W\varphi=\rho/\varepsilon_0,\qquad WA=\mu_0J\qquad\text{on }\Omega\times I.$$

The two source-free equations $\operatorname{div}B=0$ and $\operatorname{curl}E=-\partial_tB$ hold automatically for every potential pair of class $C^2$. For an arbitrary given potential pair, the conjunction of Lorenz gauge with these two wave equations implies the sourced Maxwell system, but Maxwell's equations alone do not impose $G=0$ on that representative: their exact equivalent conditions remain the residual equations of (a), whose right-hand sides retain $\partial_tG$ and $\nabla G$.

(d) [Residual generators] If the $C^2$ gauge function of (b) satisfies $W\chi=0$ on $\Omega\times I$, then the transform of a pair in Lorenz gauge is again in Lorenz gauge and has the same field pair. When $\Omega$ is nonempty the Lorenz condition does not determine the pair: the generator $\chi(x,t)=x_1$, read in numerical SI components with gauge units as in [[def-em-gauge-transformation]], has $W\chi=0$ and changes $A$ by the nonzero constant vector $(1,0,0)$.

(e) [Scope] The identities and equivalences are properties of the given $C^2$ representation. No gauge function with $W\chi=G$, and no generator meeting prescribed initial or boundary values, is asserted to exist; that is a separate PDE conclusion with its own hypotheses, treated by the gauge-reachability theorem later on this page. No boundary, decay or initial condition on the pair is imposed, and no empirical claim or observability of $\varphi$ or $A$ is included. A pair of class $C^1$ defines $E$, $B$ and $G$ but need not possess the second derivatives appearing in $W\varphi$, $WA$, $\Delta$ or $\partial_tG$, so $C^2$ is the exact standing regularity here.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$, let $\mathbb{R}^n$ be the set of functions
$n \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $d_2$ be the Euclidean metric on it
($\mathbb{R}^n$ as the set of functions $n \to \mathbb{R}$, and $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ are metrics on it). Then:

1. **Closed boxes are compact.** For reals $a_k \le b_k$ $(k < n)$ the box
   $Q = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_k \le x_k \le b_k \text{ for every } k < n \,\}$
   is a compact subset of $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ (Open cover, subcover, compact metric space, and compact subset of a metric space).
2. **Heine-Borel.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ if and only if $K$ is closed in $\mathbb{R}^n$
   (The metric topology: a set is open when every one of its points has a ball around it inside the set; closed means open complement) and bounded
   (Bounded subset, diameter, distance from a point to a set, and distance between two sets in a metric space).
3. **The real line.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$, the usual metric $d_{\mathbb{R}}(x,y) = |x-y|$
   (The absolute value makes $\mathbb{R}$ a metric space: $d(x,y) = |x-y|$ is a metric, its open balls are the intervals $(x-r, x+r)$, and it is unbounded), if and only if $K$ is closed in
   $\mathbb{R}$ and bounded.

**No choice principle is used.** The bisection below halves one coordinate at a
time and takes the **left** half whenever the left half still fails to be finitely
covered, the right half otherwise: a rule with two outcomes, decided by a
property of the box, not a selection. That is the whole reason the theorem is
available in ZF, while the general "complete and totally bounded implies compact"
(A complete, totally bounded metric space is compact, proved from countable choice used exactly once) is not.

The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is inherited from $\mathbb{R}^n$ as the set of functions $n \to \mathbb{R}$, and $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ are metrics on it, which defines
$\mathbb{R}^n$ and its metrics only there; the last remark below records what
happens at $n = 0$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Fix $n \ge 1$

$$S^{n-1}:=\{\omega \in \mathbb R^n : |\omega|=1\}.$$
Let
$$\Phi:\mathbb R^n\setminus\{0\}\longrightarrow(0,\infty)\times S^{n-1},\qquad \Phi(x)=(|x|,x/|x|).$$
This map is continuous. If $E\subseteq S^{n-1}$ is Borel, then
$(0,1]\times E$ is Borel and
$$\{r\omega:\omega\in E,\ 0<r\le1\}=\Phi^{-1}((0,1]\times E)$$
is Borel in $\mathbb R^n\setminus\{0\}$ by
[[thm-continuous-preimages-of-borel-sets-are-borel]], hence Borel in
$\mathbb R^n$ by [[thm-borel-sigma-algebra-of-a-subspace-is-the-trace]]. It is
therefore Lebesgue measurable by [[thm-borel-sets-are-lebesgue-measurable]].
Define
$$\sigma(E):=n\,\lambda_n(\{r\omega : \omega \in E,\ 0<r\le 1\}).$$

The next theorem proves that this is a Borel measure on $S^{n-1}$ and that it
is exactly the surface measure needed for polar coordinates.

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$ and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be
continuous on $[a,b]$ (Continuity of $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ at a point of $A$ and on $A$: the $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ condition, its agreement with $\lim_{x \to c} f(x) = f(c)$ at a limit point, and continuity at an isolated point, Intervals of $\mathbb{R}$: the nine order-convex forms, nondegeneracy, and length) and
differentiable at every point of $(a,b)$ as a function on $[a,b]$
(The derivative $f'(c) = \lim_{x \to c} \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c}$ of $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ at a point $c \in A$ that is a limit point of $A$, and differentiability on a set). Then there is $c \in (a,b)$ with

$$f(b) - f(a) \;=\; f'(c)\,(b - a) .$$

Equivalently, since $b - a \ne 0$, there is $c \in (a,b)$ at which
$f'(c) = \bigl(f(b)-f(a)\bigr)/(b-a)$: the derivative somewhere inside equals
the average rate of change across the whole interval.

**Continuity on the closed interval cannot be dropped.** Differentiability at
every point of $(a,b)$ alone does not suffice: a function on $[0,1]$,
differentiable at every point of $(0,1)$ with derivative constantly $1$, for
which no $c$ works, is exhibited later on this page as a false statement, and
the companion page works the same witness out in full.

citations.quote:
Assume countable choice. For every $f\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R^n)$ and every $x\in\mathbb R^n$,
$$f(x)=\int_{\mathbb R^n}\widehat f(\xi)e^{2\pi ix\cdot\xi}\,d\xi.$$
The integral is absolutely convergent.

Assume countable choice and let $n\ge1$. Fourier transformation on Schwartz space extends uniquely to a surjective complex-linear isometry $\mathcal F_2:L^2(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C)\to L^2(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C)$. It preserves the first-variable-linear inner product, and hence is unitary.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Let $(A,V,\eta,C^+)$ be an oriented time-oriented affine Minkowski space
([[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]]), let $(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ be an inertial
frame with inertial chart $x:A\to\mathbb R^4$
([[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]]), let $c>0$ be the framework's
conversion constant, and let $\delta$ be the Euclidean spatial form of that
frame on $n^\perp$, $n:=e_0$, with norm $|\cdot|$ and positive spatial
orientation ([[def-spatial-euclidean-structure-of-an-inertial-frame]]). Fix a
nonempty open interval $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ ([[def-interval]]) and a nonempty
open set $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^3$, and put

$$U:=\{p\in A:\ \text{there are }t\in I,\ y\in\Omega\text{ with }x^0(p)=ct,\ (x^1,x^2,x^3)(p)=y\}.$$

Then:

(a) [Chart restriction] $x(U)=\{(ct,y):t\in I,\ y\in\Omega\}$ and
$\Phi:U\to I\times\Omega$, $\Phi(p):=(x^0(p)/c,(x^1,x^2,x^3)(p))$, is a
bijection, because the inertial chart $x:A\to\mathbb R^4$ is a bijection and
$c>0$; its components are the **laboratory time coordinate**
$t(p):=x^0(p)/c$ and the **laboratory position**
$r(p):=(x^1(p),x^2(p),x^3(p))$. In the chart coordinates the pair
$(t(p),r(p))$ is the reading of the laboratory decomposition of $p$. Writing
$r(p)=(r^1(p),r^2(p),r^3(p))\in\mathbb R^3$, the standard basis of
$\mathbb R^3$ ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]) labels the three coordinate
directions, and the identification $\mathbb R^3\cong n^\perp$ is the linear
map $\sum_{i=1}^3 r^i e_i$ into the three-dimensional real vector space
$n^\perp$ ([[def-vector-space]], [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]).

(b) [Slices and spatial structure] For each $t\in I$ the slice
$U_t:=\{p\in U:t(p)=t\}$ is carried bijectively onto $\Omega$ by $r$; the
constant vector $n=e_0$ is future unit timelike, and $(e_1,e_2,e_3)$ is the
$\delta$-orthonormal positively oriented basis of $n^\perp$ in which the
coordinates of $r$ are expressed.

(c) [Laboratory fields] For a nonnegative integer $m$, a **laboratory field of rank $m$** is a map
$F:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^m$; it is identified with the map $U\to\mathbb R^m$,
$p\mapsto F(r(p),t(p))$, and with the family $(F(\cdot,t))_{t\in I}$ of maps
$\Omega\to\mathbb R^m$, its values at fixed time. Such a field is of class
$C^k$, for $m\ge1$, when the map $(y,t)\mapsto F(y,t)$ is $C^k$ in the sense of
[[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]. For $m=0$, set $\mathbb R^0:=\{()\}$;
the unique field into this singleton is declared $C^\infty$ (and $C^k$ for every
finite $k$), and each of its partial derivatives is the same singleton-valued
zero map. For $m\ge1$ and $k\ge1$, $\partial_{y_i}F$ (at fixed
$t$) and $\partial_tF$ (at fixed $y$) are the partial derivatives of
[[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]]. No regularity of a field is
asserted beyond the class stated for it.

(d) [Conventions] The product decomposition is a coordinate identification
inside the single inertial frame $(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$; it is not a Galilean
transformation, it does not compare two inertial frames, and it does not
assert absolute simultaneity. The objects $I,\Omega,t,r,\delta$ and the
identification $\mathbb R^3\cong n^\perp$ belong to the named frame; changes
of inertial description are the proper orthochronous maps adopted in
[[post-sr-inertial-covariance]]. The frame is an origin together with an
ordered basis; it is not a congruence of observers, and no moving observer
field is defined here.

Adopt the SI system of units for this framework, with the following quantity
table and conventions; every symbol is a quantity of this framework and the
laboratory structure is that of [[def-em-lab-geometry]].

(a) [Coordinates and constants] $x^0=ct$ and each spatial coordinate $x^i$
carries the metre (m); the time coordinate $t$ carries the second (s); the
conversion constant $c>0$ carries m s$^{-1}$ and has the exact SI defining
value $c=299\,792\,458\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$; the elementary charge $e$ has the
exact SI defining value $e=1.602\,176\,634\times10^{-19}\ \mathrm{C}$, and this
item does not assert that physical charge is quantised; the magnetic constant
$\mu_0>0$ carries N A$^{-2}$ and is measured, so no exact numerical value of
$\mu_0$ is asserted. The pre-2019 SI fixed the historical nominal
$\mu_{0,\mathrm{nom}}:=4\pi\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{H\,m^{-1}}
=4\pi\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{N\,A^{-2}}$ exactly; since the revised SI took
effect on 20 May 2019, $\mu_0$ is experimentally determined. The SI brochure
quotes the nominal $\mu_{0,\mathrm{nom}}$ as the estimate at the 2019 adoption
with relative standard uncertainty $2.3\times10^{-10}$; this is historical
estimate and uncertainty context, not an exact equality for the actual $\mu_0$
or a current measured value. The electric constant is defined within the
framework by

$$\varepsilon_0:=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$$

in F m$^{-1}$, consistent with the exact SI relation $\varepsilon_0\mu_0=1/c^2$,
so that $c^2\varepsilon_0\mu_0=1$ and $\varepsilon_0$ inherits the relative
standard uncertainty of $\mu_0$.

(b) [Electromagnetic quantities] Charge $q$ carries the coulomb (C); the
charge density $\rho$ of the framework's source definition carries C m$^{-3}$
and the current density $J$ carries A m$^{-2}$, so that the four-current
components $(c\rho,J)$ carry A m$^{-2}$; the electric field $E$ carries
V m$^{-1}$; the magnetic field $B$ carries the tesla (T), where
$1\ \mathrm{T}=1\ \mathrm{N\,A^{-1}\,m^{-1}}$; the scalar potential $\varphi$
carries V and the vector potential $A$ carries T m, so that the four-potential
components $(\varphi/c,A)$ carry T m; the components of the electromagnetic
two-form of the framework's tensor definition carry T; a force carries the
newton (N), $1\ \mathrm{N}=1\ \mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-2}}$.

(c) [Mechanical quantities] A rest mass parameter $m$ carries the kilogram
(kg) and a four-momentum $P=mU$ of the relativistic particle model carries
kg m s$^{-1}$; field energy density carries J m$^{-3}$, energy flux
W m$^{-2}$, so that $1\ \mathrm{W}=1\ \mathrm{J\,s^{-1}}=1\ \mathrm{V\,A}$.

(d) [Bookkeeping only] The unit of a quantity records the adopted system of
units; it does not show that a quantity is primitive in this or any other
framework, it contains no measurement, and it does not identify a quantity
with a similarly named quantity of another framework. The exact defining
values of $c$ and $e$ fix numerical conventions of the SI; they do not by
themselves identify $c$ with the vacuum propagation constant of ideal light,
which is the physical adoption of the framework's Minkowski postulate.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$) as carried by [[lem-em-outgoing-source-helmholtz-and-diffraction]] and [[lem-em-helmholtz-boundary-representation]] ([[def-countable-choice]]); the smooth modal full-Choice branch of the latter is not used. Adopt as a model assumption of the framework the following scalar aperture-diffraction model.

**(a) [Data.]** Fix an angular frequency $\omega>0$ and wavenumber $k:=\omega/c$, with $c$ the vacuum speed of [[def-em-si-conventions]]. Let $S\subset\{y\in\mathbb R^3:y_3=0\}\cap\{y:|y|\le a\}$ be a nonempty compact subset of a declared aperture plane $y_3=0$ with aperture radius $a>0$ (the screening plane and spatial region are read in the laboratory chart of [[def-em-lab-geometry]]), and let $\alpha$ be a finite complex measure on $\mathbb R^3$ supported in $S$ ([[def-complex-measure]], [[def-total-variation-of-a-signed-or-complex-measure]]) — the **aperture distribution** — with $\alpha$ read in volts so that the model field below carries the unit $\mathrm V\,\mathrm m^{-1}$ of an electric-field component and its pairings are those of [[def-integration-against-a-signed-or-complex-measure]].

**(b) [Model field.]** The model assigns to every observation point $x$ with $x_3>0$ the complex scalar amplitude

$$u(x):=\int G_k(x-y)\,d\alpha(y),$$

where $G_k(z)=e^{ik|z|}/(4\pi|z|)$ for $z\ne0$ is the outgoing Helmholtz kernel of [[lem-em-outgoing-source-helmholtz-and-diffraction]], together with the real scalar field $U(x,t):=\operatorname{Re}(u(x)e^{-i\omega t})$ and the model period-averaged squared field $(1/2)|u(x)|^2$. All model predictions are declared comparisons of this squared field between observation points; no absolute radiometric power or intensity calibration is adopted.

**(c) [Adopted regime and status.]** The model is the declared polarization-insensitive scalar approximation of aperture diffraction. It ignores the vector nature and polarization of the electromagnetic field, takes the aperture distribution rather than the exact screen traces as its datum, assigns no back-reaction of the diffracted field on the illumination and no screen interaction beyond the aperture, and is not derived from either branch of [[post-em-vacuum-maxwell]] or from the material-closure branches of [[post-em-material-closure]]; it is a declared optical approximation, not an exact electromagnetic model. It does not assert that $u$ or $U$ satisfies the Maxwell equations exactly, and it does not identify $\alpha$ with the unknown exact Maxwell boundary traces: assigning both $u$ and $\partial_nu$ on the aperture independently is not a well-posed exact boundary problem, as recorded in [[lem-em-helmholtz-boundary-representation]], and the error terms of [[lem-em-outgoing-source-helmholtz-and-diffraction]] are the controlled content of the model. No measured intensity, apparatus, sampling model, uncertainty budget, empirical comparison or quantitative radiometric calibration is adopted.

### Well-definedness and non-derivation notes

For fixed $x$ with $x_3>0$ and $y$ ranging over the compact support $S$ of $\alpha$, one has $|x-y|\ge x_3>0$, so $y\mapsto G_k(x-y)$ is continuous on $S$, bounded there by $1/(4\pi x_3)$; the pairing $\int G_k(x-y)\,d\alpha(y)$ is therefore the integral of a bounded continuous complex function against a finite complex measure and is defined by [[def-integration-against-a-signed-or-complex-measure]], with $|u(x)|\le\|\alpha\|_{\mathrm{TV}}/(4\pi x_3)$ in the total variation of [[def-total-variation-of-a-signed-or-complex-measure]]. The model permits the compact closed-radius support $|y|\le a$, including aperture corners: the integral, off-support regularity and closed-radius estimates at $r\ge2a$ are established for finite measures supported in $\overline{B_a(0)}$ by [[lem-em-outgoing-source-helmholtz-and-diffraction]]. The consuming diffraction theorem also supplies direct kernel estimates at that same closed radius.

The integral against a finite complex measure, the real-field reading and the squared field $\tfrac12|u|^2$ constitute the whole mathematical content adopted here; the physical reading uses the aperture plane and spatial region of [[def-em-lab-geometry]], the relation $k=\omega/c$ and the units of [[def-em-si-conventions]]. Neither the smooth nor the weak branch of [[post-em-vacuum-maxwell]] implies this scalar source model, and the finite-conductivity and material branches of [[post-em-material-closure]] contain no ideal aperture or screen model. The item uses no choice principle beyond those carried by the cited mathematical suppliers; the Countable Choice hypothesis is inherited verbatim from the kernel and boundary-representation suppliers and this postulate adds no choice use of its own. No derivation of the adopted data from the underlying postulates, and no empirical validation of the model, is claimed or implied by this item.

Use a fixed positively oriented inertial laboratory chart with spatial coordinate
$x\in\mathbb R^3$, time $t\in\mathbb R$, Euclidean dot and cross products, and
the SI vacuum speed $c>0$. A smooth amplitude is a map
$a:\mathbb R^3\setminus\{0\}\to\mathbb C^3$ whose coordinate partial
derivatives of every order exist and are continuous. Require its support
$K\subset\mathbb R^3\setminus\{0\}$ to be compact and require the bilinear
transversality condition
$k\cdot a(k):=\sum_{j=1}^3 k_j a_j(k)=0$ for every $k\ne0$. The dot in this
condition is bilinear, with no complex conjugation. The zero extension of $a$
to $k=0$ is understood.

For $R>0$, put $Q_R=[-R,R]^3$. Integrals of continuous real scalar functions on
$Q_R$ are the ordinary real Riemann integrals, defined as the common lower and
upper Darboux value. For a continuous
$F:Q_R\to\mathbb C^m$, define its Riemann integral componentwise by
$$\left(\int_{Q_R}F\,d^3y\right)_j:=\int_{Q_R}\operatorname{Re}F_j\,d^3y+i\int_{Q_R}\operatorname{Im}F_j\,d^3y\qquad(1\le j\le m),$$
where $y$ denotes the cube coordinates.
This also defines integrals of real vector fields by taking their imaginary
components to be zero; a real scalar is the case $m=1$. For a continuous real
scalar or finite-dimensional real/complex vector field $F$ on $\mathbb R^3$, write
$\int_{\mathbb R^3}F\,d^3x$ for the finite componentwise limit
$\lim_{R\to\infty}\int_{Q_R}F\,d^3x$ when each real-valued component
$\operatorname{Re}F_j$ and $\operatorname{Im}F_j$ has a finite limit. For
$F:\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb C^m$, say that $F$ is absolutely
integrable when the nonnegative real cube integrals
$$\int_{Q_R}\sum_{j=1}^m\bigl(|\operatorname{Re}F_j|+|\operatorname{Im}F_j|\bigr)\,d^3x$$
have a finite limit as $R\to\infty$. For a real scalar integrand this means
that the cube integrals of its absolute value have a finite limit. If this
absolute-integral limit is finite, every real or imaginary component integral
has a finite cube-exhaustion limit. For one such component $h$, set
$I_R:=\int_{Q_R}h$ and let $A_R$ denote the absolute component-sum cube integral
in the preceding display. Finite coordinate-slice additivity and the
absolute-value estimate give $|I_S-I_R|\le A_S-A_R$ for $S>R$. Since $A_R$
is nondecreasing by nonnegativity and additivity, if its limit is $A$ then
$0\le A_S-A_R\le A-A_R\to0$ uniformly for $S\ge R$. Thus these component
integrals are Cauchy as $R\to\infty$. The
integer-radius values form a Cauchy sequence and converge in $\mathbb R$; the
uniform tail bound then gives the same limit for all real radii, because an
integer radius can be chosen above any fixed real threshold. The argument uses
finite coordinate-slice additivity, the Riemann absolute-value estimate, and
completeness of $\mathbb R$. If $F$ is
continuous and compactly supported, its whole-space integral agrees with the
componentwise Riemann integral over any sufficiently large cube containing its
support and is independent of that cube. Every complex- or real-vector
integral below uses this convention. Define
the complex vector potential and its associated real fields by

$$A_+(x,t):=(2\pi)^{-3/2}\int_{\mathbb R^3}a(k)\exp\!\bigl(i(k\cdot x-c|k|t)\bigr)\,d^3k,\qquad A:=2\operatorname{Re}A_+,\qquad \varphi:=0,\qquad E:=-\partial_tA,\qquad B:=\operatorname{curl}A.$$

Here $k$ is a spatial wavevector with units $\mathrm{m^{-1}}$, $|k|$ is its
Euclidean norm, $t$ is in seconds, and $i^2=-1$; thus the phase is
dimensionless and real part is taken componentwise.
If $a$ carries units $\mathrm{T\,m^4}$, then $A$ carries $\mathrm{T\,m}$,
$E$ carries $\mathrm{V\,m^{-1}}$, and $B$ carries $\mathrm T$. These fields are
real and jointly smooth on $\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$; at each fixed time
$A,E,B$ are Schwartz functions of $x$, and their spatial Schwartz seminorms are
bounded on every compact time interval. They satisfy the smooth source-free
vacuum Maxwell equations and the Coulomb condition
$\operatorname{div}A=0$ with the stated scalar potential $\varphi=0$. Their
total field energy
$W(t):=\lim_{R\to\infty}\int_{[-R,R]^3}u(x,t)\,d^3x$, with $u$ the vacuum
energy density, is finite for every $t$. The amplitudes are a classical Fourier
description; no photon state is defined.

Fix a vector $\mathbf k\in\mathbb R^3$, a parameter $\omega>0$ and amplitudes $\mathbf e,\mathbf b\in\mathbb C^3$. Here $\mathbb C^3$ is the set of functions $\{0,1,2\}\to\mathbb C$ under componentwise operations, the complex analogue of the convention for $\mathbb R^n$ in [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]; we relabel the function values at $0,1,2$ by $1,2,3$ and write the coordinates of $\mathbf e$ as $(e_1,e_2,e_3)$ and those of $\mathbf b$ as $(b_1,b_2,b_3)$. For $\mathbf x\in\mathbb R^3$, $\langle\mathbf k,\mathbf x\rangle$ is the Euclidean inner product of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]], the real number $\sum_{j=1}^3k_jx_j$; for $t\in\mathbb R$ put

$$\theta(\mathbf x,t):=\langle\mathbf k,\mathbf x\rangle-\omega t\in\mathbb R .$$

Let $\exp$ be the complex exponential of [[def-complex-exponential]] (the power series $\sum_{n\ge0}z^n/n!$, convergent for every $z\in\mathbb C$), let $\operatorname{Re}$ be the real part of [[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]], and let $i$ be the imaginary unit of [[def-complex-numbers-and-arithmetic]].

For each $t\in\mathbb R$ define maps $\mathbf E(\cdot,t),\mathbf B(\cdot,t):\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R^3$ componentwise by

$$E_j(\mathbf x,t):=\operatorname{Re}\bigl(e_j\exp\bigl(i\,\theta(\mathbf x,t)\bigr)\bigr),\qquad B_j(\mathbf x,t):=\operatorname{Re}\bigl(b_j\exp\bigl(i\,\theta(\mathbf x,t)\bigr)\bigr),\qquad j\in\{1,2,3\}.$$

Equivalently, $\mathbf E(\cdot,t)$ is the real part, taken componentwise, of the complex vector $\mathbf e\exp(i\theta(\mathbf x,t))$, and likewise for $\mathbf B(\cdot,t)$ with $\mathbf b$ in place of $\mathbf e$.

### Well-definedness and conventions

For every $(\mathbf x,t)\in\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$ the number $\theta(\mathbf x,t)$ is real, so $i\,\theta(\mathbf x,t)$ is a complex number and $\exp(i\,\theta(\mathbf x,t))$ is defined by the everywhere-convergent exponential series; multiplying by the complex number $e_j$ or $b_j$ and taking real parts is likewise defined. Both amplitudes may be zero, in which case the corresponding field vanishes identically. The joint map $(\mathbf x,t)\mapsto(\mathbf E(\mathbf x,t),\mathbf B(\mathbf x,t))$ has $\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$, an open subset of $\mathbb R^4$, as its domain, so the $C^k$ conventions of [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]] apply to any regularity statement made about it; this definition asserts no regularity of its own beyond well-definedness. The exponential is entire with $\exp'=\exp$ ([[thm-complex-exponential-is-entire-with-derivative-itself]]), which is what makes the encoded expressions differentiable in the plane-wave form; derivations that differentiate them use [[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]], [[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]] and the chain rule for holomorphic maps where they are applied.

Complex notation here is an encoding of real fields and of real linear equations, not a complex physical field. The symbols $\mathbf e$ and $\mathbf b$ are constant complex amplitudes, not fields; the complex quantity $\mathbf e\exp(i\theta(\mathbf x,t))$ is an auxiliary object whose real part is the field. Real parts, imaginary parts and complex conjugation are the explicit operations of [[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]]. Since $\operatorname{Re}$ is additive and commutes with real scalar multiples, any identity obtained from the encoded expressions by sums, real scalar multiples, partial differentiation or integration may be projected by $\operatorname{Re}$ term by term; identities that multiply two encoded real fields may not be read off from a product of complex expressions without conjugation, and the correct second-order average rule is proved separately. No electromagnetic interpretation, equation of motion or physical identification is part of this definition.

Adopt as a physical postulate of this framework the following four equations for
the fields of [[def-em-fields]] and the sources of [[def-em-sources]] on the
laboratory region $U\cong I\times\Omega$ of [[def-em-lab-geometry]], with
$\mu_0>0$, $c>0$, $\varepsilon_0=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$ and the SI units of
[[def-em-si-conventions]].

(a) [Smooth branch] Let $E,B$ be jointly $C^1$ fields with the additional
derivatives required by each equation existing and continuous, and let
$\rho,J$ be continuous. Then, with the divergence and curl of
[[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]] and the partial derivative
$\partial_t$ at fixed position of
[[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]],

$$\operatorname{div}E=\rho/\varepsilon_0,\qquad \operatorname{div}B=0,\qquad \operatorname{curl}E=-\partial_tB,\qquad \operatorname{curl}B=\mu_0J+c^{-2}\partial_tE.$$

(b) [Weak branch] Let instead $E,B$ be locally integrable $\mathbb R^3$-valued
fields and $\rho,J$ locally integrable scalar and vector fields on
$I\times\Omega$, identified with their regular distributions
([[def-regular-distribution-from-a-locally-integrable-function]],
[[thm-locally-integrable-functions-embed-in-distributions]]). Let
$\operatorname{div}$, $\operatorname{curl}$ and $\partial_t$ act as
distributional derivatives, componentwise, and let $\psi$ range over
$C_c^\infty(I\times\Omega)$ ([[def-test-function-space-d-of-an-open-set]]).
Then the same four identities hold in the sense of [[def-distribution]]: the
pairings

$$\langle\operatorname{div}E-\rho/\varepsilon_0,\psi\rangle,\qquad \langle\operatorname{div}B,\psi\rangle,\qquad \langle\operatorname{curl}E+\partial_tB,\psi\rangle,\qquad \langle\operatorname{curl}B-\mu_0J-c^{-2}\partial_tE,\psi\rangle$$

all vanish for every such $\psi$, all derivatives being distributional
derivatives ([[def-distributional-derivative]]).

(c) [Scope] The postulate contains no magnetic charge: $\operatorname{div}B=0$
and no magnetic-source term appears in $\operatorname{curl}E$. Sources that
are not locally integrable functions (point or sheet sources) are covered by
neither branch and require their own definition. The equations are adopted
classical vacuum physics in the named inertial chart; they are not deduced from
charge conservation, from empirical agreement or from the special-relativity
postulates, and this item by itself asserts no covariance under changes of
inertial frame.

Let $\iota_{\mathbb R}\colon\mathbb N\to\mathbb R$ be the canonical-natural map
of [[def-canonical-natural]], and let $j\colon\mathbb R\to\mathbb C$ be the real
embedding $j(x)=x+i0$ from [[def-complex-numbers-and-arithmetic]]. For every
$n\in\mathbb N$, the factorial $n!$ is nonzero by
[[def-factorial-and-falling-factorial]], so
$\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!)>0$ by [[lem-of-naturals-positive]] and consequently
$j(\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!))\ne0$ in the complex field
[[thm-complex-numbers-form-a-field]].

For $z\in\mathbb C$, define
$$ \exp z:=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{z^n}{j(\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!))}. $$
whenever this complex series converges. Inside a complex expression we
abbreviate the embedded denominator $j(\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!))$ by $n!$, so the
same definition may be written $\exp z=\sum z^n/n!$ without identifying a
natural number with a complex number. Powers and series are those of
[[def-complex-integer-powers]] and
[[def-complex-series-power-series-and-absolute-convergence]]. The convergence
for every $z\in\mathbb C$ is discharged by
[[lem-complex-exponential-series-converges-everywhere]].

Every $z\in\mathbb C$ has unique coordinates $z=a+bi$
([[thm-complex-numbers-form-a-field]]). Define
$$\operatorname{Re}z=a,\qquad \operatorname{Im}z=b,\qquad \overline z=a-bi,$$
and define its **modulus** by
$$|z|=\sqrt{a^2+b^2}.$$
The real numbers are least-upper-bound complete
([[cor-cauchy-reals-lub-complete]]), so the nonnegative square root exists and
is unique by [[thm-of-square-roots]].

Every Cauchy sequence of real numbers (Limits and Cauchy sequences of reals) converges to a real
number. Together with The reals form a totally ordered field, this completes the
construction: $\mathbb{R}$ is a complete totally ordered field.
The proof uses no form of the axiom of choice.

Let $F$ be a complete ordered field (Complete ordered field (least-upper-bound property)). Then every
$a \in F$ with $a \ge 0$ has a **unique** $s \in F$ with $s \ge 0$ and $s^2 = a$;
we write $s = \sqrt{a}$. Consequently the positive elements of $F$ are exactly the
nonzero squares: $x > 0$ if and only if $x = y^2$ for some $y \neq 0$.

Let $F$ be an ordered field. For $a, b \ge 0$:

$$a < b \iff a^2 < b^2, \qquad a \le b \iff a^2 \le b^2.$$

More generally, for arbitrary $a, b \in F$, $a^2 < b^2 \iff |a| < |b|$.

For real $x,y$, $\exp(x+iy)=e^x(\cos y+i\sin y)$ and $|\exp(x+iy)|=e^x$. In particular $e^{i\pi}+1=0$. The conventions and prerequisite facts used below are recorded in [[thm-complex-exponential-addition-and-real-extension]], [[thm-eulers-formula]], [[lem-complex-conjugation-and-modulus-laws]], [[thm-pythagorean-and-parity-identities-for-all-six-trigonometric-functions]], [[cor-exponential-reciprocal-and-positivity]], [[thm-quarter-turn-values-and-shift-formulas]], [[def-pi-via-first-positive-cosine-zero]].

Every $z\in\mathbb C$ has unique coordinates $z=a+bi$
([[thm-complex-numbers-form-a-field]]). Define
$$\operatorname{Re}z=a,\qquad \operatorname{Im}z=b,\qquad \overline z=a-bi,$$
and define its **modulus** by
$$|z|=\sqrt{a^2+b^2}.$$
The real numbers are least-upper-bound complete
([[cor-cauchy-reals-lub-complete]]), so the nonnegative square root exists and
is unique by [[thm-of-square-roots]].

Let $F$ be an ordered field. For $a, b \ge 0$:

$$a < b \iff a^2 < b^2, \qquad a \le b \iff a^2 \le b^2.$$

More generally, for arbitrary $a, b \in F$, $a^2 < b^2 \iff |a| < |b|$.

Let $k_0>0$, $0<\delta<1$, $z\in\mathbb R$, and $s\in[0,\delta^2]$. Define

$$R(s):=1-\frac{s}{2}-\sqrt{1-s}.$$

Then

$$R(s)=\frac{s^2}{4\left(1-\frac{s}{2}+\sqrt{1-s}\right)},\qquad 0\le R(s)\le\frac{s^2}{8(1-\delta^2)^{3/2}},$$

and

$$\left|e^{izk_0\sqrt{1-s}}-e^{izk_0(1-s/2)}\right| \le \frac{|z|k_0s^2}{8(1-\delta^2)^{3/2}}.$$

More generally, for all real $a,b$,
$$|e^{ia}-e^{ib}|\le|a-b|.$$

derivations.claim: For $\boldsymbol\xi\in D_\delta$, put $\mathbf q:=2\pi\boldsymbol\xi$, $a:=k_0^2-|\mathbf q|^2$ and $b:=k_0^2(1-\delta^2)$. The support condition gives $0<b\le a\le k_0^2$. By [F6] and [F7] the roots in the definition exist; uniqueness and $k_0>0$ give $\sqrt b=k_0\sqrt{1-\delta^2}$ and $\sqrt{k_0^2}=k_0$. Applying [F8] to these nonnegative roots yields $0<k_0\sqrt{1-\delta^2}\le k_z(\boldsymbol\xi)\le k_0$.

The transverse and axial coordinates are measured in metres, while $\mathbf q,k_z,k_0$ are in $\mathrm{m}^{-1}$; thus every propagation-phase exponent is dimensionless. The multipliers preserve the unit of $u_0$.

[A1] fixes a separate scalar optical model, while the present Definition additionally restricts its plane data by $L^2$ and $D_\delta$ support; hence no existence or band-limit claim for every compact-aperture output is being made.

For $\boldsymbol\xi,\boldsymbol\eta\in D_\delta$, rationalizing gives $$|k_z(\boldsymbol\xi)-k_z(\boldsymbol\eta)|= \frac{\bigl||2\pi\boldsymbol\xi|^2-|2\pi\boldsymbol\eta|^2\bigr|} {k_z(\boldsymbol\xi)+k_z(\boldsymbol\eta)}.$$ The denominator is at least $2k_0\sqrt{1-\delta^2}>0$ by step 1.1, and the numerator is continuous in $(\boldsymbol\xi,\boldsymbol\eta)$; hence $k_z$ is continuous on $D_\delta$. The exact exponential branch is continuous on $D_\delta$; since $D_\delta$ is closed, its zero extension $m_{\mathrm{exact}}$ is measurable on $\mathbb R^2$. The paraxial phase is continuous on $\mathbb R^2$, so $m_{\mathrm{par}}$ is measurable there. [F9] gives modulus one for $m_{\mathrm{exact}}$ on $D_\delta$ and for $m_{\mathrm{par}}$ everywhere; $m_{\mathrm{exact}}$ is zero off $D_\delta$.

Both multipliers are measurable and bounded by one, so their products with $\mathcal F_2u_0$ are in $L^2$. Since $\mathcal F_2u_0$ vanishes almost everywhere off $D_\delta$, the exact multiplier's modulus one on $D_\delta$ and the paraxial multiplier's modulus one everywhere show that each product has the same $L^2$ norm as $\mathcal F_2u_0$. The unitary inverse in [F1] defines the propagated classes. For each fixed $t$, [F9] gives $|\operatorname{Re}(e^{-i\omega t}u)|\le|e^{-i\omega t}u|=|u|$, so the real scalar fields are in $L^2$ and independent of the representative.

The fixed-frequency modes named above are not identified with the three-dimensional smooth Fourier packets of [F3]; their Maxwell constraint and the longitudinal estimate are established conditionally from the real field postulate and plane-wave convention in [F4] and [A2].

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Let $(A,V,\eta,C^+)$ be an oriented time-oriented affine Minkowski space
([[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]]), let $(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ be an inertial
frame with inertial chart $x:A\to\mathbb R^4$
([[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]]), let $c>0$ be the framework's
conversion constant, and let $\delta$ be the Euclidean spatial form of that
frame on $n^\perp$, $n:=e_0$, with norm $|\cdot|$ and positive spatial
orientation ([[def-spatial-euclidean-structure-of-an-inertial-frame]]). Fix a
nonempty open interval $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ ([[def-interval]]) and a nonempty
open set $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^3$, and put

$$U:=\{p\in A:\ \text{there are }t\in I,\ y\in\Omega\text{ with }x^0(p)=ct,\ (x^1,x^2,x^3)(p)=y\}.$$

Then:

(a) [Chart restriction] $x(U)=\{(ct,y):t\in I,\ y\in\Omega\}$ and
$\Phi:U\to I\times\Omega$, $\Phi(p):=(x^0(p)/c,(x^1,x^2,x^3)(p))$, is a
bijection, because the inertial chart $x:A\to\mathbb R^4$ is a bijection and
$c>0$; its components are the **laboratory time coordinate**
$t(p):=x^0(p)/c$ and the **laboratory position**
$r(p):=(x^1(p),x^2(p),x^3(p))$. In the chart coordinates the pair
$(t(p),r(p))$ is the reading of the laboratory decomposition of $p$. Writing
$r(p)=(r^1(p),r^2(p),r^3(p))\in\mathbb R^3$, the standard basis of
$\mathbb R^3$ ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]) labels the three coordinate
directions, and the identification $\mathbb R^3\cong n^\perp$ is the linear
map $\sum_{i=1}^3 r^i e_i$ into the three-dimensional real vector space
$n^\perp$ ([[def-vector-space]], [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]).

(b) [Slices and spatial structure] For each $t\in I$ the slice
$U_t:=\{p\in U:t(p)=t\}$ is carried bijectively onto $\Omega$ by $r$; the
constant vector $n=e_0$ is future unit timelike, and $(e_1,e_2,e_3)$ is the
$\delta$-orthonormal positively oriented basis of $n^\perp$ in which the
coordinates of $r$ are expressed.

(c) [Laboratory fields] For a nonnegative integer $m$, a **laboratory field of rank $m$** is a map
$F:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^m$; it is identified with the map $U\to\mathbb R^m$,
$p\mapsto F(r(p),t(p))$, and with the family $(F(\cdot,t))_{t\in I}$ of maps
$\Omega\to\mathbb R^m$, its values at fixed time. Such a field is of class
$C^k$, for $m\ge1$, when the map $(y,t)\mapsto F(y,t)$ is $C^k$ in the sense of
[[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]. For $m=0$, set $\mathbb R^0:=\{()\}$;
the unique field into this singleton is declared $C^\infty$ (and $C^k$ for every
finite $k$), and each of its partial derivatives is the same singleton-valued
zero map. For $m\ge1$ and $k\ge1$, $\partial_{y_i}F$ (at fixed
$t$) and $\partial_tF$ (at fixed $y$) are the partial derivatives of
[[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]]. No regularity of a field is
asserted beyond the class stated for it.

(d) [Conventions] The product decomposition is a coordinate identification
inside the single inertial frame $(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$; it is not a Galilean
transformation, it does not compare two inertial frames, and it does not
assert absolute simultaneity. The objects $I,\Omega,t,r,\delta$ and the
identification $\mathbb R^3\cong n^\perp$ belong to the named frame; changes
of inertial description are the proper orthochronous maps adopted in
[[post-sr-inertial-covariance]]. The frame is an origin together with an
ordered basis; it is not a congruence of observers, and no moving observer
field is defined here.

Adopt the SI system of units for this framework, with the following quantity
table and conventions; every symbol is a quantity of this framework and the
laboratory structure is that of [[def-em-lab-geometry]].

(a) [Coordinates and constants] $x^0=ct$ and each spatial coordinate $x^i$
carries the metre (m); the time coordinate $t$ carries the second (s); the
conversion constant $c>0$ carries m s$^{-1}$ and has the exact SI defining
value $c=299\,792\,458\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$; the elementary charge $e$ has the
exact SI defining value $e=1.602\,176\,634\times10^{-19}\ \mathrm{C}$, and this
item does not assert that physical charge is quantised; the magnetic constant
$\mu_0>0$ carries N A$^{-2}$ and is measured, so no exact numerical value of
$\mu_0$ is asserted. The pre-2019 SI fixed the historical nominal
$\mu_{0,\mathrm{nom}}:=4\pi\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{H\,m^{-1}}
=4\pi\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{N\,A^{-2}}$ exactly; since the revised SI took
effect on 20 May 2019, $\mu_0$ is experimentally determined. The SI brochure
quotes the nominal $\mu_{0,\mathrm{nom}}$ as the estimate at the 2019 adoption
with relative standard uncertainty $2.3\times10^{-10}$; this is historical
estimate and uncertainty context, not an exact equality for the actual $\mu_0$
or a current measured value. The electric constant is defined within the
framework by

$$\varepsilon_0:=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$$

in F m$^{-1}$, consistent with the exact SI relation $\varepsilon_0\mu_0=1/c^2$,
so that $c^2\varepsilon_0\mu_0=1$ and $\varepsilon_0$ inherits the relative
standard uncertainty of $\mu_0$.

(b) [Electromagnetic quantities] Charge $q$ carries the coulomb (C); the
charge density $\rho$ of the framework's source definition carries C m$^{-3}$
and the current density $J$ carries A m$^{-2}$, so that the four-current
components $(c\rho,J)$ carry A m$^{-2}$; the electric field $E$ carries
V m$^{-1}$; the magnetic field $B$ carries the tesla (T), where
$1\ \mathrm{T}=1\ \mathrm{N\,A^{-1}\,m^{-1}}$; the scalar potential $\varphi$
carries V and the vector potential $A$ carries T m, so that the four-potential
components $(\varphi/c,A)$ carry T m; the components of the electromagnetic
two-form of the framework's tensor definition carry T; a force carries the
newton (N), $1\ \mathrm{N}=1\ \mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-2}}$.

(c) [Mechanical quantities] A rest mass parameter $m$ carries the kilogram
(kg) and a four-momentum $P=mU$ of the relativistic particle model carries
kg m s$^{-1}$; field energy density carries J m$^{-3}$, energy flux
W m$^{-2}$, so that $1\ \mathrm{W}=1\ \mathrm{J\,s^{-1}}=1\ \mathrm{V\,A}$.

(d) [Bookkeeping only] The unit of a quantity records the adopted system of
units; it does not show that a quantity is primitive in this or any other
framework, it contains no measurement, and it does not identify a quantity
with a similarly named quantity of another framework. The exact defining
values of $c$ and $e$ fix numerical conventions of the SI; they do not by
themselves identify $c$ with the vacuum propagation constant of ideal light,
which is the physical adoption of the framework's Minkowski postulate.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$) as carried by [[lem-em-outgoing-source-helmholtz-and-diffraction]] and [[lem-em-helmholtz-boundary-representation]] ([[def-countable-choice]]); the smooth modal full-Choice branch of the latter is not used. Adopt as a model assumption of the framework the following scalar aperture-diffraction model.

**(a) [Data.]** Fix an angular frequency $\omega>0$ and wavenumber $k:=\omega/c$, with $c$ the vacuum speed of [[def-em-si-conventions]]. Let $S\subset\{y\in\mathbb R^3:y_3=0\}\cap\{y:|y|\le a\}$ be a nonempty compact subset of a declared aperture plane $y_3=0$ with aperture radius $a>0$ (the screening plane and spatial region are read in the laboratory chart of [[def-em-lab-geometry]]), and let $\alpha$ be a finite complex measure on $\mathbb R^3$ supported in $S$ ([[def-complex-measure]], [[def-total-variation-of-a-signed-or-complex-measure]]) — the **aperture distribution** — with $\alpha$ read in volts so that the model field below carries the unit $\mathrm V\,\mathrm m^{-1}$ of an electric-field component and its pairings are those of [[def-integration-against-a-signed-or-complex-measure]].

**(b) [Model field.]** The model assigns to every observation point $x$ with $x_3>0$ the complex scalar amplitude

$$u(x):=\int G_k(x-y)\,d\alpha(y),$$

where $G_k(z)=e^{ik|z|}/(4\pi|z|)$ for $z\ne0$ is the outgoing Helmholtz kernel of [[lem-em-outgoing-source-helmholtz-and-diffraction]], together with the real scalar field $U(x,t):=\operatorname{Re}(u(x)e^{-i\omega t})$ and the model period-averaged squared field $(1/2)|u(x)|^2$. All model predictions are declared comparisons of this squared field between observation points; no absolute radiometric power or intensity calibration is adopted.

**(c) [Adopted regime and status.]** The model is the declared polarization-insensitive scalar approximation of aperture diffraction. It ignores the vector nature and polarization of the electromagnetic field, takes the aperture distribution rather than the exact screen traces as its datum, assigns no back-reaction of the diffracted field on the illumination and no screen interaction beyond the aperture, and is not derived from either branch of [[post-em-vacuum-maxwell]] or from the material-closure branches of [[post-em-material-closure]]; it is a declared optical approximation, not an exact electromagnetic model. It does not assert that $u$ or $U$ satisfies the Maxwell equations exactly, and it does not identify $\alpha$ with the unknown exact Maxwell boundary traces: assigning both $u$ and $\partial_nu$ on the aperture independently is not a well-posed exact boundary problem, as recorded in [[lem-em-helmholtz-boundary-representation]], and the error terms of [[lem-em-outgoing-source-helmholtz-and-diffraction]] are the controlled content of the model. No measured intensity, apparatus, sampling model, uncertainty budget, empirical comparison or quantitative radiometric calibration is adopted.

### Well-definedness and non-derivation notes

For fixed $x$ with $x_3>0$ and $y$ ranging over the compact support $S$ of $\alpha$, one has $|x-y|\ge x_3>0$, so $y\mapsto G_k(x-y)$ is continuous on $S$, bounded there by $1/(4\pi x_3)$; the pairing $\int G_k(x-y)\,d\alpha(y)$ is therefore the integral of a bounded continuous complex function against a finite complex measure and is defined by [[def-integration-against-a-signed-or-complex-measure]], with $|u(x)|\le\|\alpha\|_{\mathrm{TV}}/(4\pi x_3)$ in the total variation of [[def-total-variation-of-a-signed-or-complex-measure]]. The model permits the compact closed-radius support $|y|\le a$, including aperture corners: the integral, off-support regularity and closed-radius estimates at $r\ge2a$ are established for finite measures supported in $\overline{B_a(0)}$ by [[lem-em-outgoing-source-helmholtz-and-diffraction]]. The consuming diffraction theorem also supplies direct kernel estimates at that same closed radius.

The integral against a finite complex measure, the real-field reading and the squared field $\tfrac12|u|^2$ constitute the whole mathematical content adopted here; the physical reading uses the aperture plane and spatial region of [[def-em-lab-geometry]], the relation $k=\omega/c$ and the units of [[def-em-si-conventions]]. Neither the smooth nor the weak branch of [[post-em-vacuum-maxwell]] implies this scalar source model, and the finite-conductivity and material branches of [[post-em-material-closure]] contain no ideal aperture or screen model. The item uses no choice principle beyond those carried by the cited mathematical suppliers; the Countable Choice hypothesis is inherited verbatim from the kernel and boundary-representation suppliers and this postulate adds no choice use of its own. No derivation of the adopted data from the underlying postulates, and no empirical validation of the model, is claimed or implied by this item.

Use a fixed positively oriented inertial laboratory chart with spatial coordinate
$x\in\mathbb R^3$, time $t\in\mathbb R$, Euclidean dot and cross products, and
the SI vacuum speed $c>0$. A smooth amplitude is a map
$a:\mathbb R^3\setminus\{0\}\to\mathbb C^3$ whose coordinate partial
derivatives of every order exist and are continuous. Require its support
$K\subset\mathbb R^3\setminus\{0\}$ to be compact and require the bilinear
transversality condition
$k\cdot a(k):=\sum_{j=1}^3 k_j a_j(k)=0$ for every $k\ne0$. The dot in this
condition is bilinear, with no complex conjugation. The zero extension of $a$
to $k=0$ is understood.

For a compactly supported continuous integrand, write its integral over
$\mathbb R^3$ for its Riemann integral over any sufficiently large cube
$[-R,R]^3$ containing its support; this value is independent of such $R$. Define
the complex vector potential and its associated real fields by

$$A_+(x,t):=(2\pi)^{-3/2}\int_{\mathbb R^3}a(k)\exp\!\bigl(i(k\cdot x-c|k|t)\bigr)\,d^3k,\qquad A:=2\operatorname{Re}A_+,\qquad \varphi:=0,\qquad E:=-\partial_tA,\qquad B:=\operatorname{curl}A.$$

Here $k$ is a spatial wavevector with units $\mathrm{m^{-1}}$, $|k|$ is its
Euclidean norm, $t$ is in seconds, and $i^2=-1$; thus the phase is
dimensionless and real part is taken componentwise.
If $a$ carries units $\mathrm{T\,m^4}$, then $A$ carries $\mathrm{T\,m}$,
$E$ carries $\mathrm{V\,m^{-1}}$, and $B$ carries $\mathrm T$. These fields are
real and jointly smooth on $\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$; at each fixed time
$A,E,B$ are Schwartz functions of $x$, and their spatial Schwartz seminorms are
bounded on every compact time interval. They satisfy the smooth source-free
vacuum Maxwell equations and the Coulomb condition
$\operatorname{div}A=0$ with the stated scalar potential $\varphi=0$. Their
total field energy
$W(t):=\lim_{R\to\infty}\int_{[-R,R]^3}u(x,t)\,d^3x$, with $u$ the vacuum
energy density, is finite for every $t$. The amplitudes are a classical Fourier
description; no photon state is defined.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Fix a vector $\mathbf k\in\mathbb R^3$, a parameter $\omega>0$ and amplitudes $\mathbf e,\mathbf b\in\mathbb C^3$. Here $\mathbb C^3$ is the set of functions $\{0,1,2\}\to\mathbb C$ under componentwise operations, the complex analogue of the convention for $\mathbb R^n$ in [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]; we relabel the function values at $0,1,2$ by $1,2,3$ and write the coordinates of $\mathbf e$ as $(e_1,e_2,e_3)$ and those of $\mathbf b$ as $(b_1,b_2,b_3)$. For $\mathbf x\in\mathbb R^3$, $\langle\mathbf k,\mathbf x\rangle$ is the Euclidean inner product of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]], the real number $\sum_{j=1}^3k_jx_j$; for $t\in\mathbb R$ put

$$\theta(\mathbf x,t):=\langle\mathbf k,\mathbf x\rangle-\omega t\in\mathbb R .$$

Let $\exp$ be the complex exponential of [[def-complex-exponential]] (the power series $\sum_{n\ge0}z^n/n!$, convergent for every $z\in\mathbb C$), let $\operatorname{Re}$ be the real part of [[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]], and let $i$ be the imaginary unit of [[def-complex-numbers-and-arithmetic]].

For each $t\in\mathbb R$ define maps $\mathbf E(\cdot,t),\mathbf B(\cdot,t):\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R^3$ componentwise by

$$E_j(\mathbf x,t):=\operatorname{Re}\bigl(e_j\exp\bigl(i\,\theta(\mathbf x,t)\bigr)\bigr),\qquad B_j(\mathbf x,t):=\operatorname{Re}\bigl(b_j\exp\bigl(i\,\theta(\mathbf x,t)\bigr)\bigr),\qquad j\in\{1,2,3\}.$$

Equivalently, $\mathbf E(\cdot,t)$ is the real part, taken componentwise, of the complex vector $\mathbf e\exp(i\theta(\mathbf x,t))$, and likewise for $\mathbf B(\cdot,t)$ with $\mathbf b$ in place of $\mathbf e$.

### Well-definedness and conventions

For every $(\mathbf x,t)\in\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$ the number $\theta(\mathbf x,t)$ is real, so $i\,\theta(\mathbf x,t)$ is a complex number and $\exp(i\,\theta(\mathbf x,t))$ is defined by the everywhere-convergent exponential series; multiplying by the complex number $e_j$ or $b_j$ and taking real parts is likewise defined. Both amplitudes may be zero, in which case the corresponding field vanishes identically. The joint map $(\mathbf x,t)\mapsto(\mathbf E(\mathbf x,t),\mathbf B(\mathbf x,t))$ has $\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$, an open subset of $\mathbb R^4$, as its domain, so the $C^k$ conventions of [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]] apply to any regularity statement made about it; this definition asserts no regularity of its own beyond well-definedness. The exponential is entire with $\exp'=\exp$ ([[thm-complex-exponential-is-entire-with-derivative-itself]]), which is what makes the encoded expressions differentiable in the plane-wave form; derivations that differentiate them use [[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]], [[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]] and the chain rule for holomorphic maps where they are applied.

Complex notation here is an encoding of real fields and of real linear equations, not a complex physical field. The symbols $\mathbf e$ and $\mathbf b$ are constant complex amplitudes, not fields; the complex quantity $\mathbf e\exp(i\theta(\mathbf x,t))$ is an auxiliary object whose real part is the field. Real parts, imaginary parts and complex conjugation are the explicit operations of [[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]]. Since $\operatorname{Re}$ is additive and commutes with real scalar multiples, any identity obtained from the encoded expressions by sums, real scalar multiples, partial differentiation or integration may be projected by $\operatorname{Re}$ term by term; identities that multiply two encoded real fields may not be read off from a product of complex expressions without conjugation, and the correct second-order average rule is proved separately. No electromagnetic interpretation, equation of motion or physical identification is part of this definition.

natural number with a complex number. Powers and series are those of

Let $k_0>0$, $0<\delta<1$, $z\in\mathbb R$, and $s\in[0,\delta^2]$. Define

$$R(s):=1-\frac{s}{2}-\sqrt{1-s}.$$

Then

$$R(s)=\frac{s^2}{4\left(1-\frac{s}{2}+\sqrt{1-s}\right)},\qquad 0\le R(s)\le\frac{s^2}{8(1-\delta^2)^{3/2}},$$

and

$$\left|e^{izk_0\sqrt{1-s}}-e^{izk_0(1-s/2)}\right| \le \frac{|z|k_0s^2}{8(1-\delta^2)^{3/2}}.$$

More generally, for all real $a,b$,
$$|e^{ia}-e^{ib}|\le|a-b|.$$

orthogonal projection onto $T_k$; $C(k)$ is Hermitian, vanishes on the
longitudinal line, and satisfies $C(k)^2=P_T(k)$. The restrictions of

sum $P_T(k)$. Their ranges are the two helicity eigenspaces, with eigenvalues
$+1$ and $-1$ for $C(k)$.

Here $k$ is a spatial wavevector with units $\mathrm{m^{-1}}$, $|k|$ is its

dimensionless and real part is taken componentwise.

Let the metric, gauge, parameters, tortoise coordinate, harmonic $Y$, and
operator be exactly those of the charged radial scattering definition. For
$\varpi(r):=\omega-eQ/r$, a smooth separated solution
$\psi=A_{\mathrm{in}}e^{-i\omega t}Y(\Omega)u(r_*)/r$ of
$\Box_{g,A}\psi=0$ has radial function satisfying
$$\frac{d^2u}{dr_*^2}+\left[\left(\omega-\frac{eQ}{r}\right)^2-f(r)\left(\frac{\ell(\ell+1)}{r^2}+\frac{f'(r)}r\right)\right]u=0.$$
Here $f'$ denotes the derivative with respect to $r$, and derivatives of $u$
are with respect to $r_*$.

Let $u$ be any scattering solution as defined on the fixed subextremal electric
RN exterior, with real $\omega>0$, real $e,Q$, unit incoming amplitude, and
reflection and transmission coefficients $R,T$. Then its radial Wronskian
flux $j:=\operatorname{Im}(\overline u\,\partial_{r_*}u)$ is constant and
$$|R|^2=1-\frac{\omega-eQ/r_+}{\omega}|T|^2.$$
Consequently, if $0<\omega<eQ/r_+$ and $T\ne0$, the reflected radial flux
magnitude exceeds the incident radial flux magnitude, since their ratio is
$|R|^2>1$. This is conditional on an admitted scattering solution and does not
assert its existence, a complex-frequency mode, or a nonlinear instability.

Let $M>0$ and $Q\in\mathbb R$ satisfy $0<|Q|<M$. Put
$$r_\pm:=M\pm\sqrt{M^2-Q^2},\qquad f(r):=1-\frac{2M}{r}+\frac{Q^2}{r^2},\qquad r>r_+.$$
Use the static exterior
$\mathcal M_{\mathrm{ext}}=\mathbb R_t\times(r_+,\infty)_r\times S^2$
with the electric specialization $q_e=Q$, $q_m=0$, and $t=x^0$ of the
Reissner--Nordström metric and potential fixed in the preceding definition.
Thus
$$g=-f\,dt^2+f^{-1}dr^2+r^2\gamma_{S^2},\qquad A=-\frac Qr\,dt,\qquad A_t\longrightarrow0\quad(r\longrightarrow\infty).$$
Here $r_+$ is the positive outer root in the selected local model, not a claim
about an event horizon in a maximal spacetime. Set
$\Phi_H:=Q/r_+=A_t(\infty)-A_t(r_+)$ for this gauge.

For a complex scalar function $\psi$ in this fixed trivialization and a real
coupling $e$, put $D_a\psi:=(\partial_a-ieA_a)\psi$. Define the massless
charged wave operator in the static chart by
$$\Box_{g,A}\psi:=-f^{-1}D_t^2\psi+\frac1{r^2}\partial_r\!\left(r^2f\,\partial_r\psi\right)+\frac1{r^2}\Delta_{\gamma_{S^2}}\psi,\qquad D_t=\partial_t+\frac{ieQ}{r}.$$
The equation used here is $\Box_{g,A}\psi=0$; it is a fixed-background,
minimally coupled test-field equation and does not evolve or source $g$ or $A$.

Let $e\in\mathbb R$, $\omega>0$, and $\ell\in\mathbb N_0$. Supply a smooth
real function $Y:S^2\to\mathbb R$ satisfying
$$\int_{S^2}Y^2\,d\omega_{S^2}=1,\qquad \Delta_{\gamma_{S^2}}Y=-\ell(\ell+1)Y.$$
No existence assertion about $Y$ is made. Use the tortoise coordinate
$$r_*(r):=\int_{2r_+}^{r}f(\rho)^{-1}\,d\rho,$$
which is strictly increasing because $f>0$ on the exterior. Under the
subextremal hypotheses the supplied RN scalar-coordinate result proves that
$r_*$ is a smooth coordinate from $(r_+,\infty)$ onto $\mathbb R$; hence
$r_*\to-\infty$ as $r\downarrow r_+$ and $r_*\to+\infty$ as $r\to\infty$.
A separated mode has the form
$$\psi(t,r,\Omega)=A_{\mathrm{in}}e^{-i\omega t}Y(\Omega)\frac{u(r_*)}{r},$$
where $A_{\mathrm{in}}\ne0$ is a fixed incident amplitude with units
$[\psi]\,\mathrm m$, and the normalized complex radial function $u$ and its
reflection and transmission coefficients are dimensionless.

Write $\omega_H:=\omega-e\Phi_H=\omega-eQ/r_+$ and, for any reference length
$L>0$, define the Coulomb phase
$$\Theta(r_*):=\omega r_*-eQ\log(r/L),\qquad \Theta'(r_*):=\omega-\frac{eQf(r)}r.$$
A normalized scattering solution is a smooth radial solution of
$\Box_{g,A}\psi=0$ for which, for some $R,T\in\mathbb C$,
$$u=e^{-i\Theta}+R e^{i\Theta}+o(1),\qquad \partial_{r_*}u=-i\Theta'e^{-i\Theta}+i\Theta'R e^{i\Theta}+o(1)\quad(r\longrightarrow\infty),$$
and
$$u=T e^{-i\omega_Hr_*}+o(1),\qquad \partial_{r_*}u=-i\omega_HTe^{-i\omega_Hr_*}+o(1)\quad(r\downarrow r_+).$$
The error terms tend to zero in the indicated limits. These boundary
conditions prescribe unit incoming amplitude at infinity and only the
ingoing branch at the future horizon. They define admissible scattering data;
they assert neither existence nor uniqueness of such a solution.

The logarithm in $\Theta$ is required by the long-range term
$-2\omega eQ/r$ in the asymptotic radial coefficient. Changing $L$ changes
constant phases, not flux magnitudes. A constant gauge shift changes the
frequency label, so the threshold uses the potential difference
$\Phi_H$, not an absolute value of $A_t$.

Use geometric units $G=c=1$ and length coordinates, with
$[t]=[r]=[r_*]=[M]=[Q]=[L]=\mathrm m$,
$[e]=[\omega]=\mathrm m^{-1}$, $f$ dimensionless, and $A_t$ dimensionless;
then $\Theta$ is dimensionless and each term in $\Box_{g,A}$ has units
$[\psi]\,\mathrm m^{-2}$. The coupling $e$ is the charge coupling in the
chosen field normalization; restoring SI units requires restoring the
corresponding field normalization and the charge-over-$\hbar$ coupling.
This definition excludes scalar mass, magnetic charge, mirrors, anti-de Sitter
boundaries, bound states, and complex-frequency quasinormal boundary conditions.
A scalar mass would change the propagating infinity wave number to
$\sqrt{\omega^2-\mu^2}$ and requires a different scattering normalization.
Complex-frequency quasinormal modes form a distinct non-self-adjoint spectral
problem and are not covered by the real-frequency Wronskian identity.

derivations.claim:
Write $x=r_*$ and use the choices in [A1]--[A2]. By [F3], $x$ ranges over
all of $\mathbb R$ and $dr/dx=f$. The charged radial
equation [F1] becomes
$$u''(x)+\bigl(\omega^2-V(x)\bigr)u(x)=0,\qquad
V(x):=\frac{f(r(x))f'(r(x))}{r(x)}.$$
The definition gives $dr/dx=f$ and $f(r)=(r-r_+)(r-r_-)/r^2$. Since
$r_+>M>r_-$ and $r_+r_-=Q^2$, we have $f(r)>0$ and $Mr>Mr_+>Q^2$
for $r>r_+$, so $f'(r)=2(Mr-Q^2)/r^3>0$ and $V>0$. Thus $V$ is smooth
and real. Moreover,
$$\int_{\mathbb R}|V(x)|\,dx=\int_{r_+}^{\infty}\frac{f'(r)}r\,dr
=\int_{r_+}^{\infty}\frac{2(Mr-Q^2)}{r^4}\,dr<\infty.$$

Define $u_-$ by the Volterra equation
$$u_-(x)=e^{-i\omega x}+\frac1\omega\int_{-\infty}^{x}
\sin\!\bigl(\omega(x-y)\bigr)V(y)u_-(y)\,dy.$$
Iteration gives a uniformly convergent Neumann series: the absolute value of
its $n$th iterated term is at most
$\|V\|_{L^1(\mathbb R)}^n/(\omega^n n!)$, using $|\sin z|\le1$ for real $z$
and the ordered integration region. The sum is bounded on $\mathbb R$; differentiating
the integral equation shows it is a smooth solution of the equation in step
1.1. The tail integrals tend to zero as $x\to-\infty$, and differentiation
under the integral gives
$$u_-(x)=e^{-i\omega x}+o(1),\qquad
u_-'(x)=-i\omega e^{-i\omega x}+o(1)\quad(x\to-\infty).$$

Since $V u_-\in L^1(\mathbb R)$, expanding the sine in step 1.2 into
exponentials and replacing the upper integration limit by $+\infty$ gives
$$u_-(x)=a e^{-i\omega x}+b e^{i\omega x}+o(1),\qquad
u_-'(x)=-i\omega a e^{-i\omega x}+i\omega b e^{i\omega x}+o(1)$$
as $x\to+\infty$, where
$$a=1-\frac1{2i\omega}\int_{\mathbb R}e^{i\omega y}V(y)u_-(y)\,dy,
\qquad b=\frac1{2i\omega}\int_{\mathbb R}e^{-i\omega y}V(y)u_-(y)\,dy.$$
The same tail estimate after differentiating the integral equation proves the
displayed derivative asymptotic.

For $j=\operatorname{Im}(\overline{u_-}u_-')$, the real-coefficient
equation in step 1.1 gives $j'=0$. The horizon asymptotics in step 1.2 yield
$j=-\omega$, while step 2.1 yields $j=\omega(|b|^2-|a|^2)$ at infinity;
the two oscillatory cross terms have real sum and contribute no imaginary part.
Hence $|a|^2=|b|^2+1$, so $a\ne0$. Put $u=u_-/a$, $R=b/a$, and $T=1/a$.
Then $u$ has the asymptotics in [F3], with unit incoming amplitude and only
the ingoing branch at the horizon. The separated-wave substitution in the
proof of [F1] is reversible here: $Y$ is a nonzero constant, $A_{\mathrm{in}}$
and $fr$ are nonzero, and each displayed step is an equality. Therefore
$\psi=A_{\mathrm{in}}e^{-i\omega t}Y u/r$ solves $\Box_{g,A}\psi=0$ and is
an admitted scattering solution for any fixed nonzero allowed
$A_{\mathrm{in}}$.

Apply [F2] to this constructed solution. Since $e=0$ and $T=1/a\ne0$,
$$|R|^2=1-|T|^2=1-|a|^{-2}<1.$$
Thus this nonzero-charge background admits a neutral mode whose reflected
radial flux is less than the incident flux, contradicting the universal
amplification statement.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Let $u$ be any scattering solution as defined on the fixed subextremal electric
RN exterior, with real $\omega>0$, real $e,Q$, unit incoming amplitude, and
reflection and transmission coefficients $R,T$. Then its radial Wronskian
flux $j:=\operatorname{Im}(\overline u\,\partial_{r_*}u)$ is constant and
$$|R|^2=1-\frac{\omega-eQ/r_+}{\omega}|T|^2.$$
Consequently, if $0<\omega<eQ/r_+$ and $T\ne0$, the reflected radial flux
magnitude exceeds the incident radial flux magnitude, since their ratio is
$|R|^2>1$. This is conditional on an admitted scattering solution and does not
assert its existence, a complex-frequency mode, or a nonlinear instability.
