Assume the axiom of countable choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ for the smooth
tangent-bundle conventions. Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth
Lorentzian four-manifold of signature $(-,+,+,+)$ with metric-selected
connection $\nabla$ and inverse metric $g^{ab}$. Let $U\subseteq M$ be open,
let $\psi\in C^\infty(U,\mathbb R)$ be a real scalar field, and let $X$ be a
smooth vector field on $U$. Define the wave operator
$\Box_g\psi:=g^{ab}\nabla_a\nabla_b\psi$ and the symmetric covariant tensor

$$Q_{ab}[\psi]:=(\nabla_a\psi)(\nabla_b\psi)-\frac12 g_{ab}g^{cd}(\nabla_c\psi)(\nabla_d\psi).$$

Define the multiplier covector by $J^X_a[\psi]:=Q_{ab}[\psi]X^b$. The
associated energy-current vector is $j_X^a[\psi]:=-g^{ab}J^X_b[\psi]$; this
sign convention makes its flux through a future spacelike slice equal to the
density $Q_{ab}n^aX^b$ when $n$ is the future unit normal. The test-wave
equation is $\Box_g\psi=0$ on $U$. These objects are defined on the fixed
background $g$; $Q$ is not automatically an SI matter stress-energy tensor,
is not inserted into an Einstein equation here, and does not evolve $g$.

If $\psi$ is dimensionless and the coordinates have length units, the
components of $Q$ have units of inverse length squared. This dimensional fact
does not identify $Q$ with a physical stress tensor without an independently
specified field normalization and coupling.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth
Lorentzian four-manifold, let $U\subseteq M$ be open, let
$\psi\in C^\infty(U,\mathbb R)$, and let $X$ be a smooth vector field on $U$.
For the tensor $Q_{ab}[\psi]$ and multiplier covector
$J_a^X[\psi]=Q_{ab}[\psi]X^b$ defined from the metric-selected connection,

$$\nabla^aJ_a^X[\psi]=(\Box_g\psi)\,X^b\nabla_b\psi+\frac12 Q^{ab}[\psi](\mathcal L_Xg)_{ab}.$$

Consequently, when $\Box_g\psi=0$ and $X$ is Killing, the multiplier current
has zero divergence.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold
([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]) and let $\xi$ be a smooth vector field
on $M$ ([[def-smooth-vector-field-as-a-tangent-bundle-section]]). The **Lie
derivative of the metric along $\xi$**, written $\mathcal L_\xi g$, is the
smooth symmetric covariant $2$-tensor field obtained by the flow definition of
[[def-lie-derivative-of-a-tensor-field]] applied to $g$: for the local flow
$\Phi_t$ of $\xi$,

$$\mathcal L_\xi g:=\frac{d}{dt}\Big|_{t=0}\Phi_t^*g .$$

The field $\xi$ is a **Killing field** of $(M,g)$ (an **isometry generator**,
or a **Killing vector**) when

$$\mathcal L_\xi g=0 .$$

The equivalent local characterization

$$\mathcal L_\xi g=0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\nabla_a\xi_b+\nabla_b\xi_a=0,$$

where $\nabla$ is the metric-selected connection of $g$
([[def-gr-metric-selected-connection]],
[[thm-gr-nondegenerate-levi-civita-and-tensor-derivative]]) and
$\xi_b:=g_{bc}\xi^c$ is the lowered field, is proved in
[[thm-gr-killing-and-on-shell-matter-identities]] clause (a); the definition
itself asserts neither direction. Whether a given metric has Killing fields is
a property of that metric: neither existence nor uniqueness of a Killing field
is asserted here, and a general metric has none beyond the trivial field
$\xi=0$.

This item assumes the axiom of countable choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ through
the tangent-bundle structure used by
[[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]] clause (c)
([[def-countable-choice]]); no further choice principle is used.

**(a) Parameters and the Schwarzschild radius.** Let $c>0$ and $G_N>0$ be real
constants and let $m_*>0$ be a real **mass parameter**. Put

$$s:=\frac{2G_Nm_*}{c^2}>0 .$$

The number $s$ is the **Schwarzschild radius** of the datum. Neither $c$,
$G_N$ nor $m_*$ is measured here; the physical reading of $c$ and $G_N$ as the
framework's conversion and Newton constants and of $m_*$ as a mass is fixed by
the physical conventions of the framework, not by this definition.

**(b) The underlying manifold and its product charts.** Let $S^2:=S_2(0,1)=
\{y\in\mathbb R^3:\lVert y\rVert_2=1\}$ be the unit Euclidean sphere with the
subspace topology of [[def-euclidean-spheres-and-closed-balls]]. Specify its
smooth structure as the maximal atlas generated by the following two charts
([[def-smooth-manifold]]). For $\varepsilon\in\{+1,-1\}$ put
$p_\varepsilon=(0,0,\varepsilon)$ and
$U_\varepsilon=S^2\setminus\{p_\varepsilon\}$, and define

$$\sigma_\varepsilon:U_\varepsilon\to\mathbb R^2,\qquad \sigma_\varepsilon(y)=\frac{(y_1,y_2)}{1-\varepsilon y_3}.$$

These open domains cover $S^2$. Each chart is a homeomorphism onto
$\mathbb R^2$, with inverse, for $u=(u_1,u_2)$ and $q=u_1^2+u_2^2$,

$$\sigma_\varepsilon^{-1}(u)=\left(\frac{2u_1}{1+q},\frac{2u_2}{1+q},\varepsilon\frac{q-1}{1+q}\right).$$

The two inverse identities follow by substitution; all displayed denominators
are nonzero on their domains. On the overlap both transition maps are
$u\mapsto u/(u_1^2+u_2^2)$ on $\mathbb R^2\setminus\{0\}$, hence smooth.
The subspace is Hausdorff and has a countable basis given by intersections
with Euclidean balls of rational centres and positive rational radii.
Thus these charts specify a smooth two-manifold without boundary. This is
the standard sphere structure used for the round metric below: the inclusion
has the displayed smooth local parametrizations, and their differentials
are injective because composition with $\sigma_\varepsilon$ is the identity.
Let $M$ be the product manifold

$$M:=\mathbb R\times(s,\infty)\times S^2$$

with the product smooth structure
([[prop-products-of-smooth-manifolds-have-a-canonical-product-smooth-structure]]);
it is a smooth four-manifold without boundary. Write $x^0:M\to\mathbb R$ and
$r:M\to(s,\infty)$ for the first and second projections and $\iota:M\to S^2$
for the third. A **product chart** of $M$ is a smooth chart on the product
whose angular part is a smooth chart of $S^2$. In a **spherical-polar product
chart**, $0<\vartheta<\pi$ and the components of the round metric
$\gamma_{S^2}$ of [[ex-the-round-metric-on-the-sphere-as-an-induced-metric]]
are $\gamma_{22}=1$, $\gamma_{23}=\gamma_{32}=0$,
$\gamma_{33}=\sin^2\vartheta$. These polar charts omit the two poles; ordinary
smooth sphere charts around the poles complete the product atlas.

**(c) The metric.** Let $f:(s,\infty)\to(0,\infty)$ be the smooth function

$$f(r):=1-\frac{s}{r} .$$

Define $g$ globally by the coordinate-free expression

$$g=-f\,d(x^0)\otimes d(x^0)+f^{-1}\,dr\otimes dr+r^2\,\iota^*\gamma_{S^2}.$$

In every spherical-polar product chart its component functions are

$$g_{00}:=-f(r),\qquad g_{11}:=\frac{1}{f(r)},\qquad g_{22}:=r^2,\qquad g_{33}:=r^2\sin^2\vartheta,$$

and $g_{ab}:=0$ whenever $a\ne b$, $a,b\in\{0,1,2,3\}$, with the index order
$(x^0,x^1,x^2,x^3)=(x^0,r,\vartheta,\varphi)$. This is a smooth symmetric
covariant $2$-tensor field on all of $M$
([[def-gr-smooth-covariant-two-tensor-field]]); the component display is local
to spherical-polar charts, and $f>0$ because $r>s$. The pair $(M,g)$ is the **Schwarzschild exterior
metric of mass parameter $m_*$**; the datum of this definition is the
quadruple $(c,G_N,m_*,g)$. With these parameters fixed, write $(M,g,N)$
for its associated geometric datum, with $N$ as in clause (d). The geometric
datum depends on the parameters only through $s$ and does not retain $c$,
$G_N$ and $m_*$ separately. That $(M,g,N)$ is a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold
of signature $(-,+,+,+)$ is not asserted here; it is proved in the companion metric-properties lemma of this page (its
justification record in the frontmatter), which also records the equivalent
coordinate-free description
$g=-f\,d(x^0)\otimes d(x^0)+f^{-1}\,dr\otimes dr+r^2\,\iota^*\gamma_{S^2}$.

**(d) Time orientation and the Schwarzschild chart.** The field
$N:=\partial_0$ is the smooth product vector field on $M$
([[def-derivation-at-a-point-and-tangent-space]]); the chart components of $g$
are independent of $x^0$, so $N$ is the restriction of a global vector field,
and $g(N,N)=-f(r)<0$ at every point. The datum carries the time orientation
$N$. Spherical-polar product charts are **Schwarzschild charts** of the datum;
at the poles the same metric is represented in the smooth sphere charts of
the product atlas. We write $t$ for the coordinate $x^0/c$ when the datum is
read in the framework's unit conventions.

**(e) Scope.** The domain of the datum is the exterior region $r>s$; the
definition asserts nothing about $r=s$, about $r\le 0$, about any matter, or
about any equation satisfied by $g$. The horizon $r=s$ is not part of the
datum, and a continuation of the metric to $r=s$ requires the separate constructions recorded on this page, the
regularity lemma for the advanced chart and the Kruskal model-properties
lemma. Whether the datum is a solution of the
framework's field law is proved, not defined, in the Ricci-and-Einstein-tensor lemma of this
page.

Let $c>0$, $G_N>0$, $m_*>0$ and let $(M,g,N)$ be the Schwarzschild exterior
datum of mass parameter $m_*$ with Schwarzschild radius
$s=2G_Nm_*/c^2$ ([[def-gr-schwarzschild-exterior-model]]). Then:

**(a) Global metric and local components.** $M$ is a smooth four-manifold
without boundary and $g$ is the smooth symmetric covariant $2$-tensor field
globally defined by

$$g=-f\,d(x^0)\otimes d(x^0)+f^{-1}\,dr\otimes dr+r^2\,\iota^*\gamma_{S^2}.$$

In every spherical-polar product chart $(x^0,r,\vartheta,\varphi)$ its
components are

$$g_{00}=-f(r),\qquad g_{11}=\frac{1}{f(r)},\qquad g_{22}=r^2,\qquad g_{33}=r^2\sin^2\vartheta,\qquad g_{ab}=0\ (a\ne b),$$

where $f(r)=1-s/r$, $\iota:M\to S^2$ is the third projection and
$\gamma_{S^2}$ is the round metric of the unit sphere. The component display
is local to the spherical-polar charts; the global tensor formula includes
the poles.

**(b) Lorentzian signature.** At every $p\in M$ the form $g_p$ is
nondegenerate with inertia $(3,1,0)$; consequently $(M,g,N)$ is a smooth
Lorentzian four-manifold of signature $(-,+,+,+)$.

**(c) Time orientation.** The global product field $N=\partial_0$ is smooth
and nowhere vanishing, and $g_p(N_p,N_p)=-f(r(p))<0$ at every $p$; it is
therefore a time orientation of $(M,g)$. The globally defined base fields
$\partial_0,\partial_r$ are orthogonal with squared norms $-f$ and $f^{-1}$.
In a spherical-polar chart the angular coordinate fields are orthogonal with
positive squared norms $r^2$ and $r^2\sin^2\vartheta$; at a pole use any
angular chart and the positive-definite round metric instead.

**(d) Domain of the coordinates.** Product charts form an atlas covering
$M$. Spherical-polar charts are defined on the regular angular locus
$0<\vartheta<\pi$ and omit the poles; pole charts are ordinary smooth charts
of $S^2$. The functions $f$ and $f^{-1}$ are smooth on $r>s$, and the
spherical-polar component functions are smooth on their chart domains.

**(e) Conventions.** The global tensor identity holds on all of $M$; the
displayed component identities are in spherical-polar product charts. In pole
charts the sphere block is $r^2$ times the round-metric component matrix.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be the Schwarzschild exterior datum with Schwarzschild radius
$s>0$ and $f(r)=1-s/r$
([[def-gr-schwarzschild-exterior-model]]). Let
$M_{\mathrm{ext}}:=\mathbb R\times(0,\infty)\times S^2$ carry the product
smooth structure and let $\iota_{\mathrm{ext}}:M_{\mathrm{ext}}\to S^2$ be the
third projection. Its product atlas includes ordinary sphere charts at the
poles ([[prop-products-of-smooth-manifolds-have-a-canonical-product-smooth-structure]]).
Define the **tortoise function**

$$r_*(r):=r+s\log\left|\frac{r}{s}-1\right|,\qquad r>0,\ r\ne s,$$

on each of the two intervals $(0,s)$ and $(s,\infty)$, and define the
**advanced-chart metric** globally on $M_{\mathrm{ext}}$ by

$$g_{\mathrm{ext}}=-f(r)\,dv\otimes dv+dv\otimes dr+dr\otimes dv+r^2\,\iota_{\mathrm{ext}}^*\gamma_{S^2}.$$

In spherical-polar product charts its components are

$$g_{\mathrm{ext}}=-f(r)\,dv^2+2\,dv\,dr+r^2\,d\Omega^2,$$

namely $g_{vv}=-f$, $g_{vr}=g_{rv}=1$,
$g_{\vartheta\vartheta}=r^2$, $g_{\varphi\varphi}=r^2\sin^2\vartheta$ and all
other components zero. In another sphere chart the angular block is
$r^2(\gamma_{ij})$. Then:

**(a) Smooth Lorentzian metric.** $g_{\mathrm{ext}}$ is a smooth symmetric
covariant $2$-tensor field on $M_{\mathrm{ext}}$, and at every point it is
nondegenerate with inertia $(3,1,0)$; hence $(M_{\mathrm{ext}},g_{\mathrm{ext}})$
is a smooth Lorentzian four-manifold of signature $(-,+,+,+)$ on all of
$r>0$, including $r=s$.

**(b) Time orientation.** The smooth vector field

$$N_{\mathrm{ext}}:=A(r)\,\partial_v-\partial_r,\qquad A(r):=\frac{f(r)+\sqrt{f(r)^2+4}}{2}>0,$$

satisfies $g_{\mathrm{ext}}(N_{\mathrm{ext}},N_{\mathrm{ext}})<0$ everywhere
and $g_{\mathrm{ext}}(N_{\mathrm{ext}},\partial_v)<0$ everywhere; hence
$N_{\mathrm{ext}}$ is a time orientation of $g_{\mathrm{ext}}$, and on the
region $r>s$ it determines the same future cone as the datum's time
orientation $\partial_v=\partial_0$.

**(c) Isometric embedding of the exterior.** The map
$\Phi:M\to M_{\mathrm{ext}}$, $(x^0,r,\omega)\mapsto(x^0+r_*(r),r,\omega)$
restricts to a diffeomorphism of $M$ onto the open subset $\{r>s\}$ of
$M_{\mathrm{ext}}$, and $\Phi^*g_{\mathrm{ext}}=g$; the exterior datum is
therefore isometric to the region $r>s$ of the extension.

**(d) Vacuum and Kretschmann scalar of the extension.** The
metric-selected connection of $g_{\mathrm{ext}}$ exists and is unique, its
Ricci tensor, scalar curvature and Einstein tensor vanish identically on
$M_{\mathrm{ext}}$, and its Kretschmann scalar equals

$$R_{abcd}R^{abcd}=\frac{12s^2}{r^6}$$

on all of $M_{\mathrm{ext}}$. In particular the scalar is smooth and finite on
the horizon $r=s$, where it takes the value $12/s^4$.

**(e) The horizon is a null hypersurface.** The level set $\{r=s\}$ is a
smooth null hypersurface of $(M_{\mathrm{ext}},g_{\mathrm{ext}})$ whose null
generator direction is $\partial_v$; every smooth product-chart frame remains
a basis across $r=s$. In spherical-polar charts
$\det(g_{\mathrm{ext}})=-r^4\sin^2\vartheta$; in an arbitrary sphere chart
the determinant is $-r^4\det(\gamma_{ij})$, which is nonzero.

**(f) Scope.** The extension constructed here is a smooth Lorentzian
manifold containing the exterior isometrically and regular across $r=s$; it
is not claimed to be maximal, and no uniqueness or global structure theorem
is asserted. The region $r\le0$ and the surfaces relevant to the Kruskal
model of this page are outside this statement.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. At a point $p$ of a time-oriented Lorentzian
four-manifold, let $n$ be a future-directed unit timelike vector, let
$X\in T_pM$ be future causal, and let $\psi$ be a smooth real scalar. Put
$\ell:=\sharp_g(d\psi)$, $a:=d\psi(n)$,
$b:=h_n(\ell)\in n^\perp$, and $|b|^2:=g(b,b)$, where $h_n$ is the spatial
projection relative to $n$. Then

$$Q(n,n)=\frac12\bigl(a^2+|b|^2\bigr),\qquad Q(n,X)\geq0.$$

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold
([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]), let $M$ carry an orientation in the
sense of [[def-oriented-smooth-manifold-and-oriented-chart]] (so that its
charts that are oriented in that orientation have orientation-preserving
transition maps), and let $\nabla$ be its metric-selected connection. This item
fixes the metric volume form, the flux of a current through oriented $3$-faces
and finite-chain charges. The orientation of $M$ is an independent datum: it is
not determined by the metric and not by the time orientation.

**(a) Metric volume density and volume form.** Let $(U,x)$ be an oriented
chart, with metric components $g_{ab}=g(\partial_a,\partial_b)$
([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]] clause (a)). Define the **metric volume
density**

$$w:=\sqrt{|\det(g_{ab})|}>0\qquad\text{on }U,$$

a strictly positive smooth function because $g_{ab}$ is smooth and
$g_p$ is nondegenerate. In the chart define the local $4$-form

$$\mathrm{vol}_{g,U}:=w\,dx^0\wedge dx^1\wedge dx^2\wedge dx^3,$$

with the exterior product of [[def-wedge-product-of-differential-forms]] and the
coordinate covector fields of
[[prop-local-coordinate-expression-for-a-differential-form]]. That these local
forms agree on chart overlaps and therefore define one smooth nowhere-vanishing
$4$-form $\mathrm{vol}_g$ on $M$ — the **metric volume form** — is proved in
[[lem-gr-metric-volume-form-patching-and-face-normal]] clause (a), together
with the reading statement of clause (b) there: in every oriented chart
$\mathrm{vol}_g=w\,dx^0\wedge\cdots\wedge dx^3$, and on every positively
oriented $g_p$-orthonormal basis $(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ of $T_pM$ one has
$\mathrm{vol}_{g,p}(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)=1$.

**(b) Current flux through oriented $3$-faces and chains.** Let $J$ be a
smooth vector field on $M$
([[def-smooth-vector-field-as-a-tangent-bundle-section]]). The **current
$3$-form** of $J$ is the contraction

$$\iota_J\mathrm{vol}_g,$$

the interior product of the $4$-form $\mathrm{vol}_g$ with $J$
([[def-interior-product-of-a-form-by-a-vector-field]]).

By a **smooth singular $k$-simplex** of $M$ — the convention of the library
definition `def-smooth-singular-simplex` (differential-geometry track),
restated here so this page is self-contained — we mean a map
$\sigma:\Delta^k\to M$ whose domain is the standard $k$-simplex
$$\Delta^k=\Bigl\{t\in\mathbb R^{k+1}:t_i\ge0,\ \textstyle\sum_it_i=1\Bigr\},$$
for which there exist an open set $O\subseteq A^k=\{t\in\mathbb R^{k+1}:\sum_it_i=1\}$
containing $\Delta^k$ and a smooth map $\bar\sigma:O\to M$ with
$\bar\sigma|_{\Delta^k}=\sigma$; the extension is not part of the simplex
data, and degenerate parametrizations are allowed. With the integration of
forms over such simplices
([[def-integral-of-a-form-over-a-smooth-singular-simplex]]), a **$3$-face** is
a smooth singular $3$-simplex $\sigma$, and the **flux of $J$ through
$\sigma$** is the real number

$$\Phi_J(\sigma):=\int_\sigma\iota_J\mathrm{vol}_g.$$

A **finite smooth singular $k$-chain** — the convention of the library
definition `def-smooth-singular-chain-and-cochain-complexes`, restated here —
is a finite formal real linear combination $\Sigma=\sum_i c_i\sigma_i$ of
smooth singular $k$-simplices. For such a $3$-chain the **flux of $J$ through
$\Sigma$** is defined additively,

$$\Phi_J(\Sigma):=\sum_i c_i\,\Phi_J(\sigma_i),$$

a definition independent of the written expression for $\Sigma$, because a
finite formal sum is evaluated by adding the finitely many coefficients and
inserting a zero coefficient changes nothing. $\Phi_J(\Sigma)$ is the **charge**
of the current $J$ assigned to $\Sigma$ when the model reads $J$ as a conserved
current; that reading belongs to the physical postulates and is not part of
this definition.

**(c) Non-null faces and their unit normals.** A $3$-dimensional linear subspace
$H\subseteq T_pM$ is **nondegenerate** for $g_p$ when the restriction of $g_p$
to $H$ is nondegenerate, equivalently when $H\cap H^\perp=\{0\}$ in the
orthogonality of [[def-lorentz-orthogonality-and-orthogonal-complement]]. A
smooth singular $3$-simplex $\sigma$ is **non-null at** a parameter point $t$
when the span of the three velocity vectors
$\sigma_*\partial_1|_t,\sigma_*\partial_2|_t,\sigma_*\partial_3|_t$ has
dimension $3$ and is nondegenerate at $\sigma(t)$, and **non-null** when this holds at every
parameter point. For a non-null face the **unit normal** $\nu$ at that point is
the unique vector of $T_{\sigma(t)}M$ with $\nu\in H^\perp$,
$g(\nu,\nu)\in\{-1,+1\}$ and $(\nu,\sigma_*\partial_1,\sigma_*\partial_2,
\sigma_*\partial_3)$ a positively oriented basis of $T_{\sigma(t)}M$; its
existence, uniqueness and its sign $\varepsilon:=g(\nu,\nu)$ are proved in
[[lem-gr-metric-volume-form-patching-and-face-normal]] clause (c), together
with the density identity of clause (c) used to read $\iota_J\mathrm{vol}_g$ on
such a face. Rank-deficient faces and rank-three faces with degenerate induced
metric are not assigned a unit normal; their flux is defined
by the $3$-form $\iota_J\mathrm{vol}_g$ itself, as in clause (b).

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold with an
orientation, metric-selected connection $\nabla$, metric volume form
$\mathrm{vol}_g$ and current flux $\Phi_J$ as in
[[def-gr-metric-volume-form-and-current-flux]], and let $J$ be a smooth vector
field on $M$ ([[def-smooth-vector-field-as-a-tangent-bundle-section]]). Write
$\nabla_aJ^a$ for the divergence of $J$.

**(a) Exterior derivative of the current form.** As smooth $4$-forms on $M$,

$$d\bigl(\iota_J\mathrm{vol}_g\bigr)=\bigl(\nabla_aJ^a\bigr)\mathrm{vol}_g .$$

**(b) Flux balance (Stokes).** For every finite smooth singular $4$-chain $C$
of $M$ — a finite formal real sum of smooth singular $4$-simplices, the
library convention `def-smooth-singular-chain-and-cochain-complexes` restated
in [[def-gr-metric-volume-form-and-current-flux]] clause (b) — and the flux
$\Phi_J$ of the induced boundary $3$-chain
([[def-integral-of-a-form-over-a-smooth-singular-simplex]],
[[thm-stokes-theorem-for-smooth-singular-chains]]),

$$\Phi_J(\partial C)=\int_C\bigl(\nabla_aJ^a\bigr)\mathrm{vol}_g .$$

Consequently, if $\partial C=\Sigma_2-\Sigma_1+B$ for smooth singular $3$-chains
$\Sigma_1,\Sigma_2,B$, then

$$\Phi_J(\Sigma_2)-\Phi_J(\Sigma_1)=-\Phi_J(B)+\int_C\bigl(\nabla_aJ^a\bigr)\mathrm{vol}_g .$$

In particular, if $\nabla_aJ^a=0$ on $C$ then
$\Phi_J(\Sigma_2)-\Phi_J(\Sigma_1)=-\Phi_J(B)$, and if moreover
$\Phi_J(B)=0$ then $\Phi_J(\Sigma_2)=\Phi_J(\Sigma_1)$: equal charges need a
vanishing side flux, not merely a divergence-free current.

**(c) Non-null face formula.** Let $\sigma$ be a smooth singular $3$-simplex —
a map $\sigma:\Delta^3\to M$ admitting a smooth extension to a neighbourhood
of the standard $3$-simplex inside its affine plane, the convention restated
in [[def-gr-metric-volume-form-and-current-flux]] clause (b) — that is
non-null at a parameter point $t$
([[def-gr-metric-volume-form-and-current-flux]] clause (c)), with
$v_i:=\sigma_*\partial_i|_t$ spanning the hyperplane $H$ and with the unit
normal $\nu^{*}$ adapted to the ordered basis $(v_1,v_2,v_3)$ as in
[[lem-gr-metric-volume-form-patching-and-face-normal]] clause (c); write
$\varepsilon:=g_{\sigma(t)}(\nu^{*},\nu^{*})\in\{-1,1\}$. Then

$$\sigma^{*}\bigl(\iota_J\mathrm{vol}_g\bigr)(\partial_1,\partial_2,\partial_3)\big|_{t} =\varepsilon\,g_{\sigma(t)}\bigl(J,\nu^{*}\bigr)\sqrt{\bigl|\det\bigl(g_{\sigma(t)}(v_i,v_j)\bigr)\bigr|} .$$

Equivalently, the tangent vector $J$ is decomposed as
$J=\varepsilon g(J,\nu^{*})\nu^{*}+w'$ with $w'\in H$, and only the normal
component contributes to the flux through the face.
$$\sigma^{*}\bigl(\iota_J\mathrm{vol}_g\bigr)(\partial_1,\partial_2,\partial_3)\big|_{t} =\varepsilon\,g_{\sigma(t)}\bigl(J,\nu^{*}\bigr)\sqrt{\bigl|\det\bigl(g_{\sigma(t)}(v_i,v_j)\bigr)\bigr|} .$$

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

derivations.claim: In the advanced coordinates all coefficients of $g_{\mathrm{ext}}$ are independent of $v$, so the coordinate formula for $\mathcal L_{\partial_v}g_{\mathrm{ext}}$ gives $\mathcal L_Tg_{\mathrm{ext}}=0$ and $T$ is Killing by [F3]. The multiplier identity [F2] therefore gives $\nabla^aJ_a^T=0$ on $C$. Since $j_T^a=-g^{ab}J_b^T$, its divergence also vanishes.

The Statement orients each spacelike face so its adapted unit normal is the future unit normal $n_j$. By [F8] its current flux density is $-g(j_T,n_j)\,d\mu_{\Sigma_j}$. The definition $j_T^a=-g^{ab}Q_{bc}T^c$ gives $g(j_T,n_j)=-Q_{ab}n_j^aT^b$, so integration yields $\Phi_{j_T}(\Sigma_j)=\int_{\Sigma_j}Q_{ab}n_j^aT^b\,d\mu_{\Sigma_j}=E_j$.

The isometric exterior has $T$ future timelike for $r>s$, and [F5] makes $T$ future null on $\mathcal H^+$. Thus $T$ is future causal throughout the stated closure. Applying [F6] to each spacelike face gives $E_1,E_2\geq0$.

On $\mathcal H^+$, the inverse of the $(v,r)$ metric block has $g^{rv}=1$ and $g^{rr}=f=0$. Hence $j_T^r=-g^{rb}Q_{bv}=-Q_{vv}=-(T\psi)^2$, since $g_{vv}=0$ there. With
$\mathrm{vol}_{g_{\mathrm{ext}}}=r^2\,dv\wedge dr\wedge\omega_{S^2}$ and the outward boundary orientation at the inner face $r=s$, the pullback of $\iota_{j_T}\mathrm{vol}_{g_{\mathrm{ext}}}$ is $(T\psi)^2s^2\,dv\wedge\omega_{S^2}$. Therefore this face flux is exactly $F_H\geq0$.

By [F7] and step 1.1, $\Phi_{j_T}(\partial C)=0$. The stated boundary decomposition and additivity of flux give $\Phi_{j_T}(\Sigma_2)-\Phi_{j_T}(\Sigma_1)+F_H+F_{\mathrm{out}}=0$. Using step 1.2 to identify the two face fluxes with $E_2$ and $E_1$ gives the asserted balance.

On the static exterior slices $g(T,T)=-f$ and $n=f^{-1/2}T$, so $T=\sqrt f\,n$ and bilinearity gives $Q(n,T)=\sqrt f\,Q(n,n)$. By [F6] with $X=n$, $Q(n,n)\geq0$, while the coefficient $\sqrt f$ tends to zero as $r\downarrow s$. In the regular extension $g(T,T)=-f$ vanishes at $r=s$ by [F5], so $T$ becomes null there and the static Killing slice density loses its transverse coercivity.

Let $c>0$ be a fixed conversion constant in metres per second. Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be a nonempty open interval of physical time in seconds, and let $\mathbb T^3_{2\pi}=\mathbb R^3/(2\pi\mathbb Z)^3$ have dimensionless angular coordinates $x^1,x^2,x^3$. Its quotient charts are local lifts to $\mathbb R^3$; chart changes are translations by elements of $(2\pi\mathbb Z)^3$. Give $M=I\times\mathbb T^3_{2\pi}$ the product smooth structure, so $M$ is a smooth four-manifold without boundary. Here a **$C^2$ time-oriented Lorentzian metric datum** means a symmetric covariant $2$-tensor field $g$ with $C^2$ components in smooth charts, whose value at each point has inertia $(3,1,0)$, together with a smooth vector field $N$ satisfying $g(N,N)<0$ everywhere. This is the explicit $C^2$ variant of the pointwise signature and time-orientation conditions in [[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]; that supplier's metric regularity itself is smooth. Choose positive $C^2$ functions $a_i:I\to(0,\infty)$, $i=1,2,3$, with values in metres, and set

$$g=-c^2\,dt^2+\sum_{i=1}^3a_i(t)^2\,(dx^i)^2,\qquad N:=\partial_t.$$

In every lifted product chart, $g$ has matrix $\operatorname{diag}(-c^2,a_1^2,a_2^2,a_3^2)$, so it is symmetric, $C^2$, and has inertia $(3,1,0)$; $N$ is smooth and $g(N,N)=-c^2<0$. Thus $(M,g,N)$ is a $C^2$ time-oriented Lorentzian metric datum in the stated sense. This diagonal, spatially homogeneous metric datum is called a diagonal Bianchi I datum here; homogeneity means its coefficients are independent of the torus coordinates, and no isotropy is required. Define the directional expansion rates, their mean, the spatial volume scale and the squared directional shear by

$$H_i:=\frac{\dot a_i}{a_i},\qquad H:=\frac13\sum_{i=1}^3H_i,\qquad V:=a_1a_2a_3,\qquad \sigma^2:=\frac12\sum_{i=1}^3(H_i-H)^2.$$

Here $\dot a_i=d a_i/dt$; $H_i$ and $H$ have units $\mathrm{s}^{-1}$, $V$ has units $\mathrm{m}^3$, and $\sigma^2$ has units $\mathrm{s}^{-2}$. The symbol $\sigma^2$ denotes a nonnegative scalar defined by this formula, not a tensor norm on a spacetime frame. This is a geometric ansatz and makes no field-equation or observational claim. The product and quotient constructions carry the inherited axiom of countable choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ and use no stronger choice principle.

For comparison with smooth Lorentzian geometry, use the curvature convention $R(X,Y)Z=\nabla_X\nabla_YZ-\nabla_Y\nabla_XZ-\nabla_{[X,Y]}Z$ and the component order $R(\partial_c,\partial_d)\partial_b=R^a{}_{bcd}\partial_a$. The local connection and Ricci components for this $C^2$ metric are defined separately.

derivations.claim: Work in the inherited $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ context [A1]; the calculation itself uses only finite sums and differentiation. Put $P=\sum_i p_i$ and $Q=\sum_i p_i^2$. The power laws give $H_i=p_i/t$, $\dot H_i=-p_i/t^2$, and $H_\Sigma=P/t$, so [F2] yields $\operatorname{Ric}_{00}=(P-Q)/t^2$ and $\operatorname{Ric}_{ii}=a_i^2p_i(P-1)/(c^2t^2)$.

Suppose not all $p_i$ vanish and $\operatorname{Ric}=0$. Choose an index $k$ with $p_k\ne0$. Since $a_k,c,t$ are positive, the equation $\operatorname{Ric}_{kk}=0$ from step 1.1 implies $P=1$. The equation $\operatorname{Ric}_{00}=0$ then implies $Q=P=1$.
Conversely, if $P=Q=1$, step 1.1 makes every diagonal Ricci component zero, and [F2] makes every off-diagonal component zero; hence $\operatorname{Ric}=0$.

If $p_1=p_2=p_3=0$, then every $H_i$ and $\dot H_i$ is zero. Both curvature-component families in [F2] therefore vanish, and every other component is zero by that lemma, so the full curvature tensor vanishes.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ for the canonical tangent-bundle and tetrad
conventions of [[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]] and
[[def-gr-local-frame-and-tetrad-fields]]. Let $(M,g,N)$ be a smooth,
time-oriented Lorentzian four-manifold of signature $(-,+,+,+)$, let
$U\subseteq M$ be nonempty and open, and let
$E=(E_0,E_1,E_2,E_3)$ be a smooth future-directed tetrad on $U$. Thus the
$E_J$ are a pointwise basis of $TM|_U$, $g(E_I,E_J)=\eta_{IJ}$ for
$\eta=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$, and $E_0$ is future-directed. Write
$e=(e^0,e^1,e^2,e^3)^{\mathsf T}$ for the dual coframe, so
$e^I(E_J)=\delta^I{}_J$.

A **tetrad connection** is a smooth affine connection $\nabla$ on $TM|_U$;
its connection matrix $\omega=(\omega^I{}_J)$ in $E$ is defined by
$\nabla_XE_J=\sum_I\omega^I{}_J(X)E_I$. It is a **Lorentz connection** when
it is metric-compatible, equivalently when the matrix-valued one-form is
$\eta$-skew: $\omega_{IJ}:=\eta_{IK}\omega^K{}_J$ satisfies
$\omega_{IJ}=-\omega_{JI}$. A smooth local Lorentz change is a smooth map
$\Lambda:U\to SO^+(1,3)$. With the convention
$e'=\Lambda e$ (equivalently $E'=E\Lambda^{-1}$), the connection matrix
transforms as

$$e'=\Lambda e,\qquad
\omega'=\Lambda\omega\Lambda^{-1}-d\Lambda\,\Lambda^{-1}.$$

Here $d$ is the componentwise exterior derivative, and products of
matrix-valued forms use matrix multiplication and the wedge product of their
scalar form entries. Define the torsion and curvature forms by

$$T^I:=de^I+\sum_J\omega^I{}_J\wedge e^J,\qquad
F^I{}_J:=d\omega^I{}_J+\sum_K\omega^I{}_K\wedge\omega^K{}_J.$$

Thus $T$ is an $\mathbb R^4$-valued two-form and $F$ is an
$\operatorname{End}(\mathbb R^4)$-valued two-form. With this convention,
$F$ is the local curvature two-form of $\nabla$. A local $\Lambda$ is a
change of frame in a trivialization; it represents a gauge transformation in
the sense of [[def-gauge-group-of-a-smooth-principal-bundle]] only when it
extends to a principal-bundle automorphism over the identity. No such extension,
global tetrad, or spin structure is part of this definition.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $(M,g,N)$ be a smooth time-oriented
Lorentzian four-manifold, let $U\subseteq M$ be open, and let
$e=(e^0,e^1,e^2,e^3)^{\mathsf T}$ be the dual coframe of a smooth
future-directed tetrad on $U$. Let $\omega^I{}_J$ be a smooth matrix-valued
one-form with $\omega_{IJ}:=\eta_{IK}\omega^K{}_J=-\omega_{JI}$, and let
$\nabla$ be its induced affine connection as in
[[def-gr-fx-tetrad-spin-connection]]. Then

$$de^I+\omega^I{}_J\wedge e^J=0\quad\text{for every }I$$

if and only if $\nabla$ is torsion-free. There is exactly one such
$\eta$-skew connection: the Levi-Civita connection of $g$. Under a smooth
change $e'=\Lambda e$, $\Lambda:U\to SO^+(1,3)$, the torsion and curvature
forms obey

$$T'=\Lambda T,\qquad F'=\Lambda F\Lambda^{-1}.$$

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ for the cited smooth Lie-group convention. For a complex matrix $A$, write $A^\dagger:=\overline A^{\mathsf T}$. Let
$\eta=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$ and define
$SL(2,\mathbb C)=\{A\in M_2(\mathbb C):\det A=1\}$. Let
$\sigma_1=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$,
$\sigma_2=\begin{pmatrix}0&-i\\i&0\end{pmatrix}$,
$\sigma_3=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&-1\end{pmatrix}$ and
$X(x)=x^0I+x^1\sigma_1+x^2\sigma_2+x^3\sigma_3$ for
$x\in\mathbb R^4$. The real-linear map $x\mapsto X(x)$ identifies
$\mathbb R^4$ with the Hermitian $2\times2$ matrices and
$-\det X(x)=-(x^0)^2+(x^1)^2+(x^2)^2+(x^3)^2$. For $A\in SL(2,\mathbb C)$,
let $\rho(A)$ be the real linear transformation defined by

$$X(\rho(A)x)=AX(x)A^\dagger.$$

Then $\rho:SL(2,\mathbb C)\to SO^+(1,3)$ is a smooth surjective Lie-group
homomorphism, its kernel is exactly $\{I,-I\}$, and its differential at the
identity is an isomorphism. In particular, $\rho$ is a two-sheeted covering
homomorphism. This is a local group statement; it does not assert that a
spacetime admits a global spin lift.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $(M,g,N,o)$ be an oriented and
time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold, and let
$P^+_g(M)$ be its smooth oriented time-oriented orthonormal frame bundle from
[[prop-gr-fx-oriented-time-oriented-orthonormal-frame-bundle]]. Set
$\mathrm{Spin}^+(1,3):=SL(2,\mathbb C)$ and let
$\rho:SL(2,\mathbb C)\to SO^+(1,3)$ be the Hermitian-matrix covering
homomorphism of [[prop-gr-fx-spin-double-cover]]. A **Lorentzian spin
structure** is a smooth right principal $SL(2,\mathbb C)$-bundle
$\widetilde P\to M$ together with a smooth map $\lambda:\widetilde P\to
P^+_g(M)$ over the identity of $M$ such that

$$\lambda(ua)=\lambda(u)\rho(a)\qquad (u\in\widetilde P,\ a\in SL(2,\mathbb C)),$$

and the restriction of $\lambda$ to each fiber is a surjective two-sheeted
covering map. The map is over the identity, meaning $\pi^+\circ\lambda=\widetilde\pi$; the square below displays this base condition and is not used as a proof.

```tikzcd
\begin{tikzcd}
\widetilde P \arrow[r,"\lambda"] \arrow[d,"\widetilde\pi"'] & P^+_g(M) \arrow[d,"\pi^+"] \\
M \arrow[r,"\mathrm{id}_M"'] & M
\end{tikzcd}
```

A smooth finite-dimensional complex representation here consists of a
finite-dimensional complex vector space $V_\sigma$ and a smooth group
homomorphism $\sigma:SL(2,\mathbb C)\to GL(V_\sigma)$, where
$GL(V_\sigma)$ is the group of invertible complex-linear maps on
$V_\sigma$, with the smooth structure inherited as an open subset of the
real vector space of complex-linear endomorphisms of $V_\sigma$. Its
**associated vector bundle** is the quotient
$$\widetilde P\times_\sigma V_\sigma:=(\widetilde P\times V_\sigma)/\sim,$$
where $\sim$ is the equivalence relation generated by
$(ua,v)\sim(u,\sigma(a)v)$ for $u\in\widetilde P$,
$a\in SL(2,\mathbb C)$ and $v\in V_\sigma$; equivalently
$(u,v)\sim(ua,\sigma(a)^{-1}v)$, in the convention of
[[def-principal-g-bundle-and-associated-fiber-bundle]]. Write $[u,v]$ for
the class of $(u,v)$. Since every $\sigma(a)$ is complex-linear, the
fiberwise vector-space operations
$[u,v]+[u,w]=[u,v+w]$ and $z[u,v]=[u,zv]$ for $z\in\mathbb C$ are
independent of the representative. The associated-bundle proposition
[[prop-associated-bundle-is-locally-trivial-and-functorial-under-pullback]]
gives local triviality; on an overlap with local sections satisfying
$s_j(x)=s_i(x)a_{ij}(x)$, the smooth principal charts give transition maps
$(x,v)\mapsto(x,\sigma(a_{ij}(x))v)$. These are smooth because $\sigma$ is
smooth and define the smooth vector-bundle structure. When $V_\sigma$ is
chosen for spinor components, this is called its associated spinor bundle.
With the defining representation on $\mathbb C^2$ chosen for spinor
components, it is a rank-two complex spinor bundle.

To define a **lift of a Lorentz connection**, first supply a principal
connection $H^+\subset TP^+_g(M)$ on the frame bundle: it is a smooth vector
subbundle complementary to $VP^+:=\ker(d\pi^+)$ and invariant under the
right $SO^+(1,3)$ action, as in
[[def-principal-connection-and-vertical-curvature]]. This $H^+$ is additional
global data; the local affine connection and local matrix $\omega$ in
[[def-gr-fx-tetrad-spin-connection]] do not determine it unless they are
specified as restrictions of a chosen global metric-compatible affine
connection whose induced principal connection is the supplied $H^+$. A lift
is a supplied principal connection $\widetilde H\subset T\widetilde P$,
likewise a smooth
right-invariant horizontal complement to
$V\widetilde P:=\ker(d\widetilde\pi)$, such that
$d\lambda_u(\widetilde H_u)=H^+_{\lambda(u)}$ at each
$u\in\widetilde P$. It induces a covariant derivative on the associated
vector bundle by horizontal differentiation: a section is represented by a
smooth equivariant map $f:\widetilde P\to V_\sigma$ with
$f(ua)=\sigma(a)^{-1}f(u)$, and its derivative along a smooth base vector
field $X$ at $x$ is the class $[u,df_u(\widetilde X^H_u)]$ for
$u\in\widetilde P_x$, where $\widetilde X^H$ is the horizontal lift. The local
Clifford-compatibility calculation is a separate proposition about supplied
gamma matrices and does not follow from the existence of $\sigma$ alone.
A spin structure, a global spinor field, and a lifted connection are extra data: this definition asserts
neither existence nor uniqueness of a spin lift, global tetrad, or connection
lift. The matrix group and covering homomorphism are Lorentzian; the Euclidean
$\mathrm{Spin}(4)$ cover is not substituted.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $(M,g,N)$ be a smooth time-oriented
Lorentzian four-manifold, let $U\subseteq M$ be a nonempty open set, and let
$E=(E_0,E_1,E_2,E_3)$ be a smooth future-directed tetrad on $U$. Let
$\nabla$ be a smooth affine Lorentz connection on $TM|_U$ with smooth
connection matrix $\omega^I{}_J$ in $E$, meaning
$\nabla_XE_J=\sum_I\omega^I{}_J(X)E_I$ as in
[[def-gr-fx-tetrad-spin-connection]]. Write
$\omega_{IJ}:=\eta_{IK}\omega^K{}_J=-\omega_{JI}$ for
$\eta=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$, so $\eta^{IJ}$ denotes the entries of
$\eta^{-1}=\eta$. Fix an integer $n\ge1$ and constant
matrices $\gamma^I\in M_n(\mathbb C)$ satisfying

$$\gamma^I\gamma^J+\gamma^J\gamma^I=2\eta^{IJ}I_n.$$

Let $V\in\Gamma^\infty(TM|_U)$ be a smooth vector field and let
$\psi\in C^\infty(U,\mathbb C^n)$ be smooth. With $V_I:=\eta_{IJ}V^J$,
define $c(V):=V_I\gamma^I$ and, on $\mathbb C^n$-valued fields and forms,

$$D\psi:=d\psi+\Gamma\psi,\qquad \Gamma:=\frac14\omega_{IJ}\gamma^I\gamma^J,$$

where $d$ acts componentwise. Then

$$D(c(V)\psi)=c(\nabla V)\psi+c(V)D\psi,$$

where $(\nabla V)_I:=dV_I-\omega^J{}_I V_J$ are the covector components
of the induced Lorentz connection and $c(\nabla V):=(\nabla V)_I\gamma^I$.
This is precisely a local matrix identity under the stated hypotheses; it
does not assert that the matrices $\gamma^I$ or the operator $D$ are
compatible with, or induced by, a separately supplied $SL(2,\mathbb C)$
representation or principal-connection lift. Such compatibility is an
additional condition when this identity is used to describe an associated
spinor bundle.

derivations.claim: Let $J$ be the stated generator, so $\Lambda=\exp(\theta J)$. Its spatial block is an ordinary rotation, hence $\Lambda^{\mathsf T}\eta\Lambda=\eta$, $\det\Lambda=1$, and $\Lambda^0{}_0=1$; thus $\Lambda(x)\in SO^+(1,3)$. Since $d\Lambda\,\Lambda^{-1}=Jd\theta$, [F1] with initial $\omega=0$ gives $\omega'=-Jd\theta$. Because $d\theta=dx^1\ne0$ and $J\ne0$, this connection matrix is nonzero. The metric is unchanged because $\Lambda^{\mathsf T}\eta\Lambda=\eta$.

Initially $T=0$ and $F=0$. By [F2], $T'=\Lambda T=0$ and $F'=\Lambda F\Lambda^{-1}=0$. The connection is $\eta$-skew since $J^{\mathsf T}\eta+\eta J=0$; the torsion calculation and [F2] therefore identify it as the Levi-Civita connection in the rotated tetrad.

The matrix $A=\operatorname{diag}(e^{-i\theta/2},e^{i\theta/2})$ has determinant one. Conjugating $\sigma_1,\sigma_2$ by $A$ gives $A\sigma_1A^\dagger=\cos\theta\,\sigma_1+\sin\theta\,\sigma_2$ and $A\sigma_2A^\dagger=-\sin\theta\,\sigma_1+\cos\theta\,\sigma_2$, while $I$ and $\sigma_3$ are fixed. Thus [F3] sends $A(x)$ to $\Lambda(x)$, so $A$ is a local lift of this Lorentz-valued map; this asserts no global spin structure. In any chosen local $\mathbb C^n$ trivialization with constant gamma matrices satisfying the Clifford relation, [F5] gives the local matrix identity for $D=d+\frac14\omega'_{IJ}\gamma^I\gamma^J$, without asserting group-representation compatibility.

Let $M$ be a smooth manifold and $U\subseteq M$ open. A **piecewise-smooth path** in $U$ is a continuous map $\gamma:[0,1]\to U$ for which some finite partition $0=t_0<t_1<\cdots<t_n=1$ makes every restriction $\gamma|_{[t_{j-1},t_j]}$ smooth as a map of manifolds with boundary. Its source and target are $\gamma(0)$ and $\gamma(1)$. The collection of all such paths is a set: it is a subset, defined by separation, of the function set from $[0,1]$ to $U$.

Two paths $\gamma_0,\gamma_1$ with the same source $x$ and target $y$ are **thin-homotopic**, written $\gamma_0\sim_{\mathrm{thin}}\gamma_1$, if there is a continuous map $H:[0,1]^2\to U$ and a finite subdivision of the square into compact curvilinear triangles such that $H$ is smooth up to each triangle's boundary, $H(0,t)=\gamma_0(t)$, $H(1,t)=\gamma_1(t)$, $H(s,0)=x$, $H(s,1)=y$, and $\operatorname{rank}(dH_{(s,t)})\le 1$ on every smooth triangle. A **curvilinear triangle** here is a compact region $D$ equipped with a specified homeomorphism $\psi:\Delta^2\to D$ from the standard closed two-simplex which is a smooth embedding on the interior, extends smoothly to a neighborhood of $\Delta^2$ in its affine span, and maps the three edges of $\Delta^2$ to the three boundary arcs of $D$. Saying $H$ is smooth up to $D$'s boundary means that $H\circ\psi$ extends smoothly from $\Delta^2$ to an open neighborhood of $\Delta^2$ in its affine span, with values in $U$; equivalently, it is a smooth singular $2$-simplex under the neighborhood-extension convention of [[def-smooth-singular-simplex]]. The rank is the dimension of the image of the differential from the two-dimensional tangent space of the triangle to $T_{H(s,t)}M$, computed through the interior chart $\psi$ and extended to boundary points by these smooth extensions. The quotient by this relation is used only after its equivalence and compatibility properties are proved.

A **binary relation** on a set $A$ is a subset $R \subseteq A \times A$
([[def-relation-domain-range-and-field]], [[def-cartesian-product]]); we write
$a \sim b$ for $(a,b) \in R$ and read it "$a$ is related to $b$".

A binary relation $\sim$ on $A$ is an **equivalence relation** when it is reflexive
on $A$, symmetric and transitive ([[def-properties-of-a-relation-on-a-set]]), that
is, when it is

- **reflexive**: $a \sim a$ for every $a \in A$;
- **symmetric**: $a \sim b$ implies $b \sim a$, for all $a, b \in A$;
- **transitive**: $a \sim b$ and $b \sim c$ imply $a \sim c$, for all
  $a, b, c \in A$.

Let $\sim$ be an equivalence relation on $A$. For $a \in A$, the **equivalence
class** of $a$ is the subset

$$[a] \;:=\; \{\, b \in A \;:\; a \sim b \,\} \;\subseteq\; A,$$

and any $b$ with $[b] = C$ is called a **representative** of the class $C$. The
**quotient set** is the set of all classes,

$$A/{\sim} \;:=\; \{\, [a] \;:\; a \in A \,\},$$

a subset of the power set of $A$ ([[def-power-set]]). The map
$\pi : A \to A/{\sim}$ ([[def-function]]) with $\pi(a) = [a]$ is the **quotient
map**; it is surjective by construction ([[def-injection-surjection-bijection]]).

Under the definable-class convention of
[[def-language-of-set-theory]], every class below is a
formula and every function whose domain may be proper-class-sized is a
definable class-function schema. When its domain is a set, it is an ordinary
set-valued function.

A **category** $\mathcal C$ consists of a class
$\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal C)$ of **objects**, a class
$\operatorname{Mor}(\mathcal C)$ of **morphisms**, functions
$\operatorname{dom},\operatorname{cod}:\operatorname{Mor}(\mathcal C)\to
\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal C)$, an **identity morphism**
$1_A:A\to A$ for every object $A$, and a **composite**
$g\circ f:A\to C$ whenever $f:A\to B$ and $g:B\to C$.

These data satisfy, whenever the composites are defined,

$$h\circ(g\circ f)=(h\circ g)\circ f,\qquad 1_B\circ f=f=f\circ1_A.$$

We write $\mathcal C(A,B)$, or $\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal C}(A,B)$, for the
**hom-collection** of morphisms with domain $A$ and codomain $B$. The object
class is allowed to be empty; then the morphism class is empty and all axioms
are vacuous.

**Morphisms carry their domain and codomain.** A category is often presented the
other way round, by saying what the morphisms from $A$ to $B$ are for each pair
of objects. When it is, $\operatorname{Mor}(\mathcal C)$ is the **disjoint
union** of those hom-collections: a morphism is a triple $(A,B,f)$ with $f$ in
the collection assigned to $(A,B)$, and $\operatorname{dom}$ and
$\operatorname{cod}$ are the first two projections, which are then functions in
the required sense. This is not a technicality that can be dropped. In this
library a function is a set of ordered pairs and does not determine a codomain
([[def-function]]), so the empty function is a function $\varnothing\to B$ for
every $B$ at once; reading the morphisms of $\mathbf{Set}$ as bare functions
would give that one set two different codomains and leave $\operatorname{cod}$
undefined. Every concrete category below whose morphisms are described as
structure-preserving maps is to be read with this tagging, and each hom-collection
is then in canonical bijection with the corresponding collection of untagged
maps, so no size or smallness claim is affected.

In a category $\mathcal C$ ([[def-category]]), a morphism $f:A\to B$ is an
**isomorphism** if there is a morphism $g:B\to A$ with
$g\circ f=1_A$ and $f\circ g=1_B$. Such a $g$ is unique and is denoted
$f^{-1}$.

A **groupoid** is a category in which every morphism is an isomorphism. A
category is **connected** when it is nonempty and any two objects can be joined
by a finite zigzag of morphisms, with successive arrows allowed to point in
either direction. In a groupoid this is equivalent to being nonempty and having
an isomorphism between every ordered pair of objects. Nonemptiness cannot be
dropped: the empty groupoid has an isomorphism between every ordered pair of its
objects, vacuously, and is not connected.

derivations.claim: The relation is reflexive because $H(s,t)=\gamma(t)$ has rank at most one and fixed endpoints; subdivide the square along each breakpoint of a finite smooth partition of $\gamma$ and triangulate the resulting strips. It is symmetric by replacing $s$ with $1-s$ and reflecting a witnessing subdivision. For transitivity, first take finite common refinements of the boundary subdivisions of $H_0$ and $H_1$ along their common path $\gamma_1$, then paste $H_0(2s,t)$ on $0\le s\le\tfrac12$ to $H_1(2s-1,t)$ on $\tfrac12\le s\le1$. The common boundary is the same path $\gamma_1$, so this paste is continuous; the scaled finite subdivisions on the two halves give a finite curvilinear-triangle subdivision after triangulating any resulting polygons. It fixes both path endpoints, and its differential has rank at most one on each triangle. Thus the relation is an equivalence relation.

If $\gamma_0\sim_{\mathrm{thin}}\gamma_1$ and $\delta_0\sim_{\mathrm{thin}}\delta_1$ with matching endpoints, paste their homotopies on the first and second halves of the path parameter, scaling their finite subdivisions to those halves and taking a finite common refinement along their shared fixed endpoint. The shared endpoint is fixed throughout each homotopy, so the paste is continuous and piecewise smooth; on each triangle its differential has image contained in that of the corresponding homotopy differential, hence rank at most one. Therefore $\delta_0*\gamma_0\sim_{\mathrm{thin}}\delta_1*\gamma_1$, and composition of classes is well-defined.

Let $\Gamma$ be the path obtained by placing the three given paths, in order, on the three consecutive thirds of $[0,1]$. Each parenthesized concatenation is $\Gamma\circ\phi_j$ for an increasing piecewise-linear homeomorphism $\phi_j:[0,1]\to[0,1]$. Put $u(s,t)=(1-s)\phi_0(t)+s\phi_1(t)$ and $H(s,t)=\Gamma(u(s,t))$. Refine the $t$-partition by all breakpoints of $\phi_0$ and $\phi_1$. On each resulting strip $u$ is smooth and piecewise bilinear. For every breakpoint $b$ of the piecewise-smooth path $\Gamma$, also subdivide along the level set $u^{-1}(b)$; on each strip these finitely many level sets are smooth arcs, with their finitely many endpoints and intersections included in the subdivision. The resulting regions have finitely many smooth boundary arcs and can be triangulated into curvilinear triangles. On each triangle, $u$ remains in one smooth piece of $\Gamma$, so $H$ is smooth there and both differential columns are scalar multiples of the single vector $\Gamma'$. Its rank is at most one. Thus the two parenthesizations are thin-homotopic. For the right identity law use $\rho_0(t)=2t$ on $[0,\tfrac12]$ and $\rho_0(t)=1$ on $[\tfrac12,1]$, with $\rho_1(t)=t$; for the left identity law use $\rho_0(t)=0$ on $[0,\tfrac12]$ and $\rho_0(t)=2t-1$ on $[\tfrac12,1]$, again with $\rho_1(t)=t$. The corresponding homotopies $\gamma((1-s)\rho_0(t)+s\rho_1(t))$ have the required concatenated and unaltered paths as boundaries. Refine each square along the parameter-map breakpoints and the preimages of every breakpoint of $\gamma$; any region on which the argument is constant is already smooth. The same rank argument proves both identity laws.

Put $\lambda(t)=2t$ for $0\le t\le\tfrac12$ and $\lambda(t)=2(1-t)$ for $\tfrac12\le t\le1$. Then $t\mapsto\gamma(\lambda(t))$ traverses $\gamma$ and then its reverse. The map $H(s,t)=\gamma((1-s)\lambda(t))$ joins this path to the constant path at $\gamma(0)$ with both endpoints fixed. Subdivide first at $t=\tfrac12$, then along the preimages of every breakpoint of a finite smooth partition of $\gamma$ under $(s,t)\mapsto(1-s)\lambda(t)$; these are finitely many smooth arcs or constant regions on the two parameter strips. Triangulating the resulting finite curvilinear regions makes $H$ smooth on each triangle. Its differential has rank at most one because both derivatives are scalar multiples of $\dot\gamma$. Applying the same construction to $\bar\gamma$ contracts the reverse-then-forward path at $\gamma(1)$. Hence $[\bar\gamma]$ is a two-sided inverse of $[\gamma]$.

The tagged morphism set has well-defined domain and codomain by construction; step 2.1 makes composition independent of representatives, step 3.1 gives associativity, and step 3.2 gives the inverse axiom. Steps 3.1 and 3.2 also provide the two identity laws stated in [F3]. Thus the data form a category in which every morphism is invertible, which is a groupoid by [F4].

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb C$ be open, let $a\in U$, and let $f:U\to\mathbb C$. The function $f$ is **complex differentiable at $a$** if the limit

$$ \lim_{\substack{h\to0\\ h\ne0,\ a+h\in U}}\frac{f(a+h)-f(a)}{h} $$

exists in the metric of [[def-complex-metric-convergence-and-continuity]]. Its value is the **complex derivative** of $f$ at $a$, denoted $f'(a)$. The increments are nonzero and remain in the domain; because $U$ is open, all sufficiently small increments are allowed.

The function $f$ is **holomorphic on $U$** when it is complex differentiable at every point of $U$. A function holomorphic on all of $\mathbb C$ is **entire**. The word analytic is reserved for the local power-series notion.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Let $H$ be a complex Hilbert space and $T$ a linear operator on $H$ with domain $D(T)$. Write $(z-T)x=zx-Tx$ for $x\in D(T)$. The **resolvent set**
of $T$ is
$$\rho(T):=\{z\in\mathbb C:\ z-T:D(T)\to H\text{ is bijective and }(z-T)^{-1}\in\mathcal B(H)\},$$
where $\mathcal B(H)$ is the space of bounded everywhere defined operators on
$H$ ([[def-bounded-linear-operator]]); the **spectrum** is
$\sigma(T):=\mathbb C\setminus\rho(T)$. For $z\in\rho(T)$ the bounded operator
$$R_T(z):=(z-T)^{-1}\in\mathcal B(H)$$
is the **resolvent** of $T$ at $z$. This is the library convention used
throughout the page, matching the bounded resolvent of
[[def-spectrum-and-resolvent-of-a-bounded-operator]]: the shift is $zI-T$, with coefficient $-1$ on $T$.

**The resolvent determines $T$ back.** If $z\in\rho(T)$ and $R:=R_T(z)$, then
$D(T)=\operatorname{ran}R$ and $TRy=zRy-y$ for $y\in H$; equivalently
$T=zI-R^{-1}$ with $D(T)=\operatorname{ran}R$, and $R(z-T)x=x$ for
$x\in D(T)$, $(z-T)Ry=y$ for $y\in H$.

**Nonempty resolvent set forces closedness, without the closed graph
theorem.** Assume $\rho(T)\ne\varnothing$ and fix $z\in\rho(T)$ with
$R:=R_T(z)$. Choose a bound $C\ge0$ such that $\|Rv\|\le C\|v\|$.
The map $F(v,w)=w-Rv$ is continuous, since
$\|F(v,w)-F(v',w')\|\le\|w-w'\|+C\|v-v'\|$.
Its zero set $\Gamma(R)=F^{-1}(\{0\})$ is closed. Because
$D(T)=\operatorname{ran}R$ and $(z-T)Rv=v$ for every $v\in H$, the graph of $T$ is
$$\Gamma(T)=\{(x,Tx):x\in D(T)\}=\{(Rv,zRv-v):v\in H\}=\Phi(\Gamma(R)),$$
where $\Phi(v,w):=(w,zw-v)$ is a continuous linear bijection of $H\oplus H$ with
continuous inverse $\Psi(u,v)=(zu-v,u)$, since $\Phi(\Psi(u,v))=(u,z u-(zu-v))=(u,v)$
and $\Psi(\Phi(v,w))=\Psi(w,zw-v)=(v,w)$. A homeomorphism carries closed sets
to closed sets, so $\Gamma(T)$ is closed and $T$ is closed.
No closed graph theorem and hence no choice principle is used here.

For the zero operator on a nonzero $H$, $\rho(0)=\mathbb C\setminus\{0\}$: the nonzero shifts have inverse $z^{-1}I$, whereas the zero shift is not bijective. If $H=\{0\}$, every shift is the unique bijection of the zero space, so $\rho(T)=\mathbb C$ and $\sigma(T)=\varnothing$.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Assume Countable Choice. Let $T$ be a densely defined linear operator on $H$.

- $T$ is **symmetric** when $T\subseteq T^*$, that is, $D(T)\subseteq D(T^*)$ and
  $Tx=T^*x$ for all $x\in D(T)$; equivalently
  $\langle Tx,y\rangle=\langle x,Ty\rangle$ for all $x,y\in D(T)$.
- $T$ is **self-adjoint** when $T=T^*$, that is, the domains and the values
  agree.
- $T$ is **essentially self-adjoint** when its closure $\overline T$ is
  self-adjoint; by [[thm-closable-iff-adjoint-domain-is-dense]] this presupposes
  that $T$ is closable.

**Consequences, with proofs.** These are part of the content of the definition.

1. *A symmetric $T$ is closable.* $T\subseteq T^*$ and $T^*$ is closed
   ([[lem-unbounded-adjoint-is-well-defined-and-closed]]), so $T^*$ is a closed
   extension of $T$. In particular the closure $\overline T$ exists and
   $\overline T\subseteq T^*$.
2. *The closure of a symmetric operator is symmetric.* If $T\subseteq T^*$,
   the inclusion reversal of
   [[lem-unbounded-adjoint-is-well-defined-and-closed]] applied to
   $T\subseteq T^*$ gives $(T^*)^*\subseteq T^*$, that is
   $T^{**}\subseteq T^*$. Applying it once more to the inclusion
   $T^{**}\subseteq T^*$ gives $(T^*)^*\subseteq(T^{**})^*$, that is
   $T^{**}\subseteq T^{***}$. Since $\overline T=T^{**}$ and
   $(\overline T)^*=T^{***}$
   ([[thm-closable-iff-adjoint-domain-is-dense]]), this reads
   $\overline T\subseteq(\overline T)^*$: the closure is symmetric. (Each
   application is legitimate because the adjoint is defined once its operator
   is densely defined, and $D(T^{**})$ is dense because
   $T\subseteq T^{**}=\overline T$, so that $D(T^{**})$ contains the dense
   domain $D(T)$.)
3. *A self-adjoint operator has no proper symmetric extension.* If $T=T^*$ and
   $T\subseteq S\subseteq S^*$, then $S^*\subseteq T^*$ by inclusion reversal,
   so $T\subseteq S\subseteq S^*\subseteq T^*=T$ and all inclusions are
   equalities.
4. *A self-adjoint operator is closed*, being equal to the adjoint $T^*$ of the
   densely defined $T$, and *an essentially self-adjoint operator has exactly
   one self-adjoint extension*, namely $\overline T$: a self-adjoint extension
   $S$ of $T$ is closed, hence contains the least closed extension
   $\overline T$, and then $S\subseteq S^*\subseteq(\overline T)^*=\overline T$
   by item 2 and symmetry, so $S=\overline T$.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Assume Countable Choice. Let $T$ be a self-adjoint operator on $H$. Then every nonreal number belongs to
$\rho(T)$: $\mathbb C\setminus\mathbb R\subseteq\rho(T)$. More precisely, for
$z=a+ib$ with $a,b\in\mathbb R$, $b\ne0$, and every $x\in D(T)$,
$$\|(T-z)x\|^2=\|(T-a)x\|^2+b^2\|x\|^2 ,$$
and consequently $\|R_T(z)\|\le 1/|\operatorname{Im}z|$. In particular
$\sigma(T)\subseteq\mathbb R$.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Fix real parameters $m>0$, $\omega>0$, $\hbar>0$, put $\ell:=\sqrt{\hbar/(m\omega)}>0$, and let $g_0,P,(g_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ be the Hermite data of [[thm-nrqm-oscillator-hermite-recurrence]] in $L^2(\mathbb R,dy)$, so that $(g_n)$ is a complete orthonormal family by [[thm-nrqm-oscillator-hermite-completeness]]. Define

$$D:L^2(\mathbb R,dy)\to L^2(\mathbb R,dx),\qquad (Df)(x):=\ell^{-1/2}f(x/\ell),$$

and let $A$ be the self-adjoint diagonal operator of [[lem-nrqm-oscillator-diagonal-adjoint-and-graph-core-lemma]] for the complete orthonormal family $(g_n)$ and the eigenvalues $\lambda_n=2n+1$, with the core $P$ and spectrum $\{2n+1:n\in\mathbb N\}$ ([[thm-nrqm-oscillator-diagonal-spectrum]]).

Then:

(a) $D$ is a linear isometry of $L^2(\mathbb R,dy)$ onto $L^2(\mathbb R,dx)$ with two-sided inverse $(D^{-1}g)(y)=\ell^{1/2}g(\ell y)$; the functions $\psi_n:=Dg_n$, $\psi_n(x)=\ell^{-1/2}g_n(x/\ell)$, form a complete orthonormal family of $L^2(\mathbb R,dx)$;

(b) the operator

$$H_{\mathrm{osc}}:=\frac{\hbar\omega}{2}\,DAD^{-1},\qquad D(H_{\mathrm{osc}}):=\{f\in L^2(\mathbb R,dx):D^{-1}f\in D(A)\},$$

is self-adjoint, satisfies $H_{\mathrm{osc}}\psi_n=\hbar\omega(n+\tfrac12)\psi_n$ for every $n$, and has

$$D(H_{\mathrm{osc}})=\Bigl\{f:\sum_n\hbar^2\omega^2(n+\tfrac12)^2|c_n|^2<\infty\Bigr\},\qquad H_{\mathrm{osc}}f=\sum_n\hbar\omega(n+\tfrac12)c_n\psi_n,$$

where $c_n:=\langle D^{-1}f,g_n\rangle=\langle f,\psi_n\rangle$; its spectrum is $\sigma(H_{\mathrm{osc}})=\{\hbar\omega(n+\tfrac12):n\in\mathbb N\}$, its ground energy is $\hbar\omega/2$ with eigenvector $\psi_0$, and $\langle H_{\mathrm{osc}}f,f\rangle\ge\frac{\hbar\omega}{2}\|f\|^2$ for every $f\in D(H_{\mathrm{osc}})$;

(c) $D(P)=\operatorname{span}\{\psi_n\}$ is a core for $H_{\mathrm{osc}}$, and for every polynomial $p$ the function $f:=D(pg_0)$ is $C^\infty$ on $\mathbb R$ with

$$H_{\mathrm{osc}}f=-\frac{\hbar^2}{2m}f''+\frac{m\omega^2}{2}x^2f$$

pointwise on $\mathbb R$;

(d) for every $f\in D(H_{\mathrm{osc}})$ and every test function $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R)$,

$$\int_{\mathbb R}(H_{\mathrm{osc}}f)(x)\varphi(x)\,dx=\int_{\mathbb R}f(x)\Bigl(-\frac{\hbar^2}{2m}\varphi''(x)+\frac{m\omega^2}{2}x^2\varphi(x)\Bigr)dx,$$

so $H_{\mathrm{osc}}$ is the self-adjoint realization of the differential expression $-\frac{\hbar^2}{2m}\frac{d^2}{dx^2}+\frac{m\omega^2}{2}x^2$ in the weak sense; no identification of $D(H_{\mathrm{osc}})$ with a separately defined maximal differential-operator domain is asserted.

All parameters enter as positive real numbers; no physical identification of $m,\omega,\hbar$ with measured quantities is made.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $L^2=L^2(\mathbb R,dy)$ be the complex Lebesgue space with inner product $\langle\varphi,\psi\rangle=\int_{\mathbb R}\varphi(y)\overline{\psi(y)}\,dy$ linear in the first argument ([[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]], [[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]]); this pairing makes $L^2$ a complex Hilbert space by [[lem-l-two-with-the-integral-pairing-is-a-hilbert-space]]. For complex-valued functions, smoothness and derivatives use the componentwise convention of [[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]]. Write $g_0$ for the function $g_0(y):=\pi^{-1/4}e^{-y^{2}/2}$ and also for its class in $L^2$. Put

$$P:=\{p\,g_0:\ p\in\mathbb C[y]\}\subseteq L^2 ,$$

the set of classes of polynomial multiples of $g_0$. Each class in $P$ has a unique representative of the form $p g_0$: if $p g_0=qg_0$ almost everywhere, the continuous function $(p-q)g_0$ vanishes almost everywhere and therefore everywhere, and $g_0(y)>0$ for every $y$, so $p=q$. Let $Y$ be multiplication by $y$ and $\partial_y$ the derivative, acting on this unique smooth representative. Set $g_{-1}:=0$ for use in the recurrence formulas at $n=0$. Define

$$a:=\frac{Y+\partial_y}{\sqrt2},\qquad a^\dagger:=\frac{Y-\partial_y}{\sqrt2},\qquad g_n:=\frac{(a^\dagger)^ng_0}{\sqrt{n!}}\quad(n\in\mathbb N).$$

Then:

(a) $g_0\in L^2$ with $\|g_0\|=1$; more generally $y^kg_0\in L^2$ for every $k\in\mathbb N$, so $P$ is a linear subspace of $L^2$ all of whose members are represented by $C^\infty$ functions;

(b) $Y,\partial_y,a,a^\dagger$ map $P$ into $P$, and $\partial_y(pg_0)=(p'-yp)g_0$ for every polynomial $p$;

(c) for all $\varphi,\psi\in P$, $\langle a^\dagger\varphi,\psi\rangle=\langle\varphi,a\psi\rangle$ and $\langle a\varphi,\psi\rangle=\langle\varphi,a^\dagger\psi\rangle$;

(d) $a^\dagger a-a a^\dagger=-I$ on $P$, i.e. $[a,a^\dagger]=aa^\dagger-a^\dagger a=I$ on $P$, and $ag_0=0$;

(e) for every $n\in\mathbb N$: $ag_n=\sqrt n\,g_{n-1}$ (with $ag_0=0$), $a^\dagger g_n=\sqrt{n+1}\,g_{n+1}$, $a^\dagger ag_n=ng_n$ and $aa^\dagger g_n=(n+1)g_n$;

(f) the polynomials

$$H_n(y):=(-1)^ne^{y^2}\frac{d^n}{dy^n}e^{-y^2}$$

are polynomials of degree $n$ with leading coefficient $2^n$, $H_0=1$, $H_1(y)=2y$, $H_n(-y)=(-1)^nH_n(y)$, and they satisfy

$$H_n'=2nH_{n-1},\qquad H_{n+1}=2yH_n-2nH_{n-1}\qquad(n\ge1);$$

moreover

$$g_n=\frac{H_ng_0}{\sqrt{2^nn!}};$$

(g) consequently

$$\sqrt2\,y\,g_n=\sqrt n\,g_{n-1}+\sqrt{n+1}\,g_{n+1},\qquad \sqrt2\,g_n'=\sqrt n\,g_{n-1}-\sqrt{n+1}\,g_{n+1}.$$

Let $d\geq1$, let $0<\epsilon$ be a dimensionless parameter, and use the Schwartz space $\mathcal S(\mathbb R^d)$ of [[def-schwartz-space-and-its-seminorms]]. For $a\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R^{2d})$, define the Weyl quantization on $u\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R^d)$ by

$$ (\operatorname{Op}^W_\epsilon(a)u)(x):=(2\pi\epsilon)^{-d}\int_{\mathbb R^d}\int_{\mathbb R^d} e^{i(x-y)\cdot\xi/\epsilon}a\!\left(\frac{x+y}{2},\xi\right)u(y)\,d\xi\,dy . $$

The integral is absolutely convergent for each fixed $x$, since its integrand is Schwartz in $(y,\xi)$. The Wigner integral below is absolutely convergent for each $(x,\xi)$ for the same reason.

For a normalized $u\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R^d)$, define its Wigner distribution by

$$ W_\epsilon[u](x,\xi):=(2\pi\epsilon)^{-d}\int_{\mathbb R^d}e^{-iy\cdot\xi/\epsilon}u(x+y/2)\overline{u(x-y/2)}\,dy . $$

Use the inner product $\langle f,g\rangle=\int f(x)\overline{g(x)}\,dx$, linear in its first argument ([[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]]). Define the scaled Fourier transform on $\mathcal S(\mathbb R^d)$ by

$$ (\mathcal F_\epsilon u)(\xi):=(2\pi\epsilon)^{-d/2}\int_{\mathbb R^d}e^{-ix\cdot\xi/\epsilon}u(x)\,dx . $$

For the coordinate and momentum observables define $Q_j u=x_j u$ and $P_j u=-i\epsilon\partial_{x_j}u$ on $\mathcal S(\mathbb R^d)$. The product rule ([[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]]) gives
$$ [Q_j,P_k]u:=Q_jP_ku-P_kQ_ju=i\epsilon\delta_{jk}u. $$
This fixes the Poisson and Moyal signs used on this page.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $d\geq1$, $\epsilon>0$, $a\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R^{2d})$, and $u\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R^d)$ satisfy $\|u\|_2=1$. With the definitions of [def-nrqmx-weyl-symbol-wigner], the Wigner distribution $W_\epsilon[u]$ is real and integrable, and

$$ \langle\operatorname{Op}^W_\epsilon(a)u,u\rangle=\int_{\mathbb R^{2d}}a(x,\xi)W_\epsilon[u](x,\xi)\,dx\,d\xi , $$

$$ \int_{\mathbb R^d}W_\epsilon[u](x,\xi)\,d\xi=|u(x)|^2,\qquad \int_{\mathbb R^d}W_\epsilon[u](x,\xi)\,dx=|(\mathcal F_\epsilon u)(\xi)|^2. $$

The Wigner distribution need not be nonnegative.

Assume countable choice. For $n\ge1$, $t>0$, and $\xi\in\mathbb R^n$,
$$\mathcal F(e^{-\pi t|x|^2})(\xi)=t^{-n/2}e^{-\pi|\xi|^2/t}.$$
Every polynomial times a positive real Gaussian is absolutely integrable.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $d\ge1$, $0<\epsilon\le1$, and $V\in C^\infty(\mathbb R^d;\mathbb R)$ with every partial derivative of total order at least $2$ bounded. Set
$$ h(x,\xi)=\frac{|\xi|^2}{2}+V(x),\qquad H_\epsilon^0=-\frac{\epsilon^2}{2}\Delta+V(x)\quad\text{on }\mathcal S(\mathbb R^d). $$
Assume, as an explicit operator hypothesis, that for each $\epsilon$ a densely defined self-adjoint operator $H_\epsilon$ on $L^2(\mathbb R^d)$ extends $H_\epsilon^0$ and $\mathcal S(\mathbb R^d)$ is a core for $H_\epsilon$. Let $U_\epsilon(t)$, $t\in\mathbb R$, be the strongly continuous unitary group for the constant generator $H_\epsilon/\epsilon$; for $t<0$ it is the adjoint of the forward propagator at time $-t$. Define the global Hamiltonian flow by
$$ \dot x=\xi,\qquad \dot\xi=-\nabla V(x),\qquad \Phi_0=I. $$
For every $a\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^{2d})$ and finite $T>0$, there is $C_{T,V,a}<\infty$, independent of $0<\epsilon\le1$, such that
$$ \sup_{|t|\le T} \left\|U_\epsilon(t)^*\operatorname{Op}^W_\epsilon(a)U_\epsilon(t) -\operatorname{Op}^W_\epsilon(a\circ\Phi_t)\right\|_{L^2\to L^2} \le C_{T,V,a}\epsilon^2. $$
Only fixed finite times are covered by the first estimate. No Ehrenfest-time, caustic-uniformity, or physical measurement conclusion is asserted. If $V$ is a polynomial of degree at most two, the difference in that branch is identically zero.

There is also an exact statement for every real quadratic phase-space Hamiltonian. Let $z=(x,\xi)\in\mathbb R^{2d}$, let $G=G^T\in\mathbb R^{2d\times2d}$, $\ell\in\mathbb R^{2d}$ and $c\in\mathbb R$, and put
$$ h(z)=\tfrac12 z^TGz+\ell\cdot z+c. $$
Set $J=\begin{pmatrix}0&I_d\\-I_d&0\end{pmatrix}$ and $\widehat z=(Q_1,\ldots,Q_d,P_1,\ldots,P_d)$, where $Q_j u=x_j u$ and $P_j u=-i\epsilon\partial_{x_j}u$ on $\mathcal S(\mathbb R^d)$. On $\mathcal S(\mathbb R^d)$ define the Weyl realization by
$$ H_{\epsilon,h}^0:=cI+\sum_j\ell_j\widehat z_j+\tfrac14\sum_{j,k}G_{jk}(\widehat z_j\widehat z_k+\widehat z_k\widehat z_j). $$
For each $0<\epsilon\le1$, assume a densely defined self-adjoint operator $H_{\epsilon,h}$ on $L^2(\mathbb R^d)$ extends $H_{\epsilon,h}^0$ and $\mathcal S(\mathbb R^d)$ is a core for it. Let $U_{\epsilon,h}(t)$ be the strongly continuous unitary group for the constant generator $H_{\epsilon,h}/\epsilon$. The global Hamiltonian flow, defined by $\dot z=J\nabla h(z)=J(Gz+\ell)$ and $\Phi_0(z)=z$, is
$$ \Phi_t(z)=e^{tJG}z+\int_0^t e^{(t-s)JG}J\ell\,ds. $$
Here $e^{tJG}:=\sum_{n=0}^\infty t^n(JG)^n/n!$ is the matrix exponential.
Then for every $a\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R^{2d})$ and every $t\in\mathbb R$,
$$ U_{\epsilon,h}(t)^*\operatorname{Op}^W_\epsilon(a)U_{\epsilon,h}(t)=\operatorname{Op}^W_\epsilon(a\circ\Phi_t). $$

Let $A, B \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ with
$g[A] \subseteq B$ and let $f : B \to \mathbb{R}$, so that the composite
$f \circ g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ is defined. Let $c \in A$ be a limit point of
$A$ (Limit point, isolated point, adherent point, derived set, and dense subset of $\mathbb{R}$) at which $g$ is differentiable
(The derivative $f'(c) = \lim_{x \to c} \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c}$ of $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ at a point $c \in A$ that is a limit point of $A$, and differentiability on a set), put $b := g(c)$, and suppose $b$ is a limit point of $B$
at which $f$ is differentiable. Then $f \circ g$ is differentiable at $c$ and

$$(f \circ g)'(c) \;=\; f'\bigl(g(c)\bigr)\,g'(c) .$$

**Both limit-point hypotheses are needed, and neither is automatic.** That $c$
is a limit point of $A$ is what makes $g'(c)$ and $(f \circ g)'(c)$ defined
symbols; that $b = g(c)$ is a limit point of $B$ is what makes $f'(b)$ one.
Nothing forces the second: $g$ may be differentiable at $c$ and send $c$ to an
isolated point of $B$, and there $f'(b)$ is not defined and the formula asserts
nothing.

**No case analysis appears anywhere.** The naive difference-quotient proof
writes $\frac{f(g(x)) - f(g(c))}{g(x) - g(c)} \cdot \frac{g(x) - g(c)}{x - c}$
and then has to say what happens where $g(x) = g(c)$, which may occur at points
arbitrarily close to $c$. Carathéodory's factorisation never divides by the
inner increment, so the difficulty does not arise.

Assume countable choice. For complex $C^1$ functions $u,v$ on $[a,b]$, $a<b$, Lebesgue integration gives $\int_a^b u'v=u(b)v(b)-u(a)v(a)-\int_a^b uv'$ and $\int_a^b u'=u(b)-u(a)$. If instead $u,v\in C^1(\mathbb R;\mathbb C)$, $u'v,uv'\in L^1(\mathbb R)$ and $u(x)v(x)\to0$ as $x\to\pm\infty$, then $\int_{\mathbb R}u'v=-\int_{\mathbb R}uv'$.

Assume countable choice. For $n\ge1$, $t>0$, and $\xi\in\mathbb R^n$,
$$\mathcal F(e^{-\pi t|x|^2})(\xi)=t^{-n/2}e^{-\pi|\xi|^2/t}.$$
Every polynomial times a positive real Gaussian is absolutely integrable.

For all vectors $x,y$ in a real or complex inner-product space,

$$|\langle x,y\rangle|\le\|x\|\,\|y\| ,$$

with equality if and only if $x$ and $y$ are linearly dependent.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let
$(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space and let
$L^2(\mu)$ be the quotient of $\mathcal L^2(\mu)$ by the almost-everywhere zero
functions ([[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]]), with the quotient
norm $\|\cdot\|_2$ ([[thm-the-l-p-norm-descends-to-the-quotient-and-makes-l-p-a-normed-space]]).

1. On **real** $L^2(\mu)$ the formula
   $$\langle f,g\rangle:=\int fg\,d\mu$$is a well-defined inner product, linear in both variables, positive definite, with $\langle f,f\rangle=\|f\|_2^2$; with it $L^2(\mu)$ is a real Hilbert space ([[def-hilbert-space]]). 2. On **complex** $L^2(\mu;\mathbb C)$ the formula$$\langle f,g\rangle:=\int f\overline g\,d\mu$$
   is a well-defined inner product, linear in the first variable and
   conjugate-linear in the second, positive definite, with
   $\langle f,f\rangle=\|f\|_2^2$; with it $L^2(\mu;\mathbb C)$ is a complex
   Hilbert space ([[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]]).

In both cases the inner product induces exactly the established quotient
$L^2$ norm.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $U,V \subseteq \mathbb R^n$ be open and let $T : U \to V$ be a
$C^1$ diffeomorphism. If $f : V \to \mathbb C$ belongs to $L^1(\lambda_n)$,
then
$$ \int_V f(y)\,d\lambda_n(y) = \int_U f(T(x))\,|\det DT(x)|\,d\lambda_n(x). $$

derivations.claim:
The scaled oscillator eigenfunctions are polynomial multiples of $e^{-x^2/(2\epsilon)}$. To verify the core hypothesis of [[thm-nrqmx-quadratic-egorov]], take $f\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R)$ and set $L f=-\epsilon^2f''/2+x^2f/2\in L^2$. Integration by parts against each Hermite eigenfunction $\psi_n^\epsilon$, whose polynomial-Gaussian tails make the endpoint products vanish, gives
$$ \langle Lf,\psi_n^\epsilon\rangle =\langle f,L\psi_n^\epsilon\rangle =\epsilon(n+\tfrac12)\langle f,\psi_n^\epsilon\rangle. $$
Parseval for the complete basis [F1] yields
$$ \sum_{n\ge0}\epsilon^2(n+\tfrac12)^2|\langle f,\psi_n^\epsilon\rangle|^2 =\|Lf\|_2^2<\infty. $$
Thus $f\in D(H_\epsilon)$. The coefficients of $H_\epsilon f$ in the Hermite basis are $\epsilon(n+\tfrac12)\langle f,\psi_n^\epsilon\rangle$, the same coefficients as $Lf$; completeness of that basis gives $H_\epsilon f=Lf$. The finite Hermite span is contained in $\mathcal S$ and is a graph core by [F1]; since $\mathcal S\subset D(H_\epsilon)$, $\mathcal S$ is also a core. This checks every operator hypothesis of [F4].

The Gaussian integral [F5] and the positive scaling in [F8] give $\|\psi^\epsilon_{q,p}\|_2^2=(\pi\epsilon)^{-1/2}\int e^{-(x-q)^2/\epsilon}dx=1$. In its Wigner integral, the product of the two Gaussian factors is
$$ (\pi\epsilon)^{-1/2} \exp\!\left(-\frac{(x-q)^2}{\epsilon}-\frac{y^2}{4\epsilon}\right) \exp\!\left(\frac{ipy}{\epsilon}\right). $$
Multiplying by $e^{-iy\xi/\epsilon}$ and applying [F3] with $\eta=\xi-p$ gives
$$ W_\epsilon[\psi^\epsilon_{q,p}](x,\xi) =(2\pi\epsilon)^{-1}(\pi\epsilon)^{-1/2} e^{-(x-q)^2/\epsilon} 2\sqrt{\pi\epsilon}\,e^{-(\xi-p)^2/\epsilon}, $$
which is the stated nonnegative density. Its integral is $1$ by [F5] and [F8]. For its phase-space moments, apply [F8] to $x=q+\sqrt\epsilon s$ and $\xi=p+\sqrt\epsilon r$. The centered first moments vanish because $s e^{-s^2}$ and $r e^{-r^2}$ are odd; the cross-moment vanishes for the same reason. Integration by parts [F5] gives $\int s^2e^{-s^2}ds=\frac12\int e^{-s^2}ds$, so each centered variance is $\epsilon/2$. This verifies the mean and covariance definitions in the Statement.

For the operator uncertainties, direct differentiation gives $P\psi^\epsilon_{q,p}=\bigl(p+i(x-q)\bigr)\psi^\epsilon_{q,p}$, while $Q\psi^\epsilon_{q,p}=x\psi^\epsilon_{q,p}$. Thus $\bar Q_\psi=q$, $\bar P_\psi=p$, and the two squared standard deviations are both $\int(x-q)^2|\psi|^2dx=\epsilon/2$ by the same Gaussian integration by parts. To prove the lower bound for every normalized $\varphi\in\mathcal S$, first note that $Q$ and $P$ are symmetric on $\mathcal S$: for $P$ this is [F5] applied to decaying Schwartz factors, and for $Q$ it follows from real multiplication. Hence $\bar Q_\varphi,\bar P_\varphi\in\mathbb R$. Put $A=Q-\bar Q_\varphi I$ and $B=P-\bar P_\varphi I$. Cauchy–Schwarz [F6], the commutator $[A,B]=[Q,P]=i\epsilon I$ from [F2], and symmetry give
$$ \Delta_\varphi Q\,\Delta_\varphi P\ge|\langle A\varphi,B\varphi\rangle|\ge|\operatorname{Im}\langle A\varphi,B\varphi\rangle|=\frac12|\langle[A,B]\varphi,\varphi\rangle|=\frac\epsilon2. $$
Indeed, under the first-variable-linear convention, $\langle A\varphi,B\varphi\rangle=\langle BA\varphi,\varphi\rangle$ and its conjugate is $\langle AB\varphi,\varphi\rangle$. Thus the Gaussian attains the lower bound.

The classical Hamilton equations for $h(x,\xi)=(x^2+\xi^2)/2$ solve to
$$ \Phi_t(x,\xi)=(x\cos t+\xi\sin t,\ \xi\cos t-x\sin t). $$
This matrix is orthogonal with determinant $1$, and $\Phi_t(q,p)=(q_t,p_t)$. For $a\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^2)$, [F4] gives
$$ \langle W_t,a\rangle =\langle\operatorname{Op}^W_\epsilon(a\circ\Phi_t)\psi^\epsilon_{q,p}, \psi^\epsilon_{q,p}\rangle =\int_{\mathbb R^2}a(\Phi_t z)W_\epsilon[\psi^\epsilon_{q,p}](z)\,dz, $$
where the last equality is [F2]. The integrand is in $L^1$ because $a$ is compactly supported and the Gaussian is integrable. Apply [F8] to the rotation $z'=\Phi_tz$; its determinant is $1$, so the resulting density is $W_\epsilon[\psi^\epsilon_{q,p}](\Phi_{-t}z')$. Orthogonality gives
$$ |\Phi_{-t}(x,\xi)-(q,p)|^2 =|(x,\xi)-\Phi_t(q,p)|^2, $$
so this density is exactly the displayed $W_t$. The same change of variables sends its mean $(q,p)$ to $(q_t,p_t)$ and transforms covariance as $R_t(\epsilon I_2/2)R_t^T=\epsilon I_2/2$, since $R_t$ is orthogonal. This proves the asserted exact transport and covariance for every compactly supported smooth test symbol and hence for the distributional Wigner functional defined in the Statement.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Let $d\geq1$, let $0<\epsilon$ be a dimensionless parameter, and use the Schwartz space $\mathcal S(\mathbb R^d)$ of [[def-schwartz-space-and-its-seminorms]]. For $a\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R^{2d})$, define the Weyl quantization on $u\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R^d)$ by

$$ (\operatorname{Op}^W_\epsilon(a)u)(x):=(2\pi\epsilon)^{-d}\int_{\mathbb R^d}\int_{\mathbb R^d} e^{i(x-y)\cdot\xi/\epsilon}a\!\left(\frac{x+y}{2},\xi\right)u(y)\,d\xi\,dy . $$

The integral is absolutely convergent for each fixed $x$, since its integrand is Schwartz in $(y,\xi)$. The Wigner integral below is absolutely convergent for each $(x,\xi)$ for the same reason.

For a normalized $u\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R^d)$, define its Wigner distribution by

$$ W_\epsilon[u](x,\xi):=(2\pi\epsilon)^{-d}\int_{\mathbb R^d}e^{-iy\cdot\xi/\epsilon}u(x+y/2)\overline{u(x-y/2)}\,dy . $$

Use the inner product $\langle f,g\rangle=\int f(x)\overline{g(x)}\,dx$, linear in its first argument ([[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]]). Define the scaled Fourier transform on $\mathcal S(\mathbb R^d)$ by

$$ (\mathcal F_\epsilon u)(\xi):=(2\pi\epsilon)^{-d/2}\int_{\mathbb R^d}e^{-ix\cdot\xi/\epsilon}u(x)\,dx . $$

For the coordinate and momentum observables define $Q_j u=x_j u$ and $P_j u=-i\epsilon\partial_{x_j}u$ on $\mathcal S(\mathbb R^d)$. The product rule ([[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]]) gives
$$ [Q_j,P_k]u:=Q_jP_ku-P_kQ_ju=i\epsilon\delta_{jk}u. $$
This fixes the Poisson and Moyal signs used on this page.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $d\geq1$, $\epsilon>0$, $a\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R^{2d})$, and $u\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R^d)$ satisfy $\|u\|_2=1$. With the definitions of [def-nrqmx-weyl-symbol-wigner], the Wigner distribution $W_\epsilon[u]$ is real and integrable, and

$$ \langle\operatorname{Op}^W_\epsilon(a)u,u\rangle=\int_{\mathbb R^{2d}}a(x,\xi)W_\epsilon[u](x,\xi)\,dx\,d\xi , $$

$$ \int_{\mathbb R^d}W_\epsilon[u](x,\xi)\,d\xi=|u(x)|^2,\qquad \int_{\mathbb R^d}W_\epsilon[u](x,\xi)\,dx=|(\mathcal F_\epsilon u)(\xi)|^2. $$

The Wigner distribution need not be nonnegative.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $d\ge1$, $0<\epsilon\le1$, and $V\in C^\infty(\mathbb R^d;\mathbb R)$ with every partial derivative of total order at least $2$ bounded. Set
$$ h(x,\xi)=\frac{|\xi|^2}{2}+V(x),\qquad H_\epsilon^0=-\frac{\epsilon^2}{2}\Delta+V(x)\quad\text{on }\mathcal S(\mathbb R^d). $$
Assume, as an explicit operator hypothesis, that for each $\epsilon$ a self-adjoint operator $H_\epsilon$ on $L^2(\mathbb R^d)$ extends $H_\epsilon^0$ and $\mathcal S(\mathbb R^d)$ is a core for $H_\epsilon$. Let
$$ U_\epsilon(t)=U_\epsilon(t,0) $$
be the unitary propagator supplied by [[thm-nrqm-controlled-dynamics-common-domain-nonautonomous-evolution]] for the constant generator $H_\epsilon/\epsilon$. Define the global Hamiltonian flow by
$$ \dot x=\xi,\qquad \dot\xi=-\nabla V(x),\qquad \Phi_0=I. $$
For every $a\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^{2d})$ and finite $T>0$, there is $C_{T,V,a}<\infty$, independent of $0<\epsilon\le1$, such that
$$ \sup_{|t|\le T} \left\|U_\epsilon(t)^*\operatorname{Op}^W_\epsilon(a)U_\epsilon(t) -\operatorname{Op}^W_\epsilon(a\circ\Phi_t)\right\|_{L^2\to L^2} \le C_{T,V,a}\epsilon^2. $$
Only fixed finite times are covered. No Ehrenfest-time, caustic-uniformity, or physical measurement conclusion is asserted. If $V$ is a polynomial of degree at most two, the difference is identically zero.
