supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Fix real parameters $m>0$, $\omega>0$, $\hbar>0$, put $\ell:=\sqrt{\hbar/(m\omega)}>0$, and let $g_0,P,(g_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ be the Hermite data of [[thm-nrqm-oscillator-hermite-recurrence]] in $L^2(\mathbb R,dy)$, so that $(g_n)$ is a complete orthonormal family by [[thm-nrqm-oscillator-hermite-completeness]]. Define

$$D:L^2(\mathbb R,dy)\to L^2(\mathbb R,dx),\qquad (Df)(x):=\ell^{-1/2}f(x/\ell),$$

and let $A$ be the self-adjoint diagonal operator of [[lem-nrqm-oscillator-diagonal-adjoint-and-graph-core-lemma]] for the complete orthonormal family $(g_n)$ and the eigenvalues $\lambda_n=2n+1$, with the core $P$ and spectrum $\{2n+1:n\in\mathbb N\}$ ([[thm-nrqm-oscillator-diagonal-spectrum]]).

Then:

(a) $D$ is a linear isometry of $L^2(\mathbb R,dy)$ onto $L^2(\mathbb R,dx)$ with two-sided inverse $(D^{-1}g)(y)=\ell^{1/2}g(\ell y)$; the functions $\psi_n:=Dg_n$, $\psi_n(x)=\ell^{-1/2}g_n(x/\ell)$, form a complete orthonormal family of $L^2(\mathbb R,dx)$;

(b) the operator

$$H_{\mathrm{osc}}:=\frac{\hbar\omega}{2}\,DAD^{-1},\qquad D(H_{\mathrm{osc}}):=\{f\in L^2(\mathbb R,dx):D^{-1}f\in D(A)\},$$

is self-adjoint, satisfies $H_{\mathrm{osc}}\psi_n=\hbar\omega(n+\tfrac12)\psi_n$ for every $n$, and has

$$D(H_{\mathrm{osc}})=\Bigl\{f:\sum_n\hbar^2\omega^2(n+\tfrac12)^2|c_n|^2<\infty\Bigr\},\qquad H_{\mathrm{osc}}f=\sum_n\hbar\omega(n+\tfrac12)c_n\psi_n,$$

where $c_n:=\langle D^{-1}f,g_n\rangle=\langle f,\psi_n\rangle$; its spectrum is $\sigma(H_{\mathrm{osc}})=\{\hbar\omega(n+\tfrac12):n\in\mathbb N\}$, its ground energy is $\hbar\omega/2$ with eigenvector $\psi_0$, and $\langle H_{\mathrm{osc}}f,f\rangle\ge\frac{\hbar\omega}{2}\|f\|^2$ for every $f\in D(H_{\mathrm{osc}})$;

(c) $D(P)=\operatorname{span}\{\psi_n\}$ is a core for $H_{\mathrm{osc}}$, and for every polynomial $p$ the function $f:=D(pg_0)$ is $C^\infty$ on $\mathbb R$ with

$$H_{\mathrm{osc}}f=-\frac{\hbar^2}{2m}f''+\frac{m\omega^2}{2}x^2f$$

pointwise on $\mathbb R$;

(d) for every $f\in D(H_{\mathrm{osc}})$ and every test function $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R)$,

$$\int_{\mathbb R}(H_{\mathrm{osc}}f)(x)\varphi(x)\,dx=\int_{\mathbb R}f(x)\Bigl(-\frac{\hbar^2}{2m}\varphi''(x)+\frac{m\omega^2}{2}x^2\varphi(x)\Bigr)dx,$$

so $H_{\mathrm{osc}}$ is the self-adjoint realization of the differential expression $-\frac{\hbar^2}{2m}\frac{d^2}{dx^2}+\frac{m\omega^2}{2}x^2$ in the weak sense; no identification of $D(H_{\mathrm{osc}})$ with a separately defined maximal differential-operator domain is asserted.

All parameters enter as positive real numbers; no physical identification of $m,\omega,\hbar$ with measured quantities is made.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $L^2=L^2(\mathbb R,dy)$ be the complex Lebesgue space with inner product $\langle\varphi,\psi\rangle=\int_{\mathbb R}\varphi(y)\overline{\psi(y)}\,dy$ linear in the first argument ([[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]], [[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]]); this pairing makes $L^2$ a complex Hilbert space by [[lem-l-two-with-the-integral-pairing-is-a-hilbert-space]]. For complex-valued functions, smoothness and derivatives use the componentwise convention of [[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]]. Write $g_0$ for the function $g_0(y):=\pi^{-1/4}e^{-y^{2}/2}$ and also for its class in $L^2$. Put

$$P:=\{p\,g_0:\ p\in\mathbb C[y]\}\subseteq L^2 ,$$

the set of classes of polynomial multiples of $g_0$. Each class in $P$ has a unique representative of the form $p g_0$: if $p g_0=qg_0$ almost everywhere, the continuous function $(p-q)g_0$ vanishes almost everywhere and therefore everywhere, and $g_0(y)>0$ for every $y$, so $p=q$. Let $Y$ be multiplication by $y$ and $\partial_y$ the derivative, acting on this unique smooth representative. Set $g_{-1}:=0$ for use in the recurrence formulas at $n=0$. Define

$$a:=\frac{Y+\partial_y}{\sqrt2},\qquad a^\dagger:=\frac{Y-\partial_y}{\sqrt2},\qquad g_n:=\frac{(a^\dagger)^ng_0}{\sqrt{n!}}\quad(n\in\mathbb N).$$

Then:

(a) $g_0\in L^2$ with $\|g_0\|=1$; more generally $y^kg_0\in L^2$ for every $k\in\mathbb N$, so $P$ is a linear subspace of $L^2$ all of whose members are represented by $C^\infty$ functions;

(b) $Y,\partial_y,a,a^\dagger$ map $P$ into $P$, and $\partial_y(pg_0)=(p'-yp)g_0$ for every polynomial $p$;

(c) for all $\varphi,\psi\in P$, $\langle a^\dagger\varphi,\psi\rangle=\langle\varphi,a\psi\rangle$ and $\langle a\varphi,\psi\rangle=\langle\varphi,a^\dagger\psi\rangle$;

(d) $a^\dagger a-a a^\dagger=-I$ on $P$, i.e. $[a,a^\dagger]=aa^\dagger-a^\dagger a=I$ on $P$, and $ag_0=0$;

(e) for every $n\in\mathbb N$: $ag_n=\sqrt n\,g_{n-1}$ (with $ag_0=0$), $a^\dagger g_n=\sqrt{n+1}\,g_{n+1}$, $a^\dagger ag_n=ng_n$ and $aa^\dagger g_n=(n+1)g_n$;

(f) the polynomials

$$H_n(y):=(-1)^ne^{y^2}\frac{d^n}{dy^n}e^{-y^2}$$

are polynomials of degree $n$ with leading coefficient $2^n$, $H_0=1$, $H_1(y)=2y$, $H_n(-y)=(-1)^nH_n(y)$, and they satisfy

$$H_n'=2nH_{n-1},\qquad H_{n+1}=2yH_n-2nH_{n-1}\qquad(n\ge1);$$

moreover

$$g_n=\frac{H_ng_0}{\sqrt{2^nn!}};$$

(g) consequently

$$\sqrt2\,y\,g_n=\sqrt n\,g_{n-1}+\sqrt{n+1}\,g_{n+1},\qquad \sqrt2\,g_n'=\sqrt n\,g_{n-1}-\sqrt{n+1}\,g_{n+1}.$$

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Let $A, B \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ with
$g[A] \subseteq B$ and let $f : B \to \mathbb{R}$, so that the composite
$f \circ g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ is defined. Let $c \in A$ be a limit point of
$A$ (Limit point, isolated point, adherent point, derived set, and dense subset of $\mathbb{R}$) at which $g$ is differentiable
(The derivative $f'(c) = \lim_{x \to c} \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c}$ of $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ at a point $c \in A$ that is a limit point of $A$, and differentiability on a set), put $b := g(c)$, and suppose $b$ is a limit point of $B$
at which $f$ is differentiable. Then $f \circ g$ is differentiable at $c$ and

$$(f \circ g)'(c) \;=\; f'\bigl(g(c)\bigr)\,g'(c) .$$

**Both limit-point hypotheses are needed, and neither is automatic.** That $c$
is a limit point of $A$ is what makes $g'(c)$ and $(f \circ g)'(c)$ defined
symbols; that $b = g(c)$ is a limit point of $B$ is what makes $f'(b)$ one.
Nothing forces the second: $g$ may be differentiable at $c$ and send $c$ to an
isolated point of $B$, and there $f'(b)$ is not defined and the formula asserts
nothing.

**No case analysis appears anywhere.** The naive difference-quotient proof
writes $\frac{f(g(x)) - f(g(c))}{g(x) - g(c)} \cdot \frac{g(x) - g(c)}{x - c}$
and then has to say what happens where $g(x) = g(c)$, which may occur at points
arbitrarily close to $c$. Carathéodory's factorisation never divides by the
inner increment, so the difficulty does not arise.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $d\geq1$, let $H\in C^2([0,1],\operatorname{Herm}(\mathbb C^d))$ be a finite Hermitian family with energy unit joules, and let $\hbar>0$ have unit joule-seconds. A spectral cluster at $s$ is a subset $\sigma_P(s)$ of the finite spectrum of $H(s)$, and $P(s)$ is the orthogonal projection onto the sum of its eigenspaces. Coherently followed means that $s\mapsto P(s)$ is continuous in operator norm (equivalently, it agrees locally with the Riesz continuation of its initial cluster). Assume the distance from $\sigma_P(s)$ to the complementary spectrum is at least a uniform $g>0$ in joules. Let $T>0$ be a total duration in seconds, let $s=t/T$ be dimensionless, and let $U_T(0)=I$ solve
$$i\hbar\,\partial_sU_T(s)=T H(s)U_T(s).$$
Put $K(s)=[P'(s),P(s)]$. There is a $C^1$ Hermitian matrix $X(s)$ solving $[H(s),X(s)]=K(s)$. With
$$C=2\sup_{s\in[0,1]}\|X(s)\|+\int_0^1\bigl(\|X'(s)\|+\|K(s)\|\,\|X(s)\|\bigr)\,ds,$$
the leakage satisfies
$$\|(I-P(s))U_T(s)P(0)\|\leq\frac{\hbar C}{T}\qquad(0\leq s\leq1).$$
The supplier provides a $C^1$ Hermitian $X$ solving the displayed commutator equation. For that $X$, $C$ has unit joule-inverse, so $\hbar C/T$ is dimensionless. If the cluster has rank one, with $H(s)P(s)=E(s)P(s)$, define $U_A(0)=I$ by
$$i\,\partial_sU_A(s)=\left(\frac{T}{\hbar}H(s)+iK(s)\right)U_A(s).$$
For Kato transport $W'(s)=K(s)W(s)$, $W(0)=I$, the comparison evolution factors exactly on the initial eigenspace:
$$U_A(s)P(0)=\exp\!\left(-\frac{iT}{\hbar}\int_0^sE(u)\,du\right)W(s)P(0).$$
The leakage estimate is finite-dimensional and conditional on the stated uniform positive gap.

$$U_A(s)P(0)=\exp\!\left(-\frac{iT}{\hbar}\int_0^sE(u)\,du\right)W(s)P(0).$$

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $d\geq1$, let $H\in C^2([0,1],\operatorname{Herm}(\mathbb C^d))$ be a finite Hermitian family with energy unit joules, and let $\hbar>0$ have unit joule-seconds. A spectral cluster at $s$ is a subset $\sigma_P(s)$ of the finite spectrum of $H(s)$, and $P(s)$ is the orthogonal projection onto the sum of its eigenspaces. Coherently followed means that $s\mapsto P(s)$ is continuous in operator norm (equivalently, it agrees locally with the Riesz continuation of its initial cluster). Assume the distance from $\sigma_P(s)$ to the complementary spectrum is at least a uniform $g>0$ in joules. Let $T>0$ be a total duration in seconds, let $s=t/T$ be dimensionless, and let $U_T(0)=I$ solve
$$i\hbar\,\partial_sU_T(s)=T H(s)U_T(s).$$
Put $K(s)=[P'(s),P(s)]$. There is a $C^1$ Hermitian matrix $X(s)$ solving $[H(s),X(s)]=K(s)$. With
$$C=2\sup_{s\in[0,1]}\|X(s)\|+\int_0^1\bigl(\|X'(s)\|+\|K(s)\|\,\|X(s)\|\bigr)\,ds,$$
the leakage satisfies
$$\|(I-P(s))U_T(s)P(0)\|\leq\frac{\hbar C}{T}\qquad(0\leq s\leq1).$$
The supplier provides a $C^1$ Hermitian $X$ solving the displayed commutator equation. For that $X$, $C$ has unit joule-inverse, so $\hbar C/T$ is dimensionless. If the cluster has rank one, with $H(s)P(s)=E(s)P(s)$, define $U_A(0)=I$ by
$$i\,\partial_sU_A(s)=\left(\frac{T}{\hbar}H(s)+iK(s)\right)U_A(s).$$
For Kato transport $W'(s)=K(s)W(s)$, $W(0)=I$, the comparison evolution factors exactly on the initial eigenspace:
$$U_A(s)P(0)=\exp\!\left(-\frac{iT}{\hbar}\int_0^sE(u)\,du\right)W(s)P(0).$$
The leakage estimate is finite-dimensional and conditional on the stated uniform positive gap.

derivations.claim: On $\mathbb C^2$, let $e_\uparrow=(1,0)^T$, $e_\downarrow=(0,1)^T$, and $H(s)=E_0(2s-1)\operatorname{diag}(1,-1)$ for $s\in[0,1]$. For $s<1/2$ the ordered upper eigenvalue is $E_0(1-2s)$ and its projection is $P_{\rm up}(s)=e_\downarrow e_\downarrow^*$; for $s>1/2$ it is $E_0(2s-1)$ and its projection is $P_{\rm up}(s)=e_\uparrow e_\uparrow^*$. At $s=1/2$, $H(s)=0$, so the degenerate upper eigenspace is all of $\mathbb C^2$ and its spectral projection is $I_2$; the one-sided rank-one projections therefore have no continuous rank-one extension. The gap between the two eigenvalues is $2E_0|2s-1|$, which closes at $s=1/2$.

The propagator from $s=0$ solves $i\hbar U_T'(s)=T H(s)U_T(s)$ and is
$$U_T(s)=\exp\!\left(-\frac{iTE_0}{\hbar}(s^2-s)\operatorname{diag}(1,-1)\right),$$
as direct differentiation verifies. In particular $U_T(1)=I_2$.

At the endpoints, $P_{\rm up}(0)=e_\downarrow e_\downarrow^*$ and $P_{\rm up}(1)=e_\uparrow e_\uparrow^*$. Therefore
$$\bigl\|(I-P_{\rm up}(1))U_T(1)P_{\rm up}(0)\bigr\|=\|e_\downarrow e_\downarrow^*\|=1$$
for every $T>0$. No finite constant $C$ independent of $T$ can bound this leakage by $C/T$. The ordered projection fails the continuity and uniform-gap hypotheses in [F1].

The constant projection $P_\downarrow=e_\downarrow e_\downarrow^*$ commutes with every $H(s)$ and has zero leakage for all $T$. At the crossing it is not the spectral projection onto the degenerate eigenspace, which is all of $\mathbb C^2$; it is a continuous invariant rank-one subspace, not a coherently followed gapped spectral cluster. Thus the example refutes a gap-free uniform tracking claim for the ordered branch; it does not assert that every choice of state at a crossing causes transitions.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Let $X$ be a set and write $\mathcal{P}(X)$ for its power set. A **topology** on
$X$ is a family $\mathcal{T} \subseteq \mathcal{P}(X)$ such that

- **(T1)** $\varnothing \in \mathcal{T}$ and $X \in \mathcal{T}$;
- **(T2)** $\bigcup \mathcal{S} \in \mathcal{T}$ for every $\mathcal{S} \subseteq \mathcal{T}$;
- **(T3)** $U \cap V \in \mathcal{T}$ for all $U, V \in \mathcal{T}$.

A **topological space** is a pair $(X, \mathcal{T})$ consisting of a set $X$ and
a topology $\mathcal{T}$ on it; the elements of $X$ are its **points**. When only
one topology is in play we write $X$ for the pair; when several are, the topology
is always named.

The members of $\mathcal{T}$ are the **open** sets of $(X,\mathcal{T})$. A subset
$F \subseteq X$ is **closed** when its complement $X \setminus F$ is open, and
**clopen** when it is both open and closed. By (T1) both $\varnothing$ and $X$
are clopen. *Open and closed are not opposites*: a set may be neither, and it may
be both, so "not open" is never a synonym for "closed".

**Finite intersections, and the empty one.** Axiom (T3) is stated for two sets
because that is all that is ever needed: if $n \ge 1$ and
$U_1, \dots, U_n \in \mathcal{T}$, then $U_1 \cap \dots \cap U_n \in \mathcal{T}$
follows by iterating (T3) $n-1$ times. The intersection of the **empty** family
of subsets of $X$ is $X$, since the condition "lies in every member of the empty
family" is vacuous; that case is covered by (T1) rather than by (T3), which is
one of the two reasons $X \in \mathcal{T}$ is demanded outright. The other is
that (T2) alone gives only $\bigcup \varnothing = \varnothing$.

**The closed sets, and the dual axiomatisation.** Put
$\mathcal{C} := \{\, X \setminus U : U \in \mathcal{T} \,\}$, the family of closed
sets. Then

- **(C1)** $\varnothing \in \mathcal{C}$ and $X \in \mathcal{C}$;
- **(C2)** $\bigcap \mathcal{D} \in \mathcal{C}$ for every **nonempty**
  $\mathcal{D} \subseteq \mathcal{C}$;
- **(C3)** $C \cup D \in \mathcal{C}$ for all $C, D \in \mathcal{C}$.

Conversely, if a family $\mathcal{C} \subseteq \mathcal{P}(X)$ satisfies (C1),
(C2) and (C3), then $\mathcal{T} := \{\, X \setminus C : C \in \mathcal{C} \,\}$
is a topology on $X$ whose closed sets are exactly the members of $\mathcal{C}$.
So a topology may be presented equally well by its open sets or by its closed
sets, and this library uses whichever is shorter.

*Both directions are one computation, and it is carried out here rather than
assumed.* The map $U \mapsto X \setminus U$ is an involution of
$\mathcal{P}(X)$, hence a bijection, and it carries the two De Morgan identities

$$X \setminus \bigcup_{i \in I} A_i = \bigcap_{i \in I} (X \setminus A_i) \quad (I \ne \varnothing), \qquad X \setminus \bigcap_{i \in I} A_i = \bigcup_{i \in I} (X \setminus A_i) \quad (I \ne \varnothing)$$

term by term into each other. Given (T1)–(T3): $\varnothing = X \setminus X$ and
$X = X \setminus \varnothing$ lie in $\mathcal{C}$, which is (C1); for nonempty
$\mathcal{D} \subseteq \mathcal{C}$ the family
$\mathcal{S} = \{\, X \setminus C : C \in \mathcal{D} \,\}$ lies in $\mathcal{T}$
and $\bigcap \mathcal{D} = X \setminus \bigcup \mathcal{S}$ is closed by (T2),
which is (C2); and $C \cup D = X \setminus ((X \setminus C) \cap (X \setminus D))$
is closed by (T3), which is (C3). Given (C1)–(C3) the same three lines run
backwards, the empty-union case $\bigcup \varnothing = \varnothing$ being supplied
by (C1) rather than by (C2); and $\{\, X \setminus C : C \in \mathcal{C} \,\}$ has
$\mathcal{C}$ as its family of complements because complementation is an
involution.

**Comparison of topologies.** If $\mathcal{T}_1$ and $\mathcal{T}_2$ are
topologies on the same set $X$ and $\mathcal{T}_1 \subseteq \mathcal{T}_2$, then
$\mathcal{T}_1$ is **coarser** than $\mathcal{T}_2$ and $\mathcal{T}_2$ is
**finer** than $\mathcal{T}_1$; the comparison is **strict** when the inclusion
is. Inclusion is a partial order on the set of topologies on $X$
([[def-partial-order]]), and it is not a total one: two topologies on the same
set may be incomparable.

Let $(X, \mathcal{T})$ be a topological space ([[def-topological-space]]) and let
$S \subseteq X$. The **subspace topology** (also *relative topology*) on $S$ is

$$\mathcal{T}_S := \{\, U \cap S : U \in \mathcal{T} \,\},$$

the family of **traces** on $S$ of the open sets of $X$. The pair
$(S, \mathcal{T}_S)$ is a **subspace** of $X$. A subset of $S$ that lies in
$\mathcal{T}_S$ is said to be **open in $S$**, and *relatively open* where the
ambient space needs emphasis.

**$\mathcal{T}_S$ is a topology, and this is discharged here.** (T1):
$\varnothing = \varnothing \cap S$ and $S = X \cap S$ are traces. (T2): if
$\mathcal{S}' \subseteq \mathcal{T}_S$, choose for each member a set of
$\mathcal{T}$ tracing to it — no choice principle is needed, since
$U' := \bigcup \{\, U \in \mathcal{T} : U \cap S \subseteq W \,\}$ is a canonical
such set for $W \in \mathcal{T}_S$, being open by (T2) in $X$ and satisfying
$U' \cap S = W$ — and then
$\bigcup_i (U_i \cap S) = (\bigcup_i U_i) \cap S \in \mathcal{T}_S$ by (T2) in
$X$. (T3): $(U \cap S) \cap (V \cap S) = (U \cap V) \cap S \in \mathcal{T}_S$ by
(T3) in $X$.

**Closed sets of a subspace are the traces of the closed sets.** A set
$C \subseteq S$ is closed in $S$ if and only if $C = F \cap S$ for some closed
$F \subseteq X$. Indeed $S \setminus (U \cap S) = (X \setminus U) \cap S$ and
$S \setminus (F \cap S) = (X \setminus F) \cap S$, so complementation inside $S$
matches complementation inside $X$ under tracing.

**Bases and subbases trace as well.** If $\mathcal{B}$ is a basis for
$\mathcal{T}$ ([[def-topology-basis-subbasis]]) then
$\mathcal{B}_S := \{\, B \cap S : B \in \mathcal{B} \,\}$ is a basis for
$\mathcal{T}_S$: its members are open in $S$, and for $W = U \cap S$ open in $S$
and $x \in W$ there is $B \in \mathcal{B}$ with $x \in B \subseteq U$, whence
$x \in B \cap S \subseteq W$. The same computation with a subbasis $\mathcal{S}$
shows that $\{\, S_0 \cap S : S_0 \in \mathcal{S} \,\}$ is a subbasis for
$\mathcal{T}_S$, since tracing commutes with finite intersections and with
unions.

**The inclusion is continuous.** The inclusion map $\iota : S \to X$,
$\iota(s) = s$, satisfies $\iota^{-1}[U] = U \cap S$ for every $U \subseteq X$,
so preimages of open sets are open and $\iota$ is continuous
([[thm-continuity-characterisations-top]], clause (b)). Moreover
$\mathcal{T}_S$ is the **coarsest** topology on $S$ making $\iota$ continuous: any
topology on $S$ for which $\iota$ is continuous must contain every
$\iota^{-1}[U] = U \cap S$, hence contain $\mathcal{T}_S$.

**Characteristic property of a map into a subspace.** Let $(Z, \mathcal{T}_Z)$ be
a topological space and let $g : Z \to S$ be a function. Then

$$g \text{ is continuous as a map } Z \to (S,\mathcal{T}_S) \iff \iota \circ g \text{ is continuous as a map } Z \to (X,\mathcal{T}) .$$

*Proof.* For $U \in \mathcal{T}$ one has
$(\iota \circ g)^{-1}[U] = g^{-1}[\iota^{-1}[U]] = g^{-1}[U \cap S]$. If $g$ is
continuous then each $g^{-1}[U \cap S]$ is open, so $\iota \circ g$ is continuous;
conversely if $\iota \circ g$ is continuous then for any $W = U \cap S$ open in
$S$ the set $g^{-1}[W] = (\iota \circ g)^{-1}[U]$ is open, so $g$ is continuous.
Both directions use only clause (b) of [[thm-continuity-characterisations-top]].

**Restriction of a continuous map.** If $f : X \to Y$ is continuous and
$S \subseteq X$, then $f|_S : S \to Y$ is continuous, since
$(f|_S)^{-1}[V] = f^{-1}[V] \cap S$ is open in $S$ for every open $V \subseteq Y$
([[def-continuous-map-top]], [[thm-continuity-characterisations-top]]).

**When relative and ambient agree.** If $S$ is open in $X$ then a subset of $S$
is open in $S$ if and only if it is open in $X$: a trace $U \cap S$ is then an
intersection of two open sets of $X$, and conversely an open subset of $X$
contained in $S$ is its own trace. The same statement with "closed" throughout
holds when $S$ is closed in $X$. Both are used in the pasting lemma of the next
item, and both fail without the hypothesis: $S$ itself is always open and closed
in $S$, and need be neither in $X$.

**The quotient topology.** Let $(X, \mathcal{T})$ be a topological space
([[def-topological-space]]), let $Y$ be a set and let $q : X \to Y$ be a
surjection ([[def-injection-surjection-bijection]]). The **quotient topology** on
$Y$ induced by $q$ is the final topology of the one-element family $(q)$
([[def-initial-and-final-topology]]):

$$\mathcal{T}_q \;:=\; \{\, V \subseteq Y : q^{-1}[V] \in \mathcal{T} \,\} .$$

That this is a topology is discharged in [[def-initial-and-final-topology]],
where every final topology is verified to satisfy (T1), (T2) and (T3). Dually,
$C \subseteq Y$ is closed in $\mathcal{T}_q$ exactly when $q^{-1}[C]$ is closed
in $X$, because $q^{-1}[Y \setminus V] = X \setminus q^{-1}[V]$.

**Quotient map.** A surjection $q : X \to Y$ between topological *spaces* is a
**quotient map** (also *identification map*) when the topology of $Y$ is the
quotient topology of $q$, that is when

$$V \text{ is open in } Y \iff q^{-1}[V] \text{ is open in } X \qquad (V \subseteq Y).$$

The implication from left to right is exactly continuity of $q$
([[def-continuous-map-top]], [[thm-continuity-characterisations-top]] clause
(b)), so a quotient map is a continuous surjection with the extra property that
its topology is as *fine* as continuity permits. Equivalently, and this form is
used as often: $C$ is closed in $Y$ if and only if $q^{-1}[C]$ is closed in $X$.

**Saturated sets.** Let $q : X \to Y$ be a surjection. A subset $A \subseteq X$ is
**saturated** with respect to $q$ when

$$A \;=\; q^{-1}\big[\,q[A]\,\big] ,$$

equivalently when $A$ is a union of fibres $q^{-1}[\{y\}]$, equivalently when
$x \in A$ and $q(x') = q(x)$ imply $x' \in A$. The set $q^{-1}[q[A]]$ is the
**saturation** of $A$, and it is the smallest saturated set containing $A$. The
map $V \mapsto q^{-1}[V]$ is a bijection from $\mathcal{P}(Y)$ onto the saturated
subsets of $X$, with inverse $A \mapsto q[A]$, since $q$ is surjective; under it
the open sets of the quotient topology correspond exactly to the **saturated open
subsets of $X$**. That correspondence is the working description of the quotient
topology: to know the open sets of $Y$ is to know which open subsets of $X$ are
saturated.

**Quotient by an equivalence relation.** Let $\sim$ be an **equivalence relation**
on $X$, that is a relation that is reflexive ($x \sim x$), symmetric
($x \sim x'$ implies $x' \sim x$) and transitive ($x \sim x'$ and $x' \sim x''$
imply $x \sim x''$). Write $[x] := \{\, x' \in X : x' \sim x \,\}$ for the
**equivalence class** of $x$; distinct classes are disjoint and their union is
$X$. The **quotient set** is $X/\!\sim\ := \{\, [x] : x \in X \,\}$ and the
**canonical projection** is

$$\pi : X \to X/\!\sim, \qquad \pi(x) := [x] ,$$

which is a surjection by construction. The set $X/\!\sim$ always carries the
quotient topology of $\pi$, and $(X/\!\sim,\ \mathcal{T}_\pi)$ is called an
**identification space**. A subset of $X$ is saturated for $\pi$ exactly when it
is a union of equivalence classes.

**A convenient special case: collapsing a subset.** For $\varnothing \ne B \subseteq X$
let $\sim_B$ be the relation whose classes are $B$ itself and the singletons
$\{x\}$ for $x \notin B$; this is an equivalence relation, its classes being a
partition of $X$. The resulting quotient is written $X/B$, and its canonical
projection is a surjection identifying all of $B$ to a single point and doing
nothing else. Saturated sets for $\sim_B$ are the sets $A$ with $A \cap B \in
\{\varnothing, B\}$.

**Two conventions used throughout.** First, "quotient map" is a property of a map
*together with the two topologies*, never of the map alone. Second, a quotient
topology is determined by $q$ together with the topology on its domain, and not by
the underlying pair of sets $(X,Y)$: two different surjections onto the same set
can give different topologies, the same surjection gives different topologies when
its domain is retopologised, and where more than one is in play the map is named.

Let $d,m,n\ge1$, let $(F_a)_{a=1}^m$ be a finite POVM on $\mathbb C^d$ whose real span is $\mathsf H_d$, and let $\rho\in\mathsf H_d$ satisfy $\rho\ge0$ and $\operatorname{Tr}\rho=1$. Put $p_a=\operatorname{Tr}(\rho F_a)$, form the canonical dual $D_a$ from the Gram pseudoinverse, and write $D:\mathbb R^m\to\mathsf H_d$ for $D c=\sum_ac_aD_a$. Let $X(f)=\sum_af_aD_a$ be the linear-inversion output and use the induced operator norm $\|D\|_{2\to\mathrm{HS}}=\sup_{\|c\|_2=1}\|Dc\|_{\mathrm{HS}}$.

Then exact probabilities reconstruct the state: $X(p)=\rho$. For every real frequency vector $f\in\mathbb R^m$,
$$
\|X(f)-\rho\|_{\mathrm{HS}}\le\|D\|_{2\to\mathrm{HS}}\|f-p\|_2.
$$
Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space and let $Y_1,\ldots,Y_n:\Omega\to\{1,\ldots,m\}$ be measurable with the independent product law $\mathbb P(Y_1=a_1,\ldots,Y_n=a_n)=\prod_kp_{a_k}$ for every outcome tuple. Define $f_a=n^{-1}\sum_{k=1}^n\mathbf1_{\{Y_k=a\}}$. Then for every $0<\delta<1$,
$$
\mathbb P\!\left(\max_{1\le a\le m}|f_a-p_a|\le\sqrt{\frac{\log(2m/\delta)}{2n}}\right)\ge1-\delta.
$$
Consequently, with probability at least $1-\delta$,
$$
\|X(f)-\rho\|_{\mathrm{HS}}\le\|D\|_{2\to\mathrm{HS}}\sqrt m\sqrt{\frac{\log(2m/\delta)}{2n}}.
$$
These are conditional mathematical statements under the specified product sampling law; no empirical data or calibrated apparatus is asserted.

Let $d,m\ge1$, let $F_1,\ldots,F_m\in\mathsf H_d$ span $\mathsf H_d$ over $\mathbb R$, and form $S$, $G=S^*S$, $G^+$, and $D_a$ as in the preceding finite-frame definition. If $G=\sum_{\lambda>0}\lambda P_\lambda$ is its finite spectral resolution, then $G^+=\sum_{\lambda>0}\lambda^{-1}P_\lambda$. Moreover, every $X\in\mathsf H_d$ is reconstructed by
$$
X=\sum_{a=1}^m\operatorname{Tr}(XF_a)D_a.
$$
This holds for redundant families as well as bases; $G$ need not be invertible.

For an integer $d\ge1$, let $\mathsf H_d=\{A\in M_d(\mathbb C):A=A^*\}$, regarded as a real vector space. For $A,B\in\mathsf H_d$, define the trace pairing $\langle A,B\rangle_{\mathrm{HS}}:=\operatorname{Tr}(AB)$ and write $\|A\|_{\mathrm{HS}}:=\sqrt{\operatorname{Tr}(A^2)}$. The following A-page lemma verifies that the pairing is a real inner product and that this expression is its norm.

Let $m\ge1$ and let $F=(F_a)_{a=1}^m$ be a finite family in $\mathsf H_d$. It is informationally complete when its real linear span is all of $\mathsf H_d$. Its synthesis map is $S:\mathbb R^m\to\mathsf H_d$, $S c=\sum_{a=1}^m c_aF_a$. Define the Gram matrix by $G_{ab}:=\operatorname{Tr}(F_aF_b)$; the following well-definedness lemma establishes that the trace pairing makes $S^*$ well-defined and that $G=S^*S$ is real symmetric positive semidefinite.

For this positive semidefinite real matrix $G$, let $G^+$ be its unique Moore–Penrose pseudoinverse in $M_m(\mathbb R)$, defined by the four Penrose equations over $\mathbb R$. Define the canonical dual operators $D_a=\sum_{b=1}^m(G^+)_{ba}F_b$ and the reconstruction map $D:\mathbb R^m\to\mathsf H_d$, $D c=\sum_{a=1}^m c_aD_a$. A later A-page lemma identifies this finite pseudoinverse with its spectral formula.

derivations.claim: Direct multiplication gives $\sigma_j^2=I$, $\operatorname{Tr}(\sigma_j)=0$, $\sigma_x\sigma_y=i\sigma_z$, $\sigma_y\sigma_z=i\sigma_x$, and $\sigma_z\sigma_x=i\sigma_y$; reversing the order negates each mixed product. Thus $\operatorname{Tr}(\sigma_j\sigma_k)=2\delta_{jk}$. Since a Hermitian $2\times2$ matrix has two real diagonal entries and one complex off-diagonal entry, $\dim_{\mathbb R}\mathsf H_2=4$; the four nonzero orthogonal matrices $I,\sigma_x,\sigma_y,\sigma_z$ form a basis. Every trace-one Hermitian $\rho$ therefore has the stated form with $r_j=\operatorname{Tr}(\rho\sigma_j)\in\mathbb R$. Positivity [A2] restricts $|r|\le1$, since $(r_x\sigma_x+r_y\sigma_y+r_z\sigma_z)^2=|r|^2I$ and the eigenvalues of $\rho$ are $(1\pm|r|)/2$.

Each $\sigma_j$ is Hermitian with eigenvalues $1,-1$ by step 1.1, so $F_{j,\pm}$ has eigenvalues $1/3,0$ and is positive. For each $j$, $F_{j,+}+F_{j,-}=I/3$; summing over $x,y,z$ gives $I$. Also $F_{j,+}-F_{j,-}=\sigma_j/3$, so each $\sigma_j$ lies in the real span of the effects. Since $I$ is their sum, the basis in step 1.1 shows that the effects span $\mathsf H_2$.

In the coordinate order $(x+,x-,y+,y-,z+,z-)$, direct multiplication and step 1.1 give $G_{(j,s),(k,t)}=\frac1{36}\operatorname{Tr}((I+s\sigma_j)(I+t\sigma_k))=\frac1{18}(1+st\,\delta_{jk})$ for $s,t\in\{+1,-1\}$. Thus the diagonal entries are $1/9$, opposite outcomes on one axis have entry $0$, and distinct axes have entry $1/18$. Let $u=(1,1,1,1,1,1)$ and $v_j=e_{j+}-e_{j-}$. Then $Gu=u/3$, $Gv_j=v_j/9$, and $G$ vanishes on vectors $(s_x,s_x,s_y,s_y,s_z,s_z)$ with $s_x+s_y+s_z=0$. These mutually orthogonal subspaces have dimensions $1,3,2$ and span $\mathbb R^6$.

By [F2] and the eigenspaces in step 3.1, $G^+=3P_u+9\sum_jP_{v_j}$, where $P_u=uu^\mathsf T/6$ and $P_{v_j}=v_jv_j^\mathsf T/2$. The $e_{j+}$ column of $G^+$ is $u/2+9v_j/2$. Applying the canonical-dual formula [F3], using $\sum_{k,\pm}F_{k,\pm}=I$ and $F_{j,+}-F_{j,-}=\sigma_j/3$, gives $D_{j,+}=\frac12I+\frac32\sigma_j$; similarly $D_{j,-}=\frac12I-\frac32\sigma_j$. The probabilities are $p_{j,\pm}=\operatorname{Tr}(\rho F_{j,\pm})=(1\pm r_j)/6$, so $\sum_{j,\pm}p_{j,\pm}D_{j,\pm}=\frac12I+\frac12\sum_jr_j\sigma_j=\rho$, in agreement with [F1].

The frequency vector with $f_{x,+}=1$ and all other entries zero is nonnegative and sums to one. Its output is $D_{x,+}=\frac12I+\frac32\sigma_x$, whose eigenvalues are $2$ and $-1$. It is Hermitian but not positive, so the linear-inversion procedure does not preserve positivity for every frequency vector.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Let $d,m,n\ge1$, let $(F_a)_{a=1}^m$ be a finite POVM on $\mathbb C^d$ whose real span is $\mathsf H_d$, and let $\rho\in\mathsf H_d$ satisfy $\rho\ge0$ and $\operatorname{Tr}\rho=1$. Put $p_a=\operatorname{Tr}(\rho F_a)$, form the canonical dual $D_a$ from the Gram pseudoinverse, and write $D:\mathbb R^m\to\mathsf H_d$ for $D c=\sum_ac_aD_a$. Let $X(f)=\sum_af_aD_a$ be the linear-inversion output and use the induced operator norm $\|D\|_{2\to\mathrm{HS}}=\sup_{\|c\|_2=1}\|Dc\|_{\mathrm{HS}}$.

Then exact probabilities reconstruct the state: $X(p)=\rho$. For every real frequency vector $f\in\mathbb R^m$,
$$
\|X(f)-\rho\|_{\mathrm{HS}}\le\|D\|_{2\to\mathrm{HS}}\|f-p\|_2.
$$
Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space and let $Y_1,\ldots,Y_n:\Omega\to\{1,\ldots,m\}$ be measurable with the independent product law $\mathbb P(Y_1=a_1,\ldots,Y_n=a_n)=\prod_kp_{a_k}$ for every outcome tuple. Define $f_a=n^{-1}\sum_{k=1}^n\mathbf1_{\{Y_k=a\}}$. Then for every $0<\delta<1$,
$$
\mathbb P\!\left(\max_{1\le a\le m}|f_a-p_a|\le\sqrt{\frac{\log(2m/\delta)}{2n}}\right)\ge1-\delta.
$$
Consequently, with probability at least $1-\delta$,
$$
\|X(f)-\rho\|_{\mathrm{HS}}\le\|D\|_{2\to\mathrm{HS}}\sqrt m\sqrt{\frac{\log(2m/\delta)}{2n}}.
$$
These are conditional mathematical statements under the specified product sampling law; no empirical data or calibrated apparatus is asserted.

Let $m\ge1$ and let $F=(F_a)_{a=1}^m$ be a finite family in $\mathsf H_d$. It is informationally complete when its real linear span is all of $\mathsf H_d$. For this positive semidefinite real matrix $G$, let $G^+$ be its unique Moore–Penrose pseudoinverse in $M_m(\mathbb R)$, defined by the four Penrose equations over $\mathbb R$. Define the canonical dual operators $D_a=\sum_{b=1}^m(G^+)_{ba}F_b$ and the reconstruction map $D:\mathbb R^m\to\mathsf H_d$, $D c=\sum_{a=1}^m c_aD_a$. Assume AC, $r\ge1$, and the finite-mode Fock conventions of
[[def-nrqmx-finite-mode-symplectic-data]]. Let $U,V\in M_r(\mathbb C)$ obey
$$UU^*-VV^*=I_r,\qquad UV^T=VU^T,$$
where $^*$ is conjugate transpose and $^T$ is transpose without conjugation.
On the finite Hermite core define
$$a'_j=\sum_k(U_{jk}a_k+V_{jk}a_k^*).$$
Then the $a'_j$ satisfy $[a'_j,(a'_k)^*]=\delta_{jk}I$ and
$[a'_j,a'_k]=0$ on that core. The real matrix
$$S_g=\begin{pmatrix}\operatorname{Re}(U+V)&-\operatorname{Im}(U-V)\\
\operatorname{Im}(U+V)&\operatorname{Re}(U-V)\end{pmatrix}$$
is symplectic in grouped coordinate order $(Q_1,\ldots,Q_r,P_1,\ldots,P_r)$.
There is a unitary $M$ on finite-mode Fock, obtained by transporting an
individual finite symplectic implementer through the Fock–Schrödinger
unitary, such that $M^*aM=a'$ on the transported Schwartz core and
$M^*W(z)M=W(S_g^Tz)$ in grouped Weyl-label order. The transformed vacuum
$M\Omega$ has finite mean number
$$\sum_j\|a_jM\Omega\|^2=\operatorname{tr}(VV^*).$$
No infinite-mode implementability assertion is made.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $r\ge1$, fix a positive real action-scale parameter
$\hbar>0$, and let $H=\mathbb C^r$ with orthonormal basis
$e_1,\ldots,e_r$, and let $\mathcal F_s(H)=\bigoplus_{n\ge0}H^{\otimes_s n}$
be the bosonic Fock space with vacuum $\Omega$ and creation and annihilation
operators $a_j^*,a_j$ from
[[thm-nrqm-fock-and-equilibrium-hilbert-direct-sum-construction]] and
[[lem-nrqm-fock-and-equilibrium-creation-contraction-bounds]]. For
$N=(n_1,\ldots,n_r)\in\mathbb N_0^r$, set
$$|N\rangle:=\prod_{j=1}^r\frac{(a_j^*)^{n_j}}{\sqrt{n_j!}}\Omega.$$
Let $g_N(x)=\prod_{j=1}^r g_{n_j}(x_j)$ be the normalized product Hermite
function from [[thm-nrqm-oscillator-multidimensional-oscillator-completeness]].
Then $(|N\rangle)_N$ and $(g_N)_N$ are complete orthonormal families, and the
map $\mathcal U|N\rangle=g_N$ extends uniquely to a unitary
$$\mathcal U:\mathcal F_s(\mathbb C^r)\longrightarrow L^2(\mathbb R^r).$$
On the algebraic finite-particle span, $\mathcal U a_j\mathcal U^{-1}$ and
$\mathcal U a_j^*\mathcal U^{-1}$ are respectively
$(x_j+\partial_{x_j})/\sqrt2$ and $(x_j-\partial_{x_j})/\sqrt2$ on product
Hermite functions. In particular the quadratures
$$Q_j=\sqrt{\hbar/2}(a_j+a_j^*),\qquad P_j=-i\sqrt{\hbar/2}(a_j-a_j^*)$$
act there as multiplication by $\sqrt\hbar x_j$ and as
$-i\sqrt\hbar\,\partial_{x_j}$, respectively. These are core identities;
they do not assert that a finite number cutoff preserves the canonical
commutation relations.

Assume countable choice. For $n\ge1$, $t>0$, and $\xi\in\mathbb R^n$,
$$\mathcal F(e^{-\pi t|x|^2})(\xi)=t^{-n/2}e^{-\pi|\xi|^2/t}.$$
Every polynomial times a positive real Gaussian is absolutely integrable.

Assume countable choice. For complex $C^1$ functions $u,v$ on $[a,b]$, $a<b$, Lebesgue integration gives $\int_a^b u'v=u(b)v(b)-u(a)v(a)-\int_a^b uv'$ and $\int_a^b u'=u(b)-u(a)$. If instead $u,v\in C^1(\mathbb R;\mathbb C)$, $u'v,uv'\in L^1(\mathbb R)$ and $u(x)v(x)\to0$ as $x\to\pm\infty$, then $\int_{\mathbb R}u'v=-\int_{\mathbb R}uv'$.

For every $m\in\mathbb N$ and every real $a>0$,
$$\frac{x^m}{\exp(ax)}\longrightarrow0\qquad(x\to+\infty).$$

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $U,V \subseteq \mathbb R^n$ be open and let $T : U \to V$ be a
$C^1$ diffeomorphism. If $f : V \to \mathbb C$ belongs to $L^1(\lambda_n)$,
then
$$ \int_V f(y)\,d\lambda_n(y) = \int_U f(T(x))\,|\det DT(x)|\,d\lambda_n(x). $$

derivations.claim:
Apply [F5] to $x\mapsto e^{-s}x$ and $|f|^2$ to get
$$\int_{\mathbb R}|U_sf(x)|^2dx =\int_{\mathbb R}|f(y)|^2dy,$$
so $U_s$ is unitary. The chain rule for $Q=\sqrt\hbar x$ and
$P=-i\sqrt\hbar\partial_x$ gives
$U_s^*aU_s=\cosh(s)a+\sinh(s)a^*$. The scalar pair obeys
$|u|^2-|v|^2=1$ and $uv=vu$. For the $N$-mode product take
$U_N=uI_N$ and $V_N=vI_N$; the finite Bogoliubov result [F1] supplies an
implementer for these coefficients. Write
$\psi_s(x)=U_sg_0(x)=e^{-s/2}\pi^{-1/4}e^{-e^{-2s}x^2/2}$. Then
$$a\psi_s=\frac{1-e^{-2s}}{\sqrt2}x\psi_s.$$
By [F4] with $A=1,B=0$, $\int e^{-y^2}dy=\sqrt\pi$. On $[-R,R]$,
integration by parts gives
$$\int_{-R}^R y^2e^{-y^2}dy=\left[-\frac y2e^{-y^2}\right]_{-R}^R+\frac12\int_{-R}^Re^{-y^2}dy.$$
The boundary term tends to zero by [F4], so
$\int y^2|g_0(y)|^2dy=1/2$. The substitution $y=e^{-s}x$ in [F5] gives
$$\int_{\mathbb R}x^2|\psi_s(x)|^2dx=e^{2s}\int_{\mathbb R}y^2|g_0(y)|^2dy=e^{2s}/2.$$
Consequently
$$\|a\psi_s\|^2=\frac{(1-e^{-2s})^2}{2}\frac{e^{2s}}2=\sinh^2(s).$$
By [F3], the $N$-mode Fock–Schrödinger unitary sends its vacuum
$\Omega_N$ to $g_0^{\otimes N}$. On $L^2(\mathbb R^N)$ define
$$[U_s^{(N)}f](x_1,\ldots,x_N)=e^{-Ns/2} f(e^{-s}x_1,\ldots,e^{-s}x_N).$$
The $C^1$ change-of-variables formula [F5] in $\mathbb R^N$ gives
$\|U_s^{(N)}f\|_2=\|f\|_2$, so this is unitary. It is the
product of the one-mode dilations, and the coordinatewise chain rule gives
$U_s^{(N)*}a_jU_s^{(N)}=u a_j+v a_j^*$ for each $j$. The finite Bogoliubov
statement [F1] also supplies an implementer for this coefficient pair. Put
$\Psi_N=(U_s\Omega)^{\otimes N}$ under the same identification; its $j$th
number expectation is the one-mode value $\|a\psi_s\|^2=\sinh^2(s)$ already
computed above. The number operator is the sum of the $N$ mode number
operators, so linearity gives
$$\langle\Psi_N,\mathcal N_N\Psi_N\rangle=N\sinh^2(s).$$
The product unitary exists because it is the tensor product of finitely many
copies of this unitary. The same coefficient pair is covered by the finite Bogoliubov
statement [F2]; no infinite product is taken.

In Schrödinger coordinates, $\Omega=g_0$ and
$U_sg_0(x)=e^{-s/2}\pi^{-1/4}e^{-e^{-2s}x^2/2}$. Set
$A=(1+e^{-2s})/2>0$. By [F4] with $B=0$,
$$\int_{\mathbb R}e^{-Ax^2}dx=\sqrt{\pi/A}=\sqrt{\frac{2\pi}{1+e^{-2s}}}.$$
Hence
$$\langle g_0,U_sg_0\rangle=\pi^{-1/2}e^{-s/2}\sqrt{\frac{2\pi}{1+e^{-2s}}}=\sqrt{\frac{2}{e^s+e^{-s}}}=\frac1{\sqrt{\cosh s}}.$$
Since $U_s$ and $g_0$ are real and positive here, this is also the overlap
magnitude; the formula holds for every real $s$. Product inner products
factor over the $N$ modes, yielding
$$|\langle\Omega_N,\Psi_N\rangle|=(\cosh s)^{-N/2}.$$
For $s\ne0$, $\cosh s>1$, so this magnitude tends to zero as $N\to\infty$.
Together with step 1.1 this proves only the stated finite-$N$ divergence and
overlap limit. Finite-dimensional implementation does not itself provide an
infinite-mode implementer, and this example does not prove that none exists.

Assume Countable Choice and let $d\ge1$ be an integer. Work in
$H=L^2(\mathbb R^d;\mathbb C)$ with
$\langle u,v\rangle=\int_{\mathbb R^d}u\overline v$, linear in the first
variable, using the quotient and complex-function conventions of the linked
Euclidean $L^2$ definitions. Fix real scalars $m>0$, $\hbar>0$, and $q$.
Let $A=(A_1,\ldots,A_d)\in C^\infty(\mathbb R^d;\mathbb R^d)$ be real and
let $V\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\mathbb R^d;\mathbb R)$ satisfy
$V\ge-v_0$ almost everywhere for some finite $v_0\ge0$. Put
$\mathscr D=C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^d;\mathbb C)$ and, for $u\in\mathscr D$,
define
$$\Pi_j^A u=-i\hbar\,\partial_j u-qA_j u\qquad (1\le j\le d).$$
For $u,v\in\mathscr D$ define the sesquilinear form
$$q_{A,V}(u,v)=\frac1{2m}\sum_{j=1}^d\langle\Pi_j^A u,\Pi_j^A v\rangle+\int_{\mathbb R^d}V(x)u(x)\overline{v(x)}\,dx,$$
and write $q_{A,V}[u]=q_{A,V}(u,u)$. Each integral is finite: the test
functions and their magnetic derivatives are bounded with compact support,
and $V$ is integrable on compact sets. The form is Hermitian, densely
defined, and bounded below by $-v_0\|u\|_2^2$.

For $\varepsilon_0>0$ define its shifted form norm by
$$\|u\|_{q,v_0,\varepsilon_0}^2=q_{A,V}[u]+(v_0+\varepsilon_0)\|u\|_2^2.$$
The form is **closable** when every sequence $(u_n)\subset\mathscr D$ with
$\|u_n\|_2\to0$ and
$\|u_n-u_m\|_{q,v_0,\varepsilon_0}\to0$ as $n,m\to\infty$ also satisfies
$\|u_n\|_{q,v_0,\varepsilon_0}\to0$. This condition is independent of the
choice of $\varepsilon_0>0$. When it holds, the **closed form closure** is the
completion of $\mathscr D$ in this norm, identified with its $L^2$ limits;
the corresponding closed form is denoted $\overline q_{A,V}$.

Let $n\ge1$ and $f\in L^1(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C)$, with the componentwise integral and quotient conventions of [[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]], [[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]] and [[def-l-one-of-a-measure]]. Define
$$\widehat f(\xi)=\mathcal Ff(\xi):=\int_{\mathbb R^n}f(x)\exp(-2\pi i x\cdot\xi)\,dx,\qquad \xi\in\mathbb R^n.$$
Here $x\cdot\xi=\sum_{j=1}^n x_j\xi_j$, Lebesgue measure is used, and the exponential is [[def-complex-exponential]]. Its unit modulus follows from [[cor-complex-exponential-cartesian-form-modulus-and-eulers-identity]]. The integral is evaluated using any measurable representative. Absolute convergence and representative independence are the obligations discharged by [[lem-l-one-fourier-transform-is-well-defined]]. The output is a function defined at every frequency, not merely an almost-everywhere class. At frequency zero the formula reads $\widehat f(0)=\int f$. No choice selection of representatives for a family of classes is part of this definition.

Assume countable choice and let $n\ge1$. Fourier transformation on Schwartz space extends uniquely to a surjective complex-linear isometry $\mathcal F_2:L^2(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C)\to L^2(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C)$. It preserves the first-variable-linear inner product, and hence is unitary.
Assume countable choice. The Fourier transform is a topological automorphism of $\mathcal S(\mathbb R^n)$, with $\mathcal F^2=R$ and $\mathcal F^{-1}=R\mathcal F$, where $Rf(x)=f(-x)$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]), let $a,b\ge1$, and let $\lambda_n$ denote Lebesgue measure on $\mathcal L(\mathbb R^n)$ as defined in [[def-lebesgue-measure-and-the-lebesgue-sigma-algebra]] and completed from Borel measure as in [[cor-lebesgue-sigma-algebra-is-the-completion-of-borel-lebesgue-measure]]. The product measure $\lambda_a\times\lambda_b$ exists by [[thm-sigma-finite-product-measure-exists-is-rectangular-and-is-unique]], and under $\mathbb R^{a+b}=\mathbb R^a\times\mathbb R^b$, $\lambda_{a+b}$ is its completion ([[thm-euclidean-lebesgue-measure-is-the-completion-of-the-product-of-lebesgue-measures]]). Write $H_a=L^2(\mathbb R^a,\lambda_a)$ and $H_b=L^2(\mathbb R^b,\lambda_b)$, with $L^2$ understood as the almost-everywhere quotient of square-integrable measurable functions ([[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]]). Then there is a unique linear isometry

$$\Theta:H_a\widehat\otimes H_b\longrightarrow L^2(\mathbb R^{a+b})$$

with $\Theta(f\otimes g)(x,y)=f(x)g(y)$ for all $f\in H_a$, $g\in H_b$ and a.e. $(x,y)$, and $\Theta$ is onto: it is a surjective linear isometry, hence unitary. Vector-valued or spin factors follow by finite component sums. No identification of non-Euclidean product measures is asserted.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to \mathbb C$ belong to
$L^1(\mu \times \nu)$. Then:

1. for $\mu$-almost every $x$, the section $f_x$ belongs to $L^1(\nu)$;
2. for $\nu$-almost every $y$, the section $f^y$ belongs to $L^1(\mu)$;
3. after assigning the value $0$ on the exceptional parameter sets, the
   section-integral functions are integrable; and
4. the three integrals agree:
$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Assume the Axioms of Countable Choice and Dependent Choice. For $F,G\in AC[a,b]$,
$$\int_a^bFG'+\int_a^bF'G=F(b)G(b)-F(a)G(a).$$

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Fix real parameters $m>0$, $\omega>0$, $\hbar>0$, put $\ell:=\sqrt{\hbar/(m\omega)}>0$, and let $g_0,P,(g_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ be the Hermite data of [[thm-nrqm-oscillator-hermite-recurrence]] in $L^2(\mathbb R,dy)$, so that $(g_n)$ is a complete orthonormal family by [[thm-nrqm-oscillator-hermite-completeness]]. Define

$$D:L^2(\mathbb R,dy)\to L^2(\mathbb R,dx),\qquad (Df)(x):=\ell^{-1/2}f(x/\ell),$$

and let $A$ be the self-adjoint diagonal operator of [[lem-nrqm-oscillator-diagonal-adjoint-and-graph-core-lemma]] for the complete orthonormal family $(g_n)$ and the eigenvalues $\lambda_n=2n+1$, with the core $P$ and spectrum $\{2n+1:n\in\mathbb N\}$ ([[thm-nrqm-oscillator-diagonal-spectrum]]).

Then:

(a) $D$ is a linear isometry of $L^2(\mathbb R,dy)$ onto $L^2(\mathbb R,dx)$ with two-sided inverse $(D^{-1}g)(y)=\ell^{1/2}g(\ell y)$; the functions $\psi_n:=Dg_n$, $\psi_n(x)=\ell^{-1/2}g_n(x/\ell)$, form a complete orthonormal family of $L^2(\mathbb R,dx)$;

(b) the operator

$$H_{\mathrm{osc}}:=\frac{\hbar\omega}{2}\,DAD^{-1},\qquad D(H_{\mathrm{osc}}):=\{f\in L^2(\mathbb R,dx):D^{-1}f\in D(A)\},$$

is self-adjoint, satisfies $H_{\mathrm{osc}}\psi_n=\hbar\omega(n+\tfrac12)\psi_n$ for every $n$, and has

$$D(H_{\mathrm{osc}})=\Bigl\{f:\sum_n\hbar^2\omega^2(n+\tfrac12)^2|c_n|^2<\infty\Bigr\},\qquad H_{\mathrm{osc}}f=\sum_n\hbar\omega(n+\tfrac12)c_n\psi_n,$$

where $c_n:=\langle D^{-1}f,g_n\rangle=\langle f,\psi_n\rangle$; its spectrum is $\sigma(H_{\mathrm{osc}})=\{\hbar\omega(n+\tfrac12):n\in\mathbb N\}$, its ground energy is $\hbar\omega/2$ with eigenvector $\psi_0$, and $\langle H_{\mathrm{osc}}f,f\rangle\ge\frac{\hbar\omega}{2}\|f\|^2$ for every $f\in D(H_{\mathrm{osc}})$;

(c) $D(P)=\operatorname{span}\{\psi_n\}$ is a core for $H_{\mathrm{osc}}$, and for every polynomial $p$ the function $f:=D(pg_0)$ is $C^\infty$ on $\mathbb R$ with

$$H_{\mathrm{osc}}f=-\frac{\hbar^2}{2m}f''+\frac{m\omega^2}{2}x^2f$$

pointwise on $\mathbb R$;

(d) for every $f\in D(H_{\mathrm{osc}})$ and every test function $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R)$,

$$\int_{\mathbb R}(H_{\mathrm{osc}}f)(x)\varphi(x)\,dx=\int_{\mathbb R}f(x)\Bigl(-\frac{\hbar^2}{2m}\varphi''(x)+\frac{m\omega^2}{2}x^2\varphi(x)\Bigr)dx,$$

so $H_{\mathrm{osc}}$ is the self-adjoint realization of the differential expression $-\frac{\hbar^2}{2m}\frac{d^2}{dx^2}+\frac{m\omega^2}{2}x^2$ in the weak sense; no identification of $D(H_{\mathrm{osc}})$ with a separately defined maximal differential-operator domain is asserted.

All parameters enter as positive real numbers; no physical identification of $m,\omega,\hbar$ with measured quantities is made.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $U,V \subseteq \mathbb R^n$ be open and let $T : U \to V$ be a
$C^1$ diffeomorphism. If $f : V \to \mathbb C$ belongs to $L^1(\lambda_n)$,
then
$$ \int_V f(y)\,d\lambda_n(y) = \int_U f(T(x))\,|\det DT(x)|\,d\lambda_n(x). $$

Assume the Axioms of Countable Choice and Dependent Choice. For $F,G\in AC[a,b]$,
$$\int_a^bFG'+\int_a^bF'G=F(b)G(b)-F(a)G(a).$$

Let $\beta$ be the standard flat function. The **standard smooth step function** is
$$ \sigma(t):=\frac{\beta(t)}{\beta(t)+\beta(1-t)}. $$
Because $\beta$ is smooth and positive on $(0,\infty)$, the denominator is positive on $(0,1)$, while $\sigma(t)=0$ for $t\le 0$ and $\sigma(t)=1$ for $t\ge 1$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Assume Countable Choice. Let $n\ge1$, $k\in\mathbb N_0$, $1\le p<\infty$ and
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$. Then the compactly supported smooth
functions $C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb K)$ are dense in
$W^{k,p}(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb K)$: for every
$u\in W^{k,p}(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb K)$ and every $\delta>0$ there is
$\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb K)$ with
$$\|\varphi-u\|_{W^{k,p}(\mathbb R^n)}<\delta.$$
No such norm-density assertion is made for $p=\infty$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let
$(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space and let
$L^2(\mu)$ be the quotient of $\mathcal L^2(\mu)$ by the almost-everywhere zero
functions ([[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]]), with the quotient
norm $\|\cdot\|_2$ ([[thm-the-l-p-norm-descends-to-the-quotient-and-makes-l-p-a-normed-space]]).

1. On **real** $L^2(\mu)$ the formula
   $$\langle f,g\rangle:=\int fg\,d\mu$$is a well-defined inner product, linear in both variables, positive definite, with $\langle f,f\rangle=\|f\|_2^2$; with it $L^2(\mu)$ is a real Hilbert space ([[def-hilbert-space]]). 2. On **complex** $L^2(\mu;\mathbb C)$ the formula$$\langle f,g\rangle:=\int f\overline g\,d\mu$$
   is a well-defined inner product, linear in the first variable and
   conjugate-linear in the second, positive definite, with
   $\langle f,f\rangle=\|f\|_2^2$; with it $L^2(\mu;\mathbb C)$ is a complex
   Hilbert space ([[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]]).

In both cases the inner product induces exactly the established quotient
$L^2$ norm.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. All functions below have domain $X$. Let $f$ and $(f_n)$ be measurable complex-valued functions such that
$f_n\to f$ almost everywhere and $|f_n|\le g$ almost everywhere for a single
nonnegative measurable function $g$ with $\int g\,d\mu<+\infty$. Then
$f\in L^1(\mu)$,
$$\int|f_n-f|\,d\mu\longrightarrow0,$$
and hence
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\longrightarrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Let $X$ be a set and let $R \subseteq X \times X$ be a binary relation on $X$.
Call $R$ **entire on $X$** when

$$\text{for every } x \in X \text{ there is } y \in X \text{ with } x \mathbin{R} y .$$

The **Axiom of Dependent Choice**, written $\mathrm{DC}$, is the following
statement.

> For every nonempty set $X$, every relation $R$ entire on $X$, and every
> $a \in X$, there is a function $x : \mathbb{N} \to X$ (A function is a relation $f$ with $(a,b) \in f$ and $(a,c) \in f$ implying $b = c$; $f : A \to B$, the value $f(a)$, domain and codomain,
> The natural numbers $\mathbb{N}$ (von Neumann)) with
> $$x_0 = a \qquad \text{and} \qquad x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1} \ \text{ for every } n \in \mathbb{N}.$$

Here a sequence in $X$ means a function from $\mathbb{N}$ to $X$, not necessarily
a real-valued sequence. As everywhere in this library $\mathbb{N}$ contains $0$, and the sequence is
indexed from $0$; the term $x_0$ is the prescribed starting point $a$ and every
later term is related to its predecessor.

**What DC adds to what came before.** Choice function and
The Axiom of Choice select one element from each member of a family that is
fixed in advance, and The Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$) does the same for a family indexed
by $\mathbb{N}$. In both, the family is given before any selection is made. DC is
the principle needed when the $n$-th set to select from is not known until the
first $n$ selections have been made: here the admissible values of $x_{n+1}$ are
exactly the $R$-successors of $x_n$, so the family being chosen from is built
along the choosing. Thus the displayed recursion is directly an instance of
DC; it is not itself an application of the fixed-family formulation of
countable choice. This observation concerns the input to the two axioms and
makes no claim about a nonimplication between them.

**The starting point may be dropped.** The formally weaker statement obtained by
deleting the clause $x_0 = a$ — for every nonempty $X$ and every entire $R$ there
is a sequence with $x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ for all $n$ — is an immediate
consequence of the form above, since $X$ is nonempty and any of its elements may
be taken as $a$. Conversely, assume the start-free form, and fix $X$, $R$ and $a$ as above. Let $P$ be the set of all functions $p:k\to X$ with nonzero $k\in\mathbb N$, $p(0)=a$, and $p(i)\mathbin R p(i+1)$ whenever $i+1<k$. It is a set by Separation inside $\mathcal P(\mathbb N\times X)$ (The power set $\mathcal{P}(x) = \{\, z : z \subseteq x \,\}$, The Cartesian product $A \times B := \{\, z \in \mathcal{P}(\mathcal{P}(A \cup B)) : \exists a \in A\ \exists b \in B\ z = (a,b) \,\}$, The Axiom Schema of Separation: for each formula $\varphi$, $\forall \bar p\,\forall x\,\exists y\,\forall z\,(z \in y \leftrightarrow (z \in x \wedge \varphi(z,\bar p)))$); a natural is the set of its predecessors (On $\mathbb{N}$ the order is membership: $m < n \iff m \in n$). The singleton path $\{(0,a)\}$ lies in $P$.

On $P$ let $p\mathbin S q$ mean that $q$ extends $p$ by exactly one new last entry. This relation is entire: for one particular $p:k\to X$, write $k=j+1$ (Every nonzero natural number is a successor); an $R$-successor $y$ of $p(j)$ exists, and $q=p\cup\{(k,y)\}$ is the required extension. This is existential instantiation for that path, not a simultaneous choice of successors. Start-free DC now supplies a sequence $(p_n)$ with $p_n\mathbin S p_{n+1}$; its first path need not be the singleton path, but every path in $P$ already starts at $a$.

Their graphs are nested. By induction (The principle of mathematical induction), $p_n$ has at least $n+1$ entries: the initial path is nonempty, and every step adds one entry. Hence $x=\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb N}p_n$ is a function with domain $\mathbb N$ and values in $X$. Indeed, nestedness makes all common values agree, every natural index eventually lies in a path, and no path has indices outside $\mathbb N$. Each path starts at $a$, so $x(0)=a$; for any $i$, a sufficiently long path contains both $i$ and $i+1$, giving $x(i)\mathbin R x(i+1)$. Replacement and Union form this union of the sequence of graphs. Thus the start-free and prescribed-start forms are equivalent in ZF. Every use below retains the prescribed-start convention.

**$R$ need not be an order and the terms need not be distinct.** What DC delivers
is a sequence, that is a function $\mathbb{N} \to X$, not a chain in the
order-theoretic sense (Chain in a poset). The relation may be symmetric, and the
sequence may repeat a value or be constant; all that is asserted is
$x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ at every index.

Assume the Axioms of Countable Choice and Dependent Choice. For $F,G\in AC[a,b]$,
$$\int_a^bFG'+\int_a^bF'G=F(b)G(b)-F(a)G(a).$$

derivations.claim:
On the dense tensor core $a(x)b(y)$ with $a,b\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R)$,
$\mathcal F_y$ is the identity on the first factor and the unitary Fourier
transform on the second, by [F2] and the Euclidean $L^2$ product identification
in [F2]. It extends uniquely to a unitary on $L^2(\mathbb R^2)$. For each
$k$, translation $x=\xi+x_0(k)$ preserves the $x$-integral by [F4]; Fubini
then shows that $Wg(\xi,k)=g(\xi+x_0(k),k)$ is an isometry with inverse
$W^{-1}h(x,k)=h(x-x_0(k),k)$. Hence $U=W\mathcal F_y$ is unitary.

Let $u\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^2)$ and write
$F(\xi,k)=Uu(\xi,k)$. For each fixed $k$, $F(\cdot,k)$ is smooth and
compactly supported in $\xi$. Plancherel in $y$, the derivative identity
in [F2], and the substitution $x=\xi+x_0(k)$ give
$$q_B[u]=\int_{\mathbb R^2}\left(\frac{\hbar^2}{2m}|\partial_\xi F|^2+\frac{(qB)^2}{2m}\xi^2|F|^2\right)d\xi\,dk.$$
For a compactly supported smooth $g(\xi)$, put
$Lg=-\hbar^2g''/(2m)+m\omega_c^2\xi^2g/2\in L^2$. Integrating by parts
twice on a finite interval containing the support of $g$ gives
$\langle Lg,\psi_n\rangle=E_n\langle g,\psi_n\rangle$, since
$L\psi_n=E_n\psi_n$ and the boundary terms vanish. Completeness and Parseval
therefore give
$$\sum_{n=0}^\infty E_n^2|\langle g,\psi_n\rangle|^2=\|Lg\|_2^2<\infty.$$
The exact domain characterization in [F3] now implies
$g\in D(H_{\mathrm{osc}})$, and its diagonal action gives
$H_{\mathrm{osc}}g=Lg$. Hence
$$\langle H_{\mathrm{osc}}g,g\rangle=\sum_{n=0}^\infty E_n|\langle g,\psi_n\rangle|^2.$$
Integration by parts also identifies the left side with
$$\frac1{2m}\left(\hbar^2\|g'\|_2^2+(qB)^2\|\xi g\|_2^2\right).$$
Apply this identity to $F(\cdot,k)$ for almost every $k$. Tonelli [F6]
permits integrating the nonnegative series, so the displayed core form is
the coefficient form on every transformed core vector.

For $N<\infty$ and $f_0,\ldots,f_N\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R_k)$,
$F_N(\xi,k)=\sum_{n=0}^Nf_n(k)\psi_n(\xi)$ has inverse
$$U^{-1}F_N(x,y)=\frac1{\sqrt{2\pi}}\sum_{n=0}^N\int_{\mathbb R}e^{iky}f_n(k)\psi_n\!\left(x-\frac{\hbar k}{qB}\right)dk.$$
Write $v:=U^{-1}F_N$. The integrands have compact $k$-support and are Schwartz in $x$ uniformly
there by the Hermite form in [F3]; differentiating under the integral and
integrating by parts in $k$ show rapid decay in $y$, so the inverse is
Schwartz. Define
$$\chi_R(x,y)=\prod_{s\in\{x,y\}}\sigma(2-s/R)\sigma(2+s/R),$$
using [F5]. These cutoffs are one on $[-R,R]^2$, vanish outside
$[-2R,2R]^2$, and have $|\nabla\chi_R|\le C/R$. For each covariant
derivative,
$$\Pi_j^A(\chi_Rv)=\chi_R\Pi_j^Av-i\hbar(\partial_j\chi_R)v.$$
Take integer $R\ge1$. The step-function bounds in [F5] give $0\le\chi_R\le1$, and for every fixed $(x,y)$, $\chi_R(x,y)=1$ once $R\ge\max\{|x|,|y|\}$, so $\chi_R\to1$ pointwise. Since $v$ is Schwartz and $A=(0,Bx)$ is linear, $\Pi_1^Av=-i\hbar\partial_xv$ and $\Pi_2^Av=-i\hbar\partial_yv-qBxv$ are Schwartz and belong to $L^2(\mathbb R^2)$. For each $w\in\{v,\Pi_1^Av,\Pi_2^Av\}$, the functions $|(\chi_R-1)w|^2$ are measurable, tend pointwise to zero, and are bounded by the single measurable $L^1$ majorant $|w|^2$. Applying [F9] on the Lebesgue measure space $\mathbb R^2$ gives $\|(\chi_R-1)w\|_2\to0$. The derivative-cutoff term separately satisfies $\|\hbar(\partial_j\chi_R)v\|_2\le C\hbar\|v\|_2/R\to0$. Thus the displayed product identity and the triangle inequality give $\|\Pi_j^A(\chi_Rv-v)\|_2\to0$ for both $j$, as well as $\|\chi_Rv-v\|_2\to0$.
The form identity of step 2.1 also holds for Schwartz functions: the Fourier and shear maps preserve Schwartz regularity, and for each Schwartz $g(\xi)$ one has $Lg\in L^2$; its integration-by-parts pairings with the polynomial-Gaussian $\psi_n$ have vanishing boundary terms at both infinities. The same Parseval calculation and exact diagonal operator-domain criterion in [F3] therefore give $g\in D(H_{\mathrm{osc}})$ and the same oscillator energy identity. All resulting nonnegative energies can again be integrated by [F6]. Apply this extended identity to the Schwartz difference $\chi_Rv-v$. Its weighted coefficient norm squared is exactly $\frac1{2m}\sum_{j=1}^2\|\Pi_j^A(\chi_Rv-v)\|_2^2$, which tends to zero by the preceding bounds. Since $\chi_Rv\in C_c^\infty$, each $F_N$ therefore lies in the weighted-norm closure of the transformed original core, without assuming closability in advance. Finite coefficient families are dense
in the weighted target: truncate its convergent nonnegative series, then
approximate the remaining finitely many $L^2(k)$ coefficients by
$C_c^\infty(k)$ using [F7].

Let $\mathcal K_E$ be the coefficient space
$\{(f_n):\sum_nE_n\|f_n\|_2^2<\infty\}$ with squared norm
$\sum_nE_n\|f_n\|_2^2$, and let
$J:\mathcal K_E\hookrightarrow L^2(\mathbb N_0\times\mathbb R,d\#\,dk)$
be the identity inclusion. Step 2.1 maps the transformed core isometrically
into $\mathcal K_E$. Since $E_n\ge E_0=\hbar\omega_c/2>0$, $J$ is
continuous and injective, with
$\|Jf\|_2^2\le E_0^{-1}\sum_nE_n\|f_n\|_2^2$. The coefficient map is
unitary on the underlying $L^2$ space by [F2] and [F3]. Thus
$q_B[u]\ge E_0\|u\|_2^2$ on the core. For every $\varepsilon>0$,
$$q_B[u]\le q_B[u]+\varepsilon\|u\|_2^2\le(1+\varepsilon/E_0)q_B[u],$$
so each shifted form norm is equivalent to $q_B[u]^{1/2}$. Suppose a core
sequence is Cauchy in $q_B[u]^{1/2}$ and tends to zero in $L^2$. Its
weighted coefficient image converges in $\mathcal K_E$ to
some $f$; unweighted $L^2$ convergence and continuity of $J$ give $Jf=0$.
Injectivity of $J$ gives $f=0$, so $q_B[u]\to0$ along that sequence.
The equivalence above then gives convergence to zero in the defining shifted
form norm, proving closability of the core form. By [F8] the
target is complete, so the isometric image of the form completion is
closed there. Step 3.1 places a dense subspace of that target in the image;
hence the image is the whole weighted space and the form closure is exactly
the stated one.

citations.quote: Let $M$ be a smooth manifold, let $r\ge1$, and let $P:M\to M_r(\mathbb C)$ be a $C^2$ orthogonal projector of constant rank $m$, with $1\le m\le r$. Its image bundle is $E_P=\{(x,v):P(x)v=v\}$, with the projected connection $\nabla s=P\,ds$ of [[def-nrqmx-smooth-projector-bundle]]. The **determinant line bundle** is the complex line bundle

For the projector of [[def-nrqmx-determinant-line-projector]], $Q(x)=\bigwedge^mP(x)$ is a $C^2$ orthogonal projector of rank one. Its range is exactly $\det E_P(x)=\bigwedge^m\operatorname{im}P(x)$, so these ranges form the determinant line bundle.

Let $M$, $d$, and $P$ satisfy [[def-nrqmx-smooth-projector-bundle]], with constant rank $r$. Write $U(r)=\{g\in\mathbb C^{r\times r}:g^*g=gg^*=I_r\}$ for the unitary group. The curvature of the projected connection $\nabla=P\,d$, as an endomorphism-valued two-form on $\mathbb C^d$, is
$$F=P(dP\wedge dP)P.$$
For any local $C^2$ orthonormal frame $V:U\to\mathbb C^{d\times r}$ with $V^*V=I_r$ and $P=VV^*$, its connection matrix $A=V^*dV$ is anti-Hermitian and its curvature matrix is $F_{\mathrm{fr}}=dA+A\wedge A=V^*FV$. If $V'=Vg$ for a $C^2$ map $g:U\to U(r)$, then $A'=g^{-1}Ag+g^{-1}dg$ and $F'_{\mathrm{fr}}=g^{-1}F_{\mathrm{fr}}g$. Along every $C^2$ path, Kato transport is unitary and intertwines the endpoint projectors.

derivations.claim: Because the columns of $V$ are orthonormal, $w=v_1\wedge\cdots\wedge v_m$ has unit norm and spans the determinant line. Differentiating by the product rule gives $dw=\sum_j v_1\wedge\cdots\wedge dv_j\wedge\cdots\wedge v_m$. The projected connection applies $P$ to each differentiated factor. Since $P\,dv_j=\sum_a v_a A_{aj}$, each term with $a\ne j$ vanishes from a repeated wedge factor, while the $a=j$ term is $A_{jj}w$. Summing gives $Qdw=(\operatorname{tr}A)w$, so the determinant connection form is $a=\operatorname{tr}A$.

A line connection with scalar one-form $a$ has curvature $da+a\wedge a=da$, since a scalar one-form wedges with itself to zero. By [F3], $\operatorname{tr}F=\operatorname{tr}(dA)+\operatorname{tr}(A\wedge A)$. In coordinates, $\operatorname{tr}(A\wedge A)=\sum_{i,j}A_{ij}\wedge A_{ji}=0$: diagonal terms vanish and each off-diagonal pair cancels because one-forms anticommute. Therefore $da=d\operatorname{tr}A=\operatorname{tr}F_{\mathrm{fr}}=\operatorname{tr}(V^*FV)$. Finally, since $PFP=F$ and $VV^*=P$, cyclicity of finite-dimensional trace gives $\operatorname{tr}(V^*FV)=\operatorname{tr}(FVV^*)=\operatorname{tr}(FP)=\operatorname{tr}F$.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
**(a) Finite oscillator-mode data.** Choose an integer $M\ge1$, the one-particle mode space $\mathfrak h=\mathbb C^M$ with a declared orthonormal mode basis $e_1,\ldots,e_M$, and the bosonic Fock space $\mathcal F_s(\mathfrak h)=\bigoplus_{n\ge0}\mathfrak h^{\otimes_s n}$ with vacuum $\Omega$. Here $\mathfrak h^{\otimes_s n}$ is the range of the orthogonal symmetrizer in the completed $n$-fold Hilbert tensor product, with the zero-particle sector $\mathbb C\Omega$. For $\mathbf n=(n_1,\ldots,n_M)\in\mathbb N_0^M$, let $|\mathbf n\rangle$ be the normalized occupation vector. The mode operators are dimensionless and on the finite-particle core satisfy $a_j|\mathbf n\rangle=\sqrt{n_j}|\mathbf n-\mathbf e_j\rangle$ and $a_j^*|\mathbf n\rangle=\sqrt{n_j+1}|\mathbf n+\mathbf e_j\rangle$, with the first expression zero if $n_j=0$. The Fock space is infinite-dimensional for each $M\ge1$; no particle-number cutoff or tensor factorization of an individual photon into position and spin is part of this assignment.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and countable choice wherever the finite-mode Fock, quadrature, and implementability suppliers require them. These are mathematical hypotheses of the assignment, not physical postulates.

**Mode-frequency data.** For each selected mode $j$, choose a positive angular frequency $\omega_j>0$ in seconds$^{-1}$; the assigned one-quantum energy scale is $\hbar\omega_j$ joules. These are parameters of the finite-mode model, not measured frequencies.

**(b) Finite atom and dipole data.** Choose $d\ge1$, an atomic Hilbert space $\mathcal H_A=\mathbb C^d$, a Hermitian atomic energy matrix $H_A$ in joules, Hermitian compressed dipole matrices $D_j$ in coulomb-metres, and real mode field scales $\mathcal E_j$ in volts per metre. The matrix elements of $G_j:=\mathcal E_jD_j/\hbar$ have units seconds$^{-1}$, where $\hbar>0$ is retained in joule-seconds. The finite matrices and scales are chosen model data. If they are obtained by compressing a larger atomic model, that compression's error is a separate model input and is not bounded here.

The assigned dipole interaction core expression is $V_{\mathrm{dip}}=-\sum_{j=1}^{M}\mathcal E_jD_j\otimes(a_j+a_j^*)$ in the ordered space $\mathcal H_A\otimes\mathcal F_s(\mathfrak h)$; each summand has units joules and acts on the finite-particle core. This clause assigns the finite matrix expression only. It does not assert that an arbitrary such sum has a self-adjoint realization or generate an evolution; any dynamical use must state and justify its operator domain. The Jaynes–Cummings supplier below gives one specific self-adjoint direct-sum realization.

**(c) Mode transformations.** A finite mode-coordinate change is assigned only when its finite Bogoliubov matrices satisfy the exact hypotheses of the finite-mode implementability statement: for $U,V\in M_M(\mathbb C)$, $UU^*-VV^*=I_M$ and $UV^T=VU^T$. The resulting unitary acts on this finite-mode Fock space. The statement assumes the Axiom of Choice; this is a mathematical assumption, not a physical law. No infinite-mode implementability follows.

**(d) Detector outcome models.** A detector's outcome space $(X,\Sigma)$ and POVM $E:\Sigma\to\mathcal B(\mathcal H_A\otimes\mathcal F_s(\mathfrak h))$ are declared model data: each $E(B)$ is bounded and positive, $E(X)=I$, and $E$ is countably additive in the weak operator topology. For a state $\rho$, the assigned probability is $\operatorname{tr}(\rho E(B))$ under the framework's stated measurement convention. An ideal number-resolving model on the field has outcomes $\mathbf n\in\mathbb N_0^M$ and effects $I_A\otimes|\mathbf n\rangle\langle\mathbf n|$. For ideal homodyne of mode $j$ at phase $\theta\in\mathbb R$, let $R_j(\theta)|\mathbf n\rangle=e^{i\theta n_j}|\mathbf n\rangle$ and $X_{j,\theta}:=\hbar^{-1/2}R_j(\theta)Q_jR_j(\theta)^*$, where $Q_j$ is the self-adjoint quadrature fixed by [[def-nrqmx-finite-mode-symplectic-data]]. Thus $X_{j,\theta}$ is self-adjoint by unitary conjugation and on the finite-particle core equals $(e^{-i\theta}a_j+e^{i\theta}a_j^*)/\sqrt2$. Its spectral PVM $B\mapsto I_A\otimes\mathbf1_B(X_{j,\theta})$ is the ideal homodyne POVM on the product space. These are ideal outcome assignments, not claims about a detector's optical local oscillator, efficiency, bandwidth, calibration or state update. If a state update or a finite detector environment is modeled, declare its instrument separately; the optional finite product-preparation/unitary/partial-trace assignment has the exact scope of the finite open-system postulate and implies no reservoir limit.

**(e) Optional approximation regimes.** A long-wavelength identification with a spatial electromagnetic mode requires a separately declared atomic extent $L$ and wave number $k_j$ and the scale regime $k_jL\ll1$; no error bound is supplied. A rotating-wave choice keeps only the excitation-exchange terms. For a two-level transition of frequency $\omega_0$ coupled to a mode of frequency $\omega$, its usual low-excitation regime is $|g|\sqrt{n+1}\ll\omega,\omega_0$ on the declared photon-number sectors; it is not uniform over the full Fock space. A Markov/GKSL approximation is another separate model choice and must state its rates, reservoir correlation time $\tau_B$, system time scale $\tau_S$, and regime $\tau_B\ll\tau_S$. None of these optional approximations is derived from this assignment or from the finite system-environment model.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let
$\mathbb H:=\mathbb C$ with its standard inner product (linear in the first
argument), let $F(\mathbb C)$ be its Fock space as in
[[thm-nrqm-fock-and-equilibrium-hilbert-direct-sum-construction]], let
$e_n\in F(\mathbb C)$ be the unit vector supported in coordinate $n$ (so
$(e_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ is a complete orthonormal family of $F(\mathbb C)$),
let $N$ be the number operator and let $A_\pm(1)$ be the maximal creation and
annihilation operators of
[[thm-nrqm-fock-and-equilibrium-closed-adjoint-sector-domains]] for the vector
$1\in\mathbb C$. Then:

(a) *oscillator coefficients*: for every $n\in\mathbb N$,
$$A_+(1)e_n=\sqrt{n+1}\,e_{n+1},\qquad A_-(1)e_n=\sqrt n\,e_{n-1}\ (n\ge1),\qquad A_-(1)e_0=0;$$

(b) *coherent vectors*: for every $z\in\mathbb C$ the series
$$\psi_z:=e^{-|z|^2/2}\sum_{n\in\mathbb N}\frac{z^n}{\sqrt{n!}}\,e_n$$
converges absolutely in $F(\mathbb C)$
([[def-complex-exponential]], [[lem-complex-exponential-series-converges-everywhere]]),
$\|\psi_z\|=1$, $\psi_z\in D(A_-(1))$ with
$$A_-(1)\psi_z=z\,\psi_z,$$
and for all $z,w\in\mathbb C$,
$$\langle\psi_z,\psi_w\rangle=e^{-(|z|^2+|w|^2)/2+z\overline w};$$

(c) *number law*: for every $n\in\mathbb N$,
$$\bigl|\langle e_n,\psi_z\rangle\bigr|^2=e^{-|z|^2}\frac{|z|^{2n}}{n!},$$
and $\sum_{n\in\mathbb N}|\langle e_n,\psi_z\rangle|^2=1$.

The numbers in (c) are squared moduli of overlaps of unit vectors; identifying
them with outcome probabilities of a number measurement requires a separately
adopted measurement postulate, and no such physical claim is made here.
