supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Adopt the state postulate [[post-nrqm-framework-state-and-composition]] (P1), the observable and probability postulate [[post-nrqm-framework-observable-and-probability]] (P2) and the ideal conditional-measurement postulate [[post-nrqm-framework-ideal-conditional-measurement]] (P3) for the declared system, whose state space is $D(H)$ for the assigned nonzero separable complex Hilbert space $H$ ([[def-nrqm-state-geometry-framework-state-space]], [[def-nrqm-state-geometry-pure-mixed-states-and-purity]]). Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]), the hypothesis of the cited mathematics. Here the projective outcome law is supplied directly by P3(ii), and the finite-effect law by P2(iv); no spectral PVM is constructed from an assigned self-adjoint observable. The additional Axiom of Choice required by P2(ii) for that construction is therefore not used here. The following vocabulary is used by this page.

**(a) Declared ideal sharp measurement.** A **declared ideal sharp measurement** of the system is a finite or countably infinite family $(P_{a})_{a\in A}$ of bounded orthogonal projections on $H$ ([[def-hilbert-orthogonal-projection]]) that are **mutually orthogonal**, $P_{a}P_{b}=0$ for $a\ne b$, and whose **strong sum** is the identity,
$$\sum_{a\in A}P_{a}x=x\qquad(x\in H).$$
The index $a$ is the **outcome label** and the family $(P_{a})_{a\in A}$ is the **outcome structure** of the declared measurement; it is part of the declared apparatus model, not a quantity computed from the state. This is clause (i) of P3.

**(b) The Lueders instrument of a declared ideal sharp measurement.** For a preparation $\rho$ the **outcome probabilities** are
$$p_{a}:=\operatorname{tr}(\rho P_{a})\ge0,\qquad \sum_{a}p_{a}=1,$$
and for a pure preparation of the unit ray $[\psi]$ they are $p_{a}=\|P_{a}\psi\|^{2}$ (clause (ii) of P3). If $p_{a}>0$ the **conditional state** after the outcome $a$ is the selective Lueders update
$$\rho_{a}:=\frac{P_{a}\rho P_{a}}{p_{a}};$$
it is a state with $\operatorname{tr}(\rho_{a}P_{a})=1$ and $P_{a}\rho_{a}P_{a}=\rho_{a}$ ([[lem-nrqm-measurement-selective-luders-update]], clause (iii) of P3). If the outcomes are recorded but not selected, the **discarded-outcome state** is
$$\Phi(\rho):=\sum_{a\in A}P_{a}\rho P_{a},$$
the trace-norm convergent series of [[lem-nrqm-measurement-nonselective-luders-map]]; it is a state with $\Phi(\rho)=\sum_{a:p_{a}>0}p_{a}\rho_{a}$ and $\operatorname{tr}(\Phi(\rho)P_{a})=p_{a}$ (clause (iv) of P3).

**(c) Declared ideal filter.** A **declared ideal filter** is a declared ideal sharp measurement with exactly two outcomes $a=1,2$: the filter **passes** the component in the range of $P_{1}$ and **blocks** the component in the range of $P_{2}=I-P_{1}$. Repeated use of the filter in series means the sequential application of the conditional updates of clause (b).

**(d) Declared instrument.** A **declared finite or countable instrument** for an outcome set $A$ consists of a finite or countable family $(M_{a,r})_{\substack{a\in A\\r\in R_{a}}}$ of bounded operators on $H$ with
$$\sum_{a\in A}\sum_{r\in R_{a}}M_{a,r}^{*}M_{a,r}=I$$
in the strong sense ([[lem-nrqm-composites-countable-kraus-normalization]]), the **effects**
$$F_{a}:=\sum_{r\in R_{a}}M_{a,r}^{*}M_{a,r},$$
where each subseries converges strongly, independently of its enumeration. An **effect** on general $H$ is a bounded self-adjoint operator $F$ with $0\le\langle Fx,x\rangle\le\|x\|^2$ for all $x\in H$; the **order** $F\le G$ means $\langle(G-F)x,x\rangle\ge0$ for all $x$. Here $\langle F_a x,x\rangle=\sum_r\|M_{a,r}x\|^2\le\|x\|^2$, so $0\le F_a\le I$. In particular the positive partial sums $S_N$ of any subseries are contractions and have convergent quadratic forms. For a positive tail $D=S_N-S_m$, expanding $\langle D(x+ty),x+ty\rangle\ge0$ with $t=-\langle Dx,y\rangle/\langle Dy,y\rangle$ when $\langle Dy,y\rangle>0$, and varying $t\in\mathbb C$ when $\langle Dy,y\rangle=0$, gives $|\langle Dx,y\rangle|^2\le\langle Dx,x\rangle\langle Dy,y\rangle$. Since $0\le D\le I$, taking $y=Dx$ yields $\|Dx\|^4\le\langle Dx,x\rangle\langle D(Dx),Dx\rangle\le\langle Dx,x\rangle\|Dx\|^2$, hence $\|Dx\|^2\le\langle Dx,x\rangle$ (also when $Dx=0$). The partial sums therefore converge on every $x$ and their limit defines $F_a$. The **outcome probabilities** are $p_{a}:=\operatorname{tr}(\rho F_{a})$. For finite $A$ this is clause (iv) of P2, even if an outcome has countably many Kraus operators. For countably infinite $A$ outside the projective case of (a)-(b), we explicitly adopt this same probability law as an additional assumption of the declared apparatus model; P2(iv) does not state that extension. The Kraus-normalization lemma establishes that these numbers are nonnegative and sum to one, not that they describe physical outcomes. The model also explicitly stipulates the **conditional updates**
$$\rho\longmapsto\frac{1}{p_{a}}\sum_{r\in R_{a}}M_{a,r}\rho M_{a,r}^{*}\qquad(p_{a}>0),$$
and the **discarded-outcome map** $\rho\mapsto\sum_{a,r}M_{a,r}\rho M_{a,r}^{*}$. These update series converge in trace norm by the Kraus-normalization lemma, with grouping permitted by absolute trace-norm convergence for positive inputs. Their interpretation as post-measurement states is part of the instrument declaration; P3 supplies that interpretation only for its projective Lueders case. The family $(M_{a,r})$, called the **Kraus family** of the instrument, is part of the declared apparatus model. The effects $(F_{a})$ alone do not determine the conditional updates: distinct normalized Kraus families can share the same effects while defining different updates ([[lem-nrqm-composites-finite-effects-and-instruments]] clause (d); clause (v) of P3). More generally, on a specified measurable space $(X,\Sigma)$, a **declared abstract instrument** is a map $J:\Sigma\to\mathcal B(\mathcal S_{1}(H))$ into bounded complex-linear maps of trace-class operators satisfying: each $J_B$ is completely positive, meaning every finite matrix amplification preserves positive trace-class block operators; for disjoint $B_n$ with union $B$, $J_B(T)=\sum_nJ_{B_n}(T)$ in trace norm for every trace-class $T$; and $J_X$ preserves trace. Its outcome effect $F_B$ is the unique effect with $\operatorname{tr}(J_B(T))=\operatorname{tr}(TF_B)$, its probability is $p(B)=\operatorname{tr}(J_B(\rho))$, and its conditional state is $J_B(\rho)/p(B)$ only when $p(B)>0$. The interpretation of these formulas as an outcome law and a post-measurement state is likewise an explicitly adopted assumption of this abstract apparatus model. [[lem-nrqm-composites-general-trace-class-instrument-and-effect-duality]] establishes the effect duality, countably additive normalization and well-definedness of the positive-probability conditional state, not this physical interpretation. The Kraus case above is a concrete instance on $(A,2^A)$, with $J_B(T)=\sum_{a\in B,r}M_{a,r}TM_{a,r}^*$ in trace norm. This declaration does not assert that every abstract instrument has a Kraus representation or that a laboratory apparatus realizes it.

**(e) Declaration discipline.** A model of an apparatus that is used to predict post-measurement states must declare both an outcome structure (effects) and an update rule; the outcome law of P2 alone does not supply the update, and the update is not a mathematical consequence of the effects. The special case in which the Kraus family consists of the projections $P_{a}$ themselves (with a single $r$ per outcome) is the Lueders instrument of clauses (a)-(b). The claim that a concrete laboratory device realizes a particular declared measurement, filter or instrument is a physical identification with uncertainty under the preparation and apparatus postulate P7 ([[post-nrqm-framework-preparation-and-apparatus]]), not a consequence of this definition.

**(f) Limits.** Declared ideal sharp measurements are idealizations of apparatus that are idealized as repeatable and projection-valued; the framework does not assert that every apparatus, or any particular apparatus, is of this form (clause (v) of P3). The following are outside the declared class and require their own models: a measurement of an exact value of a quantity whose spectrum is continuous (no normalization of a delta symbol is intended; clauses (iii) of P2 and (v) of P3); a photon-absorption or other destructive detector, whose declared instrument need not leave an outgoing state of the same form (clause (v) of P3); and a unitary system-apparatus interaction, which by itself produces conditional correlations without selecting a unique recorded outcome or a preferred outcome family (clause (v) of P3).

**(g) Status.** Clauses (a)-(c) read the projective rules of P3, and the finite-outcome law in (d) reads P2(iv). Clause (d) additionally stipulates the countably infinite nonprojective outcome law, generalized conditional and discarded-outcome updates, and abstract-instrument law and updates as assumptions of each declared apparatus model, as permitted by P3(v)'s requirement for separate models outside its projective class. These are not consequences of P1-P3 alone. Clauses (e)-(f) fix the declaration discipline and limits used by the page's later items. The cited mathematical items ([[lem-nrqm-measurement-selective-luders-update]], [[lem-nrqm-measurement-nonselective-luders-map]], [[lem-nrqm-composites-finite-effects-and-instruments]], [[lem-nrqm-composites-countable-kraus-normalization]], [[lem-nrqm-composites-general-trace-class-instrument-and-effect-duality]]) are conditional mathematics about the displayed formulas; no physical process, outcome uniqueness or empirical fact is deduced here.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

citations.quote:
Fix a finite-dimensional real Lie algebra $\mathfrak g$, a finite index set $A$ with real basis $\{t^a\}_{a\in A}$, and a finite species index set $I$. Let $\mathfrak g_{\mathbb C}:=\mathfrak g\otimes_{\mathbb R}\mathbb C$ be the complexification of [[def-complexification-of-a-real-lie-algebra]], with complex scalar multiplication on the second tensor factor and the complex-bilinear bracket specified on pure tensors by $[X\otimes z,Y\otimes w]=[X,Y]\otimes zw$ for $X,Y\in\mathfrak g$ and $z,w\in\mathbb C$. Identify $X\in\mathfrak g$ with its canonical real embedding $X\otimes1$; in particular $t^a$ in a representation argument means $t^a\otimes1$. For each $i\in I$, let $V_i$ be a finite-dimensional complex vector space and let $\rho_i:\mathfrak g_{\mathbb C}\to\operatorname{End}_{\mathbb C}(V_i)$ be a complex-linear Lie-algebra representation, so $\rho_i([U,V])=\rho_i(U)\rho_i(V)-\rho_i(V)\rho_i(U)$. Attach the bookkeeping label $\chi_i=L$ to each species. In this interface, a “left-handed Weyl species” means exactly the data $(V_i,\rho_i,\chi_i=L)$; the label is not a spinor field or a chirality operator. No spacetime manifold, spinor bundle or field, kinetic operator or action, integration of $\rho_i$ to a gauge group, regulator, effective action, or gauge-variation map is constructed or assumed.

Set $T^a_{R_i}:=\rho_i(t^a)$ and define $\{A,B\}:=AB+BA$ for endomorphisms of $V_i$. The algebraic cubic representation coefficient is
$$d^{abc}=\sum_{i\in I}\operatorname{tr}_{V_i}\!\left(T^a_{R_i}\{T^b_{R_i},T^c_{R_i}\}\right)\in\mathbb C.$$
The basis and generator normalization are fixed as part of the data. No factor $1/2$ is included in the anticommutator. If $T^{(b}T^{c)}=(T^bT^c+T^cT^b)/2$, then $d^{abc}$ is twice $\sum_i\operatorname{tr}_{V_i}(T^a_{R_i}T^{(b}_{R_i}T^{c)}_{R_i})$. Cancellation of this coefficient means $d^{abc}=0$ for every basis triple in this convention. These are representation traces only; calling them anomaly coefficients in a physical model requires an additional theorem.

Define the separate linear representation coefficient by
$$\ell^a=\sum_{i\in I}\operatorname{tr}_{V_i}(T^a_{R_i})\in\mathbb C.$$
For one-dimensional representation spaces of a one-dimensional Abelian Lie algebra with fixed generator $t$ and $\rho_i(t)=q_i\operatorname{id}_{\mathbb C}$, this gives $\ell=\sum_iq_i$. The coefficient $\ell^a$ is recorded separately because a later mixed gauge-gravitational analysis needs its own representation data. Such an analysis must specify its spacetime and gauge connections, curvature conventions, and index polynomial; no mixed-anomaly formula is asserted by this interface.

The only local BRST obstruction statement recorded here is a separate formal result for the specific Abelian jet complex used by the mathematical supplier, not a BRST construction for the general Lie algebra $\mathfrak g$ above. In the convention of `def-qftx-brst-relative-local-cohomology`, a compactly supported local horizontal $p$-form is a finite sum of $f_{i_1\ldots i_p}(x,z)\,dx^{i_1}\wedge\cdots\wedge dx^{i_p}$, with each coefficient smooth and compactly supported in $x\in\mathbb R^4$ and polynomial in finitely many field-jet coordinates $z^i_\alpha$; $i$ indexes the field and ghost generators and $\alpha$ their derivative multi-indices. Its total derivative is $D_\mu=\partial/\partial x^\mu+\sum_{i,\alpha}z^i_{\alpha+e_\mu}\partial_L/\partial z^i_\alpha$, where $e_\mu$ is the unit multi-index and $\partial_L$ is the left graded derivative; $d_H=dx^\mu\wedge D_\mu$. The differential $s$ is the odd ghost-number-one Abelian derivation fixed by `def-qftx-abelian-local-brst`, with $sa_\mu=\partial_\mu c_{\mathrm{gh}}$, $sc_{\mathrm{gh}}=0$, $s\bar c=B$, $sB=0$, and $s\psi=igc_{\mathrm{gh}}\psi$, extended by the graded Leibniz rule and commutation with spacetime derivatives; $a_\mu,\psi,B$ are even, $c_{\mathrm{gh}},\bar c$ are odd, and their ghost numbers are $0,0,0,1,-1$, respectively. This source also fixes $s^2=d_H^2=0$ and $sd_H+d_Hs=0$, with nilpotence of $s$ established by `lem-qftx-brst-nilpotence-doublets`. For each $n$, $\mathcal K_n^{r,p}$ is an $s,d_H$-stable subcomplex of these forms, and the relative class is the quotient
$$H^{1,4}(s|d_H;\mathcal K_n)=\frac{\{a_4\in\mathcal K_n^{1,4}:s a_4+d_Ha_3=0\text{ for some }a_3\in\mathcal K_n^{2,3}\}}{\{s b_4+d_Hc_3:b_4\in\mathcal K_n^{0,4},\ c_3\in\mathcal K_n^{1,3}\}}.$$
The direct supplier `prop-qftx-anomaly-obstruction` is a draft proposition with a supplied conditional proof. Its scalar construction premise is the draft theorem `thm-qftx-scalar-eg-induction`: under the Axiom of Choice (every family of nonempty sets has a choice function) and Countable Choice (every sequence of nonempty sets has a choice function), and for admissible flat scalar free data and a local scalar polynomial class as defined by `def-qftx-local-time-ordered-system`, that theorem asserts existence of symmetric multilinear time-ordered maps satisfying its contract at every finite order, with finite graph scaling bounds and local extension ambiguities. It asserts no convergence, adiabatic limit, positivity, or Ward identity. The exact statement of `prop-qftx-anomaly-obstruction` assumes those data and a time-ordering scheme satisfying that theorem. For each ghost number $r$, define the local-functional quotient $\mathscr F_n^r:=\mathcal K_n^{r,4}/d_H\mathcal K_n^{r,3}$ and its formal series module $\mathscr F_n^r\llbracket\hbar\rrbracket$, where $\hbar$ is a formal indeterminate. For some $n\ge1$, it further assumes an odd formal ghost-number-one operator $\mathcal W_\hbar=s+\sum_{j\ge1}\hbar^j\mathcal W_j$ on this module, $\mathcal W_\hbar^2=0$, and an element $X\in\mathscr F_n^0\llbracket\hbar\rrbracket$ with $\mathcal W_\hbar X=\hbar^n\mathcal A+O(\hbar^{n+1})$, where $O(\hbar^{n+1})$ denotes terms of formal degree at least $n+1$, all lower coefficients vanish, and $\mathcal A=[a_4]_{\mathscr F_n}$ for compactly supported $a_4\in\mathcal K_n^{1,4}$. It requires $\mathcal K_n^{0,4}$ to be exactly the admissible local counterterm densities. Under these hypotheses, that proposition states that $s a_4$ is $d_H$-exact and that shifting $X$ by $-\hbar^n[b_4]_{\mathscr F_n}$, for $b_4\in\mathcal K_n^{0,4}$, cancels the order-$n$ breaking exactly when $[a_4]_{s|d_H}=0$. This is used only in the stated conditional form: it does not establish that the hypotheses hold for the representation data above or construct a physical effective action, and it does not prove a quantum action principle.

Accordingly, this interface asserts no physical anomaly-cancellation criterion from $d^{abc}$. A later physical theorem must specify its spacetime, field space, action, regulator and renormalized effective-action map, and the map that assigns a local gauge-variation density to that data. It must then prove the relation of that density to an explicitly specified local BRST cohomology class and invariant six-form polynomial, with mixed gauge-gravitational coefficients and loop-order hypotheses stated separately. No conclusion about transformations outside the identity component of a separately specified full gauge-transformation group follows from this infinitesimal representation tensor. Vanishing $d^{abc}$ alone proves neither a nonperturbative gauge theory nor the absence of failures under such transformations.

derivations.claim: In one dimension the trace of a scalar is that scalar, and $\{q,q\}=2q^2$, $\{-q,-q\}=2q^2$. Therefore the two contributions to the cubic coefficient sum to $q(2q^2)+(-q)(2q^2)=2(q^3+(-q)^3)=0$.

Let $D\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^n$ be open, let $F:D\to\mathbb R^n$, and let $n\ge1$. The equation

$$x'(t)=F(t,x(t))$$

is a **first-order system**. An **initial value problem** consists of this equation and data $(t_0,x_0)\in D$, written $x(t_0)=x_0$.

A **solution on an interval** $I$ is a function $x:I\to\mathbb R^n$ such that $t_0\in I$, $(t,x(t))\in D$ for every $t\in I$, $x$ is differentiable on $I$ in the domain-relative sense of [[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]], and

$$x(t_0)=x_0,\qquad x'(t)=F(t,x(t))\quad(t\in I).$$

Endpoints of $I$ use the corresponding one-sided, domain-relative derivative. A local solution is one whose interval contains a nondegenerate neighborhood of $t_0$ relative to the time projection of $D$.

Let $n\in\mathbb N$ with $n\ge1$, let $D\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^n$ be open, and let $F:D\to\mathbb R^n$. The map $F$ is **locally Lipschitz in the state variable, locally uniformly in time**, if every compact time-state cylinder $C\subseteq D$ has a finite $L\ge0$ such that

$$\|F(t,x)-F(t,y)\|_2\le L\|x-y\|_2$$

whenever $(t,x),(t,y)\in C$ have the same time coordinate.

On every compact time-state cylinder the state-variable inequality holds with one finite constant $L$. More generally, let $p\ge1$, let $\Lambda\subseteq\mathbb R^p$, let $D_\Lambda\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^n\times\Lambda$ be open in its relative Euclidean topology, and let $F:D_\Lambda\to\mathbb R^n$. The parameter family is **locally Lipschitz in the state variable, locally uniform in time and parameters** when every compact time-state-parameter cylinder $C\subseteq D_\Lambda$ has one finite $L\ge0$ such that

$$\|F(t,x,\lambda)-F(t,y,\lambda)\|_2\le L\|x-y\|_2$$

whenever $(t,x,\lambda),(t,y,\lambda)\in C$ have the same time and parameter coordinates.

Let $D\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^n$ be open, let $F:D\to\mathbb R^n$ be continuous and locally Lipschitz in the state variable, and let $(t_0,x_0)\in D$. Then a unique local solution of the IVP exists on some interval around the initial time. More quantitatively, if $h,r>0$ make

$$[t_0-h,t_0+h]\times\overline B(x_0,r)\subseteq D,$$

if $\|F\|_2\le M$ and $F$ has state-Lipschitz constant $L$ on this cylinder, and if $hM\le r$ and $Lh<1$, then there is exactly one solution on $[t_0-h,t_0+h]$ through $(t_0,x_0)$ whose graph lies in the cylinder. Any two solutions through the same initial data agree on every common subinterval containing $t_0$.

In particular, a unique local solution exists on an interval around the initial time.

The functor $(y,\beta,x,\alpha)\mapsto(x,\beta\circ q(\alpha))$ maps it to $(\mathcal X)_z$. A quasi-inverse sends $(x,\gamma:q(p(x))\to z)$ to $(p(x),\gamma,x,\operatorname{id}_{p(x)})$. The composite on $(\mathcal X)_z$ is the identity. For any iterated object, the isomorphism $\alpha:p(x)\to y$ and $\operatorname{id}_x$ give a natural isomorphism from the quasi-inverse image back to that object. Hence the functor is an equivalence.

Fix an isomorphism class $[e]$ of $\mathcal E$, set $y=b(e)$, and write $A=\operatorname{Aut}_{\mathcal Y}(y)$, $B=\operatorname{Aut}_{\mathcal E}(e)$, $I=\operatorname{im}(B\to A)$, and $N=\ker(B\to A)$. The classes in the homotopy fiber $\mathcal E_y$ represented by this $[e]$ are the orbits of $I$ on the $A$-torsor of isomorphisms $b(e)\cong y$, so there are $|A|/|I|$ of them; each has automorphism group $N$. Their contribution after the outer factor $1/|A|$ is $f([e])/(|I||N|)=f([e])/|B|$, by the finite homomorphism counting identity $|B|=|I||N|$. Summing over $[e]$ proves $\int_{y\in\mathcal Y} b_!f(y)=\int_{e\in\mathcal E} f(e)$.

Such an arrow satisfies $\tau'\circ v=\tau$ and $c(v)\circ\alpha=\alpha'\circ b(u)$, so its image satisfies $\beta'\circ b(u)=\beta$. Conversely, for any such $u$ between images $(e,\beta)$ and $(e',\beta')$, the only possible lift has $v=(\tau')^{-1}\circ\tau:f'\to f''$; the equation $\beta'\circ b(u)=\beta$ implies $c(v)\circ\alpha=\alpha'\circ b(u)$, so this lift exists and is unique. Use the shift convention $M(1)_d=M_{d+1}$; on the split Grothendieck ring it is recorded by $v[M]=[M(1)]$. Let $K^b(\mathrm{SBim}_n)$ denote the category of bounded cochain complexes in $\mathrm{SBim}_n$ with chain maps modulo chain homotopy.

For $1\le i<n$, let $F_i=[B_i\xrightarrow{\varepsilon_i}R(1)]$ in cohomological degrees $0,1$ and $F_i^{-1}=[R(-1)\xrightarrow{\eta_i}B_i]$ in degrees $-1,0$, with the maps and grading conventions of the positive and negative Rouquier generator complexes. For a signed word $\sigma=\sigma_{i_1}^{\epsilon_1}\cdots\sigma_{i_r}^{\epsilon_r}$, $\epsilon_k\in\{+1,-1\}$, let $F(\sigma)=F_{i_1}^{\epsilon_1}\otimes_R\cdots\otimes_R F_{i_r}^{\epsilon_r}$, using signed tensor totalization and left-to-right bracketing; the empty word gives $R$ in degree zero. If $\beta\in B_n$ is the braid represented by $\sigma$, the **Rouquier categorified line operator** $F(\beta)$ is this complex considered up to the canonical homotopy equivalence between words representing $\beta$. Tensor product is the categorical stacking operation. The comparison maps give the unit and coherent multiplication maps $F(\beta)\otimes_R F(\gamma)\simeq F(\beta\gamma)$; equivalently, left tensoring defines the coherent braid-group action on $K^b(R\text{-grmod})$.

A **physical defect realization** is additional data. A monoidal category $\mathcal D$ here means a category with a tensor bifunctor, a unit object, associator and unit isomorphisms satisfying the pentagon and unit triangles; its objects are declared line-defect types, its morphisms are declared junction maps, and its tensor product is the chosen stacking operation. The realization is a strong monoidal functor $\mathcal R:K^b(\mathrm{SBim}_n)\to\mathcal D$, meaning a functor with natural product and unit isomorphisms satisfying those same coherence equations and assigning images to every morphism, including junction maps, in its domain. Calling $\mathcal D$ a category of defects in a particular quantum field theory also requires an independently specified physical model. The Soergel and Rouquier data alone supply neither $\mathcal D$ nor this functor.

**Setting.** Fix $n\ge2$ and the two graded additive monoidal categories of this
page: the type-A Soergel category $\mathrm{SBim}_n$, the idempotent completion of
the category of Bott–Samelson bimodules
([[def-the-type-a-soergel-category]]), and the Karoubi envelope
$\operatorname{Kar}(D)$ of the type-A diagrammatic category
$D$ ([[def-type-a-diagrammatic-soergel-category-and-its-bimodule-functor]]).
Both are graded: an object $X$ has a shift $X(1)=X\{-1\}$, and both are monoidal
with unit the one-object bimodule $R$ respectively the empty word. Both are
additive in the sense of [[def-additive-category]].

**The split Grothendieck group.** For such a category $C$ choose a *small
skeleton*, that is, a set $\operatorname{sk}(C)$ of representative objects
meeting every isomorphism class exactly once — for $\mathrm{SBim}_n$ one may take
the graded direct summands of finite direct sums of shifts of Bott–Samelson
bimodules with a fixed underlying set of words, and for
$\operatorname{Kar}(D)$ the idempotents in finite direct sums of shifts of words,
so that the representatives form a set rather than a proper class. Define
$$K_0^{\mathrm{split}}(C):=\Bigl(\bigoplus_{X\in\operatorname{sk}(C)}\mathbb Z[X]\Bigr)\Big/\,\bigl\langle[X]-[X']-[X'']\ :\ X\cong X'\oplus X''\ \text{in }C\bigr\rangle,$$
the free abelian group on the isomorphism classes of representative objects
modulo the relations $[X]=[X']+[X'']$ whenever $X$ is isomorphic to a direct sum
of $X'$ and $X''$.

**Ring structure.** For representatives $X,Y$ the tensor product $X\otimes Y$
is again an object of $C$, whose isomorphism class is represented by a unique
element of the skeleton; the assignment $(X,Y)\mapsto X\otimes Y$ is additive in
each variable up to isomorphism, so $[X][Y]:=[X\otimes Y]$ descends to a
well-defined bilinear product on $K_0^{\mathrm{split}}(C)$, with the unit
$1:=[\mathbf 1]$ the class of the monoidal unit $R$ (respectively the empty
word). Associativity and unitality of the tensor product make
$K_0^{\mathrm{split}}(C)$ a ring; it is not commutative in general, and
$K_0^{\mathrm{split}}(\mathrm{SBim}_n)$ is not commutative for $n\ge3$, since
the classes of two adjacent one-color products do not commute. The grading
shift is an additive
autoequivalence commuting with the tensor product, so setting
$$v[X]:=[X(1)]=[X\{-1\}]$$
equips $K_0^{\mathrm{split}}(C)$ with the structure of a
$\mathbb Z[v,v^{-1}]$-algebra, with $v^{-1}[X]=[X(-1)]=[X\{1\}]$.

**The two charts.** For the bimodule category the classes are those of the
Bott–Samelson products, $[B_{i_1}\otimes_R\cdots\otimes_RB_{i_r}]$, and for
every object $X$ the shift rule is $[X\{k\}]=v^{-k}[X]$; for the diagrammatic
category the class of a word is $[B_{\underline i}]$, with the same shift rule.
The standard bimodules $R_x$, $\Delta_x(d)$ and $\nabla_x(d)$ with $x\ne e$ are
not objects of $\mathrm{SBim}_n$ — they occur only as the successive quotients
of the support flags of its objects — so this definition attaches no object
class to them; the Hecke algebra's basis elements indexed by $x$ are written
$T_x,\widetilde T_x,H_x$, as in
[[def-type-a-hecke-algebra-in-soergel-normalization]]. Under the
dictionary of [[def-type-a-diagrammatic-soergel-category-and-its-bimodule-functor]]
the two rings are compared by sending $[B_{\underline i}]$ to
$[B_{i_1}\otimes_R\cdots\otimes_RB_{i_r}]$; the comparison is an isomorphism only
after the equivalence of the two categories is proved later on this page.

Let $C,D$ be bounded cochain complexes of graded $(R,R)$-bimodules whose terms
lie in the type-A Soergel category $\mathrm{SBim}_n$ (for instance Rouquier
word complexes), and define the alternating class
$$\chi(C):=\sum_{m\in\mathbb Z}(-1)^m[C^m]\ \in\ K_0^{\mathrm{split}}(\mathrm{SBim}_n),$$
the cochain indexing being translated to the chain indexing of
[[def-mapping-cone-of-a-chain-map]] by $C_m:=C^{-m}$. Then:

1. $\chi$ is a homotopy invariant: if $C\simeq D$ in $K^b$, then
   $\chi(C)=\chi(D)$, so $\chi$ is well defined on isomorphism classes of the
   homotopy category;
2. $\chi$ is multiplicative: $\chi(C\otimes_RD)=\chi(C)\chi(D)$ for the signed
   tensor totalization and more generally for every finite tensor product;
3. for every chain map $f\colon C\to D$ one has
   $\chi(\operatorname{Cone}(f))=\chi(D)-\chi(C)$, and $\chi$ is additive on
   distinguished triangles of the homotopy category, so it descends to a
   homomorphism $K_0^{\mathrm{tri}}\to K_0^{\mathrm{split}}(\mathrm{SBim}_n)$ on
   the triangulated Grothendieck group of the full triangulated subcategory of
   complexes with terms in $\mathrm{SBim}_n$;
4. for every signed word $\sigma=\sigma_{i_1}^{\epsilon_1}\cdots\sigma_{i_r}^{\epsilon_r}$,
   the iterated signed tensor totalization
   $F_{i_1}^{\epsilon_1}\otimes_R\cdots\otimes_RF_{i_r}^{\epsilon_r}$ (the word
   complex $F(\sigma)$ once that notation is introduced) satisfies
   $\chi(F(\sigma))=\prod_{k=1}^r\chi(F_{i_k}^{\epsilon_k})$.

In particular the alternating class of a Rouquier complex depends only on its
homotopy class and is compatible with tensor products.

**Additive setting.** Fix an additive category $\mathcal A$
([[def-additive-category]]): every hom-set is an abelian group, finite
biproducts exist, and every object has an identity morphism. All morphisms below
are morphisms of $\mathcal A$, sums and negatives are taken in the hom-groups,
and $0$ denotes the zero morphism between the indicated objects.

**Cochain complexes.** A **cochain complex** $C^\bullet=(C^n,d^n)_{n\in\mathbb Z}$
consists of objects $C^n$ of $\mathcal A$ and morphisms $d^n:C^n\to C^{n+1}$
with
$$d^{n+1}d^n=0\qquad\text{for all }n\in\mathbb Z .$$
The morphisms $d^n$ are the **differentials** of $C^\bullet$. No boundedness,
finiteness or nonvanishing condition is imposed on the family of objects.

**Cochain maps.** A **cochain map** $f:C^\bullet\to D^\bullet$ is a family of
morphisms $f^n:C^n\to D^n$ with
$$f^{n+1}d^n_C=d^n_Df^n\qquad\text{for all }n\in\mathbb Z .$$
Identities and composites of cochain maps are cochain maps, so cochain complexes
and cochain maps form a category; this category is written
$\operatorname{Ch}^\bullet(\mathcal A)$ when the ambient category needs to be
recorded.

**Homotopies.** A **homotopy** $h:f\simeq g$ between cochain maps
$f,g:C^\bullet\to D^\bullet$ is a family of morphisms $h^n:C^n\to D^{n-1}$, one
in each degree, such that
$$f^n-g^n=d^{n-1}_Dh^n+h^{n+1}d^n_C\qquad\text{for all }n\in\mathbb Z .$$
Thus $h$ has degree $-1$, and the right-hand side is the $n$-th component of the
graded map
$$dh+hd:=(d^{n-1}_Dh^n+h^{n+1}d^n_C)_{n\in\mathbb Z},$$
written with $d$ on both sides. A **null
homotopy** of a cochain map $f:C^\bullet\to D^\bullet$ is a homotopy
$f\simeq0$ to the zero map with the same source and target; $D^\bullet$
need not be the zero complex. A map admitting such a homotopy is
**null-homotopic**.

**Homotopy equivalence.** A cochain map $f:C^\bullet\to D^\bullet$ is a
**homotopy equivalence** when there is a cochain map
$g:D^\bullet\to C^\bullet$ with $gf\simeq1_{C^\bullet}$ and
$fg\simeq1_{D^\bullet}$; the complexes are then **homotopy equivalent**. The maps
$f$ and $g$ are homotopy inverses of one another.

**Contractibility.** A cochain complex $C^\bullet$ is **contractible** when its
identity is null-homotopic, $1_{C^\bullet}\simeq0$: that is, when there is a
family of morphisms $h^n:C^n\to C^{n-1}$ with
$$1_{C^n}=d^{n-1}h^n+h^{n+1}d^n\qquad\text{for all }n\in\mathbb Z .$$
A complex is contractible exactly when it is homotopy equivalent to the zero
complex, since a homotopy equivalence onto the zero complex is a pair of
null-homotopies of the identities.

**Degreewise biproducts.** If $C^\bullet$ and $D^\bullet$ are cochain complexes,
then defining
$$(C\oplus D)^n:=C^n\oplus D^n,\qquad d^n_{C\oplus D}:=d^n_C\oplus d^n_D$$
gives a cochain complex, because
$(d^{n+1}_C\oplus d^{n+1}_D)(d^n_C\oplus d^n_D)=0\oplus0=0$. The degreewise
injections and projections are cochain maps, and the biproduct identities hold in
each degree and are therefore identities of cochain maps; hence $C\oplus D$ is a
biproduct of $C$ and $D$. Iterating, finite direct sums of cochain complexes are
formed degreewise, and finite direct sums of cochain maps and of homotopies are
formed degreewise as well. Under the reindexing below this is the additive
structure on complexes over an additive category recorded in
[[thm-the-category-of-complexes-in-an-additive-category-is-additive]].

**Dictionary with the published chain convention.** Reindex by
$C_n:=C^{-n}$ and $d_n:=d^{-n}$. Then $d_n:C_n\to C_{n-1}$ and
$$d_{n-1}d_n=d^{-(n-1)}d^{-n}=d^{-n+1}d^{-n}=0,$$
so $(C_\bullet,d_\bullet)$ is an ordinary chain complex. A cochain map $f$
becomes the chain map with components $f_n:=f^{-n}$, and a homotopy
$h:f\simeq g$ becomes the chain homotopy $s_n:=h^{-n}:C_n\to D_{n+1}$, because
substituting $n\mapsto-n$ into the displayed homotopy equation produces exactly
$$f_n-g_n=d^D_{n+1}s_n+s_{n-1}d^C_n .$$
Consequently, when $\mathcal A$ is abelian, these definitions restrict under this
dictionary to the published [[def-chain-homotopy]] and
[[def-contractible-complex]], which are stated for chain complexes in an abelian
category. Reindexing reverses the sign of the differential degree ($+1$ for
cochains, $-1$ for chains) and of the homotopy degree ($-1$ for cochains, $+1$
for chains), and introduces no further sign.

**What is not asserted.** The definitions use only zero morphisms, addition,
negatives, composition and identities. No kernel, cokernel, image, homology
object or exactness is assumed or defined, no linear structure on the hom-groups
beyond the additive one is used, and no homology object is attached to a complex
in an arbitrary additive category; contractibility is the existence of the
displayed family $h$, not the vanishing of homology.

derivations.claim: The complex $C$ is bounded and its two nonzero terms are objects of $\mathrm{SBim}_n$. Its Euler class is $\chi(C)=[R]-[R]=0$ by [F2] and [F3].
Since every differential is zero, $H^0(C)=R$ and $H^1(C)=R$. Each is nonzero because $1\in\mathbb Q[x_1,\ldots,x_n]$ is nonzero.

If $C$ were contractible, the equation of [F4] in degree $0$ would give $1_R=d^{-1}h^0+h^1d^0=0$, contradicting $1_R\ne0$. Thus $C$ is not contractible although its Euler class vanishes, refuting the Statement.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Fix an integer $n\ge2$, let $R=\mathbb Q[x_1,\ldots,x_n]$ with $\deg x_j=2$, and let $S_n$ act on $R$ by permuting variables. Let $\mathrm{SBim}_n$ be the idempotent-complete additive monoidal category of graded $(R,R)$-Soergel bimodules generated by the unit bimodule $R$, the bimodules $B_i=R\otimes_{R^{s_i}}R(1)$ for the adjacent transpositions $s_i=(i\ i+1)$, internal grading shifts, finite direct sums, tensor products over $R$, and direct summands. Use the shift convention $M(1)_d=M_{d+1}$; on the split Grothendieck ring it is recorded by $v[M]=[M(1)]$. Let $K^b(\mathrm{SBim}_n)$ denote the category of bounded cochain complexes in $\mathrm{SBim}_n$ with chain maps modulo chain homotopy.

For $1\le i<n$, let $F_i=[B_i\xrightarrow{\varepsilon_i}R(1)]$ in cohomological degrees $0,1$ and $F_i^{-1}=[R(-1)\xrightarrow{\eta_i}B_i]$ in degrees $-1,0$, with the maps and grading conventions of the positive and negative Rouquier generator complexes. For a signed word $\sigma=\sigma_{i_1}^{\epsilon_1}\cdots\sigma_{i_r}^{\epsilon_r}$, $\epsilon_k\in\{+1,-1\}$, let $F(\sigma)=F_{i_1}^{\epsilon_1}\otimes_R\cdots\otimes_R F_{i_r}^{\epsilon_r}$, using signed tensor totalization and left-to-right bracketing; the empty word gives $R$ in degree zero. If $\beta\in B_n$ is the braid represented by $\sigma$, the **Rouquier categorified line operator** $F(\beta)$ is this complex considered up to the canonical homotopy equivalence between words representing $\beta$. Tensor product is the categorical stacking operation. The comparison maps give the unit and coherent multiplication maps $F(\beta)\otimes_R F(\gamma)\simeq F(\beta\gamma)$; equivalently, left tensoring defines the coherent braid-group action on $K^b(R\text{-grmod})$.

A **physical defect realization** is additional data. A monoidal category $\mathcal D$ here means a category with a tensor bifunctor, a unit object, associator and unit isomorphisms satisfying the pentagon and unit triangles; its objects are declared line-defect types, its morphisms are declared junction maps, and its tensor product is the chosen stacking operation. The realization is a strong monoidal functor $\mathcal R:K^b(\mathrm{SBim}_n)\to\mathcal D$, meaning a functor with natural product and unit isomorphisms satisfying those same coherence equations and assigning images to every morphism, including junction maps, in its domain. Calling $\mathcal D$ a category of defects in a particular quantum field theory also requires an independently specified physical model. The Soergel and Rouquier data alone supply neither $\mathcal D$ nor this functor.

page: the type-A Soergel category $\mathrm{SBim}_n$, the idempotent completion of
the category of Bott–Samelson bimodules
([[def-the-type-a-soergel-category]]), and the Karoubi envelope
$\operatorname{Kar}(D)$ of the type-A diagrammatic category
$D$ ([[def-type-a-diagrammatic-soergel-category-and-its-bimodule-functor]]).
Both are graded: an object $X$ has a shift $X(1)=X\{-1\}$, and both are monoidal
with unit the one-object bimodule $R$ respectively the empty word. Both are
additive in the sense of [[def-additive-category]].

**The split Grothendieck group.** For such a category $C$ choose a *small
skeleton*, that is, a set $\operatorname{sk}(C)$ of representative objects
meeting every isomorphism class exactly once — for $\mathrm{SBim}_n$ one may take
the graded direct summands of finite direct sums of shifts of Bott–Samelson
bimodules with a fixed underlying set of words, and for
$\operatorname{Kar}(D)$ the idempotents in finite direct sums of shifts of words,
so that the representatives form a set rather than a proper class. Define
$$K_0^{\mathrm{split}}(C):=\Bigl(\bigoplus_{X\in\operatorname{sk}(C)}\mathbb Z[X]\Bigr)\Big/\,\bigl\langle[X]-[X']-[X'']\ :\ X\cong X'\oplus X''\ \text{in }C\bigr\rangle,$$
the free abelian group on the isomorphism classes of representative objects
modulo the relations $[X]=[X']+[X'']$ whenever $X$ is isomorphic to a direct sum
of $X'$ and $X''$.

**Ring structure.** For representatives $X,Y$ the tensor product $X\otimes Y$
is again an object of $C$, whose isomorphism class is represented by a unique
element of the skeleton; the assignment $(X,Y)\mapsto X\otimes Y$ is additive in
each variable up to isomorphism, so $[X][Y]:=[X\otimes Y]$ descends to a
well-defined bilinear product on $K_0^{\mathrm{split}}(C)$, with the unit
$1:=[\mathbf 1]$ the class of the monoidal unit $R$ (respectively the empty
word). Associativity and unitality of the tensor product make
$K_0^{\mathrm{split}}(C)$ a ring; it is not commutative in general, and
$K_0^{\mathrm{split}}(\mathrm{SBim}_n)$ is not commutative for $n\ge3$, since
the classes of two adjacent one-color products do not commute. The grading
shift is an additive
autoequivalence commuting with the tensor product, so setting
$$v[X]:=[X(1)]=[X\{-1\}]$$
equips $K_0^{\mathrm{split}}(C)$ with the structure of a
$\mathbb Z[v,v^{-1}]$-algebra, with $v^{-1}[X]=[X(-1)]=[X\{1\}]$.

**The two charts.** For the bimodule category the classes are those of the
Bott–Samelson products, $[B_{i_1}\otimes_R\cdots\otimes_RB_{i_r}]$, and for
every object $X$ the shift rule is $[X\{k\}]=v^{-k}[X]$; for the diagrammatic
category the class of a word is $[B_{\underline i}]$, with the same shift rule.
The standard bimodules $R_x$, $\Delta_x(d)$ and $\nabla_x(d)$ with $x\ne e$ are
not objects of $\mathrm{SBim}_n$ — they occur only as the successive quotients
of the support flags of its objects — so this definition attaches no object
class to them; the Hecke algebra's basis elements indexed by $x$ are written
$T_x,\widetilde T_x,H_x$, as in
[[def-type-a-hecke-algebra-in-soergel-normalization]]. Under the
dictionary of [[def-type-a-diagrammatic-soergel-category-and-its-bimodule-functor]]
the two rings are compared by sending $[B_{\underline i}]$ to
$[B_{i_1}\otimes_R\cdots\otimes_RB_{i_r}]$; the comparison is an isomorphism only
after the equivalence of the two categories is proved later on this page.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
**Additive setting.** Fix an additive category $\mathcal A$
([[def-additive-category]]): every hom-set is an abelian group, finite
biproducts exist, and every object has an identity morphism. All morphisms below
are morphisms of $\mathcal A$, sums and negatives are taken in the hom-groups,
and $0$ denotes the zero morphism between the indicated objects.

**Cochain complexes.** A **cochain complex** $C^\bullet=(C^n,d^n)_{n\in\mathbb Z}$
consists of objects $C^n$ of $\mathcal A$ and morphisms $d^n:C^n\to C^{n+1}$
with
$$d^{n+1}d^n=0\qquad\text{for all }n\in\mathbb Z .$$
The morphisms $d^n$ are the **differentials** of $C^\bullet$. No boundedness,
finiteness or nonvanishing condition is imposed on the family of objects.

**Cochain maps.** A **cochain map** $f:C^\bullet\to D^\bullet$ is a family of
morphisms $f^n:C^n\to D^n$ with
$$f^{n+1}d^n_C=d^n_Df^n\qquad\text{for all }n\in\mathbb Z .$$
Identities and composites of cochain maps are cochain maps, so cochain complexes
and cochain maps form a category; this category is written
$\operatorname{Ch}^\bullet(\mathcal A)$ when the ambient category needs to be
recorded.

**Homotopies.** A **homotopy** $h:f\simeq g$ between cochain maps
$f,g:C^\bullet\to D^\bullet$ is a family of morphisms $h^n:C^n\to D^{n-1}$, one
in each degree, such that
$$f^n-g^n=d^{n-1}_Dh^n+h^{n+1}d^n_C\qquad\text{for all }n\in\mathbb Z .$$
Thus $h$ has degree $-1$, and the right-hand side is the $n$-th component of the
graded map
$$dh+hd:=(d^{n-1}_Dh^n+h^{n+1}d^n_C)_{n\in\mathbb Z},$$
written with $d$ on both sides. A **null
homotopy** of a cochain map $f:C^\bullet\to D^\bullet$ is a homotopy
$f\simeq0$ to the zero map with the same source and target; $D^\bullet$
need not be the zero complex. A map admitting such a homotopy is
**null-homotopic**.

**Homotopy equivalence.** A cochain map $f:C^\bullet\to D^\bullet$ is a
**homotopy equivalence** when there is a cochain map
$g:D^\bullet\to C^\bullet$ with $gf\simeq1_{C^\bullet}$ and
$fg\simeq1_{D^\bullet}$; the complexes are then **homotopy equivalent**. The maps
$f$ and $g$ are homotopy inverses of one another.

**Contractibility.** A cochain complex $C^\bullet$ is **contractible** when its
identity is null-homotopic, $1_{C^\bullet}\simeq0$: that is, when there is a
family of morphisms $h^n:C^n\to C^{n-1}$ with
$$1_{C^n}=d^{n-1}h^n+h^{n+1}d^n\qquad\text{for all }n\in\mathbb Z .$$
A complex is contractible exactly when it is homotopy equivalent to the zero
complex, since a homotopy equivalence onto the zero complex is a pair of
null-homotopies of the identities.

**Degreewise biproducts.** If $C^\bullet$ and $D^\bullet$ are cochain complexes,
then defining
$$(C\oplus D)^n:=C^n\oplus D^n,\qquad d^n_{C\oplus D}:=d^n_C\oplus d^n_D$$
gives a cochain complex, because
$(d^{n+1}_C\oplus d^{n+1}_D)(d^n_C\oplus d^n_D)=0\oplus0=0$. The degreewise
injections and projections are cochain maps, and the biproduct identities hold in
each degree and are therefore identities of cochain maps; hence $C\oplus D$ is a
biproduct of $C$ and $D$. Iterating, finite direct sums of cochain complexes are
formed degreewise, and finite direct sums of cochain maps and of homotopies are
formed degreewise as well. Under the reindexing below this is the additive
structure on complexes over an additive category recorded in
[[thm-the-category-of-complexes-in-an-additive-category-is-additive]].

**Dictionary with the published chain convention.** Reindex by
$C_n:=C^{-n}$ and $d_n:=d^{-n}$. Then $d_n:C_n\to C_{n-1}$ and
$$d_{n-1}d_n=d^{-(n-1)}d^{-n}=d^{-n+1}d^{-n}=0,$$
so $(C_\bullet,d_\bullet)$ is an ordinary chain complex. A cochain map $f$
becomes the chain map with components $f_n:=f^{-n}$, and a homotopy
$h:f\simeq g$ becomes the chain homotopy $s_n:=h^{-n}:C_n\to D_{n+1}$, because
substituting $n\mapsto-n$ into the displayed homotopy equation produces exactly
$$f_n-g_n=d^D_{n+1}s_n+s_{n-1}d^C_n .$$
Consequently, when $\mathcal A$ is abelian, these definitions restrict under this
dictionary to the published [[def-chain-homotopy]] and
[[def-contractible-complex]], which are stated for chain complexes in an abelian
category. Reindexing reverses the sign of the differential degree ($+1$ for
cochains, $-1$ for chains) and of the homotopy degree ($-1$ for cochains, $+1$
for chains), and introduces no further sign.

**What is not asserted.** The definitions use only zero morphisms, addition,
negatives, composition and identities. No kernel, cokernel, image, homology
object or exactness is assumed or defined, no linear structure on the hom-groups
beyond the additive one is used, and no homology object is attached to a complex
in an arbitrary additive category; contractibility is the existence of the
displayed family $h$, not the vanishing of homology.

For probability vectors $p=(p_i)_{i\in I}$ and $q=(q_i)_{i\in I}$ on a finite nonempty set $I$, define

$$D(p\|q):=\begin{cases}\displaystyle\sum_{i:p_i>0}p_i\ln\frac{p_i}{q_i},&p_i>0\Rightarrow q_i>0,\\+\infty,&\text{otherwise.}\end{cases}$$

Then $D(p\|q)\ge0$, and $D(p\|q)=0$ if and only if $p=q$.

For $x>0$, define $\log x$ to be the unique real $y$ such that $\exp(y)=x$. This is well-defined because The exponential is a continuous bijection from $\mathbb{R}$ onto $(0,\infty)$ states that $\exp:\mathbb R\to(0,\infty)$ is a bijection.

Thus $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is the inverse function of $\exp$. In particular, $\log(\exp y)=y$ for every $y\in\mathbb R$ and $\exp(\log x)=x$ for every $x>0$.

The function $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is continuous and strictly increasing, is onto $\mathbb R$, and satisfies, for $x,y>0$,
$$\log(xy)=\log x+\log y,\qquad \log(x/y)=\log x-\log y,\qquad \log(1/x)=-\log x.$$
Also $\log 1=0$.

derivations.claim:
Write $p_x=P_X(x)$ and $q_x=Q_X(x)$. Strict positivity of $Q$ gives $q_x>0$ and $Q_{Y|x}(y)>0$ for each $x,y$. If $P(x,y)>0$, then $p_x>0$ and
$$\ln\frac{P(x,y)}{Q(x,y)}=\ln\frac{p_x}{q_x}+\ln\frac{P_{Y|x}(y)}{Q_{Y|x}(y)}$$
by [F2]. Multiply by $P(x,y)$ and sum over positive joint atoms. For each $x$ with $p_x>0$, summing the first term over $y$ gives $p_x\ln(p_x/q_x)$, and summing the second gives $p_xD(P_{Y|x}\|Q_{Y|x})$. Atoms with $p_x=0$ contribute no terms. This is exactly the claimed chain rule.

If $C$ is empty or all of $I\times J$, then $P(C)=Q(C)$ is respectively $0$ or $1$, so the binary divergence is $0$ under the stated zero-weight convention. The grouping bound is then $D(P\|Q)\ge0$, with equality exactly when $P=Q$ by [F1]. For a nonempty proper $C$, strict positivity gives $0<Q(C)<1$. Put $a=P(C)$ and $b=Q(C)$. When $a>0$, the conditional laws on $C$ are $P_C(z)=P(z)/a$ and $Q_C(z)=Q(z)/b$; the latter is strictly positive on $C$. The logarithmic identity $\ln(P(z)/Q(z))=\ln(a/b)+\ln(P_C(z)/Q_C(z))$ for each $z\in C$ with $P(z)>0$ yields
$$\sum_{z\in C:P(z)>0}P(z)\ln\frac{P(z)}{Q(z)}=a\ln\frac ab+aD(P_C\|Q_C).$$
If $a=0$, both the sum and the weighted conditional term are zero, so the same identity holds with that term omitted. Applying the identical calculation to $C^c$ and adding gives $D(P\|Q)=d(a\|b)+aD(P_C\|Q_C)+(1-a)D(P_{C^c}\|Q_{C^c})$, with zero-weight conditional terms omitted. Both weighted conditional divergences are nonnegative by [F1], which proves the grouping inequality, including $a=0$ or $1$. Equality holds precisely when every conditional divergence with positive weight vanishes; by the equality clause of [F1], this is equivalent to agreement of the conditional probability vectors on each positive-$P$-mass block. Zero-$P$-mass blocks impose no conditional-law condition.

An abstract polymer model consists of an at most countable set $\Gamma$ (finite or in bijection with $\mathbb N$), a reflexive symmetric relation $\sim$ on $\Gamma$ (so $\gamma\sim\gamma$ and $\gamma\sim\eta$ implies $\eta\sim\gamma$), and an activity function $z:\Gamma\to\mathbb C$. Its elements are called polymers, and $\gamma\sim\eta$ means that the two polymers are incompatible. A subset $X\subseteq\Gamma$ is compatible when no two distinct elements of $X$ are related by $\sim$. For real and natural summands, finite-index sums and products are enumeration-independent. For complex summands, define a finite sum or product by any enumeration and repeated addition or multiplication in $\mathbb C$; associativity and commutativity make the result independent of the enumeration. The empty sum is $0$ and the empty product is $1$. For each finite $V\subseteq\Gamma$, define the finite-volume partition polynomial

$$Z_V(z):=\sum_{\substack{X\subseteq V\\X\text{ compatible}}}\ \prod_{\gamma\in X}z_\gamma,$$

where the empty subset contributes $1$.

Write $[n]:=\{1,\ldots,n\}$ and $\binom{[n]}2:=\{\{i,j\}:i,j\in[n],\ i\ne j\}$. A simple graph on $[n]$ is a pair $([n],E)$ with $E\subseteq\binom{[n]}2$; a path is a finite vertex list with distinct vertices and each consecutive pair an edge. A graph is connected when every two vertices are joined by a path. A cycle is a vertex list $(v_0,\ldots,v_k)$ with $k\geq3$, $v_k=v_0$, $v_0,\ldots,v_{k-1}$ distinct, and each consecutive pair an edge; a tree is a connected simple graph with no cycle. For $n\in\mathbb N$ with $n\geq1$, let $\mathcal C_n$ be the set of connected simple graphs on $[n]$ and let $\mathcal T_n$ be the set of trees on $[n]$. The set $[n]$ is finite; its power set is finite, so its subset $\binom{[n]}2$ is finite; the power set of that edge set is finite as well. Each simple graph on $[n]$ is determined by an edge set in this last power set, so $\mathcal C_n$ and $\mathcal T_n$ are finite.

For an ordered tuple $(\gamma_1,\ldots,\gamma_n)\in\Gamma^n$, put $f_{ij}:=-\mathbf 1_{\{\gamma_i\sim\gamma_j\}}$ and define the connected coefficient

$$U_n(\gamma_1,\ldots,\gamma_n):=\sum_{G\in\mathcal C_n}\ \prod_{\{i,j\}\in E(G)}f_{ij}.$$

For $n=1$, $\mathcal C_1$ contains the one-vertex graph and the empty edge product equals $1$. These are finite polynomial and coefficient definitions; they assert no convergence.

Let $(\Gamma,\sim,z)$ be an abstract polymer model, and let $a:\Gamma\to[0,\infty)$. Interpret each countable sum over polymer labels of nonnegative terms as the supremum of its finite subsums in $[0,+\infty]$, and interpret a nonnegative series as the supremum of its increasing partial sums in $[0,+\infty]$. Suppose

$$\sum_{\eta\sim\gamma}|z_\eta|e^{a_\eta}\leq a_\gamma\qquad(\gamma\in\Gamma).$$

For each fixed root $\gamma\in\Gamma$, define the nonnegative rooted connected-cluster sum

$$R_\gamma:=\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac1{(n-1)!}\sum_{\gamma_2,\ldots,\gamma_n\in\Gamma}|U_n(\gamma,\gamma_2,\ldots,\gamma_n)|\prod_{j=2}^n|z_{\gamma_j}|$$

Then $R_\gamma$ is well-defined as a possibly extended nonnegative series and satisfies $R_\gamma\leq e^{a_\gamma}$.

Let $\iota_{\mathbb R}\colon\mathbb N\to\mathbb R$ be the canonical-natural map
of [[def-canonical-natural]], and let $j\colon\mathbb R\to\mathbb C$ be the real
embedding $j(x)=x+i0$ from [[def-complex-numbers-and-arithmetic]]. For every
$n\in\mathbb N$, the factorial $n!$ is nonzero by
[[def-factorial-and-falling-factorial]], so
$\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!)>0$ by [[lem-of-naturals-positive]] and consequently
$j(\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!))\ne0$ in the complex field
[[thm-complex-numbers-form-a-field]].

For $z\in\mathbb C$, define
$$ \exp z:=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{z^n}{j(\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!))}. $$
whenever this complex series converges. Inside a complex expression we
abbreviate the embedded denominator $j(\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!))$ by $n!$, so the
same definition may be written $\exp z=\sum z^n/n!$ without identifying a
natural number with a complex number. Powers and series are those of
[[def-complex-integer-powers]] and
[[def-complex-series-power-series-and-absolute-convergence]]. The convergence
for every $z\in\mathbb C$ is discharged by
[[lem-complex-exponential-series-converges-everywhere]].

For all $z,w\in\mathbb C$, $\exp(z+w)=\exp z\exp w$. For real $x$, the complex value $\exp(x+0i)$ equals the published real exponential $e^x$. The conventions and prerequisite facts used below are recorded in [[def-complex-exponential]], [[lem-complex-exponential-series-converges-everywhere]], [[lem-cauchy-product-of-absolutely-convergent-complex-series]], [[def-real-exponential-function-and-e]], [[lem-binomial-theorem-over-complex-numbers]], [[thm-binomial-closed-formula]].

Let $f(z)=\sum_{n\ge0}c_n(z-a)^n$ have radius $R$. If $|z-a|<R$, then $f$ is complex differentiable at $z$ and
$$f'(z)=\sum_{n\ge1}n c_n(z-a)^{n-1}.$$
Consequently $f$ is holomorphic on its open disc of convergence ([[def-complex-differentiability-holomorphic-and-entire]]).

Every $z\in\mathbb C$ has unique coordinates $z=a+bi$
([[thm-complex-numbers-form-a-field]]). Define
$$\operatorname{Re}z=a,\qquad \operatorname{Im}z=b,\qquad \overline z=a-bi,$$
and define its **modulus** by
$$|z|=\sqrt{a^2+b^2}.$$
The real numbers are least-upper-bound complete
([[cor-cauchy-reals-lub-complete]]), so the nonnegative square root exists and
is unique by [[thm-of-square-roots]].

Complex conjugation is a real-field automorphism satisfying
$$\overline{z+w}=\overline z+\overline w,\qquad \overline{zw}=\overline z\,\overline w,\qquad \overline{\overline z}=z.$$
For every $z,w\in\mathbb C$,
$$z\overline z=|z|^2,\qquad |z|\ge0,\qquad |z|=0\Longleftrightarrow z=0,$$
$$|zw|=|z||w|,\qquad |z+w|\le |z|+|w|.$$

For every real $r$, write $\lambda_r$ for its canonical image in $\mathbb C$. Then
$$
|\lambda_r|_{\mathbb C}=|r|_{\mathbb R}.
$$

Let $S$ be a finite set, $n := \lvert S\rvert$ (The cardinality $\lvert A\rvert$ of a finite set), and
let $a : S \to \mathbb{R}$ or $a : S \to \mathbb{N}$, written $a_i$ for $a(i)$.
Choose a bijection $\varphi : n \to S$, which exists because $S \approx n$
(Equinumerous sets, $A \approx B$ and $A \preceq B$), and set

$$\sum_{i \in S} a_i := \sum_{k<n} a_{\varphi(k)}, \qquad \prod_{i \in S} a_i := \prod_{k<n} a_{\varphi(k)},$$

the right-hand sides being the iterated operations of Finite sums and finite products, by recursion when the
values are real and of Finite sums and finite products of natural numbers, $\sum_{k<n} a_k$ and $\prod_{k<n} a_k$ in $\mathbb{N}$ when they are natural.

**Independence of the enumeration, which is the content of the definition.** Let
$\varphi, \psi : n \to S$ be two bijections. Then $\pi := \varphi^{-1} \circ \psi$
is a bijection $n \to n$ (Injection, surjection, bijection), and
$a_{\psi(k)} = a_{\varphi(\pi(k))}$ for every $k < n$. Applying
A finite sum is unchanged by a permutation of its index range: $\sum_{k<n} a_{\pi(k)} = \sum_{k<n} a_k$ for every bijection $\pi : n \to n$ to the list $c_k := a_{\varphi(k)}$
gives

$$\sum_{k<n} a_{\psi(k)} = \sum_{k<n} c_{\pi(k)} = \sum_{k<n} c_k = \sum_{k<n} a_{\varphi(k)},$$

and identically for products. So the value does not depend on which bijection is
used, and $\sum_{i \in S} a_i$ is a single well-determined element.

**No choice principle is involved.** The definition does not select an
enumeration: it asserts that all enumerations give the same value, and that value
is what the notation names. Only one bijection is ever produced at a time, from a
set already known to be nonempty.

**Three clauses, recorded here because the page uses them constantly.**

**(a) The bridge to the old notation.** Taking $S = n$ and $\varphi = \mathrm{id}_n$,
which is legitimate since $\lvert n\rvert = n$, gives

$$\sum_{i \in n} a_i = \sum_{k<n} a_k, \qquad \prod_{i \in n} a_i = \prod_{k<n} a_k .$$

So the new notation **extends** the sum over an initial segment rather than
competing with it, and every law proved for the latter is available for the
former whenever the index set is a natural number.

**(b) Reindexing along a bijection.** If $h : T \to S$ is a bijection of finite
sets, then $\sum_{j \in T} a_{h(j)} = \sum_{i \in S} a_i$, and likewise for
products. Indeed $\lvert T\rvert = \lvert S\rvert = n$ by transport
(The cardinality $\lvert A\rvert$ of a finite set), and if $\varphi : n \to S$ is a bijection then
$h^{-1} \circ \varphi : n \to T$ is one, so
$\sum_{j \in T} a_{h(j)} = \sum_{k<n} a_{h(h^{-1}(\varphi(k)))} = \sum_{k<n} a_{\varphi(k)} = \sum_{i \in S} a_i$.

**(c) The empty index set and a constant summand.** $\lvert\varnothing\rvert = 0$,
so $\sum_{i \in \varnothing} a_i = 0$ and $\prod_{i \in \varnothing} a_i = 1$ by
the base clause of the recursion. And for a constant $c$, clause (a) together
with the constant clause of Laws of finite sums and products in $\mathbb{N}$, and $\iota\big(\sum_{k<n} a_k\big) = \sum_{k<n} \iota(a_k)$
in $\mathbb{N}$, or clause 2 of Laws of finite sums and finite products in $\mathbb{R}$, gives

$$\sum_{i \in S} c = \lvert S\rvert \cdot c \quad (c \in \mathbb{N}), \qquad \sum_{i \in S} c = \iota(\lvert S\rvert)\cdot c \quad (c \in \mathbb{R}),$$

the second with $\iota$ written out because $\lvert S\rvert$ is a natural number
and not an element of $\mathbb{R}$ (The canonical natural $\iota(n) = n \cdot 1_F$ of a field).

An abstract polymer model consists of an at most countable set $\Gamma$ (finite or in bijection with $\mathbb N$), a reflexive symmetric relation $\sim$ on $\Gamma$ (so $\gamma\sim\gamma$ and $\gamma\sim\eta$ implies $\eta\sim\gamma$), and an activity function $z:\Gamma\to\mathbb C$. Its elements are called polymers, and $\gamma\sim\eta$ means that the two polymers are incompatible. A subset $X\subseteq\Gamma$ is compatible when no two distinct elements of $X$ are related by $\sim$. For real and natural summands, finite-index sums and products are enumeration-independent. For complex summands, define a finite sum or product by any enumeration and repeated addition or multiplication in $\mathbb C$; associativity and commutativity make the result independent of the enumeration. The empty sum is $0$ and the empty product is $1$. For each finite $V\subseteq\Gamma$, define the finite-volume partition polynomial

$$Z_V(z):=\sum_{\substack{X\subseteq V\\X\text{ compatible}}}\ \prod_{\gamma\in X}z_\gamma,$$

where the empty subset contributes $1$.

Write $[n]:=\{1,\ldots,n\}$ and $\binom{[n]}2:=\{\{i,j\}:i,j\in[n],\ i\ne j\}$. A simple graph on $[n]$ is a pair $([n],E)$ with $E\subseteq\binom{[n]}2$; a path is a finite vertex list with distinct vertices and each consecutive pair an edge. A graph is connected when every two vertices are joined by a path. A cycle is a vertex list $(v_0,\ldots,v_k)$ with $k\geq3$, $v_k=v_0$, $v_0,\ldots,v_{k-1}$ distinct, and each consecutive pair an edge; a tree is a connected simple graph with no cycle. For $n\in\mathbb N$ with $n\geq1$, let $\mathcal C_n$ be the set of connected simple graphs on $[n]$ and let $\mathcal T_n$ be the set of trees on $[n]$. The set $[n]$ is finite; its power set is finite, so its subset $\binom{[n]}2$ is finite; the power set of that edge set is finite as well. Each simple graph on $[n]$ is determined by an edge set in this last power set, so $\mathcal C_n$ and $\mathcal T_n$ are finite.

For an ordered tuple $(\gamma_1,\ldots,\gamma_n)\in\Gamma^n$, put $f_{ij}:=-\mathbf 1_{\{\gamma_i\sim\gamma_j\}}$ and define the connected coefficient

$$U_n(\gamma_1,\ldots,\gamma_n):=\sum_{G\in\mathcal C_n}\ \prod_{\{i,j\}\in E(G)}f_{ij}.$$

For $n=1$, $\mathcal C_1$ contains the one-vertex graph and the empty edge product equals $1$. These are finite polynomial and coefficient definitions; they assert no convergence.

derivations.claim: Write $f_{ij}=-\mathbf 1_{\{\gamma_i\sim\gamma_j\}}$. Reflexivity makes $\prod_{i<j}(1+f_{ij})$ zero when a tuple repeats a polymer, and otherwise this product is one exactly for a compatible subset. Hence $Z_V(t)=\sum_{n\geq0}\frac{t^n}{n!}\sum_{\vec\gamma\in V^n}(\prod_iw_{\gamma_i})\prod_{i<j}(1+f_{ij})$ as a formal series. Expanding the pair product gives all simple graphs. A set partition of $[n]$ is a finite family of nonempty pairwise-disjoint blocks whose union is $[n]$; write $\Pi_n$ for the set of such partitions. This set is finite since it is contained in $\mathcal P(\mathcal P([n]))$. The connected components of each finite graph give its unique partition into connected graph blocks. Each graph's edge weight factors over these blocks. The coefficient of $t^n$ in $\exp(L_V(t))$ is $\frac1{n!}\sum_{\pi\in\Pi_n}\sum_{\vec\gamma\in V^n}(\prod_{B\in\pi}U_{|B|}(\vec\gamma_B))(\prod_{i=1}^nw_{\gamma_i})$: for ordered block sizes $m_1,\ldots,m_k$, assigning the $n$ labels to those blocks contributes $n!/(m_1!\cdots m_k!)$, and the exponential's factor $1/k!$ removes the ordering of the $k$ blocks. These factors leave exactly the connected-component expansion of the all-graph coefficient. Thus $Z_V$ and $\exp(L_V)$ have identical formal coefficients.

Let $d_n$ be the coefficient of $t^n$ in $L_V$, and apply [F2] to the finite polymer set $V$ with activities $r w_\eta$. Since $r>0$, [F5] gives $|r w_\eta|=r|w_\eta|$, so [A1] implies the rooted criterion. For each fixed root $\gamma_1$, the $n$th nonnegative term of that rooted sum is at most $e^{a_{\gamma_1}}$. The finite-sum triangle inequality, multiplicativity in [F5], and agreement of the complex modulus with real absolute value give $r^n|d_n|\leq\frac1{n!}\sum_{\gamma_1\in V}r|w_{\gamma_1}|\sum_{\gamma_2,\ldots,\gamma_n\in V}|U_n(\gamma_1,\ldots,\gamma_n)|\prod_{j=2}^n|r w_{\gamma_j}|\leq\frac1n\sum_{\gamma\in V}r|w_\gamma|e^{a_\gamma}$. Thus on $|t|\leq s<r$, the series is dominated by a constant times $\sum_{n\geq1}(s/r)^n/n$, and its derivative series by a constant times $\sum_{n\geq1}(s/r)^{n-1}$. Both converge uniformly on every such closed subdisc.

By [F4], $L_V$ differentiates term by term throughout $|t|<r$. For each fixed $t$ with $|t|<r$, step 1.2 gives $\sum_{n\geq1}|d_n||t|^n<\infty$, so the total absolute sum after expanding $\exp(L_V(t))$ is at most $\sum_{k\geq0}(\sum_{n\geq1}|d_n||t|^n)^k/k!<\infty$. The products may therefore be regrouped by total degree; their coefficients are the formal coefficients identified in step 1.1, so $Z_V(t)=\exp(L_V(t))$ on the disc. By [F3], $\exp(L_V(t))\exp(-L_V(t))=1$, so $Z_V(t)$ is nonzero and $L_V$ is its analytic logarithm with $L_V(0)=0$.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]) and let
$\mathbb T=\mathbb R/\mathbb Z$ with its normalized Haar integral
$dm_{\mathbb T}$ ([[def-the-one-dimensional-torus-and-normalized-haar-integral]]).

**Characters.** For $k\in\mathbb Z$ define $e_k:\mathbb T\to\mathbb C$ by
$e_k(x):=\exp(2\pi i\,k\,\widetilde x)$ for $x=[\widetilde x]\in\mathbb T$,
where $\exp$ is the complex exponential ([[def-complex-exponential]]). The
definition is independent of the representative $\widetilde x$: replacing
$\widetilde x$ by $\widetilde x+n$ with $n\in\mathbb Z$ adds the period
$2\pi kn$ to the argument of sine and cosine. Each $e_k$ is continuous, hence
Borel, and satisfies

$$e_k(x)e_l(x)=e_{k+l}(x),\qquad |e_k(x)|=1,\qquad \overline{e_k(x)}=e_{-k}(x) ,$$

the last two by the cartesian form $\exp(i\theta)=\cos\theta+i\sin\theta$ of
[[cor-complex-exponential-cartesian-form-modulus-and-eulers-identity]] and
[[lem-complex-conjugation-and-modulus-laws]]. In particular $e_0=1$ and every
$e_k$ is bounded and nonzero everywhere.

**Fourier coefficients.** Let $f\in L^1(\mathbb T;\mathbb C)$
([[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]]), that is, a class
of Borel functions with $\int_{\mathbb T}|f|\,dm_{\mathbb T}<+\infty$. Define the
**Fourier coefficient** of $f$ at $k\in\mathbb Z$ by

$$\widehat f(k):=\int_{\mathbb T}f(x)e_{-k}(x)\,dm_{\mathbb T}=\int_{\mathbb T}f(x)\exp(-2\pi ikx)\,dm_{\mathbb T}.$$

This is well defined: $|f\,e_{-k}|=|f|$ because $|e_{-k}|=1$, so
$f\,e_{-k}\in L^1(\mathbb T;\mathbb C)$ and its integral is finite; and the
integral depends only on the class of $f$, because it is unchanged when $f$ is
modified on a null set
([[thm-the-lebesgue-integral-respects-almost-everywhere-equality]]). The map
$f\mapsto\widehat f(k)$ is complex-linear for each $k$
([[thm-linearity-of-the-lebesgue-integral-on-l-one]]).

**Trigonometric polynomials.** A **trigonometric polynomial** on $\mathbb T$ is
a finite complex linear combination of characters, $p=\sum_{k\in F}c_ke_k$, for
a finite $F\subseteq\mathbb Z$ and scalars $c_k\in\mathbb C$. The set of all
trigonometric polynomials is the span of $\{e_k:k\in\mathbb Z\}$; it is closed
under addition, scalar multiplication, multiplication and complex conjugation
(by the identities for $e_ke_l$ and $\overline{e_k}$), and it contains $e_0=1$.
Nothing is claimed here about uniqueness of the coefficients in an expansion,
nor about the size of $\widehat p$; those are properties of the characters
proved below.

**The finite torus.** On $\mathbb T^n$, $n\ge1$, the characters are
$e_k(x):=\exp(2\pi i\,k\cdot x)$ for $k\in\mathbb Z^n$, where $k\cdot x$ is the
Euclidean dot product of a representative tuple; trigonometric polynomials are
finite complex linear combinations of these, and Fourier coefficients of
$f\in L^1(\mathbb T^n;\mathbb C)$ are
$\widehat f(k)=\int_{\mathbb T^n}f\,e_{-k}\,dm_{\mathbb T^n}$. Fubini computes
integrals of products of characters on the product measure
([[thm-fubini-theorem-for-l-one-on-sigma-finite-product-spaces]]); for
$f\in L^2(\mathbb T^n;\mathbb C)$ Hölder's inequality makes $f\,e_{-k}$
integrable ([[thm-complex-holder-minkowski-and-the-quotient-norm]],
[[thm-finite-measure-l-r-includes-into-l-p-for-p-less-r]]).

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $n\ge1$
and let $e_k(x)=\exp(2\pi i\,k\cdot x)$, $k\in\mathbb Z^n$, be the coordinate
characters on $\mathbb T^n$
([[def-the-one-dimensional-torus-and-normalized-haar-integral]],
[[def-fourier-coefficients-and-trigonometric-polynomials]]). Then:

1. $(e_k)_{k\in\mathbb Z^n}$ is an orthonormal family in the complex Hilbert
   space $L^2(\mathbb T^n)$;
2. it is an orthonormal basis: its closed linear span is $L^2(\mathbb T^n)$;
3. consequently the Fourier expansion
   $f=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^n}\widehat f(k)e_k$ and Parseval's identity
   $$\|f\|_2^2=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^n}|\widehat f(k)|^2,\qquad \langle f,g\rangle=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^n}\widehat f(k)\overline{\widehat g(k)}$$
   hold for all $f,g\in L^2(\mathbb T^n)$, in the finite-subset-net sense; and
4. the Fourier coefficient map is a surjective linear isometry of
   $L^2(\mathbb T^n)$ onto $\ell^2(\mathbb Z^n,\mathbb C)$.

No Hilbert tensor-product identification is used anywhere.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$), meaning every at most countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function. Let $d\ge1$, let $\mathbb T^d=(\mathbb R/\mathbb Z)^d$ carry the normalized product Haar measure $dx$ with $dx(\mathbb T^d)=1$, and let $\rho_0$ be a real measurable function on $\mathbb T^d$ with $0\le\rho_0\le1$ almost everywhere. For a finite $T\ge0$, a **weak heat solution with datum $\rho_0$** is a family $(u_t)_{0\le t\le T}$ of real essentially bounded measurable-function classes (elements of $L^\infty(\mathbb T^d,dx;\mathbb R)$), with $u_0=\rho_0$ as a function class, such that for every complex-valued smooth periodic test function $G$, the map $t\mapsto\int_{\mathbb T^d}u_t(x)G(x)\,dx$ is continuous and

$$\int_{\mathbb T^d}u_t(x)G(x)\,dx=\int_{\mathbb T^d}\rho_0(x)G(x)\,dx+\int_0^t\int_{\mathbb T^d}u_s(x)\Delta G(x)\,dx\,ds$$

for every $0\le t\le T$. Here $\Delta=\sum_{i=1}^d\partial_{x_i}^2$ is the periodic Laplacian; equality of function classes means equality almost everywhere with respect to $dx$. For the Fourier convention on this torus, set $e_k(x)=\exp(2\pi i k\cdot x)$ for $k\in\mathbb Z^d$ and $\widehat f(k)=\int_{\mathbb T^d}f(x)e_{-k}(x)\,dx$ for $f\in L^1(\mathbb T^d,dx)$.

derivations.claim: Since $0\le\rho_0\le1$ and $dx(\mathbb T^d)=1$, $\rho_0\in L^1$ and $|\widehat\rho_0(k)|\le1$ for every $k$. For any smooth $G$ and integer $m\ge1$, periodic integration by parts gives $(1+4\pi^2|k|^2)^m\widehat G(k)=\widehat{(1-\Delta)^mG}(k)$, hence $|\widehat G(k)|\le\|(1-\Delta)^mG\|_{L^1}(1+4\pi^2|k|^2)^{-m}$. If $q\ge0$ is fixed, choose $m>(d+q)/2$; grouping lattice points by $r=\|k\|_\infty$ gives at most $(2r+1)^d-(2r-1)^d\le C_dr^{d-1}$ points in shell $r$. The shell contribution to $\sum_k(1+|k|)^q|\widehat G(k)|$ is at most $C r^{d-1+q-2m}$. Grouping shells into dyadic blocks $2^j\le r<2^{j+1}$ bounds the $j$th block by $C'2^{j(d+q-2m)}$, a convergent geometric series since $2m>d+q$. Thus $\sum_k(1+|k|)^q|\widehat G(k)|<\infty$.

For each $t>0$ and each fixed derivative order, multiplication of the coefficients by any corresponding polynomial in $k$ still leaves an absolutely summable sequence, because $|\widehat\rho_0(k)|\le1$ and the Gaussian factor $e^{-4\pi^2|k|^2t}$ dominates every inverse power on lattice shells. Therefore the heat series and all fixed-order differentiated series converge uniformly on $\mathbb T^d$ for $t\ge\varepsilon>0$. Pairing the $k$ and $-k$ terms shows $\rho_t$ is real. Termwise differentiation is valid on every such compact time interval; both $\partial_t$ and $\Delta$ multiply the $k$th term by $-4\pi^2|k|^2$, so $\partial_t\rho_t=\Delta\rho_t$.

The decay estimate in step 1.1 makes the Fourier series for $G$ and for each fixed space or time derivative of $P_tG$ uniformly absolutely convergent even at $t=0$. By [F2], the series at $t=0$ equals $G$ in $L^2$; both are continuous, so equality almost everywhere implies equality everywhere. Uniform convergence of the differentiated series proves smoothness and uniform derivative bounds on $[0,T]\times\mathbb T^d$. Also $\|P_tG-G\|_\infty\le\sum_k|\widehat G(k)|\,|e^{-4\pi^2|k|^2t}-1|\to0$ by splitting into a finite set of modes and an absolutely summable tail. Termwise differentiation gives $\partial_tP_tG=\Delta P_tG$.

Absolute convergence permits termwise integration against $\rho_0\in L^1$. Reindexing $k\mapsto-k$ and using the even multiplier $e^{-4\pi^2|k|^2t}$ gives $\int\rho_tG=\sum_k e^{-4\pi^2|k|^2t}\widehat\rho_0(k)\widehat G(-k)=\int\rho_0P_tG$. By step 2.2 this pairing tends to $\int\rho_0G$ as $t\downarrow0$. Differentiating the pairing for $t>0$ and using $\Delta P_tG=P_t\Delta G$ yields $\frac{d}{dt}\int\rho_tG=\int\rho_t\Delta G$; integration from $0$ proves the weak identity in [F3]. Thus the constructed family is a weak heat solution.

Parseval and the heat coefficients give $\|\rho_t-\rho_0\|_2^2=\sum_k|\widehat\rho_0(k)|^2|e^{-4\pi^2|k|^2t}-1|^2\to0$ as $t\downarrow0$: choose a finite set whose tail in the convergent series $\sum_k|\widehat\rho_0(k)|^2$ is small, then take the limit on that finite set. For $\epsilon>0$ put $a_\epsilon(z)=\frac12(1-z/\sqrt{z^2+\epsilon^2})$ and $\Phi_\epsilon(z)=\int_0^z\int_0^r a_\epsilon(q)\,dq\,dr$. Then $\Phi_\epsilon$ is smooth and convex, $\Phi_\epsilon(0)=\Phi_\epsilon'(0)=0$, and $0\le\Phi_\epsilon(z)\le z^2/2$. On any interval $[a,b]\subset(0,T]$, the heat equation, chain rule, and periodic integration by parts give $\int\Phi_\epsilon(\rho_b)-\int\Phi_\epsilon(\rho_a)=-\int_a^b\int\Phi_\epsilon''(\rho_s)\sum_{i=1}^d|\partial_{x_i}\rho_s|^2\,dx\,ds\le0$. For each real $z$, the defining double integral tends to $\frac12(z^-)^2$, where $z^-:=\max\{-z,0\}$; dominated convergence on the bounded range of $\rho$ over $[a,b]\times\mathbb T^d$ gives the same monotonicity for $\|\rho_t^-\|_2^2$. Letting $a\downarrow0$, the $L^2$ continuity just proved and $\rho_0\ge0$ imply $\rho_t^-=0$. The assumed datum already gives the required bound when $T=0$.

For the upper bound put $b_\epsilon(z)=\frac12(1+(z-1)/\sqrt{(z-1)^2+\epsilon^2})$ and $\Psi_\epsilon(z)=\int_1^z\int_1^r b_\epsilon(q)\,dq\,dr$. This is smooth and convex with $\Psi_\epsilon(1)=\Psi_\epsilon'(1)=0$ and $0\le\Psi_\epsilon(z)\le(z-1)^2/2$. The same integration by parts gives $\int\Psi_\epsilon(\rho_b)\le\int\Psi_\epsilon(\rho_a)$ for $0<a<b$, and $\Psi_\epsilon(z)\to\frac12((z-1)^+)^2$, where $r^+:=\max\{r,0\}$. Dominated convergence and $L^2$ continuity at zero, together with $\rho_0\le1$, give $(\rho_t-1)^+=0$. The zero Fourier coefficient is unchanged by the heat multiplier, so $\int\rho_t=\widehat\rho_0(0)=\int\rho_0$. The assumed datum already gives the bound when $T=0$.

Let $(u_t)$ be any weak heat solution in the sense of [F3]. Testing its weak identity with $e_{-k}$ shows $g_k(t):=\widehat u_t(k)$ is continuous and satisfies $g_k(t)=\widehat\rho_0(k)-4\pi^2|k|^2\int_0^t g_k(s)\,ds$. Hence $g_k$ is differentiable and solves $g_k'=-4\pi^2|k|^2g_k$, so $g_k(t)=e^{-4\pi^2|k|^2t}\widehat\rho_0(k)$, the coefficient of the constructed $\rho_t$. For each $t$, both functions are in $L^2$; equality of all Fourier coefficients and completeness in [F2] imply $u_t=\rho_t$ almost everywhere. Thus the weak heat solution is unique.

modified on a null set
([[thm-the-lebesgue-integral-respects-almost-everywhere-equality]]). The map
$f\mapsto\widehat f(k)$ is complex-linear for each $k$
([[thm-linearity-of-the-lebesgue-integral-on-l-one]]).

**Trigonometric polynomials.** A **trigonometric polynomial** on $\mathbb T$ is
a finite complex linear combination of characters, $p=\sum_{k\in F}c_ke_k$, for
a finite $F\subseteq\mathbb Z$ and scalars $c_k\in\mathbb C$. The set of all
trigonometric polynomials is the span of $\{e_k:k\in\mathbb Z\}$; it is closed
under addition, scalar multiplication, multiplication and complex conjugation
(by the identities for $e_ke_l$ and $\overline{e_k}$), and it contains $e_0=1$.
Nothing is claimed here about uniqueness of the coefficients in an expansion,
nor about the size of $\widehat p$; those are properties of the characters
proved below.

**The finite torus.** On $\mathbb T^n$, $n\ge1$, the characters are
$e_k(x):=\exp(2\pi i\,k\cdot x)$ for $k\in\mathbb Z^n$, where $k\cdot x$ is the
Euclidean dot product of a representative tuple; trigonometric polynomials are
finite complex linear combinations of these, and Fourier coefficients of
$f\in L^1(\mathbb T^n;\mathbb C)$ are
$\widehat f(k)=\int_{\mathbb T^n}f\,e_{-k}\,dm_{\mathbb T^n}$. Fubini computes
integrals of products of characters on the product measure
([[thm-fubini-theorem-for-l-one-on-sigma-finite-product-spaces]]); for
$f\in L^2(\mathbb T^n;\mathbb C)$ Hölder's inequality makes $f\,e_{-k}$
integrable ([[thm-complex-holder-minkowski-and-the-quotient-norm]],
[[thm-finite-measure-l-r-includes-into-l-p-for-p-less-r]]).

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $n\ge1$
and let $e_k(x)=\exp(2\pi i\,k\cdot x)$, $k\in\mathbb Z^n$, be the coordinate
characters on $\mathbb T^n$
([[def-the-one-dimensional-torus-and-normalized-haar-integral]],
[[def-fourier-coefficients-and-trigonometric-polynomials]]). Then:

1. $(e_k)_{k\in\mathbb Z^n}$ is an orthonormal family in the complex Hilbert
   space $L^2(\mathbb T^n)$;
2. it is an orthonormal basis: its closed linear span is $L^2(\mathbb T^n)$;
3. consequently the Fourier expansion
   $f=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^n}\widehat f(k)e_k$ and Parseval's identity
   $$\|f\|_2^2=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^n}|\widehat f(k)|^2,\qquad \langle f,g\rangle=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^n}\widehat f(k)\overline{\widehat g(k)}$$
   hold for all $f,g\in L^2(\mathbb T^n)$, in the finite-subset-net sense; and
4. the Fourier coefficient map is a surjective linear isometry of
   $L^2(\mathbb T^n)$ onto $\ell^2(\mathbb Z^n,\mathbb C)$.

No Hilbert tensor-product identification is used anywhere.
