citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Fix a period $L>0$ metres and let $\mathbb T_L:=\mathbb R/(L\mathbb Z)$. A smooth periodic function on $\mathbb T_L$ means an $L$-periodic $C^\infty$ function on $\mathbb R$. For a periodic integrable function $g$, use the normalized spatial measure $dm_L=dx/L$ on a period and write

$$\|g\|_{2,L}^2:=\frac1L\int_0^L |g(x)|^2\,dx.$$

Elements of $L^2(\mathbb T_L,dm_L;\mathbb C)$ are equivalence classes modulo equality almost everywhere. For $n\in\mathbb Z$, define the wave number $\kappa_n:=2\pi n/L$, character $e_n(x):=\exp(i\kappa_n x)$, and Fourier coefficient $\widehat g(n):=L^{-1}\int_0^L g(x)e^{-i\kappa_nx}\,dx$. These formulas are independent of the chosen representative of $x$ in $\mathbb T_L$.

Let $c>0$ be a speed in $\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, let $\lambda>0$ be a switching-rate parameter in $\mathrm{s^{-1}}$, and let $\epsilon>0$ be dimensionless. For smooth real initial data $f_{+,0},f_{-,0}$ on $\mathbb T_L$, the two-velocity periodic model is the linear Cauchy problem below; when these functions represent physical densities, also require $f_{\pm,0}\ge0$.

$$\partial_t f_+^\epsilon+\frac{c}{\epsilon}\partial_x f_+^\epsilon=\frac{\lambda}{\epsilon^2}(f_-^\epsilon-f_+^\epsilon),\qquad \partial_t f_-^\epsilon-\frac{c}{\epsilon}\partial_x f_-^\epsilon=\frac{\lambda}{\epsilon^2}(f_+^\epsilon-f_-^\epsilon),\qquad f_\pm^\epsilon(\cdot,0)=f_{\pm,0}.$$

Here $x\in\mathbb T_L$, $t\ge0$ is measured in seconds, and $f_\pm$ have the units of a linear number density, $\mathrm{m^{-1}}$. The speed magnitude is $c/\epsilon$, and from either velocity state the rate of switching to the opposite state is $\lambda/\epsilon^2$. Define the total density $\rho^\epsilon:=f_+^\epsilon+f_-^\epsilon$, the flux $j^\epsilon:=(c/\epsilon)(f_+^\epsilon-f_-^\epsilon)$, and the total mass $M^\epsilon(t):=\int_0^L\rho^\epsilon(x,t)\,dx$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $n\ge1$
and let $e_k(x)=\exp(2\pi i\,k\cdot x)$, $k\in\mathbb Z^n$, be the coordinate
characters on $\mathbb T^n$
([[def-the-one-dimensional-torus-and-normalized-haar-integral]],
[[def-fourier-coefficients-and-trigonometric-polynomials]]). Then:

1. $(e_k)_{k\in\mathbb Z^n}$ is an orthonormal family in the complex Hilbert
   space $L^2(\mathbb T^n)$;
2. it is an orthonormal basis: its closed linear span is $L^2(\mathbb T^n)$;
3. consequently the Fourier expansion
   $f=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^n}\widehat f(k)e_k$ and Parseval's identity
   $$\|f\|_2^2=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^n}|\widehat f(k)|^2,\qquad \langle f,g\rangle=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^n}\widehat f(k)\overline{\widehat g(k)}$$
   hold for all $f,g\in L^2(\mathbb T^n)$, in the finite-subset-net sense; and
4. the Fourier coefficient map is a surjective linear isometry of
   $L^2(\mathbb T^n)$ onto $\ell^2(\mathbb Z^n,\mathbb C)$.

No Hilbert tensor-product identification is used anywhere.

Let $a < b$ be reals, let $G : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at every
point of $[a,b]$ as a function on $[a,b]$ (The derivative $f'(c) = \lim_{x \to c} \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c}$ of $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ at a point $c \in A$ that is a limit point of $A$, and differentiability on a set; at $a$ and $b$
this is the one-sided derivative), let $f := G'$, and suppose $f$ is integrable
on $[a,b]$ (The lower and upper Darboux integrals of a bounded $f$ on $[a,b]$ as $\sup_P L(f,P)$ and $\inf_P U(f,P)$, Darboux integrability as their equality, and the notation $\int_a^b f$). Then

$$\int_a^b f \;=\; G(b) - G(a) .$$

**Both hypotheses are needed and neither is removable.** A function may be
differentiable everywhere with $G'$ not integrable — then the left-hand side does
not exist (an everywhere differentiable function with unbounded derivative) — and an
integrable $f$ need not be the derivative of anything
(the sign function); both witnesses are on the
companion page.

**No continuity of $f$ is assumed**, which is what makes this the working form:
the theorem evaluates $\int_a^b f$ for every integrable derivative, not only for
continuous integrands.

Let $I=[a,b]\subseteq\mathbb R$ be a nonempty compact interval, let
$C:I\to M_n(\mathbb R)$ be continuous, let $t_0\in I$, and let
$Y_0\in M_n(\mathbb R)$. For $n=0$, there is exactly one map $Y:I\to M_0(\mathbb R)$, namely the empty-matrix map, and all entrywise differential identities are vacuous. For $n\ge1$ and $a<b$, the linear matrix initial value problem

$$Y'(t)=C(t)Y(t),\qquad Y(t_0)=Y_0,$$

has a unique solution on all of $I$, with domain-relative one-sided
derivatives at the endpoints. If $n\ge1$ and $a=b$, then $t_0=a$ and there is exactly
one map $Y:I\to M_n(\mathbb R)$ with $Y(a)=Y_0$. This singleton map
extends to a solution of $Z'=C(a)Z$, $Z(a)=Y_0$, on an open interval
around $a$; any two such local continuations agree on their common interval
containing $a$. No time derivative or IVP solution on the singleton itself
is asserted.

Let $X$ be a real or complex Banach space and let $A\in\mathcal B(X)$ ([[def-bounded-linear-operator]]). For $t\in\mathbb R$ define $E(t):=\sum_{n=0}^\infty\frac{t^n}{n!}A^n$. Then the series converges absolutely in the operator norm $\|\cdot\|$ of $\mathcal B(X)$, uniformly for $t$ in compact subsets of $\mathbb R$; $E(t)\in\mathcal B(X)$ with $\|E(t)\| \le e^{|t|\|A\|}$; $E(0)=I$ and $E(t+s)=E(t)E(s)$ for all $s,t\in\mathbb R$; $t\mapsto E(t)$ is of class $C^\infty$ in the operator norm with $$E'(t)=AE(t)=E(t)A,$$ and $\|E(t)-I-tA\| \le\frac{t^2}{2}\|A\|^2e^{|t|\|A\|}$, so that $\frac{E(t)-I}{t}\to A$ in operator norm as $t\to0$. In particular $E$ is a uniformly continuous (hence strongly continuous) group of bounded operators on $X$ whose generator is the bounded operator $A$.

1. $(\mathbb{R}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$ with the usual metric $d_{\mathbb{R}}(x,y) = |x-y|$
   ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]) is a complete metric space
   ([[def-complete-metric-space]]).
2. Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$ and let $d_2$ be the Euclidean metric on
   $\mathbb{R}^n$ ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). Then $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ is complete.

**The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is inherited and is not decoration.**
[[lem-metrics-on-rn]] defines $\mathbb{R}^n$ and its three metrics only for
$n \ge 1$, because at $n = 0$ the metric $d_\infty$ would be a maximum over the
empty index set. Every statement about $\mathbb{R}^n$ in this library carries the
hypothesis, and this one does too.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and let $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$, with the Euclidean
inner product and the Euclidean norm as in The Euclidean inner product $\langle x,y\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k y_k$ on $\mathbb{R}^n$. Then:

1. **Cauchy-Schwarz.**
   $$\lvert\langle x,y\rangle\rvert \;\le\; \lVert x\rVert_2\,\lVert y\rVert_2 ,$$
   with equality if and only if there is a pair $(\lambda,\mu) \ne (0,0)$ of
   reals with $\lambda x_k = \mu y_k$ for every $k < n$.
2. **$\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm on $\mathbb{R}^{n}$**
   (A norm on a real vector space, the induced metric, and the dictionary with the metric axioms), for **every** $n \in \mathbb{N}$; the metric
   it induces is $d_2$ of $\mathbb{R}^n$ as the set of functions $n \to \mathbb{R}$, and $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ are metrics on it whenever $n \ge 1$.
3. **Parallelogram law.**
   $$\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} + \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2} \;=\; 2\lVert x\rVert_2^{2} + 2\lVert y\rVert_2^{2} .$$
4. **Polarisation.**
   $$\langle x,y\rangle \;=\; \tfrac14\Bigl(\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} - \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2}\Bigr),$$
   so the inner product is recovered from the norm it induces.

**Clause 1 is a citation, not a new proof.** The inequality and its equality case
are the published The Cauchy-Schwarz inequality for finite sums, stated there for two lists of
reals; all that happens below is that it is read in the vector notation of
The Euclidean inner product $\langle x,y\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k y_k$ on $\mathbb{R}^n$. Re-proving it here would put two proofs of one
statement in the library.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$. A natural number is a von Neumann natural, that is a set,
and $n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ (The natural numbers $\mathbb{N}$ (von Neumann),
On $\mathbb{N}$ the order is membership: $m < n \iff m \in n$), so

$$\mathbb{R}^{n} \;=\; \{\, x \;:\; x \text{ is a function } n \to \mathbb{R} \,\}$$

is the function space of The vector space $F^{X}$ of all functions $X \to F$ with pointwise operations, and $F^{n}$ as the case $X = n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ at $F = \mathbb{R}$ and $X = n$,
a vector space over $\mathbb{R}$ under the pointwise operations
(Vector space over a field). We write $x_k := x(k)$ for $k < n$, and two elements of
$\mathbb{R}^{n}$ are equal exactly when they agree at every $k < n$. This is the
same set that $\mathbb{R}^n$ as the set of functions $n \to \mathbb{R}$, and $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ are metrics on it calls $\mathbb{R}^{n}$.

The **Euclidean inner product** of $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ is the real number

$$\langle x, y\rangle \;:=\; \sum_{k<n} x_k\,y_k ,$$

the finite sum of Finite sums and finite products, by recursion applied to the list $k \mapsto x_k y_k$
(extended by $0$ beyond $n$, as every finite list in this library is). The
**Euclidean norm** of $x$ is

$$\lVert x\rVert_2 \;:=\; \sqrt{\langle x, x\rangle},$$

which is defined because $\langle x,x\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k^{2} \ge 0$ (a sum
of nonnegative terms, Laws of finite sums and finite products clause 4 and
Squares of nonzero elements are positive, the case $x_k = 0$ giving $x_k^2 = 0$ by
Integer powers $a^m$) and every nonnegative real has a unique nonnegative square
root (Square roots exist: a unique $\sqrt{a} \ge 0$ with $(\sqrt{a})^2 = a$; the positives are $\{x^2 : x \neq 0\}$).

### Both are defined for every $n$, including $n = 0$

At $n = 0$ the set $\mathbb{R}^{0}$ has exactly one element, the empty function,
and it is the zero vector space (The standard list $e : n \to F^{n}$ with $e_i(i) = 1_F$ and $e_i(j) = 0_F$ for $j \ne i$ is an ordered basis of $F^{n}$; hence $\dim_F F^{n} = n$, and $F^{0}$ is the zero space with basis $\varnothing$ and dimension $0$ clause 5); the sum
above is the empty sum, so $\langle x,y\rangle = 0$ and $\lVert x\rVert_2 = 0$.
**This is the first place on this page where the two index regimes diverge, and
the divergence is deliberate.** The published metrics $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ of
$\mathbb{R}^n$ as the set of functions $n \to \mathbb{R}$, and $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ are metrics on it are defined only for $n \ge 1$, because $d_\infty$ would
otherwise be a maximum over the empty index set; the algebra above needs no such
restriction. The boundary in this page runs between the algebra and the metric,
not where a reader would guess, and Conventions of this page, the standing $n \ge 1$ hypothesis, and what is taken up elsewhere in the reading order lists
exactly which items inherit $n \ge 1$.

### The algebra of the inner product

For all $x, y, z \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

1. **Symmetry.** $\langle x,y\rangle = \langle y,x\rangle$, since $x_ky_k = y_kx_k$
   termwise.
2. **Additivity in the first argument.**
   $\langle x + y, z\rangle = \langle x,z\rangle + \langle y,z\rangle$: the list
   $k \mapsto (x_k+y_k)z_k$ is the termwise sum of $k \mapsto x_kz_k$ and
   $k \mapsto y_kz_k$, so Laws of finite sums and finite products clause 1 applies.
3. **Homogeneity in the first argument.**
   $\langle \lambda x, y\rangle = \lambda\langle x,y\rangle$, by
   Laws of finite sums and finite products clause 2.
4. **Bilinearity.** Clauses 2 and 3 together with symmetry give the same two laws
   in the second argument.
5. **Positive definiteness.** $\langle x,x\rangle \ge 0$, and
   $\langle x,x\rangle = 0$ if and only if $x = 0$. Indeed a vanishing sum of
   nonnegative terms has every term $0$ (Laws of finite sums and finite products clause 4), so
   $x_k^{2} = 0$ for every $k < n$, and a nonzero real has a positive square
   (Squares of nonzero elements are positive), whence $x_k = 0$ for every $k < n$ and $x = 0$.
6. **Agreement with the published Euclidean metric.** For $n \ge 1$ and
   $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$,
   $\lVert x - y\rVert_2 = \sqrt{\sum_{k<n}(x_k-y_k)^{2}} = d_2(x,y)$, the two
   sides being the same expression ($\mathbb{R}^n$ as the set of functions $n \to \mathbb{R}$, and $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ are metrics on it). In particular
   $\lVert x\rVert_2 = d_2(x, 0)$.

That $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm in the sense of A norm on a real vector space, the induced metric, and the dictionary with the metric axioms
is proved in Cauchy-Schwarz $\lvert\langle x,y\rangle\rvert \le \lVert x\rVert_2\lVert y\rVert_2$ with its equality case, the triangle inequality for $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$, the parallelogram law and polarisation, where the triangle
inequality is obtained from the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality; it is not assumed
here.

Let $X$ and $Y$ be normed spaces over the same scalar field, and let
$T:X\to Y$ be bounded in the sense of [[def-bounded-linear-operator]]. The
**operator norm** of $T$ is

$$\|T\| := \sup\{\|Tx\| : x \in X,\ \|x\| \le 1\}.$$

The set on the right contains $0$ and every bound $C$ for $T$ bounds it
above. Thus its finite real supremum exists by the proved least-upper-bound
property of the library's real field ([[cor-cauchy-reals-lub-complete]]).
In particular every number strictly below the supremum is exceeded by a
member of this set; otherwise it would be a smaller upper bound. No choice
principle is used for this assertion.

The same number is the least bound of $T$:

$$\|T\| = \inf\{C \ge 0 : \|Tx\| \le C\|x\| \text{ for all } x \in X\}.$$

If $X \ne \{0\}$, positive homogeneity also gives

$$\|T\| = \sup\{\|Tx\| : \|x\| = 1\}.$$

When $X = \{0\}$, the unit sphere is empty and the unit-ball supremum is $0$,
so $\|T\| = 0$.

derivations.claim: For $n\in\mathbb Z$, put $U_n=(\widehat f_+^\epsilon(n),\widehat f_-^\epsilon(n))^{\mathsf T}$, $v=c/\epsilon$, and $\alpha=\lambda/\epsilon^2$. Integrating by parts in the real and imaginary parts separately, using [F3], gives $U_n'=M_nU_n$, with $M_n=\begin{pmatrix}-i\kappa_n v-\alpha&\alpha\\ \alpha&i\kappa_n v-\alpha\end{pmatrix}$. Realify $z\in\mathbb C^2$ by $\mathcal Rz=(\operatorname{Re}z_1,\operatorname{Re}z_2,\operatorname{Im}z_1,\operatorname{Im}z_2)\in\mathbb R^4$, and for $M=P+iQ$ put $\mathcal RM=\begin{pmatrix}P&-Q\\Q&P\end{pmatrix}$. Direct coordinate multiplication gives $\mathcal R(Mz)=(\mathcal RM)\mathcal Rz$ and $|\mathcal Rz|_2^2=|z_1|^2+|z_2|^2$. By [F6], $\mathbb R^4$ is Banach; [F7] applied rowwise bounds $\mathcal RM_n$ as an operator, and [F8]–[F9] specify the Euclidean and operator norms. Hence [F5] makes $t\mapsto e^{t\mathcal RM_n}\mathcal RU_n(0)$ a solution of the realified constant-matrix IVP; [F4] gives uniqueness on each compact interval $[0,T]$, so these compatible solutions define the unique global complex Fourier mode solution after pulling back by $\mathcal R$. Since real initial data satisfy $U_{-n}(0)=\overline{U_n(0)}$ and $M_{-n}=\overline{M_n}$, uniqueness gives $U_{-n}(t)=\overline{U_n(t)}$, so the reconstructed Fourier series is real. The skew-Hermitian transport part contributes zero to the derivative of $|U_n|^2$, and direct multiplication of the collision matrix gives $(|U_n|^2)'=-2\alpha|\widehat f_+^\epsilon(n)-\widehat f_-^\epsilon(n)|^2\le0$. For every integer $r\ge0$ and every integer $q>r+1$, repeated integration by parts gives $|\widehat f_{\pm,0}(n)|\le |\kappa_n|^{-q}\|\partial_x^q f_{\pm,0}\|_{L^1(dm_L)}$ for $n\ne0$; grouping $2^j\le |n|<2^{j+1}$ shows $\sum_n(1+|\kappa_n|)^r|U_n(0)|<\infty$. The mode bound preserves these summable tails, and $M_n$ grows at most linearly in $|n|$, so the Fourier series and every space-time derivative converge uniformly on compact time intervals. They define a global smooth solution of the Cauchy problem. Any other smooth solution has the same mode ODEs and initial coefficients; [A1] and [F2] make the solutions equal as $L^2(\mathbb T_L,dm_L;\mathbb C^2)$ classes, hence almost everywhere. Both solutions are smooth and therefore continuous in $x$. If their difference were nonzero at some $x_0$, continuity would give a nonempty open arc on which its norm is bounded below by a positive constant; every nonempty open arc has positive normalized Lebesgue measure $dm_L$, contradicting equality almost everywhere. Thus they agree pointwise on $\mathbb T_L$.

Put $F_0=(f_{+,0},f_{-,0})$. For $h\ge0$, free transport $T_h(g_+,g_-):=(g_+(\cdot-vh),g_-(\cdot+vh))$ preserves nonnegativity and pair norm. It preserves each component mass because a change of variable turns its integral into an integral of a smooth periodic function over another full period, which is unchanged by [F3]. The pointwise collision operator $C_h$ is the matrix $\frac12\begin{pmatrix}1+e^{-2\alpha h}&1-e^{-2\alpha h}\\1-e^{-2\alpha h}&1+e^{-2\alpha h}\end{pmatrix}$. Its entries are nonnegative and its column sums are one. The orthonormal vectors $(1,1)/\sqrt2$ and $(1,-1)/\sqrt2$ have eigenvalues $1$ and $e^{-2\alpha h}\in[0,1]$, so $C_h$ preserves nonnegativity and total mass and contracts the pair norm pointwise, hence in pair $L^2$. Thus the alternating products $(T_{t/m}C_{t/m})^mF_0$ are nonnegative when $F_0$ is and are $L^2$ contractions.

Fix a Fourier mode $k\in\mathbb Z$ and let $A_k=\operatorname{diag}(-i\kappa_kv,i\kappa_kv)$ and $B=\alpha\begin{pmatrix}-1&1\\1&-1\end{pmatrix}$. Under the realification of step 1.1, their generators are real $4\times4$ matrices $\widetilde A_k=\mathcal R(A_k)$ and $\widetilde B=\mathcal R(B)$. Transport on this mode is $e^{\widetilde A_kh}$, and collision is $e^{\widetilde Bh}$ because the eigenvectors and eigenvalues in step 1.2 diagonalize $B$. By [F6], $\mathbb R^4$ with its Euclidean norm is Banach; applying [F7] rowwise bounds every real matrix as an operator, and [F8]–[F9] give the Euclidean and operator norms used in [F5]. For $X\in\{\widetilde A_k,\widetilde B,\widetilde A_k+\widetilde B\}$, [F5] gives $e^{Xh}=I+hX+R_X(h)$ with $\|R_X(h)\|\le K_Xh^2$ on $0\le h\le t$, where $K_X:=\tfrac12\|X\|^2e^{t\|X\|}$. Multiplying the first two expansions and subtracting the third shows $\|e^{\widetilde A_kh}e^{\widetilde Bh}-e^{(\widetilde A_k+\widetilde B)h}\|\le C_{k,\epsilon,t}h^2$, where one may take $C_{k,\epsilon,t}=\|\widetilde A_k\|\|\widetilde B\|+K_{\widetilde A_k}+K_{\widetilde B}+K_{\widetilde A_k+\widetilde B}+t(\|\widetilde A_k\|K_{\widetilde B}+\|\widetilde B\|K_{\widetilde A_k})+t^2K_{\widetilde A_k}K_{\widetilde B}$. All factors are contractions: the split factors by step 1.2, and the exact mode evolution by the energy identity in step 1.1. Telescoping the $m$-fold products with $h=t/m$ bounds the error by $mC_{k,\epsilon,t}(t/m)^2=C_{k,\epsilon,t}t^2/m$, so the split evolution converges to the exact solution in each fixed mode.

The zero mode in the equations of [F1] satisfies $(\widehat f_+(0)+\widehat f_-(0))'=0$, since the switching terms cancel and the transport frequency is zero. As $M^\epsilon(t)=L(\widehat f_+^\epsilon(0,t)+\widehat f_-^\epsilon(0,t))$, this proves total-mass conservation.

For a finite set of modes, step 2.1 gives convergence of the split evolution to the exact solution. Let $P_{>K}$ be the Fourier projection onto $|k|>K$, applied componentwise. Its initial pair tail tends to zero by [A1] and [F2]. Every split product preserves modes and contracts this tail by step 1.2. The exact evolution also preserves modes; applying the mode energy identity in step 1.1 and summing by Parseval [F2] shows it contracts the same tail. Hence the split products converge in pair $L^2$ to the solution from step 1.1.

The nonnegative cone is closed in real $L^2$: if classes $g_m$ have nonnegative representatives almost everywhere and $g_m\to g$, then for representatives of $g$ and $g_m$ the inequality $g^-\le|g-g_m|$ holds almost everywhere, so $\|g^-\|_2\le\|g-g_m\|_2\to0$. Applying this componentwise, the split products are nonnegative by step 1.2 and converge by step 3.1, so each component of the exact solution is nonnegative almost everywhere. Fix $t\ge0$. Step 1.1 gives smooth, hence continuous, functions $x\mapsto f_\pm^\epsilon(x,t)$. If either component were negative at some $x_0$, continuity would give a nonempty open arc on which it is bounded above by a negative constant. Such an arc has positive $dm_L$ measure, contradicting nonnegativity almost everywhere. Thus both components are nonnegative pointwise for every $t\ge0$.

Under [A1], apply the mode identity in step 1.1 to the difference of two solutions; summing over $n$ by Parseval [F2] gives the stated contraction. Step 1.1 gives uniform convergence of the solution and time-derivative Fourier series, so termwise differentiation of Parseval's sum is valid. derivations.claim: The elementary integral is well-defined: adjoining an endpoint splits an interval into two whose lengths sum to its original length, so finite common refinement leaves each integral unchanged. Indicators of finite-box sets, their fixed-coordinate sections, and their finite products and differences are rectangular step functions. Common refinement proves linearity, positivity and the integral triangle inequality. It also proves equality of iterated and full integrals, because both sum the same finitely many cell values times products of lengths; outer grid endpoints have zero length. A translation preserves side lengths, so a piecewise translation bijectively exchanging finitely many boxes preserves these integrals. These are all the continuous-cube integration rules used below.

For $1\le p\le2$ and real $u,v$, we prove $(u^2+(p-1)v^2)^{1/2}\le((|u+v|^p+|u-v|^p)/2)^{1/p}$. At $p=1$ this follows from the triangle inequality, and at $p=2$ it is equality. For $1<p<2$ signs can be removed. If $|v|>|u|$, interchange their absolute values: the right side is unchanged and the squared left side increases by $(2-p)(v^2-u^2)$. It therefore suffices to take $u>0$ and $0\le t=v/u\le1$, apart from the trivial zero case. For $t<1$ put $H(t)=((1+t)^p+(1-t)^p)/2$. The convexity of $s^{p-2}$, obtained by two differentiations, gives $H''(t)\ge p(p-1)$. Since $H(0)=1$ and $H'(0)=0$, integration twice gives $H(t)\ge1+p(p-1)t^2/2$. Concavity of $s^{p/2}$ gives $(1+(p-1)t^2)^{p/2}\le1+p(p-1)t^2/2$. Multiply by $u^p$ and take the $p$th root; continuity includes $t=1$. This proves the claimed two-point inequality.

On a uniform bit $x\in\{-1,1\}$ define $T_\rho(u+vx)=u+\rho vx$, for $0\le\rho\le1$. Step 1.2 with $p=1+\rho^2$ proves $\|T_\rho h\|_2\le\|h\|_p$. To extend this to $d$ bits, first note that finite-sum Minkowski gives $\|h\|_{L_y^2(L_x^p)}\le\|h\|_{L_x^p(L_y^2)}$ for finite probability spaces and $1\le p\le2$: its $p$th-power form is the triangle inequality for $\mathbb E_x|h(x,\cdot)|^p$ in $L_y^{2/p}$. For completeness, finite weighted Minkowski at exponent $r>1$ follows by multiplying $|z+w|\le|z|+|w|$ by $|z+w|^{r-1}$, summing, applying Hölder and dividing by $\|z+w\|_r^{r-1}$ if nonzero. Weighted Hölder follows by normalizing the two norms and summing Young's inequality $ab\le a^r/r+b^{r'}/r'$, which follows by minimizing $a^r/r-ab$ in $a\ge0$; zero norms and $r=1$ are immediate. If $T_X,T_Y$ contract $L^p$ into $L^2$ on two blocks, apply the $X$ contraction pointwise in $y$, the mixed-norm inequality, and then the $Y$ contraction pointwise in $x$ to obtain $\|T_XT_Yh\|_2\le\|T_Yh\|_{L_y^2(L_x^p)}\le\|T_Yh\|_{L_x^p(L_y^2)}\le\|h\|_p$. Induction therefore gives $\|T_\rho h\|_2\le\|h\|_{1+\rho^2}$ on every finite Boolean cube, where $T_\rho$ applies the one-bit operator in each coordinate.

Put $N=2^m$ for $m\ge1$ and partition $[0,1)^n$ into the dyadic cells $Q_a=\prod_i[a_i/N,(a_i+1)/N)$, with $0\le a_i<N$. On $Q_a$ let $\ell_m=f(a/N)$, $u_m=f((a+\mathbf1)/N)$ and $g_m=N^n\int_{Q_a}f$. Faces at coordinate one may be assigned arbitrary values for integration. Monotonicity gives $\ell_m\le f,g_m\le u_m$. Telescope each difference $u_m-\ell_m$ one coordinate at a time. For coordinate $i$, summation over $a_i$ at fixed remaining upper/lower corner coordinates telescopes to a difference of values at coordinate one and zero, at most one. There are $N^{n-1}$ choices of the other indices, hence $\int(u_m-\ell_m)\le n/N$ and $\delta_m:=\int|g_m-f|\le n/N$. Cell averaging gives $\int g_m=\int f=a$, while $|g_m^2-f^2|\le2|g_m-f|$. Therefore $|\operatorname{Var}(g_m)-a(1-a)|\le2\delta_m\to0$. This uses an explicit numerical error bound, not a theorem interchanging a limit and an integral.

On $\{-1,1\}^d$ let $x^{(j)}$ flip bit $j$ and set $D_jh=(h(x)-h(x^{(j)}))/2$. Suppose numbers $b_j\in[0,1]$ satisfy $\|D_jh\|_p\le b_j^{1/p}/2$ for every $1\le p\le2$. We will prove $\operatorname{Var}(h)\le\sum_j b_j/(1+\log(1/b_j))$, interpreting the summand at zero as zero. For $S\subseteq\{1,\ldots,d\}$ define $\chi_S(x)=\prod_{j\in S}x_j$. Independence and zero mean of each bit show these $2^d$ functions are orthonormal. Since the function space has dimension $2^d$, they form a basis; write $h=\sum_S\widehat h(S)\chi_S$. Then $D_jh=\sum_{S\ni j}\widehat h(S)\chi_S$ and $T_\rho\chi_S=\rho^{|S|}\chi_S$. Parseval and finite-sum integration yield the exact identity
$$\operatorname{Var}(h)=2\sum_j\int_0^1\|T_\rho D_jh\|_2^2\,\frac{d\rho}{\rho},$$
because the coefficient of each $\widehat h(S)^2$ for nonempty $S$ is $2|S|\int_0^1\rho^{2|S|-1}\,d\rho=1$. These are ordinary one-variable Riemann integrals of finite polynomials after cancellation of the factor $\rho$; no singularity at zero occurs.

Identify each cell index $a_i$ with its $m$ binary digits, most significant first; the uniform distribution of the $nm$ bits is the uniform distribution of the equal-volume cells. Regard $g_m$ as a real function on this finite Boolean cube. For $1\le k\le m$, let $R_{ik}$ flip the $k$th binary digit of coordinate $i$ on $[0,1)$: in every prefix interval of length $2^{1-k}$ translate its lower half up by $2^{-k}$ and its upper half down by $2^{-k}$. Define it arbitrarily at coordinate one. This is a finite piecewise translation preserving elementary integrals, and it pairs the level-$m$ cells with that digit flipped. Let $b_{ik}=\int|f-f\circ R_{ik}|$. The bit derivative of $g_m$ on a cell is the cell average of $(f-f\circ R_{ik})/2$. For such an average $z=|Q|^{-1}\int_Q(f-f\circ R_{ik})$, the finite triangle inequality gives $|z|\le|Q|^{-1}\int_Q|f-f\circ R_{ik}|\le1$, so $|z|^p\le|z|$ for $p\ge1$. Multiplying by $2^{-p}|Q|$ and summing cells yields $\|D_{ik}g_m\|_p^p\le2^{-p}b_{ik}$, the hypothesis of step 3.1.

Write $D_jh=x_jg_j(x_{-j})$. The product noise operator gives $T_\rho D_jh=\rho x_jT_\rho g_j$, so step 2.1 and the norm hypothesis in step 3.1 imply $\|T_\rho D_jh\|_2^2\le\rho^2 b_j^{2/(1+\rho^2)}/4$. For $b=b_j>0$ put $L=\log(1/b)$. Its contribution to the integral in step 3.1 is at most
$$\frac12\int_0^1\rho b^{2/(1+\rho^2)}\,d\rho\le\frac b4\int_0^1e^{-Ls/2}\,ds\le\frac b{1+L}.$$
The middle inequality substitutes $s=1-\rho^2$ and uses $2/(1+\rho^2)\ge1+(1-\rho^2)/2$. The last integral is at most one, proving the last inequality when $0\le L\le1$, and at most $2/L$, proving it when $L\ge1$. At $b_j=0$ the norm hypothesis gives $D_jh=0$. Summing establishes the variance estimate claimed in step 3.1.

Fix the coordinates other than $i$. The fiber indicator is an increasing zero-one function of one real variable, hence a threshold indicator except possibly at its threshold. If the endpoint values agree it is constant everywhere. Otherwise flipping the $k$th digit can change its value only in the single prefix interval of length $2^{1-k}$ containing the threshold. If the threshold is a prefix endpoint, disagreement at that endpoint has length zero; other intervals are constant. Thus the disagreement length is at most $2^{1-k}(f(x_{-i},1)-f(x_{-i},0))$. All these sections and disagreement sets are finite-box sets. Finite-sum iterated integration from step 1.1 gives $b_{ik}\le2^{1-k}F_i$, and consequently $\sum_{k=1}^m b_{ik}\le2F_i$ and $b_{ik}\le M$.

If $M=0$, steps 4.1–5.1 make every bit derivative of every $g_m$ zero, so every $g_m$ is constant, and step 2.2 gives $a(1-a)=0$. If $M>0$, apply the variance bound of step 4.2 to $g_m$, using steps 4.1–5.1. Each nonzero denominator is at least $1+\log(1/M)$, giving $\operatorname{Var}(g_m)\le2\sum_iF_i/(1+\log(1/M))$. Taking the limit with the explicit error in step 2.2 proves the first stated inequality.

If $0<M<n^{-1/2}$, step 6.1 gives $a(1-a)\le4nM/\log n$, which is the required lower bound on $M$. If $M\ge n^{-1/2}$, use $a(1-a)\le1/4$ and $\log n\le\sqrt n$ to get $a(1-a)\log n/(4n)\le1/(16\sqrt n)\le M$. The elementary bound $\log t\le\sqrt t$ for $t\ge1$ follows by differentiating $(\log t)/\sqrt t$: its maximum is $2/e<1$. The case $M=0$ was settled in step 6.1. This proves the stated bound for every integer $n\ge2$.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $H$ be a complex Hilbert space and
$\mathcal B(H)$ the space of bounded linear operators on $H$
([[def-space-of-bounded-linear-operators]]). For a set
$\mathcal S\subseteq\mathcal B(H)$, write

$$\mathcal S':=\{T\in\mathcal B(H):Ts=sT\text{ for every }s\in\mathcal S\}, \qquad \mathcal S'':=(\mathcal S')'.$$

The strong operator topology on $\mathcal B(H)$ is the topology of pointwise
norm convergence: $T_\alpha\to T$ strongly exactly when
$\|(T_\alpha-T)\xi\|\to0$ for every $\xi\in H$. The weak operator topology is
the topology of pointwise matrix-coefficient convergence: $T_\alpha\to T$
weakly exactly when $\langle T_\alpha\xi,\eta\rangle\to\langle T\xi,\eta\rangle$
for every $\xi,\eta\in H$. Use the linear-first inner-product convention.

A **concrete von Neumann algebra** on $H$ is a unital star subalgebra
$M\subseteq\mathcal B(H)$ satisfying $M=M''$. Under Choice, the double
commutant theorem makes this equivalent to being closed in the weak operator
topology.

An operator $a\in\mathcal B(H)$ is **positive** when $a=a^*$ and
$\langle a\xi,\xi\rangle\ge0$ for every $\xi\in H$, using the bounded
adjoint convention of [[thm-hilbert-adjoint-properties]]. Write $M_+$ for the
positive operators in $M$ and $a\le b$ when $b-a$ is positive.

A vector $\Omega\in H$ is **cyclic** for $M$ when
$\overline{M\Omega}=H$, and is **separating** for $M$ when
$x\Omega=0$ for $x\in M$ implies $x=0$. For a unit vector $\Omega$, define its
vector functional by $\omega_\Omega(x)=\langle x\Omega,\Omega\rangle$.
It is **faithful** when $\omega_\Omega(x^*x)=0$ implies $x=0$; this is
equivalent to $\Omega$ being separating because
$\omega_\Omega(x^*x)=\|x\Omega\|^2$.

For a bounded linear functional $\varphi:M\to\mathbb C$, **positive** means
$\varphi(a)\ge0$ for every $a\in M_+$. A positive functional is **normal**
when $\varphi(\sup_\alpha x_\alpha)=\sup_\alpha\varphi(x_\alpha)$ for each
bounded increasing net $(x_\alpha)$ in $M_+$ whose supremum is taken in $M$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $H$ be a complex Hilbert space with inner product linear in its first argument, let $M\subseteq\mathcal B(H)$ be a concrete von Neumann algebra, and let $\Omega$ be a unit vector cyclic and separating for $M$. Define $D(S_0)=M\Omega$ and $S_0(x\Omega)=x^*\Omega$ for $x\in M$. Let $S=\overline{S_0}$ and write its polar decomposition as $S=J\Delta^{1/2}$. The preceding Tomita-operator lemma ensures this closure and polar data are well defined, with $\Delta$ positive self-adjoint and injective. For $x\in\mathcal B(H)$ and dimensionless $t\in\mathbb R$, define
$$\sigma_t(x):=\Delta^{it}x\Delta^{-it}.$$
Set $\omega(x)=\langle x\Omega,\Omega\rangle$. The powers $\Delta^{it}$ are the bounded unitary imaginary powers from the unbounded Borel functional calculus. At this definition stage $\sigma_t$ is defined on $\mathcal B(H)$; preservation of $M$ is established by a separate theorem.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $H$ be a complex Hilbert space with inner product linear in its first argument, let $M\subseteq\mathcal B(H)$ be a concrete von Neumann algebra, and let $\Omega$ be a unit vector that is cyclic and separating for $M$. Define $S_0(x\Omega)=x^*\Omega$ on $M\Omega$ and $F_0(x'\Omega)=x'^*\Omega$ on $M'\Omega$. Let $S=\overline{S_0}$ and $F=S^*$. Then $S$ is a densely defined closed antilinear involution, its polar decomposition is $S=J\Delta^{1/2}$ with $J$ antiunitary and $\Delta$ positive self-adjoint and injective, and
$$J=J^*=J^{-1},\qquad J\Delta J=\Delta^{-1},\qquad J\Delta^{it}J=\Delta^{it}\ (t\in\mathbb R),\qquad F=J\Delta^{-1/2}=\Delta^{1/2}J,\qquad J\Omega=\Omega,\qquad \Delta\Omega=\Omega.$$

Assume the Axiom of Choice and the standard modular data of a concrete von Neumann algebra $M\subseteq\mathcal B(H)$ with unit cyclic-separating vector $\Omega$. Let $F=S^*$, where $S$ is the closure of $S_0(x\Omega)=x^*\Omega$, and let $F_0(x'\Omega)=x'^*\Omega$ on $M'\Omega$. For every $\lambda\in\mathbb C$ with $|\lambda|=1$ and $\lambda\ne-1$,
$$(\Delta+\lambda)^{-1}M'\Omega\subseteq M\Omega.$$
The modular conjugation and operator satisfy
$$JMJ=M',\qquad \Delta^{it}M\Delta^{-it}=M\quad(t\in\mathbb R),\qquad \overline{F_0}=F=S^*.$$

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $H$ be a complex Hilbert space with inner product linear in its first argument, let $M\subseteq\mathcal B(H)$ be a concrete von Neumann algebra, and let $\Omega$ be a unit vector cyclic and separating for $M$. Define $D(S_0)=M\Omega$ and $S_0(x\Omega)=x^*\Omega$ for $x\in M$. Let $S=\overline{S_0}$ and write its polar decomposition as $S=J\Delta^{1/2}$. The preceding Tomita-operator lemma ensures this closure and polar data are well defined, with $\Delta$ positive self-adjoint and injective. For $x\in\mathcal B(H)$ and dimensionless $t\in\mathbb R$, define
$$\sigma_t(x):=\Delta^{it}x\Delta^{-it}.$$
Set $\omega(x)=\langle x\Omega,\Omega\rangle$. The powers $\Delta^{it}$ are the bounded unitary imaginary powers from the unbounded Borel functional calculus. At this definition stage $\sigma_t$ is defined on $\mathcal B(H)$; preservation of $M$ is established by a separate theorem.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $H$ be a complex Hilbert space with inner product linear in its first argument, let $M\subseteq\mathcal B(H)$ be a concrete von Neumann algebra, and let $\Omega$ be a unit vector that is cyclic and separating for $M$. Define $S_0(x\Omega)=x^*\Omega$ on $M\Omega$ and $F_0(x'\Omega)=x'^*\Omega$ on $M'\Omega$. Let $S=\overline{S_0}$ and $F=S^*$. Then $S$ is a densely defined closed antilinear involution, its polar decomposition is $S=J\Delta^{1/2}$ with $J$ antiunitary and $\Delta$ positive self-adjoint and injective, and
$$J=J^*=J^{-1},\qquad J\Delta J=\Delta^{-1},\qquad J\Delta^{it}J=\Delta^{it}\ (t\in\mathbb R),\qquad F=J\Delta^{-1/2}=\Delta^{1/2}J,\qquad J\Omega=\Omega,\qquad \Delta\Omega=\Omega.$$

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $H$ be a complex Hilbert space and let $A$ be a self-adjoint operator whose spectral projection valued measure $E$ is supported on $(0,\infty)$. For $\xi\in H$, put $\mu_\xi(B)=\langle E(B)\xi,\xi\rangle$. Define
$$D(A^{1/2})=\left\{\xi\in H:\int_{(0,\infty)}\lambda\,d\mu_\xi(\lambda)<\infty\right\}.$$
For $z\in S=\{z\in\mathbb C:0\leq\operatorname{Im}z\leq1\}$ and $\xi\in D(A^{1/2})$, define $A^{-iz/2}\xi$ by the unbounded Borel functional calculus for the function $\lambda\mapsto \exp(-iz\log(\lambda)/2)$. This vector is defined, strongly continuous in $z$ on $S$, and satisfies
$$\|A^{-iz/2}\xi\|^2\leq\|\xi\|^2+\|A^{1/2}\xi\|^2.$$
The map $z\mapsto A^{-iz/2}\xi$ is norm-holomorphic on the open strip $S^\circ$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $M\subseteq\mathcal B(H)$ be a concrete von
Neumann algebra on a complex Hilbert space $H$, and define
$$M_\perp:=\{T\in\mathcal S_1(H):\operatorname{Tr}(Tx)=0 \text{ for every }x\in M\}.$$
Equip the coset space $Q:=\mathcal S_1(H)/M_\perp$ with the quotient norm.
Then the trace pairing
$$\Psi:M\to Q^*,\qquad (\Psi(x))([T])=\operatorname{Tr}(Tx),$$
is a well-defined isometric bijection, and $Q$ is a Banach space. Thus $Q$ is
an isometric predual of $M$, and its dual unit ball is weak-star compact.
Every vector functional $x\mapsto\langle x\xi,\xi\rangle$ and every positive
functional in $Q$ preserves suprema of bounded increasing positive nets in
$M$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $H$ be a complex Hilbert space, and let
$\mathcal S_1(H)$ be its trace-class operators with trace norm $\|\cdot\|_1$
and trace $\operatorname{Tr}$. Finite-rank operators are dense in
$(\mathcal S_1(H),\|\cdot\|_1)$. For every bounded linear functional
$\Phi:\mathcal S_1(H)\to\mathbb C$, there is a unique $X\in\mathcal B(H)$ such
that
$$\Phi(T)=\operatorname{Tr}(TX)\qquad(T\in\mathcal S_1(H)),$$
and the correspondence is isometric:
$\|\Phi\|=\|X\|$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $M\ne\{0\}$ be a concrete von Neumann algebra on a complex Hilbert space. Use the predual $M_*=Q$ of [[lem-qsmx-von-neumann-predual]]; its elements are the normal linear functionals, and the induced topology $\sigma(M,Q)$ is the ultraweak topology. A **normal state** on $M$ is a bounded complex-linear functional $\omega:M\to\mathbb C$ with $\omega(I)=1$, $\omega(a)\geq0$ for every positive $a\in M$, and
$$\omega\!\left(\sup_i a_i\right)=\sup_i\omega(a_i)$$
for every increasing net $(a_i)$ of positive elements with $0\leq a_i\leq C I$ for a common finite $C$ and supremum taken in $M$.
An automorphism of $M$ is **normal** when it preserves the suprema of all such bounded increasing positive nets.
A **point-ultraweakly continuous one-parameter automorphism group** is a family $(\alpha_t)_{t\in\mathbb R}$ of bijective unital complex-linear maps $M\to M$ preserving multiplication and adjoints, with $\alpha_0=\operatorname{id}_M$, $\alpha_s\alpha_t=\alpha_{s+t}$, and $t\mapsto\varphi(\alpha_t(x))$ continuous for every $x\in M$ and every normal linear functional $\varphi\in Q$.
For dimensionless $t$ and dimensionless $\beta>0$, the normal state $\omega$ satisfies the **upper-strip $(\alpha,\beta)$ KMS condition** when, for every $A,B\in M$, there is a bounded scalar function $F_{A,B}$ on $S_\beta=\{z\in\mathbb C:0\leq\operatorname{Im}z\leq\beta\}$ that is continuous on $S_\beta$, holomorphic in its interior, and satisfies
$$F_{A,B}(t)=\omega(A\alpha_t(B)),\qquad F_{A,B}(t+i\beta)=\omega(\alpha_t(B)A)\quad(t\in\mathbb R).$$

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $H$ be a complex Hilbert space and let $A$ be a positive self-adjoint injective operator with spectral projection valued measure $E$ supported on $(0,\infty)$. For $t\in\mathbb R$, the unbounded Borel functional calculus defines $A^{it}$ as a unitary on all of $H$. For every $\xi\in H$, the map $t\mapsto A^{it}\xi$ is norm-continuous.

derivations.claim: By [F2], $\sigma_t(M)=M$. Each $\sigma_t$ is conjugation by the unitary $\Delta^{it}$, so it is complex-linear, multiplicative, adjoint-preserving and bijective, with inverse $\sigma_{-t}$. The spectral calculus gives $\Delta^{i(s+t)}=\Delta^{is}\Delta^{it}$, hence $\sigma_s\sigma_t=\sigma_{s+t}$ and $\sigma_0=I$. To check normality, let $0\leq a_i\uparrow a$ be a bounded increasing net in $M$. Unitary conjugation is an order isomorphism of $\mathcal B(H)$: if $b$ bounds every $\Delta^{it}a_i\Delta^{-it}$, then $\Delta^{-it}b\Delta^{it}$ bounds every $a_i$, so $a\leq\Delta^{-it}b\Delta^{it}$ and $\Delta^{it}a\Delta^{-it}\leq b$. Thus $\Delta^{it}a_i\Delta^{-it}\uparrow\Delta^{it}a\Delta^{-it}$ in $\mathcal B(H)$. By [F2] the limit is in $M$, hence is also the supremum in $M$. By the definition in [F7], each restriction is a normal $*$-automorphism.

For $A,B\in M$, both $A^*\Omega$ and $B\Omega$ lie in $D(\Delta^{1/2})$, because $Sx\Omega=x^*\Omega$ for $x\in M$ and $\|Sx\Omega\|=\|\Delta^{1/2}x\Omega\|$. Define $$F_{A,B}(z)=\bigl(\Delta^{i\overline z/2}A^*\Omega\,\big|\,\Delta^{-iz/2}B\Omega\bigr),$$ where $(u|v)=\langle v,u\rangle$ is linear in its second argument. By [F3], both vectors $A^*\Omega$ and $B\Omega$ belong to $D(\Delta^{1/2})$; [F4] then makes each vector factor bounded and continuous on the closed strip. The first is anti-holomorphic as a vector-valued function of $z$ and enters the first, conjugate-linear slot, while the second is holomorphic in the second slot. Hence $F_{A,B}$ is bounded and continuous on the strip and holomorphic inside.

By [F8], $t\mapsto\Delta^{it}\xi$ is norm-continuous for every $\xi\in H$. For fixed $x\in M$ and $\xi,\eta\in H$, the coefficient $\langle\sigma_t(x)\xi,\eta\rangle$ is therefore continuous. If $T$ is finite rank, $\operatorname{Tr}(T\sigma_t(x))$ is a finite sum of such continuous coefficients. Since $\Delta^{it}\Omega=\Omega$ and $\Delta^{it}$ is unitary, $$\omega(\sigma_t(x))=\langle\Delta^{it}x\Omega,\Omega\rangle=\langle x\Omega,\Delta^{-it}\Omega\rangle=\omega(x).$$ So $\omega$ is invariant under $\sigma_t$ and under $\alpha_t=\sigma_{-t}$. For real $t$, unitarity of $\Delta^{it/2}$ and the identity $\Delta^{-it}B\Omega=\sigma_{-t}(B)\Omega$ give $$F_{A,B}(t)=(A^*\Omega|\Delta^{-it}B\Omega)=(\Omega|A\Delta^{-it}B\Omega)=\omega(A\alpha_t(B)).$$ This is the lower boundary in [F7].

At $z=t+i$, $\Delta^{i\overline z/2}A^*\Omega=\Delta^{it/2}J A\Omega$ and $\Delta^{-iz/2}B\Omega=\Delta^{-it/2}J B^*\Omega$, because $Sx\Omega=x^*\Omega$ and $S=J\Delta^{1/2}$. $f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume the Axiom of Choice as inherited through the cited Hall supplier. Let
$V=\mathbb C^2$ with ordered orthonormal basis $|\uparrow\rangle,|\downarrow\rangle$.
On $V$ define
$$ E=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\0&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad F=\begin{pmatrix}0&0\\1&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad H=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&-1\end{pmatrix}. $$
They satisfy $[H,E]=2E$, $[H,F]=-2F$, and $[E,F]=H$, and therefore define
the standard two-dimensional representation of $\mathfrak{sl}_2(\mathbb C)$.
Write $S^+=E$, $S^-=F$, and $S^z=H/2$.

For each integer $N\geq1$, the spin space is
$\mathcal H_N=V^{\otimes N}$ with its tensor-product inner product. If $A$ is
an endomorphism of $V$, let $A_j$ act as $A$ on factor $j$ and as the identity
on the other factors. Define the diagonal generators
$$ S_N^+=\sum_{j=1}^N E_j,\qquad S_N^-=\sum_{j=1}^N F_j,\qquad S_N^z=\frac12\sum_{j=1}^N H_j. $$
For $m\in\{-N/2,-N/2+1,\ldots,N/2\}$, its weight space is
$\mathcal H_{N,m}=\ker(S_N^z-mI)$. These are dimensionless matrices in the
algebraic spin convention.

For each integer $r\geq0$, define $V(r)$ to be the vector space
$\mathbb C[x,y]_r$ of homogeneous polynomials of degree $r$, with
$\mathfrak{sl}_2$ action
$$ E=x\partial_y,\qquad F=y\partial_x,\qquad H=x\partial_x-y\partial_y. $$
The ordered monomials $x^{r-k}y^k$ for $0\leq k\leq r$ form its basis.
Under $x\mapsto|\uparrow\rangle$ and $y\mapsto|\downarrow\rangle$,
$V(1)$ is the representation on $V$ above. A tensor power $V(1)^{\otimes N}$
uses the diagonal action defined by the sums $S_N^+,S_N^-,2S_N^z$.

Let $q_H>1$ be a prime power, fix a finite field $\mathbb F_{q_H}$, and put
$\nu=\sqrt{q_H}>1$ and $K=\mathbb Q(\nu)$. The representation category
$\mathcal A=\mathrm{Vect}^{\mathrm{fd}}_{\mathbb F_{q_H}}$ of the one-vertex,
no-arrow quiver has one simple isomorphism class, represented by
$S=\mathbb F_{q_H}$. For objects $M,N$, write
$\chi_0(M,N)=\dim_{\mathbb F_{q_H}}\operatorname{Hom}(M,N)-
\dim_{\mathbb F_{q_H}}\operatorname{YExt}^1(M,N)$. In the Hall convention of
[[def-euler-twisted-hall-algebra]], the Hall space is
$H_{\mathcal A,\nu}=\bigoplus_{[M]}K[M]$, with basis $[M]$ indexed by
isomorphism classes and product
$$[M]\star[N]=\nu^{\chi_0(M,N)}\sum_{[L]}g^L_{M,N}[L],$$
where $g^L_{M,N}$ counts subspaces $N'\subseteq L$ with $N'\cong N$ and
$L/N'\cong M$, or equivalently short exact sequences
$0\to N\to L\to M\to0$. Thus the twist is part of the multiplication.
For $M\cong\mathbb F_{q_H}^{m}$ and $N\cong\mathbb F_{q_H}^{n}$,
$\dim\operatorname{Hom}(M,N)=mn$ and every short exact sequence splits, so
$\operatorname{YExt}^1(M,N)=0$ and $\chi_0(M,N)=mn$.

By [[def-extended-hall-algebra-and-composition-subalgebra]], the composition
subalgebra is the subalgebra of this Hall algebra generated by the classes of
simple objects; its torus extension is the distinct extended composition
subalgebra. Denote the former by $\mathcal C$ here, so
$\mathcal C=K\langle[S]\rangle\subseteq H_{\mathcal A,\nu}$. The rank-one
positive quantum half is $U_\nu^+(\mathfrak{sl}_2)=K[E]$, the polynomial
algebra on one generator. The Ringel map $E\mapsto[S]$ embeds this positive
half with image $\mathcal C$; since the one-vertex graph is finite Dynkin type
$A_1$, the finite-Dynkin criterion identifies $\mathcal C$ with the full Hall
algebra in this case. The simple object is unique up to isomorphism, not as a
chosen representative. The Axiom of Choice is inherited through the cited
Ringel supplier.

Let $d\ge1$, let $A\in M_d(\mathbb C)$ act on $\mathbb C^d$ with its standard complex inner product, and let $z\in\mathbb C$. Define the finite-dimensional matrix exponential by
$$e^{zA}:=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\frac{z^kA^k}{k!},\qquad A^0=I_d.$$
Every matrix $B=(b_{ij})\in M_d(\mathbb C)$ is bounded on $\mathbb C^d$: since $|x_j|\le\|x\|$ for the standard Euclidean norm, $\|Bx\|^2\le\sum_{i=1}^d(\sum_{j=1}^d|b_{ij}|)^2\|x\|^2$. Thus its operator norm is defined by the unit-ball supremum in [[def-operator-norm]]. For $B,C\in M_d(\mathbb C)$ and $\|x\|\le1$, that definition and the bound $\|By\|\le\|B\|\|y\|$ give $\|BCx\|\le\|B\|\|Cx\|\le\|B\|\|C\|$; taking the supremum over the unit ball proves $\|BC\|\le\|B\|\|C\|$. Since $d\ge1$, the standard unit ball contains a unit vector and $\|I_d\|=1$. Hence $\|A^0\|=1$, while induction using submultiplicativity gives $\|A^k\|\le\|A\|^k$ for every $k\ge1$. The terms are therefore dominated by the convergent scalar exponential series $\sum_{k\ge0}(|z|\|A\|)^k/k!$; the displayed series converges absolutely in operator norm. The scalar exponential uses the convention $\exp z=\sum_{k\ge0}z^k/k!$.

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional vector space over $F$ and let $T:V\to V$ be
linear. Choose any ordered basis $\mathcal B$ of $V$ and define the **trace of
the endomorphism $T$** by

$$\operatorname{tr}(T):=\operatorname{tr}([T]_{\mathcal B}^{\mathcal B}).$$

This is independent of the chosen basis: matrices of the same endomorphism in
two ordered bases are similar, and similar matrices have equal trace. When
$V$ is the zero space, the empty basis gives trace $0$.

Under [A1], apply [F1] to the KLR datum in the Given. Its hypotheses are
the datum and field specified in [F2], and its conclusion is exactly the
isomorphism $\gamma_D:A f_D\to K_0(R_D)$ with the Laurent grading parameter

In $V(1)$, $H$ has eigenvalue $1$ on $|\uparrow\rangle$ and $-1$ on
$|\downarrow\rangle$. The elementary tensor basis of $V(1)^{\otimes n}$
therefore consists of $H$-eigenvectors. A tensor with exactly $k$ down
factors has eigenvalue $n-2k$, and there are exactly $\binom nk$ such
tensors. Hence its weight character is
$(z+z^{-1})^n=\sum_{k=0}^n\binom nk z^{n-2k}$.

The monomials $x^{n-k}y^k$ form a basis of $V(n)$. Applying
$H=x\partial_x-y\partial_y$ gives
$H(x^{n-k}y^k)=(n-2k)x^{n-k}y^k$, so each listed weight space is
one-dimensional. For $k>0$, $E(x^{n-k}y^k)=k x^{n-k+1}y^{k-1}$ is nonzero;
for $k<n$, $F(x^{n-k}y^k)=(n-k)x^{n-k-1}y^{k+1}$ is nonzero. Any nonzero
submodule has a nonzero $H$-weight vector, since the eigenvalues are distinct
and the corresponding projections are polynomials in $H$. Repeated $E$
then reaches $x^n$, and repeated $F$ from $x^n$ reaches every basis
monomial. Thus $V(n)$ is irreducible and its weights have multiplicity one.

On a tensor basis vector with $k$ down factors,
$S_n^z$ has eigenvalue $(n-2k)/2$, so $H_n^{(0)}$ has eigenvalue
$-h(n-2k)/2$. Summing the exponentials over the basis gives
$$ Z_n(\beta)=\sum_{k=0}^n\binom nk e^{\beta h(n-2k)/2} =\bigl(e^{\beta h/2}+e^{-\beta h/2}\bigr)^n =\bigl(2\cosh(\beta h/2)\bigr)^n. $$
The series [F4] acts diagonally on this eigenbasis, and [F5] identifies its
trace with the sum of these diagonal entries. This is an exact finite-matrix
trace identity for the stated operator.

a spin-chain spectrum therefore requires additional data.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Assume the Axiom of Choice as inherited through the cited Hall supplier. Let
$V=\mathbb C^2$ with ordered orthonormal basis $|\uparrow\rangle,|\downarrow\rangle$.
On $V$ define
$$ E=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\0&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad F=\begin{pmatrix}0&0\\1&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad H=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&-1\end{pmatrix}. $$
They satisfy $[H,E]=2E$, $[H,F]=-2F$, and $[E,F]=H$, and therefore define
the standard two-dimensional representation of $\mathfrak{sl}_2(\mathbb C)$.
Write $S^+=E$, $S^-=F$, and $S^z=H/2$.

For each integer $N\geq1$, the spin space is
$\mathcal H_N=V^{\otimes N}$ with its tensor-product inner product. If $A$ is
an endomorphism of $V$, let $A_j$ act as $A$ on factor $j$ and as the identity
on the other factors. Define the diagonal generators
$$ S_N^+=\sum_{j=1}^N E_j,\qquad S_N^-=\sum_{j=1}^N F_j,\qquad S_N^z=\frac12\sum_{j=1}^N H_j. $$
For $m\in\{-N/2,-N/2+1,\ldots,N/2\}$, its weight space is
$\mathcal H_{N,m}=\ker(S_N^z-mI)$. These are dimensionless matrices in the
algebraic spin convention.

For each integer $r\geq0$, define $V(r)$ to be the vector space
$\mathbb C[x,y]_r$ of homogeneous polynomials of degree $r$, with
$\mathfrak{sl}_2$ action
$$ E=x\partial_y,\qquad F=y\partial_x,\qquad H=x\partial_x-y\partial_y. $$
The ordered monomials $x^{r-k}y^k$ for $0\leq k\leq r$ form its basis.
Under $x\mapsto|\uparrow\rangle$ and $y\mapsto|\downarrow\rangle$,
$V(1)$ is the representation on $V$ above. A tensor power $V(1)^{\otimes N}$
uses the diagonal action defined by the sums $S_N^+,S_N^-,2S_N^z$.

Let $q_H>1$ be a prime power and fix a finite field $\mathbb F_{q_H}$ of that
cardinality. Put $\nu=\sqrt{q_H}>1$ and $K=\mathbb Q(\nu)$. The representation category of
the one-vertex, no-arrow quiver over $\mathbb F_{q_H}$ is the category of
finite-dimensional $\mathbb F_{q_H}$-vector spaces, with unique simple object
$S=\mathbb F_{q_H}$. Its Hall composition algebra is the subalgebra generated
by the class $[S]$ in the twisted Hall algebra with the normalization of the
Ringel supplier. The rank-one positive quantum half is
$U_\nu^+(\mathfrak{sl}_2)=K[E]$. The canonical Ringel map $E\mapsto[S]$
identifies this positive half with the composition algebra; the finite-Dynkin
criterion identifies it with the full Hall algebra in this one-vertex case.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Let $Q$ be a KLR datum as in [[def-quiver-hecke-klr-algebra-for-a-symmetrizable-cartan-datum]] over any field $k$. Then the homomorphism $\gamma:Af\to K_0(R)$ of [[thm-klr-projective-grothendieck-group-satisfies-the-negative-quantum-serre-relations]] is an isomorphism of $\mathbb Z[q,q^{-1}]$-algebras and of $\mathbb N[I]$-graded twisted bialgebras:
(i) **Surjectivity.** Every class in $K_0(R(\beta))$ is a $\mathbb Z[q,q^{-1}]$-linear combination of classes of divided-power projectives $[P_\theta]$, $\theta$ a sequence of divided powers of weight $\beta$; hence $\gamma$ is onto.
(ii) **Injectivity.** $\gamma$ is injective, because it preserves the forms by [[thm-klr-cartan-pairing-agrees-with-lusztigs-bilinear-form]] and the source form $B_L$ (equivalently $B_K$) is nondegenerate on each finite weight component.
(iii) **Compatibility.** $\gamma$ intertwines the multiplications ($[\mathrm{Ind}]$ against the product in $Af$), the comultiplications ($[\mathrm{Res}]$ against $r$), the bar involutions and the forms; the free $A$-rank of $K_0(R(\beta))$ equals the free $A$-rank of $Af_\beta$; no rank or dimension comparison of the infinite-dimensional algebra $R(\beta)$ itself with $f_\beta$ is asserted.
Equivalently, $K_0(R)$ is a free $A$-module with the classes of the indecomposable graded projective $R$-modules as a shift-orbit basis ([[lem-klr-module-categories-are-krull-schmidt-with-shift-orbit-bases]]), and the divided-power classes span; the triangularly selected classes $[P(Y_b)]$ form an $A$-basis, whereas the family of all divided-power words is generally redundant.

citations.quote:
Fix either a finite open chain with sites $\{1,\ldots,L\}$, $L\ge2$, or a periodic chain with sites $\mathbb Z/L\mathbb Z$, $L\ge3$, and denote its site set by $\Lambda_L$. Let $\mathcal H_L$ be a nonzero finite-dimensional complex Hilbert space. For each site $j$, let $q_j=q_j^*$ be a bounded charge observable, with physical unit $\mathsf Q$. For each oriented nearest-neighbor bond $(j,j+1)$, let $h_{j,j+1}=h_{j,j+1}^*$ be an energy operator in joules. Require $[h_{k,k+1},q_j]=0$ whenever $j\notin\{k,k+1\}$, and require local charge conservation $[h_{j,j+1},q_j+q_{j+1}]=0$. On an open chain set $H_L=\sum_{j=1}^{L-1}h_{j,j+1}$; on a ring set $H_L=\sum_{j\in\mathbb Z/L\mathbb Z}h_{j,j+1}$ with periodic indices. For an open chain define the absent boundary currents $j_{0,1}=j_{L,L+1}=0$. Use $\hbar>0$ in joule-seconds. These finite local data may be realized on a tensor-product spin space or on a finite fixed-particle site space, provided the stated commutation conditions hold.

The oriented bond current from $j$ to $j+1$ is
$$j_{j,j+1}:=\frac{i}{\hbar}[h_{j,j+1},q_{j+1}].$$
It has unit $\mathsf Q\,\mathrm{s}^{-1}$. The total current is the sum over existing bonds, $J_L:=\sum_{(j,j+1)}j_{j,j+1}$, and its Heisenberg evolution for $t\in\mathbb R$ is $J_L(t):=e^{iH_Lt/\hbar}J_Le^{-iH_Lt/\hbar}$. For finite inverse temperature $\beta>0$ in joules$^{-1}$, define $\rho_{\beta,L}:=e^{-\beta H_L}/\operatorname{Tr}(e^{-\beta H_L})$ and $\omega_{\beta,L}(A):=\operatorname{Tr}(\rho_{\beta,L}A)$. Write $J_L^\circ:=J_L-\omega_{\beta,L}(J_L)I$ and $J_L^\circ(t):=e^{iH_Lt/\hbar}J_L^\circ e^{-iH_Lt/\hbar}$. Define the real, connected, symmetrized correlation per site by
$$C_L(t):=\frac{1}{L}\operatorname{Re}\,\omega_{\beta,L}\!\left(J_L^\circ(t)J_L^\circ\right)=\frac{1}{2L}\omega_{\beta,L}\!\left(J_L^\circ(t)J_L^\circ+J_L^\circ J_L^\circ(t)\right).$$
The correlation has unit $\mathsf Q^2\,\mathrm{s}^{-2}$ per site.

This definition assigns no transport coefficient by itself. Any proposed finite-volume or thermodynamic transport quantity must additionally state its time cutoff, frequency regulator (for example $e^{-\eta t}$ with $\eta>0$ in seconds$^{-1}$), spatial normalization, and the exact order in which $L\to\infty$, the time cutoff tends to infinity, and any regulator is removed. Existence of those limits is not part of this definition.

Use the finite open or periodic chain and bond-current definition in [[def-qsmx-lattice-current-and-limits]]. Each $j_{j,j+1}$ is self-adjoint, and with $\dot q_j:=(i/\hbar)[H_L,q_j]$ the exact local identity
$$\dot q_j=j_{j-1,j}-j_{j,j+1}$$
holds at every site. Consequently the total charge $Q_L:=\sum_{j\in\Lambda_L}q_j$, where $\Lambda_L$ is the open-chain site set or periodic site set from the definition, is conserved: $[H_L,Q_L]=0$. The current orientation is from $j$ to $j+1$, so positive outgoing current lowers the charge at site $j$.

Under the finite-dimensional unitary dynamics of [[thm-qsm-dt-finite-unitary]], let $P_E$ be the orthogonal spectral projection of $H$ for its distinct energy $E$. For every density matrix $\rho$,

$$\frac1T\int_0^T U(t)\rho U(t)^*\,dt\longrightarrow\sum_E P_E\rho P_E$$

in trace norm as $T\to\infty$. The diagonal energy blocks, including all blocks within degenerate eigenspaces, remain. This is Cesaro convergence of the averaged state; pointwise convergence of $U(t)\rho U(t)^*$ is not asserted.

Use the following conventions on a complex inner-product space $H$ of dimension $D\geq1$, with inner product linear in its first argument. For an endomorphism $A$, define $\operatorname{Tr}A:=\sum_{j=1}^D\langle Ae_j,e_j\rangle$ in an orthonormal basis; step 3.1 proves basis independence. For any Hermitian $M$, its **positive spectral subspace** (called its positive support here) is $S_M:=\bigoplus_{\lambda>0}\ker(M-\lambda I)$; when $M\geq0$ this equals $(\ker M)^\perp$. Its support logarithm is $\log(M|_{S_M}):=\sum_{\lambda>0}(\log\lambda)P_\lambda|_{S_M}$, where $P_\lambda$ is the orthogonal projection onto that eigenspace. No value $\log0$ is assigned; for $M=0$ this is the unique endomorphism of the zero space. For the set $\mathcal D(H)$ of positive semidefinite Hermitian endomorphisms with trace one, a point $\rho$ is **extreme** if every equality $\rho=t\sigma+(1-t)\tau$ with $\sigma,\tau\in\mathcal D(H)$ and $0<t<1$ implies $\sigma=\tau=\rho$.

Let $H$ be a complex inner-product space of finite dimension $D\geq1$, with inner product linear in its first argument. Every Hermitian endomorphism $M$ has an orthonormal eigenbasis with real eigenvalues. For a real function $f$ on its finite spectrum, define $f(M)$ by its spectral projections; this definition is independent of the choice of eigenbasis. In particular positive square roots, exponentials, and logarithms on positive supports are well defined.

For a density matrix $\rho$ on $H$, meaning a Hermitian positive semidefinite operator with $\operatorname{Tr}\rho=1$, $\operatorname{Tr}(\rho A)=\sum_jp_j\langle Au_j,u_j\rangle$ for bounded $A$, where $\rho=\sum_jp_j|u_j\rangle\langle u_j|$. The weighted form $(X,Y)_\rho=\operatorname{Tr}(\rho X^*Y)$ satisfies Cauchy–Schwarz, $|(X,Y)_\rho|^2\leq(X,X)_\rho(Y,Y)_\rho$. Finally, $\operatorname{Tr}(\rho^2)\leq1$, with equality exactly for rank-one densities, and those are exactly the extreme points of the finite density-matrix set.

derivations.claim: The lattice-current definition fixes $J_L=\sum_jj_{j,j+1}$, and the local-current lemma gives $J_L=J_L^*$. Subtracting its real mean $\omega(J_L)$ preserves self-adjointness, so $J$ is a matrix observable in $\mathcal B(\mathcal H)$.

On $\mathcal B(\mathcal H)$ define $(A,B)_\rho:=\operatorname{Tr}(\rho A^*B)$, linear in its second argument. It is positive definite: if $(A,A)_\rho=0$, then $\rho\ge cI$ for some $c>0$ in finite dimension, so $0=\operatorname{Tr}(\rho A^*A)\ge c\operatorname{Tr}(A^*A)$ and hence $A=0$. The invariance $[\rho,H]=0$ gives $(\alpha_t(A),\alpha_t(B))_\rho=(A,B)_\rho$ by cyclicity of the finite trace, so $\alpha_t$ is unitary on this finite-dimensional Hilbert space of matrices.

Write $H=\sum_E E P_E$ over its distinct eigenvalues. Then $\alpha_t(J)=\sum_{E,F}e^{it(E-F)/\hbar}P_EJP_F$. For $E\ne F$,
$$\left|\frac1T\int_0^T e^{it(E-F)/\hbar}\,dt\right|\le\frac{2\hbar}{T|E-F|}\longrightarrow0,$$
while for $E=F$ the coefficient is $1$. The sum is finite, so $M_TJ:=T^{-1}\int_0^T\alpha_t(J)\,dt$ converges in matrix norm to $PJ:=\sum_E P_EJP_E$. This block map is the orthogonal projection onto $\mathcal N:=\{A:[H,A]=0\}$ in $(\cdot,\cdot)_\rho$: $PJ\in\mathcal N$, and each off-diagonal block of $J-PJ$ has zero weighted trace pairing with a block-diagonal matrix because $\rho$ is block diagonal. It is the same energy-block projection as the density-matrix dephasing in [F3]; [F3] states the density-matrix version, while the explicit finite expansion here proves the observable version used.

Since $J=J^*$, $(\alpha_t(J),J)_\rho=\omega(\alpha_t(J)J)$. Norm convergence in step 2.1 therefore gives
$$\lim_{T\to\infty}\frac1T\int_0^T\operatorname{Re}\,\omega(\alpha_t(J)J)\,dt=\operatorname{Re}(PJ,J)_\rho=\|PJ\|_\rho^2,$$
because $J-PJ$ is orthogonal to $\mathcal N$ and $PJ\in\mathcal N$.

Set $S:=\operatorname{span}\{Q_1,\ldots,Q_m\}\subseteq\mathcal N$, and let $P_S$ be its orthogonal projection. Then $P_SJ=P_SPJ$, so $\|PJ\|_\rho^2\ge\|P_SJ\|_\rho^2$. The Gram matrix $G$ is positive definite by linear independence and the positive-definite inner product. Writing $P_SJ=\sum_a c_aQ_a$, orthogonality gives $Gc=v$, so $c=G^{-1}v$ and $\|P_SJ\|_\rho^2=c^*Gc=v^*G^{-1}v$. Together with step 3.1 this proves the bound.

The total current is the sum over existing bonds, $J_L:=\sum_{(j,j+1)}j_{j,j+1}$, and its Heisenberg evolution for $t\in\mathbb R$ is $J_L(t):=e^{iH_Lt/\hbar}J_Le^{-iH_Lt/\hbar}$. For finite inverse temperature $\beta>0$ in joules$^{-1}$, define $\rho_{\beta,L}:=e^{-\beta H_L}/\operatorname{Tr}(e^{-\beta H_L})$ and $\omega_{\beta,L}(A):=\operatorname{Tr}(\rho_{\beta,L}A)$. Write $J_L^\circ:=J_L-\omega_{\beta,L}(J_L)I$ and $J_L^\circ(t):=e^{iH_Lt/\hbar}J_L^\circ e^{-iH_Lt/\hbar}$. Define the real, connected, symmetrized correlation per site by
$$C_L(t):=\frac{1}{L}\operatorname{Re}\,\omega_{\beta,L}\!\left(J_L^\circ(t)J_L^\circ\right)=\frac{1}{2L}\omega_{\beta,L}\!\left(J_L^\circ(t)J_L^\circ+J_L^\circ J_L^\circ(t)\right).$$
The correlation has unit $\mathsf Q^2\,\mathrm{s}^{-2}$ per site.

This definition assigns no transport coefficient by itself. Existence of those limits is not part of this definition.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Use the following conventions on a complex inner-product space $H$ of dimension $D\geq1$, with inner product linear in its first argument. For an endomorphism $A$, define $\operatorname{Tr}A:=\sum_{j=1}^D\langle Ae_j,e_j\rangle$ in an orthonormal basis; step 3.1 proves basis independence. For any Hermitian $M$, its **positive spectral subspace** (called its positive support here) is $S_M:=\bigoplus_{\lambda>0}\ker(M-\lambda I)$; when $M\geq0$ this equals $(\ker M)^\perp$. Its support logarithm is $\log(M|_{S_M}):=\sum_{\lambda>0}(\log\lambda)P_\lambda|_{S_M}$, where $P_\lambda$ is the orthogonal projection onto that eigenspace. No value $\log0$ is assigned; for $M=0$ this is the unique endomorphism of the zero space. For the set $\mathcal D(H)$ of positive semidefinite Hermitian endomorphisms with trace one, a point $\rho$ is **extreme** if every equality $\rho=t\sigma+(1-t)\tau$ with $\sigma,\tau\in\mathcal D(H)$ and $0<t<1$ implies $\sigma=\tau=\rho$.

Let $H$ be a complex inner-product space of finite dimension $D\geq1$, with inner product linear in its first argument. Every Hermitian endomorphism $M$ has an orthonormal eigenbasis with real eigenvalues. For a real function $f$ on its finite spectrum, define $f(M)$ by its spectral projections; this definition is independent of the choice of eigenbasis. In particular positive square roots, exponentials, and logarithms on positive supports are well defined.

For a density matrix $\rho$ on $H$, meaning a Hermitian positive semidefinite operator with $\operatorname{Tr}\rho=1$, $\operatorname{Tr}(\rho A)=\sum_jp_j\langle Au_j,u_j\rangle$ for bounded $A$, where $\rho=\sum_jp_j|u_j\rangle\langle u_j|$. The weighted form $(X,Y)_\rho=\operatorname{Tr}(\rho X^*Y)$ satisfies Cauchy–Schwarz, $|(X,Y)_\rho|^2\leq(X,X)_\rho(Y,Y)_\rho$. Finally, $\operatorname{Tr}(\rho^2)\leq1$, with equality exactly for rank-one densities, and those are exactly the extreme points of the finite density-matrix set.

Let $M$ be a smooth four-manifold without boundary, so that $M$ is Hausdorff
and second countable and carries a maximal smooth atlas
([[def-smooth-manifold]]). Let $g$ be a smooth covariant $2$-tensor field on $M$
in the sense of [[def-gr-smooth-covariant-two-tensor-field]]. Then $g$ assigns
to every $p\in M$ a bilinear form $g_p:T_pM\times T_pM\to\mathbb R$
([[def-derivation-at-a-point-and-tangent-space]]).

**(a) Lorentzian metric.** The field $g$ is a **Lorentzian metric of signature
$(-,+,+,+)$** on $M$ when it is symmetric and nondegenerate, and at every
$p\in M$ the pair $(T_pM,g_p)$ is a Lorentz vector space of signature
$(-,+,+,+)$ in the sense of [[def-lorentz-form-and-inertia]]: that is, $g_p$ has
inertia $(3,1,0)$, so that some — equivalently every — basis of $T_pM$ in which
the matrix of $g_p$ is diagonal has exactly one negative and three positive
diagonal entries. The pair $(M,g)$ is a **smooth Lorentzian four-manifold** (or
Lorentzian manifold of signature $(-,+,+,+)$). In a smooth chart $(U,x)$ the
**components** of $g$ are the $C^\infty$ functions
$g_{ab}(q)=g_q(\partial_a|_q,\partial_b|_q)$ of
[[def-gr-smooth-covariant-two-tensor-field]], and $g_{ab}=g_{ba}$ by symmetry.
We use indices $a,b,c,d=0,1,2,3$ and the Einstein summation convention, with
components in a chart written as lower-case indexed symbols and equations
between indexed fields understood basis-independently. These conventions are
fixed once for this library and the physical reading of the symbols is recorded
with the framework postulates, separately from this mathematical definition.

**(b) Pointwise causal structure.** For every $p\in M$ the vocabulary of
[[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]] applies to the Lorentz vector
space $(T_pM,g_p)$: a tangent vector $v\in T_pM$ is **timelike** when
$g_p(v,v)<0$, **null** when $v\neq0$ and $g_p(v,v)=0$, **spacelike** when
$g_p(v,v)>0$, and **causal** when it is timelike or null. Every nonzero
$v\in T_pM$ has exactly one causal character. The **timelike set**
$T_p:=\{v\in T_pM:g_p(v,v)<0\}$ has exactly two connected components, each
nonempty, open, convex and path-connected; each $g_p$-orthonormal basis
$e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3$ of $T_pM$ satisfies $g_p(e_a,e_b)=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)_{ab}$
for some ordering, so in particular nonzero orthonormal vectors exist at every
point ([[lem-lorentz-form-has-orthonormal-basis]],
[[lem-timelike-cone-has-two-convex-components]]).

**(c) Time orientation.** A **time orientation** of $(M,g)$, also called a
**choice of future cone**, is a smooth vector field $N$ on $M$
([[def-smooth-vector-field-as-a-tangent-bundle-section]], whose tangent-bundle
smooth structure uses the axiom $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ of
[[def-countable-choice]]; this is the only use of that axiom in this
definition) such that

$$g_p(N_p,N_p)<0\qquad\text{for every }p\in M .$$

The function $p\mapsto g_p(N_p,N_p)$ is $C^\infty$ because $g$ is a smooth
covariant $2$-tensor field and $N$ a smooth field, so the condition is a
pointwise strict inequality between a smooth function and $0$; since
$g_p(N_p,N_p)<0$ implies $N_p\neq0$, a time orientation is nowhere vanishing.
A **time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold** is a triple $(M,g,N)$
consisting of a smooth Lorentzian four-manifold and a time orientation $N$.

Given a time orientation $N$ and $p\in M$, the vector $N_p$ is timelike, and we
**define** a nonzero causal vector $v\in T_pM$ to be **future-directed** when
$g_p(v,N_p)<0$ and **past-directed** when $g_p(v,N_p)>0$. The classification of
nonzero causal vectors into exactly these two classes, and its agreement with
the two components of the timelike set (the future component is the component
$C_p^+$ containing $N_p$, and the future causal vectors form
$\operatorname{cl}(C_p^+)\setminus\{0\}$), is proved in
[[lem-gr-future-causal-classification-by-a-timelike-field]]; in particular no
nonzero causal $v$ satisfies $g_p(v,N_p)=0$, so the definition is exhaustive and
mutually exclusive. Replacing $N$ by $-N$ reverses every future/past label, and
two time orientations $N,N'$ determine the same future-directed causal vectors
at every point where $g_p(N_p,N'_p)<0$, while they determine opposite ones
where $g_p(N_p,N'_p)>0$, by
[[lem-gr-timelike-fields-define-equal-or-opposite-future-cones]]; that lemma
also shows the sign of $p\mapsto g_p(N_p,N'_p)$ is constant on every connected
component of $M$.

**(d) The inverse metric.** Because $g_p$ is nondegenerate, it induces at each
$p$ an isomorphism $\flat_p:T_pM\to T_p^*M$, $v\mapsto g_p(v,\cdot)$, and an
inverse metric $g_p^{-1}$ on the dual space; the inverse metric, the musical
isomorphisms and the components $g^{ab}$ are defined separately on this page,
where the smoothness of those components is also proved. Neither construction
uses any choice principle beyond the one already recorded in (c).


**(e) Smooth timelike curves and their scalar normalization.** Before using
these quantities in the physical conventions, fix a positive real scaling
parameter $c$ (with no physical meaning or dimension in this mathematical
item). A **smooth future timelike curve** is a smooth map $\gamma:I\to M$
from a nonempty open real interval $I$ ([[def-interval]],
[[def-c-r-and-smooth-maps-between-smooth-manifolds]]) whose velocity derivation
$\gamma'(s)\in T_{\gamma(s)}M$
([[def-velocity-derivation-of-a-smooth-curve]]) satisfies
$g(\gamma',\gamma')<0$ and $g(\gamma',N)<0$ at every $s\in I$.
In a chart its components are $d(x^a\circ\gamma)/ds$, $a=0,1,2,3$.
For a supplied base point $s_0\in I$ and additive constant $\tau_0\in\mathbb R$
define

$$h(s):=\sqrt{-g_{\gamma(s)}(\gamma'(s),\gamma'(s))},\qquad \tau(s):=\tau_0+\frac1c\int_{s_0}^{s}h(r)\,dr,\qquad U(s):=\frac{c\gamma'(s)}{h(s)}.$$

The integral is oriented when $s<s_0$. The function $\tau$ is called
**proper time** for this scaling and $U$ the **four-velocity** of the smooth
curve; its increment times $c$ is the Lorentzian length. The well-definedness
proof below shows $\tau'>0$, that $\tau:I\to\tau(I)$ is a smooth
diffeomorphism, and that $U$ is the velocity of $\gamma\circ\tau^{-1}$.
Thus $g(U,U)=-c^2$ and $U$ is future timelike. This introduces the smooth
case before any physical unit reading; the later worldline definition extends
it to its stated $C^k$, endpoint and piecewise-$C^1$ classes. It asserts no
clock coupling, motion law or physical value of $c$.

**Convention and scope.** The physical reading of a smooth time-oriented
Lorentzian four-manifold as a classical spacetime model, and the domain in which
that reading is adopted, are recorded in the framework postulate
`post-gr-spacetime-and-classical-domain`; the words spacetime and event carry no
mathematical content beyond this definition, and this item asserts no claim
about nature. The dimension $4$ and the absence of boundary are part of the
data; nothing in the definition assumes that $M$ is nonempty or connected, and
no completeness, extendibility or maximality property of $(M,g)$ is asserted.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold
([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]) and let $\xi$ be a smooth vector field
on $M$ ([[def-smooth-vector-field-as-a-tangent-bundle-section]]). The **Lie
derivative of the metric along $\xi$**, written $\mathcal L_\xi g$, is the
smooth symmetric covariant $2$-tensor field obtained by the flow definition of
[[def-lie-derivative-of-a-tensor-field]] applied to $g$: for the local flow
$\Phi_t$ of $\xi$,

$$\mathcal L_\xi g:=\frac{d}{dt}\Big|_{t=0}\Phi_t^*g .$$

The field $\xi$ is a **Killing field** of $(M,g)$ (an **isometry generator**,
or a **Killing vector**) when

$$\mathcal L_\xi g=0 .$$

The equivalent local characterization

$$\mathcal L_\xi g=0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\nabla_a\xi_b+\nabla_b\xi_a=0,$$

where $\nabla$ is the metric-selected connection of $g$
([[def-gr-metric-selected-connection]],
[[thm-gr-nondegenerate-levi-civita-and-tensor-derivative]]) and
$\xi_b:=g_{bc}\xi^c$ is the lowered field, is proved in
[[thm-gr-killing-and-on-shell-matter-identities]] clause (a); the definition
itself asserts neither direction. Whether a given metric has Killing fields is
a property of that metric: neither existence nor uniqueness of a Killing field
is asserted here, and a general metric has none beyond the trivial field
$\xi=0$.

Let $(M,g,N_0)$ be a smooth time-oriented Lorentzian four-manifold of signature
$(-,+,+,+)$ in the sense of [[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]], and let
$\nabla$ be its unique torsion-free $g$-compatible connection supplied by
[[thm-gr-nondegenerate-levi-civita-and-tensor-derivative]]. Fix a nonempty
connected open set $O\subseteq M$. A **selected stationary thermal carrier** on
$O$ consists of a smooth future timelike vector field $\xi$ and a smooth
positive scalar field $T:O\to(0,\infty)$, where $T$ is measured in kelvins,
such that $\xi$ is a Killing field of $g$ in the sense of
[[def-gr-killing-field]]. Equivalently, the criterion is
$\nabla_{(a}\xi_{b)}=0$ by
[[thm-gr-killing-and-on-shell-matter-identities]]. The round brackets mean
symmetrization with factor $1/2$. The choice of $\xi$ specifies the thermal congruence; no
coordinate chart or universal observer field is selected.

Set $N_\xi:=\sqrt{-g(\xi,\xi)}>0$ and $u:=\xi/N_\xi$. Then
$g(u,u)=-1$. In the length-coordinate convention $x^0=ct$, $u$ is
dimensionless and $cu$ is the physical four-velocity, with $c>0$ in
$\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. For a fixed Boltzmann constant $k_B>0$ in
$\mathrm{J\,K^{-1}}$, define the inverse-temperature vector
$\beta:=u/(k_BT)$, with units $\mathrm{J^{-1}}$, and the Killing-normalized
temperature field $T_K:=N_\xi T$. Thus $\beta=\xi/(k_BT_K)$; this definition
does not assert that $T_K$ is constant.

For a smooth chemical-potential scalar $\mu:O\to\mathbb R$ in joules, put
$\zeta:=\mu/(k_BT)$, a dimensionless scalar. Define the rest-space metric,
derivative, acceleration, expansion and shear by
$$h_{ab}:=g_{ab}+u_au_b,\qquad D:=u^a\nabla_a,\qquad a_b:=u^a\nabla_au_b,\qquad \theta:=\nabla_au^a,\qquad \sigma_{ab}:=h_a{}^ch_b{}^d\nabla_{(c}u_{d)}-\frac13\theta h_{ab}.$$
Here $a$, $\theta$ and $\sigma$ have inverse-length units; the physical
proper acceleration is $c^2a$. The smooth tangent-bundle structure used by
the cited GR suppliers assumes the Axiom of Countable Choice
[[def-countable-choice]]; no stronger choice principle is part of this
definition.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

derivations.claim: The scalar $s:=-g(\beta,\beta)$ is smooth and strictly positive on $O$. Hence $s^{-1/2}$ is smooth and positive, so $T=(k_B\sqrt{s})^{-1}$ is a smooth positive kelvin-valued scalar and $u=\beta/\sqrt{s}$ is a smooth future-directed vector field. Direct contraction gives $g(u,u)=g(\beta,\beta)/s=-1$.

Lowering the smooth vector field $\beta$ with $g$ gives a smooth one-form, and its covariant derivative is a smooth covariant two-tensor. Antisymmetrizing this tensor gives the smooth two-form $\varpi$; the inverse-length derivative of the inverse-joule components of $\beta$ gives its stated units. Since $\mu$ and $k_BT>0$ are smooth, $\zeta$ and $\alpha=-\zeta$ are defined and dimensionless on all of $O$. The only foundational assumption in this construction is the inherited $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ in [F4]; no selection or stronger choice principle is used.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring with unit and $\delta\in R$. For each $n\ge0$, let $F_n:=R\langle u_1,\ldots,u_{n-1}\rangle$ be the free associative unital $R$-algebra on the indicated symbols ([[lem-hh-free-associative-ring-and-relations-descent]]). When $n=0$ or $n=1$, the symbol set is empty and $F_n=R$.

Let $I_n$ be the two-sided ideal generated by

$$u_i^2-\delta u_i\quad(1\le i<n),\qquad u_i u_j-u_j u_i\quad(|i-j|>1),$$

and

$$u_i u_{i+1}u_i-u_i,\qquad u_{i+1}u_i u_{i+1}-u_{i+1}\quad(1\le i\le n-2).$$

The abstract **rank-$n$ Temperley–Lieb algebra** is the presented $R$-algebra

$$P_n(R,\delta):=F_n/I_n.$$

Thus its defining relations are $u_i^2=\delta u_i$, $u_i u_{i\pm1}u_i=u_i$, and $u_i u_j=u_j u_i$ for $|i-j|>1$. The definition of a presented $R$-algebra and its universal property are those of [[lem-hh-free-associative-ring-and-relations-descent]].

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Let $R$ be a commutative ring with unit ([[def-algebra-over-a-commutative-ring]]) and let $\delta\in R$. The object labels are the nonnegative integers $n=0,1,2,\ldots$. For labels $m,n$, place bottom points $b_1,\ldots,b_m$ and top points $t_1,\ldots,t_n$ along the rectangle from left to right on their respective edges. Their cyclic order is $t_1,\ldots,t_n,b_m,\ldots,b_1$. When $m=n=0$, the empty matching is included.

An $(m,n)$ **diagram** is a perfect matching of these $m+n$ boundary labels which is noncrossing: there are no four labels $a,b,c,d$ in cyclic order whose matched pairs are $\{a,c\}$ and $\{b,d\}$. A picture consists of disjoint arcs realizing the matching; equality is equality of the matching, so planar deformation that fixes the boundary does not change a diagram. If $m+n$ is odd, there are no such diagrams. Write $\mathcal D(m,n)$ for this set and define the $R$-module

$$M_R(m,n):=R^{(\mathcal D(m,n))},$$

the free $R$-module on the set of diagrams ([[def-free-module-on-a-set-and-standard-basis]]). In particular, its diagram basis is empty when $m+n$ is odd.

For basis diagrams $D:m\to n$ and $E:n\to p$, stack $E$ above $D$ and identify the $n$ matching boundary points. The resulting finite graph has degree two at each identified point, where degree means the number of incident arcs. Each component is a path joining two exterior boundary points or a closed cycle. Remove every cycle and multiply the remaining exterior matching by $\delta^c$, where $c$ is the number of removed cycles. Denote this output by $E\circ D$ and extend the rule $R$-bilinearly to a map $M_R(n,p)\times M_R(m,n)\to M_R(m,p)$. A following result proves closure of these operations on the diagram modules and the category axioms.

The matching $1_n:n\to n$ pairs each bottom point to the top point directly above it. Horizontal juxtaposition, with the left diagram placed first, defines $m\otimes m'=m+m'$ on object labels and $D\otimes D'$ on basis diagrams; extend it $R$-bilinearly to the modules. A following result proves that these operations give a strict monoidal category.

For $1\le i<n$, let $d_i\in M_R(n,n)$ be the diagram with a cap joining top points $i,i+1$, a cup joining bottom points $i,i+1$, and vertical through strands at every other position. Define $\mathrm{TL}_n(R,\delta)$ to be the $R$-module $M_R(n,n)$ with bilinear multiplication $xy:=x\circ y$ and distinguished element $1_n$. A following result proves that it is a unital associative $R$-algebra and identifies it with the endomorphism algebra at object $n$.

The left factor is stacked above the right factor. The loop value is $\delta$; no invertibility or nonzero condition on $\delta$ is part of these data.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Let $R$ be a commutative ring with unit and $\delta\in R$. Define the quantum integers by

$$[0]_\delta=0,\qquad [1]_\delta=1,\qquad [r+1]_\delta=\delta[r]_\delta-[r-1]_\delta\quad(r\ge1).$$

The **quantum characteristic** of $(R,\delta)$ is the least positive integer $\ell$ with $[\ell]_\delta=0$, if one exists, and $\ell=\infty$ otherwise. No element of $R$ is inverted in this definition.

For $q\in\mathbb C^\times$ and $\delta=q+q^{-1}$, write $[r]_q=[r]_\delta$. If $q\ne\pm1$, this agrees with $(q^r-q^{-r})/(q-q^{-1})$; at $q=\pm1$ the recurrence gives $[r]_q=rq^{r-1}$. For complex-parameter classification, write $\kappa=\operatorname{ord}(q^2)$, with $\kappa=\infty$ when $q^2$ has infinite order. If $q\ne\pm1$, the quantum characteristic equals $\kappa$ when $\kappa<\infty$ and is $\infty$ otherwise. At $q=\pm1$, $\kappa=1$ but the complex quantum characteristic is $\infty$, because $[r]_q=rq^{r-1}\ne0$ for every positive $r$.

For a field $K$ of positive characteristic $p$, set $p(0)=1$ and, when $\ell<\infty$, set $p(i)=\ell p^{i-1}$ for $i\ge1$. In characteristic zero and finite $\ell$, the finite digit scale is $p(1)=\ell$; the separate characteristic-zero criterion below uses $a\ell-1$ for arbitrary positive integers $a$. If $\ell=\infty$, every finite index is already in the range $n<\ell$.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Let $R$ be a nonzero commutative ring with unit, $\delta\in R$, and suppose $[2],\ldots,[n]$ are units. The projector $p_n$ of [[def-temperley-lieb-jones-wenzl-recursion-over-unit-denominators]] has coefficient $1$ on the identity diagram, is nonzero and idempotent, and is annihilated on both sides by each $U_i$ for $1\le i<n$. Its corner is $p_n\mathrm{TL}_n p_n=R p_n$, so it is the unique idempotent with identity coefficient $1$ and those two-sided annihilation conditions. For $n\ge1$,

$$\operatorname{ptr}_n(p_n)=\frac{[n+1]}{[n]}p_{n-1},\qquad \operatorname{Tr}_n(p_n)=[n+1].$$

Only the displayed denominator units are assumed; $\delta$ need not be a unit.

For a linear map $T:V\to W$, its **kernel** and **image** are respectively

$$\ker T:=\{v\in V:T(v)=0_W\},\qquad \operatorname{im}T:=\{T(v):v\in V\}.$$

That both sets are linear subspaces, and that a trivial kernel characterises
injectivity, is proved in [[thm-linear-kernel-image-and-injectivity]].
